Additionally, it recorded the death of Duncan McIntosh at Aux Cayes on the 26th of the previous month, praising him for risking his life during the revolutionary troubles of 1793 in St. Domingo to save numerous inhabitants from the blacks.

records.summary_en: According to the *Phenix gazette* of June 26, 1826, Audain relocated to St. Domingo as a trader after abdicating his pulpit, where he subsequently shot two black general officers in a quarrel. When Christophe threatened to hang him if either man died, Audain escaped by night in an open boat to St. Eustatius. There, he resumed his role as a clergyman, offering his services to multiple religious sects by celebrating mass in French, reading the Church of England liturgy, and conducting the Dutch service.
records.summary_es: Según la *Phenix gazette* del 26 de junio de 1826, Audain se trasladó a Santo Domingo como comerciante tras renunciar al púlpito, donde posteriormente hirió de bala a dos oficiales generales negros durante una disputa. Cuando Christophe amenazó con ahorcarlo si alguno de ellos fallecía, Audain huyó de noche en un bote descubierto hacia San Eustaquio. Allí reanudó su ministerio religioso, ofreciendo sus servicios a diversas confesiones al celebrar misa en francés, leer la liturgia de la Iglesia de Inglaterra y oficiar el servicio holandés.

records.full_text:
A WEST INDIA PARSON.
[From Colgridge's Six Months in the West Indies.]
The church in Roseau is well situated and tolerably finished without, but the interior is in a miserable state. The common pitch pine, white unpainted, has a particularly unpleasant effect in a hot climate; it always oppressed me in a remarkable manner. About a hundred persons, chiefly colored, attended the morning service, they had few books, and apparently came for the purpose of seeing the bishop; certainly with one or two exceptions, they were entirely unacquainted with the ordinary ritual of the established religion. The Church of England indeed does not flourish in Dominica, which, considering the great capacity and spirituous affections of the people, is a matter of some character of surprise. I believe there are 2,000 protestants in this colony, of which number the Methodists form the larger part, about 16,000 are Papists, under the care of three Spanish priests; so that it is consolatory to the sympathies of obese and liquescent men to know that if true religion thrive not in Dominica, at least its minister does, since he is worth his salary, and just so much breathing exercise o' Sundays as may conduce to a good digestion for the rest of the week. Not that I would be thought to impeach the zeal of the rector of Roseau; very far from it; it is too well-known to be questioned, and it argues an unusual degree of apathy or stubbornness in those who are the daily witnesses of it, that its effects are not more perceptible.
Mr. Newman is great and remarkable; but he is not so great and remarkable as his predecessor Mr. Audain. This Mr. Audain was a patriot; few of his cloth like him; he was not content with praying against the enemies of his country—he fought against them also. St. Peter certainly owned a boat, and the authorized translation (Mr. Audain loved literal orthodoxy) intimates a partnership amongst some of the Apostles in a ship. So, Mr. Audain built a schooner, and carried on for many years a system of polemical politics with the disputants of the French school to his own abundant profit and notoriety. It is even yet fresh in the recollections of the inhabitants of Roseau, with how joyful a rapture this holy Dominican once broke off the service on a Sunday, unable to repress the emotions of his triumph on seeing the vessel of his faith sail into the bay with a dismantled bark laden with sugar, rum and other gallic vanities from Martinique.*
It was shortly after this event that the star of Audain began to wax dim. His zeal was equally great, his courage undaunted, but his evil destiny met him at every turn. An acquaintance of mine met him one day in the streets of Bassaterre, in St. Kitts, surrounded by negroes, to whom he was distributing plantains, yams, potatoes and other eatables, and holding private talk with them all by turns. Having caught my friend's eye, he came up to him and said, 'I am going to smuggle all these rascals into St. Eustatius.' He did so in his schooner, but remained himself on shore. A privateer of Nevis captured the smuggler before she could get to her market. Audain became furious, went himself to Nevis, and challenged the owner of the privateer to fight. The challenge was not accepted; and Audain immediately possessed the name of the recusant, as that of a scoundrel, on the court house. He himself for two days kept watch upon the platform with a sword by his side and four pistols stuck in his belt, to see if any one dared to touch the shields.
Audain fired another schooner and cruised in her himself. But fate was too heavy for him, though he struggled against it like a man. On the second day a large vessel was seen to leeward; he ascertained her to be worthy his armed, bore down on her as upon a certain prey. When he came within pistol shot, fourteen masked ports were opened and as many guns pointed at him through them. Audain was obliged to strike in an instant, and, with his carpenter, succeeded in secreting himself under the water casks in the hold of his schooner. The rest of the crew were taken out in the morning, upon further search their asylum was discovered. They were brought upon deck, and the Spaniards were on the point of sawing them by inches, when their captain exclaimed with rapidity, 'Hold all! this man's life is sacred, and the other's too for his sake.' Audain had formerly done the Spaniard great service at St. Thomas's, and it now saved his own and his carpenter's life.
Up to this time Audain, though occasionally and quietly for the above-mentioned, had continued the minister of Rosseau. He was a singularly eloquent preacher in the pathetic and suasory style, and he rarely failed to draw down tears from the cheeks of most of those who heard him. His manners were fine and gentle, and his appearance even venerable. He was hospitable to the rich and gave alms to the poor. But his repeated losses were such as to bear a royal merchant down, and the Dominicians became more scrupulous, and a governor came who knew not Audain. So Audain abdicated the pulpit of Rosseau.
Privateering and smuggling had lulled; so now he commenced honest trader. He went to St. Domingo with a cargo of Corn, sold it well, and lived on the island. But his star grew fainter and fainter. He quarrelled with two black general officers, challenged them both and shot them both severely. Christophe sent for him and told him that, if the men recovered, it was well, but if either of them died, he would hang him on the tamarind tree before his own door. Audain thought the men would die, and escaped from the tamarind tree by night in an open boat.
He now settled in St. Eustatius, put on his black coat again and recommenced clergyman—St. Eustatius is a fine place yet for the soul—his labor has made surprisingly slow advances in it. There were many religious, but no priest, in the island when Audain made his appearance there. He was become liberally minded by misfortune, and he was always actuated by a faith of such immense catholicity that it comprehended within its limits every variation of opinion from the centre of Christianity, as the jelly embraceth the spokes of a wheel. Audain offered to minister to all the sects respectively, which the free traders thankfully accepted. In the morning he celebrated mass in French, in the forenoon read the liturgy of the Church of England, in the afternoon spackened the Dutch service, and in the evening harangued the Methodists.
His star descended proner and proner, though he seemed to be gaining wealth and fame. Audain was a married man, but his wife resided and still resides at Bristol. A Dutch widow, rich, pious and large, cast a widow's eye on Audain; the rigor of creed violetly softened under the afternoon spackeneding of Audain, as Dutch butter melts under the kisses of Titan, and she told Audain that, if Heaven had made her such a man, she would have married twice. The hint was as broad as herself, but Audain liked it the better for its dimensions, and married her on the spot, spackening the service himself.
Audain has fought thirteen duels, and is a good boxer. Once upon a time, he fired twice without hitting; upon which he threw down his pistol on the ground, and said sternly to his second, 'Take care that does not happen again!' suggesting his pistol had not been charged with ball. A delay occurred; he fired again for the third time, upon which Audain went up to his antagonist, squared his body, saying 'Something however, sometimes between, good sir,' knocked him down with a flush hit on the nose.
Audain is now about sixty years of age, and has wholly reformed his manners. He loves his Dutch wife, and says his prayers so loud at night as to disturb his neighbors. His English wife sends him a Christmas box annually. He is a man of infinite talent, and has seen the world. I trust the report is true, that, like Lazarillo de Tormes and Gil Blas, he is writing a life of himself. It would be the most interesting book of this age If he does not, these few lines may happily serve to rescue him from an oblivion which he does not seem to deserve.
* This is like the Cornish vicar. He was preaching one afternoon in a seaside church during a heavy southwest gale, when all on a sudden his audience began to leave, take down their hats, and push towards the door. The vicar, having the advantage of pulpit eminence and long experience, immediately perceived the cause, and, animated with a just indignation at their conduct, ordered them, as they valued their souls' welfare, to remain quiet till the end of the sermon. The good man in his eagerness to restrain them even left the pulpit, and, like Aaron, ran into the midst of the congregation, following and exhorting them, till he reached the porch; when, tucking up his gown under his arm, he shouted out, 'Now, my boys, let us start fair!' and immediately outran them all, as in his days of his heels, to administer Cornish relief to a distressed merchantman.
My friend Mr. Oxley, in Barbadoes, says he was present at a scene in Tortola, where Audain figured in the manner mentioned in the text; probably it happened twice.

records.headline: A WEST INDIA PARSON
records.summary_en: The *Daily National Intelligencer* reported on the life and travels of Audain, a former clergyman and privateer who traded corn in St. Domingo after losing his position in Roseau. Following a quarrel in which he shot two black general officers, Audain fled by night to escape King Christophe's threatened execution and subsequently settled in St. Eustatius to resume his clerical duties, offering to minister to all religious sects on the island.
records.summary_es: El *Daily National Intelligencer* dio cuenta de la vida y los viajes de Audain, un antiguo clérigo y corsario que comerciaba con maíz en Santo Domingo tras perder su puesto en Roseau. A raíz de una disputa en la que hirió a tiros a dos oficiales generales negros, Audain huyó de noche para evadir la amenaza de ejecución dictada por el rey Christophe y luego se estableció en San Eustaquio para reanudar sus deberes clericales, ofreciéndose a ministrar a todas las confesiones religiosas de la isla.

He was become liberally minded by misfortune, and he was always humane; so a kind of an immense catholicity, that it comprehended within its circle every radiation of opinion from the centre of Christianity, as the folly embraceth the spokes of a wheel. Audain offered to minister to all the sects respectively, which the free traders thankfully accepted. In the morning he celebrated mass in French, in the forenoon read the liturgy of the Church of England, in the afternoon spackened the Dutch service, and at nightfall chanted to the Methodists.
His star descended proner and proner, though he seemed to be gaining wealth and fame. Audain was a married man, but his wife resided, and still resides, at Bristol. A Dutch widow, rich, pious, and large, cast a widow's eye on Audain; the rigor of creole viduity softened under the afternoon spackening of Audain, as Dutch butter melts under the sun. It was said by Audain, that, if Heaven had made her such a man, she would have married twice. The hint was followed up herself, but Audain liked it the better for its dimensions, and married her on the spot, spackening the service himself.
Audain was deeply read, and was a good boxer. Once upon a time, he fired twice, without hitting; upon which he threw down the pistols, and proposed a few rounds of fisticuffs. "Take care that does not happen again!" supposing his pistol had not been charged with ball. A delay occurred in re-loading for the third time, upon which Audain went up to his antagonist, squared his body, saying, "Something between, something between, good sir!" and knocked him down with a flush hit on the nose.
Audain is now about sixty years of age, and has lately collected his scattered family. He loves his Dutch wife, and says his prayers so loud at night as to disturb his neighbors. His English wife sends him a Christmas box annually. He is a man of infinite talent, and has seen the world. I trust the report is true, that, like Lazarillo de Tormes and Gil Blas, he is writing a history of his life. It would be the most entertaining book of this age. If he does not, these few lines may happily serve to rescue him from an oblivion which he does not seem to deserve.

records.full_text:
Your committee on F. Missions present the following Report:—
The past year has been an eventful period in the history of F. Missionary operations.
While we have occasion to mourn the loss of some valuable Missionaries; the unparalleled success that has marked the proceedings of the Board, and that has attended the labours of the Missionaries, calls loudly for gratitude to Almighty God. Rostan of France, a "standard-bearer" indeed, has fallen. Miss Cummings of Burmah, O'Brynt and Mrs. Lewis of the Indian Stations, were "faithful unto death," and have all, doubtless, gone to the "rest that remaineth to the people of God." Still we have by far, greater reason to "sing of mercy" than of "judgment." Indeed, the past year may be said to have introduced a new era in the history of F. Missions, under the patronage of American Baptists. Many new and promising fields have come to light, inviting labourers to gather in the whitening harvest; China with her immense benighted population, now accessible at the nearest point of approach—the Bombay and Madras Presidencies, where are already scattered converts, both European and native, and where 40 millions of immortal souls are perishing for "lack of vision;"—Germany, where the leaven of Calvinistic Baptist sentiments, is already beginning powerfully to operate upon the putrid mass of neology; where Oncken, Lewis, and other kindred spirits are pouring light upon the surrounding darkness; Africa, ill fated and too long neglected, but now promising health, and successful effort, to our Missionaries; and the Island of Hayti with her numerous Catholic population.
Not only have these new fields been opened; but measures have been taken by the Board, to occupy most of them, and greatly to augment the number of labourers in fields previously occupied.
On the first of July 1834, a reinforcement of 11 missionaries, accompanied bro. Wade on his return to Burmah. Two of these with their wives were to be stationed among the Karens; one, with his wife, was to join the Siam Mission; another, with his wife, was to form a station in Arracan; Mr. Osgood, a printer, and his wife, were to remain at Maulmein; and sister Gardner was to reside in the family of bro. Wade, in the capacity of a School teacher. These missionaries had acquired a considerable knowledge of the language of the people where they were to be stationed, before they left this country, and have, doubtless, been successfully labouring in their respective spheres since the time of their arrival, the 1st of Dec. last.
On the 11th of July last, 3 Missionaries—Crocker, and Mylne and his wife, were sent out to Africa.
On the 21st of Sept. 14 other Missionaries embarked for the east. Five of these were destined for the Burman Mission; two others (one a printer) with their wives, were designated to Bankok, Siam there to prepare for laboring among the Chinese. The five others were to labor among the Taling's on the Madras coast. With this last deputation, sailed Rev. Howard Malcom, appointed by the Board to visit the several Mission stations in the east, and to confer with the Missionary brethren on subjects pertaining to the interests of Eastern Missions.
Your committee hail with joy his appointment, as a measure promising great and important results.
Your committee learn with pleasure that the Board have secured the services of two valuable Missionaries, Willard and Shelden, with their wives, to join Porchat and Wilmarth in France; also, that they have designated a colored brother to Hayti.
The completion of the whole Bible in the Burman language, opens a wide field of labor, which ought thankfully and perseveringly to be cultivated; until every son and daughter of Burmah are permitted to read, how they may escape an "Eternal Hell." Viewing these enlarged operations, in connexion with the fact, that the Treasury is now, for the first time, almost empty, the inference is irresistible, that, while we are called upon by every consideration that is soul-stirring, to increase our contributions for Home Missions, Domestic Missions, and Ministerial Education, we must increase and greatly increase our contributions to the Foreign Mission Treasury.
Your committee feel, that the death of those Missionaries above mentioned, and the numerous instances in which the lives of others have been periled, ought forcibly to remind us of our dependence upon Him, "in whose hand our breath is," and of our duty to persevere in prayer for the lives, health, and success of those who are yet spared.
In closing their Report, your committee would offer the following resolutions:
Resolved, That this Convention cordially responds to the appeal of the Baptist General Convention, for the support and enlargement of their Mission in the heathen, and will use all suitable means in its power to carry into effect their resolution, to raise one hundred thousand dollars for Missionary purposes during the current year.
Resolved, That as the diffusion of authentic Missionary intelligence is a highly important means of calling forth the energies of the Christian church in extending the Redeemer's kingdom throughout the earth; And as the American Baptist Magazine is devoted specially to this object, and can now be furnished to subscribers at the very low price of one dollar a year; Therefore, be it further resolved, that we will use our efforts to secure its general circulation, and we do hereby cordially commend it to the patronage of all who are interested in the promotion of the glory of Christ, and the salvation of the heathen.
MARK CARPENTER, Chairman.

records.headline: Cape Haytien-Haiti.
records.summary_en: The *New York Herald* reported that Spanish General Salcedo sent a flag of truce and a letter to Haytien General Pierot, stating his mission was to occupy the Dominican Republic's frontiers rather than engage in hostilities. General Pierot responded by seizing the officers and men, stripping them of their belongings, and confining them together in a narrow dungeon without communication. Meanwhile, the Spaniards retired before General Pierot's advancing forces—who marched from Dajabon to take Santiago and join the President—while Salcedo, unaware of his first envoy's fate, dispatched a second flag of truce to Pierot.
records.summary_es: El *New York Herald* informó que el general español Salcedo remitió una bandera de parlamento y una carta al general haitiano Pierot, exponiendo que su misión consistía en ocupar las fronteras de la República Dominicana y no en trabar hostilidades. El general Pierot reaccionó capturando a los oficiales y a la tropa, despojándolos de sus pertenencias y encerrándolos juntos e incomunicados en una estrecha mazmorra. Entretanto, los españoles retrocedieron ante el avance de las fuerzas del general Pierot —que marchaban desde Dajabón para tomar Santiago y sumarse al presidente—, al tiempo que Salcedo, desconociendo el destino de sus primeros emisarios, despachó una segunda bandera de parlamento ante Pierot.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
Since I last had the pleasure, in the month of January, Haiti was reposing in the sweet sleep of confidence and tranquility, and we all looked forward to a season of renewed life and prosperity in her affairs.
This was but a deceitful calm only to burst forth into a more terrible revolution and bloody warfare.
The Spaniards who occupy the eastern and most valuable part of the island, and who have never been well affected to the black government of this part, which was in some measure forced upon them, suddenly showed a manifest of their grievances and flew to arms on the 7th of March, declaring themselves a free and independent state, divided and separate forever from the Haitien Republic—the semi-black chickens from the black ones.
The President, Herard, immediately proceeded to arms the whole male population of the French part of the island, and marched with a large force to overrun the Spanish part with his forces at one blow. The Spanish population do not number one-third of the French.
The forces of Pierot on the side of the north, soon mustered 30,000 men, with which he set out for St. Domingo. His first resistance from the enemy was at Azua, a small town of about 600 inhabitants, where it is said our regiments of the advanced guard were cut to pieces; however, coming up with the main body, the main body of the army, he forced the Spaniards to retire, and ultimately retreated the town, which he found totally abandoned, without a single soul in it. The loss on both sides is variously stated at 100 to 1,000 men, and by our last accounts from Port au Prince, the President was still at Azua, waiting and calling for further reinforcements. He had only removed the dead bodies from the streets of Azua, where the stench from the dead bodies, which it appears were not buried.
On this, the north side of the island, General Pierot advanced on the frontiers of the north, with ten thousand men. In the mean time, the Spanish General, Salcedo, having marched from Santiago, advanced to within eight miles of the Haytien forces, where he remained some days in suspense. He ultimately sent two officers, escorted by four dragoons, with a flag of truce, to Gen. Pierot, as bearers of a letter, communicating that the object of his mission was not hostilities, but merely to occupy the frontiers of the Dominican Republic. To this flag of truce Gen. Pierot paid no respect, but immediately had the officers and men seized, stripped of their arms and horses, and these, together with their horses, he distributed among his own officers. He then sent the officers to a safe place, where the six individuals are at present confined in a small room, and all possibility of communication with them prohibited. So much for respect to a flag of truce.
The Spaniards after this, in order to entice Gen. Pierot further into the interior, gradually retired before him, as soon as he set out from Daxabon on the 24th of March, and on his march he put to the sword all the National Guards and troops of the line that fell into his hands, leaving behind him nothing but women and children.
The Spaniards in their movement of retiring without any sacrifice of life, drew them to the cross of the roads of Santiago, on the 29th of March, for a combined attack upon the city of Santiago.
General Salcedo, however, in the face of his enemies, despatched another flag of truce to Gen. Pierot, to inform him that the city of St. Domingo was surrounded and fired upon; several were killed and wounded on both sides. This was the first opening of the campaign on the part of the Haytiens, and where Spanish blood first watered the soil of their country.
Gen. Pierot reached the neighborhood of Santiago on the 29th of March, and made his dispositions for attacking the Spaniards, who had assembled a force of about five thousand men, advantageously posted on a rising ground in the outskirts of the town.
The Haytien army was divided into three divisions; the right, commanded by General Cadet Antoine, was ordered to cross the river Yaqui, and the river Yaqui in the rear of Quinones' brickery, and to attack the Spanish in the flank. Gen. St. Louis, commanded the left division, to cross the river at Paso Colorado; and Gen. Pierot, the centre division, to cross at Paso Yaqui. The whole was done with much skill and precision, and the three columns almost simultaneously advanced to the attack, about three on Saturday the 30th of March. The Spaniards very quietly allowed them to come close up, when they suddenly poured out such showers of grape and musketry as to cause confusion in the Haytien ranks; however, they rallied, and three different times returned with coolness to the assault, but the Spaniards kept up such a fire that, finding it in vain, Gen. Pierot was finally forced to retreat, after suffering great loss. His army is now completely broken up; for it is reported by the wounded and stragglers who are coming in, that he has scarcely one thousand men together.
The Spaniards never left their lines during the engagement, and are supposed to have suffered little or no loss. After the action, Gen. Pierot found it necessary to send a flag of truce to the Spaniards, the result of which has not transpired—though we know they were well treated, notwithstanding Pierot's treatment of theirs.
There is no doubt that the other division in the interior must be the same; and, from the liberal and enlightened policy proclaimed by them, it is thought the existence of the Spanish part will soon become powerful and wealthy.

records.headline: Cape Haytien—Haiti.
records.summary_en: According to *The New York Herald* on April 29, 1844, Spanish forces forced a retreat and occupied the town of Azua, with private loss estimates reaching eleven hundred men while the President awaited reinforcements near Port-au-Prince. Meanwhile, on the northern side of the island, General Pierot mustered eighteen thousand men at Dajabon while Spanish General Salcedo advanced nearby. When Salcedo sent a flag of truce and a letter stating his mission was to occupy the frontiers rather than wage war, General Pierot seized the officers and men, stripped them, and confined them together in a narrow dungeon without communication.

Por su parte, en el flanco norte de la isla, el general Pierot congregó a dieciocho mil hombres en Dajabón mientras el general español Salcedo avanzaba en las proximidades. Cuando Salcedo envió una bandera de parlamento con una misiva indicando que su propósito era ocupar las fronteras y no emprender la guerra, el general Pierot apresó a los oficiales y soldados, los despojó y los confinó juntos e incomunicados en una angosta mazmorra.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
Affairs in the Haytien Empire—Negro Respect for a Flag of Truce—To al Overthrow of the Black Troops under Pierot, &c.
When I last had this pleasure, in the month of January, Haiti was reposing in the sweet sleep of profound and honorable peace; all looked forward to a season of renewed life and prosperity in her affairs.
This was but a deceitful calm only to burst forth anew with tenfold fury, in revolution and bloody warfare.
The Spaniards who occupy the eastern and most valuable part of the island, and who have never been well affected to the negro rule on that part, which was in some measure forced upon them, suddenly hoisted a standard of their grievances and flew to arms on the 7th of March, declaring themselves a free and independent State, divided and separate forever from the Haitien Republic—the news of which reached here on the 10th.
The President Rivière lost no time in ordering to arms the whole male population of the French part of the island, to march on the rebels, to crush to overrun the Spanish part with his forces at one blow, for the Spanish population do not exceed one-third of the French.
He left Port au Prince on the 10th of March, and soon mustered 30,000 men, with which he set out for St. Domingo. His advanced guard met the enemy at Azua, a small town of about 600 inhabitants, where a severe and night fight took place; his advanced guard were cut to pieces; however, coming up the next day with the main body of his army, he forced the Spaniards to retire, and ultimately occupied the town, which he found totally abandoned, without a single soul in it. The loss before Azua is privately stated at eleven hundred men, and by our last accounts from Port au Prince, the President had not yet advanced, but is awaiting further reinforcements. He had only removed to a short distance from the place, on account of the stench from the dead bodies, which it appears were never buried.
On this, the north side of the island, General Pierot assembled on the frontiers of Hinche, eight or ten thousand men. In the mean time, the Spanish General, Salcedo, having also collected a force, had advanced to within eight miles of the Haytien forces, where he remained some days in camp. He ultimately sent two officers, escorted by four dragoons, with a flag of truce, to Gen. Pierot, as bearers of a letter, communicating that the object of the Spanish was not hostilities, but merely to occupy the frontiers of the Dominican Republic, and to live in peace, as they had made no reply, but immediately had the officers and their escort disarmed, and taken from the arms, &c., which, together with their horses, he distributed among his soldiers, and then marched them off on foot to this place, where they arrived yesterday, and are now living together, in one narrow dungeon, and all communication with them prohibited. So much for respect to a flag of truce.
The Spaniards after this, in order to entice Gen. Pierot into the interior, gradually retired before him, as soon as he set out from Hinche, on the 24th March, at the head of the combined force of all the Northern Guards and troops of the line. The North was mustered, leaving behind him nothing but women and children.
His orders were to take possession of Santiago at any sacrifice of life, from thence to cross the country and form a junction with the President for a combined attack upon the city of St. Domingo.
General Salcedo, ignorant of the fate of his first envoys, despatched another flag of truce to Gen. Pierot, on the Plains of Talanquero; this party was surrounded and fired upon; several were killed and the rest escaped with difficulty. This was the opening of the campaign on the part of the Haytiens, and where Spanish blood first watered the soil of their country.
Gen. Pierot reached the neighborhood of Santiago on the 29th of March, and made his dispositions for attacking the Spaniards, who had assembled a force of about five thousand men, advantageously posted on a hill, at the entrance of the town.
The Haytien army was divided into three divisions; the right, commanded by General Cadet Antoine, was ordered to cross the Yaqui river, and the river Yaqui is the rear of Guimonea's brickery, on the left of the town; the left, under General St. Louis, commanded the left division, to cross the Yaqui at Paso Colorado; and Gen. Pierot the centre division, to cross at Paso Yaqui. The whole was done with much skill and precision, and the three columns almost simultaneously advanced to the attack, about noon, on Saturday, the 30th ult. The Spaniards very quietly allowed them to come within the reach of their artillery, when such showers of grape and musketry as to cause confusion in the Haytien ranks; however, they rallied, and three different times returned with coolness to the assault, but the fire of the Spaniards was too dogged obstancy, until Gen. Pierot was finally obliged to retreat. He has not been heard of or seen since his army completely broken up; for it is reported that he has not more than five hundred men, some say that he has scarcely one thousand men with him.
The Spaniards never left their lines during the whole attack, and are reported to have suffered little or no loss. After the action, Gen. Pierot made a movement to enter a flag of truce to the Spaniards, the result of which has not transpired—though we know they were well treated, notwithstanding strong reasons for retaliation.
There is no doubt of the ultimate success and independence of the Spaniards; and, from the liberal policy of the new government of St. Domingo, it is generally anticipated that the Spanish part will soon become powerful and prosperous.

records.headline: FROM PORT AU PLATT—By the Hero, Boyd, arrived last night in eight days from Port au Platt, we learn that everything was tranquil in that place when she left. Business was entirely at a stand still. The other portions of the island were in a fine condition, but from want of attendance would fall short, on account of the planters being engaged in the revolution. The following is the capitulation between the French and Spaniards of Hayti:—
records.summary_en: The May 9, 1844 issue of *The New York herald* reported on the terms of capitulation involving the fort and garrison at Port-au-Plat. The agreement outlined protections for Haytian citizens and their legally acquired property, established conditions and a one-month timeframe for residents to swear allegiance to Dominican independence or be considered strangers, and guaranteed safe departure and transport options for those wishing to leave. Additionally, it detailed provisions allowing foreign property to be respected, the National guard and regular troops to retain their arms as members of the Dominican Republic, and General C. Antonio and others to embark on vessels of their choice.
records.summary_es: El ejemplar del 9 de mayo de 1844 de *The New York herald* reseñó las capitulaciones convenidas respecto al fuerte y la guarnición de Puerto Plata. Las estipulaciones garantizaban la protección de los ciudadanos haitianos y sus bienes legítimamente adquiridos, establecían condiciones y un término de un mes para que los residentes jurasen lealtad a la independencia dominicana o fuesen considerados forasteros, y aseguraban salvoconductos y facilidades de transporte para quienes decidiesen marcharse. De igual modo, preveía el respeto a la propiedad extranjera, la conservación de las armas por parte de la Guardia Nacional y las tropas regulares en calidad de miembros de la República Dominicana, y la autorización al general C. Antonio y a otros jefes para embarcarse en los navíos de su preferencia.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
This day March 14th, 1844, the members of the Commission appointed by J. Beuchot, the moment the Haytien flag was lowered, to treat with the Junta of the Dominican republic, and the officers appointed by General Cadet Pierre, the following articles agreed upon to wit:—
1st. The Haytien flag shall be lowered with honor and respect.
2d. Immediately after lowering the Haytien flag, the Dominican flag unfurled, with the soldiers, national guards, and the citizens who wish to leave this city shall embark with them and their families and baggage.
3d. Every thing found in the fort belonging to the Haytien government, after which the keys shall be delivered the moment his leaving it.
4th. Haytien citizens without any distinction of persons will be respected and protected.
5th. The property legally bought by the Haytiens, free from hypotheques, shall be respected and guaranteed. The owners shall dispose of them as they please.
6th. The Haytiens who wish to reside at Port au Plate as Dominican citizens, shall be permitted to do so with the consent of the governmental junta with St. Domingo. Passports shall be delivered to them until 15 days after which time, those that shall not have given their names shall be considered as foreigners.
7th. No opposition whatever shall be made at the departure of the Haytiens who wish to leave.
8th. Passports shall be given to those who will prefer to go to another harbor.
9th. No person shall be made answerable who shall have manifested any opinion whatever before the Capitulation.
10th. The property of foreigners shall be respected.
11th. The Haytien guard shall keep their arms, and the regular troops comprising the garrison of Port au Plate as members of the commission of safety. The public officers who wish to leave, shall keep their arms, and soldiers shall deposit theirs in the arsenal.
12th. A sufficient number of vessels shall be given to those who wish to follow him, to embark in whatever vessel they please, provided it does not belong to the Haytien treasury. The passage money of him and those who follow him shall be paid by the junta of the Dominican government. The embarkments shall be made behind the fort.
13th. As to the wages which are due to the members of the administration to this day, they shall be paid in the term of 15 days after the 4th article of the capitulation of Santo Domingo.
14th. French and Spaniards shall live as good allies and mates. Made in double expeditions, the day, month, and year as above said.
The commission appointed by General C. Antonio—A. Pichardo, E. Guerrero, M. S. Guerrero, P. Robert, (Signed) C. ANTONIO.
The commission appointed by the Junta Governmental of St. Domingo—Abad Alfau, Lieut. Col. of the Staff, Domingo D. Pichardo, P. Elchuquier Guerrier, Michel fils Sanches, (Signed) C. ANTONIO.
Sanctioned—The Brigadier General commanding at Port au Plate. (Signed) C. ANTONIO.

records.headline: RECENT RIOTS IN HAYTI.
records.summary_en: According to the newspaper report, the Haytien armies from Port au Prince and the Cape advanced to the frontiers, where they were checked and subsequently driven back over the borders by Dominican forces after a series of combats and an attack at Azua on the 9th of the previous month. Additionally, a naval engagement in the bay of Azua resulted in the Haytien fleet of three vessels being driven onto reefs and sunk by the Dominican fleet of equal force, with heavy casualties reported among the Haytien crews and none on the Dominican side. The report also notes that the Cape army had lost 500 men to desertion by the time it reached the frontiers.
records.summary_es: Según la reseña periodística, los ejércitos haitianos provenientes de Puerto Príncipe y de El Cabo marcharon hacia las fronteras, donde las fuerzas dominicanas lograron contenerlos y luego rechazarlos tras sucesivos combates y un asalto en Azua el día 9 del mes previo. Además, un combate naval en la bahía de Azua culminó con la flotilla haitiana de tres navíos encallada en arrecifes y echada a pique por la escuadrilla dominicana de similar porte, reportándose considerables pérdidas entre las tripulaciones haitianas frente a ninguna baja dominicana. El parte añade que el ejército de El Cabo había sufrido quinientas bajas por deserción antes de alcanzar la frontera.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
The following letter, which the Journal of Commerce ascribes to an intelligent source at Port au Plata, Hayti, gives the most connected view of the recent events in that distracted island than we have elsewhere seen:
"PORTO PLATA, MAY, 1844.
"Since my last to you the chief events have been here as follows: The blacks and mulattoes of the West quickly assembled and armed to reorganize the government of the island. Many letters were sent up here from the Cape and Port au Prince, exaggerating the force of the armies that were on their march. Among others Gen. Cadet wrote, saying that the President was marching at the head of 25,000 men from Port au Prince upon the city of St. Domingo; that Gen. Pierrot was marching with 15,000 men from the Cape for Santiago; while he would march with 1,500 men direct from the Cape for this place. From what I can learn, the Port au Prince army, when it started, was about 8,000; the Cape army 6,500; while Gen. Cadet's force was incorporated in the 6,500 of the army of the Cape. The army of Port au Prince, as there is very little organization or discipline in the Haytien armies, possibly, when it arrived on the frontiers, was 7,000. It was there met and checked by the army of St. Domingo, which, it is said, consisted of only about 800 Dominicans; three combats, in the last of which it suffered very severely, and was obliged to retreat to Azua, where they now are. The second of the last month the army of the Cape attacked the Dominicans and driven over the frontiers; but they left encamped on a mountain near 1,000 men, who were small-pox, and were only firing for some person's attention. In the bay of Azua there has been a naval engagement; the Haytien fleet of three schooners was attacked and sunk by the fleet of the city of the same force. The greater part of the crews of the Haytien vessels were killed or drowned, and report says not one person was injured on board of the Dominican vessels. One of the vessels of the city is what was formerly the Grand Canal pilot-boat of New York. She was armed with 50 Frenchmen, spared from the French fleet that was in the city of St. Domingo previous to that affair.
"When the Haytien army of the Cape Haytien reached the frontiers it had lost 500 men by desertion. It was there met and checked by Gen. Imbert, and also by Gen. Don Titus Salcedo, who may be called the Cincinnatus of this country. He left a beautiful country residence, and has aroused his countrymen on this side, and was by them chosen General-in-Chief. He has been joined by Gen. Alfau, the advance of the Western army of the Cape, and caused it to retreat by the Port au Prince road. This movement caused the army of Santiago to fall back, and the retreat took place. The people of the La Sierra retired up their mountains, and from there they can defend the only mountain pass which commands the road from the Cape and Santiago to this place.
"On the 30th March, the Cape army arrived before and immediately attacked Santiago. They have lost thousands on their march, by desertion and fatigue, to about 4,000 men. They attacked in three columns, and were repulsed by the artillery of the city, with a terrible carnage. They again assembled, again attacked, and were again repulsed. They fled for the frontiers, leaving on the field, it is said, about 1,000 killed and desperately wounded, many more being drowned in the river Yaqui. It is said by those who were on the route to the frontiers they were repeatedly attacked by the army of La Sierra, and it is thought they will not have more than 2,000 reached the frontier. There they were met by Gen. Pierrot, who was on his march to Santiago, to whom they communicated their panic. The whole force, when organized, again made an attempt, unsuccessfully. In order to the defence of Santiago, not one person was killed on the part of the Dominicans was killed, and only one slightly wounded. This appears almost incredible, but it is nevertheless a fact. It may be called, with the naval action at Azua, miraculous. Gen. Pierrot, finding it impossible to induce the rest of the army of the north to remarch to Santiago, he sent to the General-in-chief, Pierrot, an order to shoot every third man in the army.
"The General refused to execute so atrocious an order, and sent a message to the President to that effect, who immediately ordered General-in-chief Pierrot, who was at the Cape, to arrest the General-in-chief and send him to Port au Prince. In the mean time the army had disbanded itself. When the last news arrived at the Cape, an officer who bore it had an order for fifteen brass field pieces, which are at the Cape, to be sent to the army of Pierrot; he was also the bearer of $30,000 towards the raising of a new army. The people of the North, on the arrival of the order, decided to keep the field pieces and the money—have declared the North to be a separate and independent State, and have appointed the same General-in-chief, Pierrot, to be their General-in-chief. The Port au Prince and Cape of the Cape are in this movement; they are now raising an army to march against Port au Prince, and I think it very probable that Hayti will witness the spectacle of another intestine war. The State of the North will take in all the old kingdom of Christophe.
"On the South, an army marched from Aux Cayes for the Port au Prince, being some four or five thousand men. They commenced an indiscriminate massacre of the mulattoes and their families. That is the last information we have from the South. All the Haytian armies are principally blacks.
"The Dominican Republic consists of all the country from the frontier to the East. It is here that the Consul for the United States is expected.
"When the Haytien armies commenced their march to this end, an order was received from the President to kill all the whites, and also all the mulattoes; but the blacks would have made few prisoners; all are killed.
"The country of the Dominicans, or Spanish, which is the classic soil of the New World, is not short of three hundred miles in length, and about one hundred fifty in width; white; many are the descendants of the first discoverers. In the interior the color is—the people are white. On the other hundred thousand are blacks, mulattoes, the different combinations of the two races, and some pure-blooded aborigines. The heads of the revolution are the white men of the country. By casting your eye over the names of the signers of their manifesto, you will see many noble Spanish names.
"The ten per cent. extra duty on goods and tonnage has been annulled by the new Government, and also the American vessel that has been here since the revolution. I enclose to you with this the official notice of the new duty. This letter and the document accompanying it, if you think proper, I wish laid before the Chamber of Commerce of your city, that they may judge whether it is advisable for them to request the United States Government to send a proper person to this country, to ascertain if they are worthy to be acknowledged as a nation. The rulers and the mass of the people are of our own complexion, and they have liberated themselves from the ignominious bondage of the blacks and mulattoes of Hayti. You will see by the manifesto of the people of the North, that they wish a Confederation. The Dominicans do not wish of this, and most certainly will not, for they are an inoffensive people; but they are determined that they are to remain a separate Republic, (or feelings, an entirely distinct people,) to have no confederation with them."

records.headline: LATE FROM HAYTI
records.summary_en: The *New-York daily tribune* reported that Port au Prince and the South were submissive to Guerrier's Government, and that ex-President Hérard and his kinsman were ordered to leave the island after his troops were beaten by the Dominicans. The newspaper also noted the presence of several naval vessels, including five French brigs-of-war and a steamer, the British frigate *Spartan*, and the U.S. sloop *Preble*, alongside reports that the vessel *Baltimore* had sheltered American Consul Mr. Usher and numerous refugees during tumults.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
LATE FROM HAYTI—By the brig Phil. Enquirer, Capt. King, arrived yesterday from Cape Haytien, intelligence has been received at the Merchants' Exchange as late as the 28th ult.
Tranquility was restored at Cape Haytien. Guerrier had been proclaimed President of the North, and accordingly acknowledged.
The different divisions of the Island are to be erected into States, somewhat after the plan of the United States. If the Dominicans reject this offer, another expedition will be sent against them.
There were five French brigs-of-war and a steamer off the island.
The additional duty of $10 per M. on coffee had been removed.
H. B. M. frigate Spartan, of 26 guns, Captain Elliott, arrived at the Cape on the 26th, from Port au Prince.
Port au Prince and the South was submissive to Guerrier's Government.
Ex-President Herard, and his kinsman, late President of the Assembly, had been ordered to leave the Island.
No new expedition was designed against the Dominicans, for which the government had then no means. The army had suffered from the small pox, hunger, nakedness, &c. in their retreat after the late battle by the Dominicans.
The U. S. sloop Preble was at Aux Cayes a few days before the Phil. Enquirer sailed. She was expected at Port au Prince.
While there, the 'Baltimore' was at different times a means of shelter, not only to our American Consul, Mr. Usher, but at one time to near 40 of our citizens. Their lives were in danger during the late tumults; added to which was a large amount of property, and mostly sent off to the Baltimore for safety. Even at midnight the boats were kept in motion to receive them. The prospect of returning quiet caused the disembarkation of both persons and property.
Phil. Enq.

records.headline: LATE FROM HAYTI.
records.summary_en: According to the June 15, 1844 issue of the *Daily National Intelligencer*, Gurrier was proclaimed President of the North on the 18th, with plans to erect the island's divisions into States similar to the United States and potentially propose that the Dominicans join as a State. The newspaper reported that the ex-President and Herard Dumesle were ordered to be banished to Jamaica, that Aux Cayes and the South remained submissive, and that no new expedition was currently designed against the Dominicans, who had severely beaten Herard’s troops. Additionally, it noted unconfirmed talk of a treaty between the Dominicans and France, the arrival of the British frigate *Spartan* from Port au Prince, and the presence of the U.S. sloop *Preble* at Aux Cayes.
records.summary_es: Conforme al ejemplar del 15 de junio de 1844 del *Daily National Intelligencer*, Gurrier fue proclamado presidente del Norte el día 18, proyectando estructurar las demarcaciones insulares en estados a semejanza de Estados Unidos y plantear en su caso que los dominicanos se integrasen en calidad de estado. El periódico refirió que se dispuso el confinamiento en Jamaica del expresidente y de Herard Dumesle, que Aux Cayes y el Sur acataban la autoridad y que no se preparaba de momento ninguna expedición contra los dominicanos, quienes habían desbaratado a los destacamentos de Hérard. Además, aludió a negociaciones no confirmadas de un tratado dominicano con Francia, al arribo de la fragata británica *Spartan* desde Puerto Príncipe y a la estancia de la corbeta estadounidense *Preble* en Aux Cayes.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
The following intelligence, from the Philadelphia United States Gazette, confirms the reports which have previously reached us of another change of Government in Hayti. The intelligence is brought by the schooner Mary Ann, which left Cape Haytien on the 30th ultimo. While there this vessel was at different times a means of shelter, not only to the American Consul, Mr. Usher, but to others, and as many as two hundred females whose lives were in danger during the late tumults. There was also a considerable amount of property placed on board of her for safety, but the prospect of returning quiet caused the disembarkation of both persons and property.
CAPE HAYTIEN, MAY 28, 1844.
This place has been rather quiet for the last week or two. The 'Council of State,' learning from Port au Prince that Rivera, or Herard, as he is called indifferently, had been deposed from office, and Gen. Guerrier appointed President in his place, concluded to accept Gurrier as President of the 'North' also, and he was accordingly proclaimed on the 18th. The Government is not to be consolidated, as heretofore; but it is in contemplation to erect the several divisions of the Island into States, somewhat in imitation of the United States Government, and Commissioners have gone to Port au Prince for that purpose. Their plans, however, do not appear to be very clearly developed at present. It is said this arrangement will be made to the Dominicans to join the new Government as a State, which, if they reject, another expedition will be sent against them. But it is the general opinion that they will be able to sustain their position as a distinct Government. There is some talk of their having made a treaty with France, but this wants confirmation.
The British frigate Spartan, 26 guns, Capt. Elliot, arrived here on the 26th instant from Port au Prince, whence she sailed for Jamaica. The British Consul went along with them. The ex-President has been ordered to leave the island, and his kinsman, Hérard Dumesle, late President of the Council of State, has also been banished, and they are to retire to Jamaica.
The South and the South-west generally continued submissive to the Government of Guerrier; and no new expedition is, at present, designed against the Dominicans, by whom Herard's troops were severely beaten. Both men and horses are said to have suffered extremely on the return march from hunger, nakedness, disease, and vermin.
The U. S. sloop Preble was at Aux Cayes a few days since, and when the Spartan left was daily expected at Port au Prince. The French force about the island consists of five frigates and a steamer.

records.headline: Hayti
records.summary_en: According to *The Liberator*, the new administration sought to restore peace and national unity following a period of civil war, sending influential deputations across the island that successfully garnered support for union beyond the ancient Spanish limits. Furthermore, correspondence between the Haytien Secretary of War and General Pedro Santana, commander-in-chief of the Dominican army, indicated a favorable disposition on both sides toward the ultimate incorporation of the entire island into one body politic.
records.summary_es: De acuerdo con *The Liberator*, el nuevo régimen procuró afianzar la concordia y la unidad nacional tras la guerra civil, comisionando representaciones notables a lo ancho de la isla que consiguieron adhesiones a la unión más allá de las antiguas lindes españolas. Por otra parte, la correspondencia intercambiada entre el ministro de Guerra haitiano y el general Pedro Santana, general en jefe de las fuerzas dominicanas, reveló una inclinación propicia en ambas partes orientada a la fusión definitiva de toda la isla en una sola entidad política.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
The Government of the 3d of May, at the head of which is General Philippe Guerrier, an old soldier of the first army, which, under Dessalines, achieved the independence of the country, has adopted moderate counsels, and evinces a most anxious solicitude to conciliate the popular favor, and to repair the evils effected by its predecessor. That administration precipitated Hayti into an abyss of civil war. This strives to restore peace and concord, and is laying broad and solid the foundations on which it hopes to establish these national blessings. Deputations, composed of men of the first character and influence, have been sent to every part of the island, with views of promoting the spirit of concord and of union, and their success has happily been proportionate to the importance of the mission with which they were actuated, and with the benevolence of the sentiments by which they were commanded. Ed.
The whole country beyond the ancient limits of the Republic of Hayti, has declared itself implicitly and cordially in favor of union and national unity; and, by an act, in conformity with the law of federalism, they have acted, in the existing conjunction, with exalted wisdom and laudable patriotism. All sectional animosity and hatred seem to have vanished; and, from the tone of a correspondence in reference to prisoners of war and state prisoners, carried on by the Haytien Secretary of War on the one part, and General Pierrot, lately commander-in-chief of the army of the Dominican republic, on the other, we are led to believe that a disposition exists, on both sides, the most favorable to an ultimate incorporation of the whole island into one body politic.
The Government has not neglected other means of pacification. It has not only arrested the conflagration and pillage of Azua, but it has taken measures effective to succor the families of the despoiled. By the aid of conduct so firmly wise, so dignified, and so well calculated to inspire confidence, it cannot fail to succeed in establishing itself in the affections and respect of the people. Already it manifests its eagerness to revive the sources of production, and to increase the revenue of the State by depending little upon arbitrary measures to meet the public expenditures. This is the true way to obtain and render durable, peace and the blessings which attend it.

records.headline: FROM ST. DOMINGO.
records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that the legal Junta reinstated by General Santa Ana had ceded Samana to the French, a move opposed by the faction led by President Duarte. Meanwhile, the French were actively engaging Port-au-Prince and Cape Haytien to create a diversion against the East, while General Santa Ana marched on St. Domingo with an army, was made President, and was reported to favor French protection.
records.summary_es: El periódico informó que la Junta legal reinstaurada por el general Santana había traspasado Samaná a los franceses, disposición resistida por el bando del presidente Duarte. Entre tanto, los buques franceses hostilizaban Puerto Príncipe y Cabo Haitiano con el fin de propiciar una distracción frente a la región oriental, al tiempo que el general Santana se dirigía sobre Santo Domingo al frente de un ejército, asumía la presidencia y se manifestaba partidario de la tutela francesa.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
A Dominican man-of-war schooner, belonging to General Santa Ana, called the Separacion, formerly the pilot boat Romp, arrived off here to-day, with letters from General Santa Ana to Gen. Villanueve, informing him that he, Santa Ana, had been legally chosen by the legal Junta, President of the Republic, in the city of St. Domingo. Gen. Villanueve sent his son, and aid, Colonel Toutio, on board of her to invite the Captain to bring his vessel in, which he did. He saluted the town, which was returned by the fort. The same legal Junta that Gen. Santa Ana has reinstated, are the self-chosen or appointed, who wished to, or who in fact did cede Samana to the French. The party that President Duarte is the chief of, are opposed to the French protection. Since the arrival of the French Admiral with the Junta, the French have been actively employed in Port-au-Prince, to create there a diversion of the Black Government against the East. The same activity in intrigue has been displayed at Cape Haytien. It is not yet ascertained with what success.

At the time that Gen. Duarte was proclaimed President at La Vega and on this side of the island, Gen. Santa Ana was on the frontiers with his army. While there, he received a commission from the Junta at St. Domingo, and he commenced his march on St. Domingo—his army increasing on the route. Report says he appeared before the city with an army of 6,000 men, in a tolerable state of discipline, and was by them made President. He is in favor of French protection—so report says. Whether such protection would benefit the country is hard to say. On the principle that a powerful friend is a benefit, the protection of the French may possibly benefit these people, provided their commerce with other nations, and their own internal Government, are not interfered with.

As I before informed you, Gen. Duarte is a white man, about 30 years old; Gen. St. Ana is a Spanish white, about 55 years old. The last named has devoted all his fortune to this revolution; two of the man-of-war schooners are his private property. The existing difficulties may be amicably arranged; but I believe myself there will be some fighting, if the two Presidents can bring their followers up to it. The people don't like that sort of work.—N. Y. Jour. of Commerce.

records.headline: FROM HAYTI.
records.summary_en: The newspaper reports that a French squadron was waiting at Port-au-Prince for an indemnity installment, though funds were scarce. It also states that General Accau, leader of the late revolution in Aux Cayes, was decoyed to Port-au-Prince by President Gurriere and made prisoner upon arrival. Additionally, patriots in the Spanish part of the island rejected French protection, while Dominican President General Santa Anna's movements suggested he might retain his post and form a confederacy with Gurriere's government.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
The United States ship Vandalia, Commander JOHN S. CHAUNCEY, arrived at Pensacola, on the 12th ultimo, last from Port au Prince, via Aux Cayes, which latter port she left on the 12th ultimo.

Though the island of St. Domingo is in a very unsettled and precarious position, still all was quiet. At Port au Prince a French squadron, consisting of one frigate, a barque, and two brigs, was waiting for an instalment of the indemnity due the French Government; but, from all accounts, it was supposed they would have to await some time, as money was a scarce article in the market.

An arrival at New York in ten days from Port au Prince reports that General ACCAU, the leader of the late revolution in Aux Cayes, is now in Port au Prince, having been decoyed down by President GUERRIER, under the pretence of conferring the appointment of general of that part of the island, and, on his arrival, thrown into a prison. He was made prisoner immediately on his arrival.

The Patriots of the Spanish part of the island have declared against a French protectorate. SANTA ANNA, the President of the Dominicans, rendered it probable that he would retain his post, and unite his Government to that of Guerrier as a confederacy.

records.full_text:
M. THIERS has brought up his Report from the Commission on the Deputies on the Education Bill as fashioned by the Peers. It is a grand tractate, which occupied nearly three hours in the reading, and requires seven or eight columns of the journals. There is much of verbiage, sciolism, false social philosophy, pretension, and rhetoric in this work of a professor, anti-christian design. The alterations proposed in the bill reverse the work of the Peers, and re-establish the University monopoly and privileges. Frequent were the plaudits of the Deputies, a majority of whom belong to the school of Voltaire. During the recitation, the Monarchy betrayed their chagrin at the success of one who stands perpetually in their van or rear as a premier candidate or leader of the most formidable of their adversaries. THIERS, observes a Legitimist oracle, is Voltairean, Revolutionary, Imperialist, Monarchist, Doctrinaire, Radical—head of none. The Jansenist journal of Public Instruction will come from his incubator. GUIZOT took up a small share of the debates, space is consumed by the serial report of a criminal trial at Auch, in the extreme South, which lasted eight days, and in which the accused and distant nearly two hundred leagues from Paris. The case is of a beautiful and opulent widow accused of poisoning her husband with arsenic; it teems with romantic circumstances quite as congenial for the French temperament as those of the Suire-de-Boissy. All the reporters from the capital announced that they would have reporters at Auch, and receive the stimulating matter by special couriers; the details in the newspapers are devoured; and the avidity with which they are grasped at the reading rooms equals at least any interest connected with the Education bill. Count MOLÉ made a sage to excite any where in the Union. I enclose a summary of the accusation; the whole story is a drama of real life. Gravity, dignity, high tone, scandal, and forensics were never more remarkably mixed and exhibited. There is not a suspect proof of guilt—no conclusive presumption—but God knows, only an impressionable jury could convict. In the Court of Appeal of Paris, the bar of the Royal Court having resigned, a new election took place on the 14th instant. Their Spanish candidate, M. BRESSON, received 217 votes out of their brethren entitled to vote. The number of these was five hundred and one, and the whole body is not as pleased by that number and with six votes, greater by ninety-six than any poll on the records of the bar. Octogenary judges and councilors, aged from sixty to eighty-five years, had long ceased to practise claimed the right of suffrage; particular homage was paid to BERRYER; the Council is twenty-eight in full, contemporary and friend of the GERBIERS and TRONSON DU COUDRAY. They are directly related to professors, and the lecturers who have succeeded them in jurisprudence in the Colleges, bustled in the suite. Animosity exists in some measure between this bar and arriere-ban of the Council—this professional clanship shown in the resurrection of so many antique and decrepit bodies; the old bar was ended the batonnier (staffman) of the Council delivered an address, in which he congratulated the Elders and his colleagues on the success of their activity, their perseverance, and their pecuniary sacrifices for the dignity and independence and the moral influence of the profession. To the Count, he repeals the strife will be between the esprit de corps of the bar and that of the magistracy. Three rounds of applause followed the address. Up to this date the result of the Cabinet conference at Barcelona is the dissolution of the Cortes so long suspended, and the convocation of a new assembly, to be opened and organized, and the convocation of the Spanish electors college in their proper districts, on the 10th October. You may judge how fair and regular the elections may prove; and, nevertheless, it is quite possible that NARVAEZ & Co. may not be unable to control the new body and be quickly brought to the alternative of another suspension or a dictatorship. A letter of July 3d, from Madrid, called from London, resigned because he would have proceeded without Cortes: NARVAEZ appointed himself in his stead, and now holds the double office of Minister of War, Minister of Foreign Affairs, Commander-in-chief of the Army—a political dictator, pure and simple. The press has not reprinted the prate of the farce of constitutional freedom after the tragedy of military despotism; and for this look at the remonstrance of the British Minister, who with drugs from his bed and consigned to the stomach ... How fine and sincere the language of Lord ABERDEEN, in his reply to Lord CLANRICARDE'S question concerning the proposals of DON CARLOS to marry his son to the young Queen of Spain! His Lordship said:

"He would just observe that if the question in Spain were only one between a Carlist contender, and a Carlist princess, that proposed, if adopted by the Spanish people, might be regarded as an eligible means of terminating differences and putting an end to civil war; but if it were proposed to change the nature of the affair had completely changed; it was no longer a question of a Carlist pretender, but of a pretender to Government—a question between a constitutional Government and absolute rule."

Such a division in favor of the Narvaez party and Moderado system rivals the declaration from the same source of French favorite-ship and French concurrence in the insurrection against the ESPARTERO Regency. A Barcelona decree of the 4th instant, countermanded the tax-abatement and privileges for the Basque provinces according to the ancient fueros. This measure precludes national concord, but tends to strengthen the cause of the Pretender's Government against the Carlists, who have relied chiefly on those provinces.

In Switzerland the split is temporizing, and seems willing to see realized in the federal concerns the French notion: "In general the most vexed questions decide themselves natively." The No. 234 Athens was disturbed and alarmed by a mob crying, "Down with the Ministers and Constitution!" the Emeute was quelled by the troops, not without much effusion of blood: the elections in the interior of Greece have been generally and very contentious for the present Cabinet: lately, in our own Chamber of Deputies, Mr. GUIZOT related that the French Plenipotentiary at Athens had, conformably to his instructions, exerted himself to maintain the original coalition in the National Councils of the Metaxist party and Coletti party—the English and French; but the rupture came, and no control could be attempted. Greece is too crude as a nation, and foreign influence too strong for a regular, familiar, to allow firm and steady management of the representative system. The Paris Commerce of yesterday has an article on the French Navy in the Pacific, occasioned by the news by the Burgundy from New York. That anti-Ministerial sheet is charged by the Commerce with instigating Mexico to her warlike "armor and attitude," and French Admirals to usurp authority and act at discretion either on the Mexican or American side. The Commerce is said to have passed into the hands of the Press party—the Conservative anti-Guizot party—led by Messrs. DE TOCQUEVILLE, DE BEAUMONT, and LANGUINAIS. The recall of Admiral DE MOGES, who is replaced by Admiral LAPLACE on the Antilles station, forms a ground of Opposition complaint. DE MOGES mediated between the Dominican Republic and Negro Hayti, and favored or welcomed the overture of the Spanish party for French protectorate. A Conservative journal supposes the French Cabinet to apprehend that Great Britain would claim the protectorate of the North of the island—far the most valuable, and the true French portion. Admirals, continues the journal, must not be allowed to anticipate, with regard to Saint Domingo or Tahiti, the proper work of Cabinets. Those of London and Paris are blamed for employing themselves in the detection and frustration of the conspiracies and enterprises against the Governments of Italy. A natural fellow-feeling prompts them. Their success has not been great, for it seems that some forty political zealots and adventurers was more preposterous and not more lucky than M. MAZZINI'S band of 1833. The two Cabinets have reached arrangements for terminating the quarrel of Mexico with Texas, and guaranteeing Texas independence, on condition that Texas will not annex to any other party. French affairs at Montevideo afford plentiful ammunition to the Paris Opposition in the Chamber of Deputies.

The Revue des Deux Mondes, issued to-day, contains an article of fifty pages, entitled Texas and the United States, and signed A. CAUCHY. It refers mainly to the question of annexation. The editor gave read, in manuscript, to M. DE TOCQUEVILLE, Colonel BUTLER, General HOUSTON, Mr. VAN BUREN, Mr. CLAY, Mr. ADAMS, with MEXICO, &c. TEXAS, in regard to English policy and designs. He condemns them all as Machiavelian; he relates the proceedings of Mr. TYLER, and the formation, management, and ultimate defeat of the Annexation treaty. He gives the purport, with quotations, of each principal document; he exhibits, as he understands them, the agents, their spirit and aims, as well as the political chiefs; he dwells on the respective interests and views of the South and the North, and the British Government, the latter and the United States; of Great Britain with respect to Texas; he exposes the late treaty as the offspring of President TYLER'S treaty and the approaching Presidential election; the whole abolition strife is explained and analyzed. Touching the policy of France in the matter, Monsieur CAUCHY thinks that she should insist, as far as possible, against the revival of the Mexican claim, or that, at least, the independence of Mexico should be permanently secured from the encroachments and institutions of the slaveholders who possess Texas, provided Texas remain an independent State with England in obtaining from the U. States a certain absolute guaranty of Mexican independence. The author of the essay had, from his personal acquaintance of the writer with events, persons, publications, documents, and publications of every description, representing all the views. In the body of this essay has an extract from an American paper of last December—the correspondence between Captain ELLIOT and the Texan Government—which has engaged my attention on account of the identity of some of its statements and inferences with our impressions here.

The Journal du Havre tells us that Edward CONROY, Esq., specialized as British Consul, has embarked for the United States at that port. Our morning papers say that the telegraph reports the acquittal of M. DE BRUGEQ, at Paris, charged with breach of the criminal calendar. Curiosity is still alive in Paris about the results of the inquiry by the secret committee of the British House of Lords touching the Government prerogative and practice of opening letters. Let us leave, observes the Constitutionnel, Lord RADNOR, BANNERMAN, and DUNCOMBE to search the internal system of Cabinet noirs. We may smile at such pharisaism. The houses of the Duke of MORNY and M. ROUL, and M. DE LAGRANGE have just been thoroughly searched—all papers found (letters, wills) were duly opened; and, if you enter any coffee-house with a political turn of mind, domiciliary visits and arrests are performed, you may learn a little, and of the legal formalities too, of the system. M. DUNCOMBE got the proceedings of the Peers yesterday afternoon.

"VISCOUNT DEROUCHAGE referred to the certain prevention of small-pox by the vaccine matter, and stated that M. Charbonnier de la Guesnerie, who had been brought from the prison of Saint Lazare to the Civil Tribunal of Paris, and afflicted with acute rheumatism, was kept for ninety-six hours in a damp cell...

"THE MINISTER OF PUBLIC INSTRUCTION begged leave to say that the noble peer was greatly mistaken in supposing that the police of Paris acted...

"M. J. DEL ESSERT bore testimony to the truth of these facts...

"M. DE BRUGEQ was acquitted on the 30th ultimo; arrears, however, frequent. The official report of the proceeds of the French indirect taxes and contributions for the first six months of this year shows an increase of nearly eight millions of francs over those of the corresponding period of 1843. Washington and Paris appear to be equal, at present, in mended health. The Narvaez Government is selling Church property as fast as possible, notwithstanding the remonstrances and solemn protests of the Holy See. We have lost by death two eminent literati—one FAURIEL, aged 69, of the Academy of Inscriptions and Belles-Lettres, who wrote the famous Bipolante, PANCKOUCKE, to whom we owe a good translation and an excellent edition of Tacitus, aged 64. A small French force of fifteen hundred vics from the frontiers of Morocco. The Spaniards promise to occupy Tangiers with six thousand infantry. Abdul-Rhaman's force in Morocco is exceedingly doubtful, and even abstruse for the quiddance.

records.headline: FROM ST. DOMINGO.
records.summary_en: The *Daily National Intelligencer* reported that the project to divide the island into states was abandoned, leaving the government restored to its pre-revolution status minus municipalities, with Port au Prince serving as the capital and Port au Platt maintaining the Dominican flag. Additionally, authorities at Port au Platt arranged a treaty granting the French a patent for the Samana mines, though it was expected to fail due to popular opposition, while President Guerriere was on an island tour expected to reach Cape Haytien.
records.summary_es: El *Daily National Intelligencer* consignó que la iniciativa de erigir estados en la isla quedó desestimada, restituyéndose el orden administrativo existente con anterioridad a la rebelión salvo en las municipalidades, con Puerto Príncipe en calidad de capital y Puerto Plata desplegando el pabellón dominicano. Paralelamente, las autoridades de Puerto Plata estipularon un convenio otorgando a los franceses la concesión minera de Samaná, cuya ratificación se juzgaba inviable por el rechazo popular, al paso que el presidente Guerrier recorría el país con destino a Cabo Haitiano.

IMPORTANT FROM ST. DOMINGO.—The Island continues in a very unsettled state, in consequence of an expected attack by the Haytiens. Gen. Boewavo had been recalled to the capital, and was succeeded by Gen. St. Jago. The Spaniards are being appointed to office in place of the Dominicans, and every possible effort was made to defend the town.

records.full_text:
From St. Domingo.—We learn from Capt. Wilson of the brig Republic, just arrived from Port au Prince, that on the 12th of March the Haytien man of war Herard, in the schr. La Granada, had been seen off the South side of the Island, five miles off, by five gun boats. The whole coast was guarded by vessels of war, to prevent the ex-President and his adherents from landing. The government called out all the militia, and the whole of that part of the Island belonging to the Haytien government was under martial law. Several of the adherents of Herard had been taken and shot, and there was a great excitement throughout the Island. Coffee was very scarce and high on account of all the country men having been taken for soldiers, and no persons left to bring the Coffee to market. The markets were glutted with American produce.

Although numerous arrests were made in different parts of the Republic, among whom were some of the journalists, there was no general sympathy for Herard, who was viewed as an ambitious usurper, and by all parties of government, that his attempts to revolutionize the country would prove abortive.

It was rumored at Port Republican, that a revolution had taken place at St. Domingo, which had resulted in the expulsion of Gen. Santana from the Presidency, and in the elevation to that office of Major Moru, a mulatto of splendid character, and the respectable family of the Alvares of Zagnate (Saint Domingo.) If true, this change of government in the Dominican Republic would be the triumph of an enlightened policy over military rule, and demagogism personified in Santana and Bobadilla.
