records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
MR. SLICER—Since the return of Mr. Hogan from his secret mission to St. Domingo, a strong disposition has been manifested to learn the result of his researches.

The Washington correspondents of several northern papers, particularly of New-Hampshire, have drawn largely upon what they understand to be the Secret Report of Mr. Hogan. These communications have given an impression that a splendid arrangement has been made by Mr. Hogan, on our part, with the Eastern part of St. Domingo. One writer even asserts that an empire has been bought, and found in that region a population of 190,000, including 90,000 whites.

His astonishment is certainly natural, for the majority of the population of St. Domingo does not exceed 65,000, and the whites not more than 3,000 and 4,000.

In the second place, it is said that the territory of the Dominicans is very rich and fertile—a land of milk and honey—and that the sun has seldom shone upon such a garden of Eden as this; but the whole Dominican country contains less than 60,000 all told; at this time it probably does not exceed 50,000, including 5,000 or 6,000 whites.

As to the idea of annexing the whole Island, there is no ground for it; for since the sun of Haytien freedom has shone upon such a garden of Eden as this, the Dominicans have been able to raise less than 300 millions of pounds of coffee which we can call our own—a small portion of which they export; moreover, the Haytien President does not acknowledge the independence of the Dominicans, or to give them a title to their own territory; and that perhaps it may be well to turn over a few pages of the history of the country, that we may have a true view of the relations which exist between the parties.

It is not my intention to go into a history of the country; but as an effort will be made hereafter to carry out the views of the secret agent, there exists not a doubt:

First—The Dominicans, finding that they could not, of themselves, maintain their independence against France, sent a "shining blade for Boyer, but decline a union;" but sent a delegation to Boyer, at Port au Prince, and proposed to notice briefly some of the principal events of the Revolution, which caused all the calamities and miseries under which the country now suffers—a cruel and unoffending government being overthrown.

In the first place there is no ground for the common opinion that the Dominicans were forced to submit to the government of the French part—against their consent. The people of the country had suffered from the French, and when Boyer, to prevent further bloodshed and destruction of property, marched into the Spanish part, he was received with open arms. At that period the Spanish part of the island was under a weak government, and a revolution broke out between Spain and her revolted provinces in South America, which so shocked the Spanish inhabitants, while the seas which thronged the Caribbee seas were continuously plundered by pirates, and Spain could not protect this part; moreover, there were many persons in that division of the island who were in favor of a union with Hayti, and the Haytien President was invited, no one officer opposing such a step. Such was the state of things when Boyer entered the Spanish part of the Island. After maturely reflecting upon the difficulties by which they were surrounded, the people of the Spanish part sought protection in an union with the Haytiens; and the Haytiens, on their part, willingly gave its consent to the annexation of the Eastern part to the Haytien Republic, as much so as Massachusetts have to any of the States of this Union. Thus it appears that the Dominicans adopted the Haytien Government, not only voluntarily, but joyfully. Shortly after this, the French (with an overwhelming force in the harbor of Port au Prince) demanded an indemnity for the property sacrificed in the Revolution, The people of the country had “supped full of horrors,”* and Boyer, to prevent farther bloodshed and destruction of property, agreed to the payment of 150,000,000 of francs to France; and other European powers demanded an indemnity for the loss of property, and an equality of commerce and an acknowledgment from the Haytiens. The sum was so great that it was impossible to pay it, and nothing was effected.

Here was the grand cause of the revolt of the people of the Island. This was the signal, in the Spanish part, for an insurrection, and, without the least hesitation, they declared themselves independent of it. It does not appear that they took any steps towards a union with Howard, or from a conviction that his course was wrong; but they felt that they had been deceived, and as soon as they found themselves in a condition to do so, they declared themselves independent. In other words, Boyer's acts were wrong, and the consequences of Boyer's absurd attempt to raise an indemnity for the French, by taxing the whole country, was the real cause of discontent; and when he was deposed, the Haytiens and Pierrot, his successors and opponents in everything, have pursued a similar course, and brought about the same results.

About two years since, agents were despatched by the Dominicans to our Government, asking aid and protection. Their proposals were favorably received by Mr. Upshar, which, had he lived, would probably have led to a treaty that was some mark remarkable. After the death of Mr. Upshur, Mr. Calhoun sent Mr. Hogan to the Island to see if the Spanish part found a kindred spirit in Mr. Calhoun. Mr. Hogan, no doubt, executed his mission well; but the distinguished honor of sending a secret agent to a country which has declared its independence, but whose independence is not recognized, is a violation of the constitution of the country, and in opposition to nine-tenths of the Democratic party. A secret agent, our Government ought to encourage, in order to prove that blacks are not capable of governing, and that it is for their own country; indeed they are supposed to have any rights in the case. This course of our Government towards Santo Domingo is not only contrary to the spirit of our Constitution, which acknowledges their independence—but who believes that they have any right to send an agent in the movement? The commerce of our country has been very small with the Island; but hundreds of thousands of dollars might have been saved in our trade, by making a treaty with the Government of Hayti. It was asked during the administration of General Jackson that a commissioner should be sent to Hayti; but the goods imported into Hayti in American vessels were subject to a tonnage duty of 10 per cent. and an extra duty of ten per cent., matching an equal amount on English vessels. The interest of the country has been thus sacrificed to gratify the vulgar prejudice of southern statesmen, as "Aristocratic England" could acknowledge the independence of Hayti, and we, with our "Democratic" principles, trade, which naturally belongs to us—but "Democratic principles" forbid us to acknowledge it! Had the commerce of the country was made subservient to the public good, our commerce with Hayti would be as much to us as Massachusetts has to any of the States of this Union. Why, an untrammeled trade with one million of Haytiens, using a thousand articles of our manufacture, is worthy of the slightest consideration. But we are told that the Dominicans presented a petition to Mr. Hogan, and Christophe is often held up as an evidence of the fact. Christophe, we know, had no other title to his position than that of being the first, and he took it by force of arms; Napoleon, in about the same manner, brought his army into Paris, and held it to his distinct wish, to blood, and by the same means; and Boyer, when he marched through seas of slaughter to subjugate other nations, might have done the same; but to a popular man, for it is a grand and philanthropic truth that

The Haytiens universally hold in utter detestation the memory of Boyer and his acts.

The government of Christophe, as has been stated, was a despotism; but under Christophe the Haytiens were free from the influence of foreign powers, and he never suffered those who consider a colored Republic an anomaly, to interfere in the affairs of Hayti; and during the whole of his administration of twenty years, there was less taking of life for political offences, than there has been since the eruption among the officers, less plundering of the treasury, and far greater security for property, than there was seen in this country during the same period. Why should it be said that Hayti will not succeed under a free government? Look at the short period under Boyer—greater degree, it is true, than under Christophe—but look at his acts. Let it be remembered that the country has been divided into three parts—1804 declared, and in 1842 divided and besieged; yet under all these difficulties, trade and commerce flourished in the North. Three calamities have checked the decline of commerce in Hayti—which, perhaps, have checked the decline of commerce among the children of the soil and in the find the characteristics of the Haytiens—despotism, combined with an unmanageable earthquake, which destroyed Port au Prince, as well as (both publicly and private), in the principal towns. Still under all these calamities, trade and commerce flourish in the North. If under all these difficulties trade and commerce flourish, how much more would the Dominicans "ring" from their resources if they were under a similar government?

As regards the other, and more important attributes of a free government, Hayti is by no means deficient. The "blood-thirsty barbarians," it may safely be affirmed will compare favorably with those of the U. States; while as regards morality, peace and order, industry, intelligence, hospitality, freedom from vice, and, above all, religious toleration, the Haytiens are far superior to the Dominicans—touching who have been slender circumstances—have declared their independence, and have sought for protection and aid.

These circumstances have gladened more yearly brought to light.

"From Greenland's icy mountains
* * * * *

But it is a melancholy fact that Hayti has been overlooked. Is not the Dominican Republic small, weak, and insignificant to compare in comparative darkness? How can our Government have compromised its character by sending one of our Government towards these Islands, may be inferred by those who are familiar with American politics.

In this state of things, a manifest disposition on the part of the United States to aid the Dominicans cannot fail to produce a disastrous effect on Hayti. It will be considered by the world as anti-Republican, ungenerous and unjust. How far Hayti has cause for complaint, may be inferred by those who are familiar with American politics. As to the payment of the indemnity which was been granted by him, with the American expressions of good will. France will not allow us to tamper with her debt with impunity; and by an ill-timed, imprudent interference with another government, destroy her chance for the recovery of her debt. A difference with the French, however, is little to be shunned than the foul dishonor of a fraudulent trick upon the debt of another Government, less powerful than our own, for our own portion of its territory.
B. C. C.

*Although we cannot but feel that Slavery speaks to this editor through his article, as well as through most of the Boston press, we do not wish to discuss the subject here; but we cannot help remarking that the editor of the Journal, who takes his facts from his correspondent in St. Domingo or from some other tap-room, does not represent our Southern brethren any more than he does the true principles of Hayti or the Dominicans.

†Look at the condition of our one missionary in Hayti from the American Board of Foreign Missions! He is living in a hut, in a small, uncomfortable schooner, for Port au Prince, or in a hovel on shore; while the French missionaries are able to allude to demonstrations, in view of a "Surprise of Soldiers at High Mass," or a procession of Priests in full robes, at Port au Prince.

records.full_text:
Your number of yesterday, which arrived here this morning, containing the important news from your correspondents in Hayti and St. Domingo, fell like a bomb shell among all the politicians, from the Capitol to the White House, and throughout every hotel, tavern, and oyster cellar in the city. 'Have you seen the Herald this morning?' said one. 'No; what's in it?' 'Why the news from Hayti.' 'Why the d—l,' the first would reply—'go get a copy and read for yourself.' But alas, for his comfort, there were no Heralds to be let round upon such a basis.—Every place, where one could be found, was secured in order to read the news; from St. Domingo, which filled one entire page of interesting and important matter. In both Houses of Congress might be seen groups of members talking together upon the subject, perfectly amazed, and wondering at Bennett's industry in getting such information even in advance of the government. Nothing that has occurred for the last ten years was calculated to cause more excitement throughout this country and Europe, than the information thrown before the public in those letters, respecting that island, in your columns. Oregon and Texas are completely cast in the shade by them, and it would not surprise me much, were I to see 10,000 men on their way to that island before one month. They want such a force there at this time, in order to rescue the island from negro domination, and restore it to the white race, to whom it properly belongs. I have heard a gentleman say, who has just returned from there, that five thousand able-bodied men, in addition to the Dominican forces, would conquer, in forty-eight hours, the whole island and subjugate all the blacks. There are no existing treaties between the United States and Hayti, to prevent our citizens from going there in any character they please, and I know, from what I have learned on the subject, that any force of this sort would be accepted by the Dominican government, and ample portions of land for settlement would be given to those who would emigrate there for the purpose of sustaining the white Dominicans and others against the black savages, with whom they are contending for liberty and independence.
There is something serious going on here at present between Mr. Pakenham and Mr. Calhoun, in relation to public affairs. Whether it is the Oregon question or not, I cannot say; but the fact is, that yesterday, that has started Her Majesty's representative, for he was known to be there. Since Mr. Pakenham sent Mr. Bidwell, his attaché, in hot haste after Mr. Calhoun, who was on a visit to the Hermitage, the communication between the British Minister and the late Secretary of State, is the subject of much talk. Something is forthcoming in the settlement of our difficulties with Great Britain. It is said that Mr. Calhoun, although named in my letter of yesterday, intends to take upon himself the responsibility of proposing to suspend the joint occupancy of that territory. The South, it is said, will sustain him. He will separate himself and fall on this question, will sound his death knell, and forever bury the nullification party. From henceforth, they will not discover any difference between a Calhoun Democrat and a Nullifier. The term will be synonymous.
The friends of Mr. Calhoun in the Senate, are preparing to make a move to-day in the Senate. The latter offered them in the Senate, after the speech of Mr. Hannegan, and prefaced their introduction with some remarks, in which they took occasion to let it be known how much they hate both Calhoun and the war party. They will not be taken by surprise, and a twelve months' notice—thereby bringing the whole question to a close. If they were to act otherwise than by them, it would be tantamount to any tariff they might propose. It is well known that the whole manufacturing interest of this country would receive an impetus, and the manufacturing and commercial interests of England, by excluding the whole of her manufactures from this country. Both parties are now politicians, and will do nothing, but like a pig in a poke, or a cat in the gutter. It is also said that Mr. Calhoun will go in for annexing Cuba. He says he will do it to prevent the British. Whether Mr. Levy was serious or not, in offering a resolution to annex this island, is not known; but there are those who consider the motion rather premature. It is not so much. Among them is the British Minister, who it is rumored, remarked when he heard of it, that 'Mr. Levy was a clever young man, but a very great ass.'—His name is mentioned in this connection, and his friends say with the opposition to it at the North. The southern men will say very little, by-and-by, that they will have to annex for themselves, without consulting southern politicians.

records.headline: IMPORTANT NEWS FROM ST. DOMINGO—PROGRESS OF GENERAL ANNEXATION.
records.summary_en: *The Liberator* reprinted reports from the *New York Herald* regarding a conspiracy against Hayti and the progress of general annexation concerning the island of San Domingo. According to these reports, documents and diplomatic correspondence obtained by a special correspondent indicated that the United States and San Domingo were preparing for U.S. recognition of the Dominican republic, following a policy similar to the one used with Texas that led to its annexation.
records.summary_es: *The Liberator* reprodujo informaciones de *The New York Herald* relativas a una conspiración contra Haití y a la marcha general de las tentativas anexionistas sobre la isla de Santo Domingo. Según dichos despachos, documentos y correspondencia diplomática obtenidos por un enviado especial indicaban que Estados Unidos y Santo Domingo preparaban el reconocimiento estadounidense de la República Dominicana, siguiendo una pauta análoga a la empleada con Texas que condujo a su anexión.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
In further proof of the existence of this frightful conspiracy against the freedom and independence of Hayti, read, mark and inwardly digest the extraordinary contents of the following articles from the New-York Herald—

IMPORTANT NEWS FROM ST. DOMINGO—PROGRESS OF GENERAL ANNEXATION.
The news which we have received here, during the last two days, by two vessels from different ports of the Island of San Domingo, or Hayti, in the West Indies, and which will be found in this day's paper, is of the highest importance to this country and to the world—nay, even to the course and progress of republican government in this hemisphere, for all time to come.
Through the energy and industry of a special agent and correspondent, whom we sent to San Domingo last autumn, we have received, exclusively, a series of several interesting and diplomatic correspondence which have already passed between the government of the United States and that of San Domingo, preparing the way for the great movement of the annexation of the latter to the former, according to the same policy, or plan, which was pursued towards Texas, and which has, in a few years, terminated in the absorption or annexation of the latter into this great republic of the North. These documents consist of a proposal, presented to the United States government at Washington, by the agent of the Dominican republic, some time ago, together with copies of highly interesting letters, written by certain public functionaries in that island, and addressed, during the last summer, to Mr. Hogan, the agent of the United States, then in San Domingo, to which island he was sent by Mr. Calhoun, then Secretary of State, in order to investigate the condition and ascertain the importance and capabilities of that new republic in the West Indies.
Thus far, the movement has been highly prosperous and successful. The war between San Domingo and Hayti is rapidly coming to an end, and it is highly probable that the black and sturdy republic will be overcome by the white and more civilized races of the other. As soon as that point shall have been accomplished, there will follow other movements, leading to the natural termination of the annexation of the whole island to the United States.
It will be perceived that the diplomatic correspondence which we give, only comes up to the period at which Mr. Hogan, the United States agent, left San Domingo. The report which Mr. Hogan has already made to the Secretary of State at Washington, or the action of our government on that information, we can only as yet conjecture. One thing, however, is certain, that these great diplomatic movements, of such mighty interest to the destiny of the West Indies, and to the world in general annexation, were not alluded to in the slightest degree, in the recent message of the President. How far, therefore, the present administration may be carrying out this magnificent policy, so auspiciously begun under Mr. Calhoun, we can only conjecture. We have no doubt, however, but that such is the policy of the day—to the spirit of the age—to his destiny—and to the great principles of republican progress, which we have seen so happily begun in the annexation of Texas.
Hispaniola, or the island of San Domingo, favored by God and nature, is surely marching, with a step as regular as the movement of the spheres, to accomplish that great destiny which is allotted to her to fulfil—that is, the union and incorporation, in one great and mighty republic, of a grand confederation of regular democracies, the whole of the islands of the West Indies, and all the lands thereunto naturally belonging. In Cuba, in Mexico, and, indeed, in all the neighboring countries, there is that will, in the course of a few years, lead to the realization of every article and a central system. The difference between England and the United States, respecting the 49th parallel in the Oregon Territory, is a mere bagatelle compared to the movements contemplated and begun in reference to those portions of the southern hemisphere, not yet united to this republic. Our government might, if necessary, easily settle that question by giving England all she asks in Oregon—for in less than a quarter of a century, she can pay with the whole peach, fall into the lap of the United States, along with other territories to which it may be attached. The annexation of the whole of the West Indies, and a stable government in San Domingo, in Mexico and in the California territories, will only be the coming events that already cast their shadows over the present and the future, and make the mountains of Europe look pale with fear.

records.headline: CONSPIRACY AGAINST HAYTI.
records.summary_en: The January 9, 1846 issue of *The Liberator* published an account alleging that the black population of Dominica lives without marriage, religion, or clothing, leading a state of extreme immorality. According to the excerpt, the white inhabitants of Dominica successfully emancipated themselves from this oppression through valor and are now appealing to the United States for sympathy and protection against threatened extermination by the negroes. Additionally, the text notes that the French government is seeking redress from the Haitians for the spoliation of French property.
records.summary_es: El número del 9 de enero de 1846 de *The Liberator* publicó un relato en el que se afirmaba que la población negra de Santo Domingo vivía al margen del matrimonio, la religión y el vestuario, sumida en una extrema inmoralidad. Según el extracto, los habitantes blancos de Santo Domingo lograron emanciparse valerosamente de dicha opresión y apelaban entonces a la simpatía y protección de Estados Unidos frente a la amenaza de exterminio por parte de los negros. Asimismo, el texto señala que el gobierno francés exigía reparaciones a los haitianos por el despojo de bienes pertenecientes a súbditos galos.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
CONSPIRACY AGAINST HAYTI.

There cannot be a doubt that, flushed with their success in the seizure and annexation of Texas, the southern slaveholding banditti are conspiring for the dismemberment of the Haytian republic in the first instance, and its subsequent absorption by this country for slaveholding purposes! They are aiming to establish slavery in Hayti as they have done in Texas. The following letter, which is from a highly respectable source in Washington, is a start-ling character, and renders it highly probable that the conspirators are even among ourselves, on the soil of Massachusetts!

Ipswich, Dec. 29th, 1845.
I casually heard, to-day, that a young seaman of this place, named Leon, had gone up to Boston, to go on a voyage to Hayti. I was anxious to see him; and on inquiry, I learned that he had been offered high wages, $25 per month, by a captain who was fitting out a vessel for Hayti, with the agreement, after the arrival of the vessel there, that they should all serve for the same wages, $25 per month; and it was implied that he was to have very high wages, and it would seem to imply that any bold, daring man might procure very easy high wages, by going out in this vessel. I do not know the name, or whether there is any such vessel fitting out in Boston, for such a purpose, or whether there are any of the Dominicans engaged in fitting out a vessel; but if true, it would seem to imply that there are persons in Boston, who are willing to aid in this conspiracy, and that they are actually fitting out a vessel for this purpose, or are violating the laws of the United States, and may not this be remedied? Is Hayti to be a second edition of Texas? I hope not. I hope that New-England has no citizens who are willing to aid slavery in such a project.

In further proof of the existence of this frightful conspiracy against the freedom and independence of Hayti, read, mark and inwardly digest the extract below, which we copy from the editorial columns of the New-York Herald:—

IMPORTANT NEWS FROM ST. DOMINGO—CONSPIRACY AGAINST HAYTI.

The news which we have received here, during the last two days, by two vessels from different parts of the island of San Domingo, or Hayti, in the West Indies, and which will be found in this day's paper, is of the highest importance to this country and to the world—may, even to the course and progress of Republican government in this hemisphere, for all time to come.

Through the energy and industry of a special agent and correspondent, whom we sent to San Domingo last autumn, we have received, exclusively, copies of several documents and diplomatic correspondence which have already passed between the government of the United States and that of San Domingo, preparing the way for the great measure of the annexation of the latter republic to the former, according to the same policy, or plan, which has annexed Texas; and which must, in a few years, terminated in the absorption or annexation of the latter into this great republic of the North. These documents consist of a report... presented to the United States government at Washington by the agent of Mr. Calhoun to San Domingo, together with copies of highly interesting letters written by various public functionaries in that island, and addressed, during the last summer, to Mr. Hogan, the agent of the United States, sent to San Domingo, to which island he was sent by Mr. Calhoun, then Secretary of State, in order to investigate the condition and ascertain the resources and capabilities of that new republic in the West Indies.

Thus far, the movement has been highly prosperous and successful. The contest between San Domingo and Hayti is rapidly coming to an end, and it is highly probable that the black and mulatto republic will be overcome by the white and more civilized races of the other. As soon as that point shall have been accomplished, there will follow other movements, leading to the natural termination of the whole affair, in the absorption or annexation of both by the United States.

It will be perceived that the diplomatic correspondence which we give, only comes up to the period when Mr. Hogan, the agent, had just left San Domingo. The report which Mr. Hogan has himself made to the Secretary of State at Washington, or the action of our government on that information, we can only as yet conjecture. One thing, however, is certain, that movements, diplomatic movements, of such mighty interest to the destiny of the West Indies, and to the world in general annexation, were not alluded to in the late message of the President to Congress... How far, therefore, the present administration may carry out the views of Mr. Calhoun, we can only conjecture. We have no doubt, however, but Mr. Polk will follow them up, to their full extent. In proof of this, we give below a letter, which we received a few days since, from a gentleman who is favored by God and nature, is surely marching, with rapid strides, to take a place among the nations—that great accomplishment which that great destiny which is allotted to her to fulfill—that is, the union and incorporation, or annexation of Hayti to San Domingo, or a confederation of regular democracies, the whole of Hispanic America, in a short time, and the whole of the trade naturally belonging. In Cuba, in Mexico, in California, and all the rest of Hispanic America, that will, in the course of a few years, lead to the formation of great, free, Anglo-Saxon states. The difference between England and the United States, respecting the 49th parallel in the Oregon boundary, is a mere "flea-bite" compared to the movements contemplated and begun in reference to these millions of square miles, belonging to countries not yet united to this republic. Our government might, to-morrow, settle with Mr. Pakenham, all that England all she asks in Oregon—for less than a quarter of a century—and yet it would be a mere peach, fall into the lap of the United States, along with other territories to which it may be attached. What a magnificent vision of future power, great, and stable government in San Domingo, in Mexico and Oregon, is now opening to our country! The coming events that already cast their shadows over the future, leave no doubt on our mind that the millions of Hispanic race look with favor

MR. HOGAN'S MISSION TO ST. DOMINGO.
To the Editor of the New-York Herald.

The great and important considerations involved in this mission ought not to be lightly overlooked by the country. What are they? They are simply these:—

First—One of the most beautiful and fertile islands in the West Indies, is occupied by a barbarous race, rapidly sinking into a state of savageism, or civil order, a prey to every species of licentiousness and crime, the very details of which would be as monstrous to our sober thinking citizens as Gulliver's travels, or the flights of Baron Munchausen; yet, as true as God is in heaven. They have set aside the ceremonial of marriage, and look upon religion as a farce: and so far have they carried their obscenity, that a majority of the black population, both male and female, go entirely naked, and have not the decency to cover themselves with fig leaves, as our first parents are represented to have done in paradise, after their fall. Can any thing in the organic structure of male and female bodies authorize any one pretending to the least respect for human nature countenance such a state of immorality at our very doors? Surely not.

Secondly—The white inhabitants of Dominico, and those who have fled to other countries, save the honorable position in which these people have placed themselves, to defend their rights, and protect themselves from this oppression, and who have actually taken up arms, and with their own stretched arms to protect them, at least, by their sympathy, from the extermination with which the black population of Hayti threaten them, as they did in the Spanish part of the island.

Thirdly—The interests of humanity in behalf of suffering thousands of our own race and religion, who have been driven from their homes, and forced into the subject, and which, with our government ought to take into consideration, and aid the government, which is seeking redress from the Haytiens for spoliations of the property of French subjects. St. Domingo, thousands of French subjects fled to the United States at the period of the revolution, and become citizens, they, or their offspring, are now living among us, and both humanity and interest, and government may afford them, with other reasons, which might be brought in support of giving the Dominicans our aid, at this moment, when their officers come to us from their government to recognize their independence at once, and open commercial relations with us, or alliance with the white government there. I hope Congress will take up this subject, and examine into it through their hands, while their time is taken up with less important matters. We must have the whole of the paper, standard, or full, this session; and Congress must set in time upon it, before foreign nations step in and take the prize from us.

records.full_text:
There has been an arrival at New York from St. Domingo, bringing dates to the 22d November.

A battle is reported to have taken place on the 27th of October, between the Dominican and Haytien armies. It commenced by attacking a fort, which the Haytiens occupied.

After a combat of two hours, the Dominicans entered and took possession of the fort, and completely destroyed the enemy, killing 350 Haytiens, and making a prize of two pieces of cannon, 8 drums, and all the musical instruments belonging to the 28th regiment of the Cape, 3 flags and more than 200 muskets.

The blockade promulgated on the 5th September, is a mere paper affair, there being not a solitary Haytien vessel to enforce it. A few vessels were preparing by the Dominicans to cruise around the coast, they appearing determined to sustain their independence, having been victorious in all the battles since the revolution last year.

records.headline: EFFECTS OF THE NEWS FROM HAYTI.
records.summary_en: The *Anti-slavery Bugle* reported that letters published regarding St. Domingo caused widespread amazement and excitement in Congress and across the United States and Europe, completely overshadowing the Oregon and Texas questions. The published information claimed that 5,000 to 10,000 men could easily conquer the Black-occupied portion of the island within forty-eight hours to restore it to the white race, and that the Dominican government would accept such assistance from U.S. citizens.
records.summary_es: El *Anti-slavery Bugle* consignó que las cartas divulgadas sobre Santo Domingo provocaron general asombro y revuelo en el Congreso, en todo Estados Unidos y en Europa, opacando enteramente los litigios de Oregón y Texas. La información publicada sostenía que entre 5.000 y 10.000 hombres podrían subyugar con facilidad en cuarenta y ocho horas la porción de la isla ocupada por negros para devolverla a la raza blanca, y que el gobierno dominicano admitiría gustoso ese auxilio de ciudadanos estadounidenses.

records.full_text: Your number of yesterday, which arrived here this morning, containing the important news from your correspondents in Hayti and St. Domingo, fell like a bomb shell among all the politicians, from the Capitol to the White House, and throughout every hotel, tavern, and oyster cellar in the city.— 'Have you seen the Herald this morning?' said one. 'No; what is in it?' said the person spoken to—'Why the d—l,' the first would reply—'go get a copy, and read for yourself.' But alas, for his comfort, there were no Heralds to be found after nine o'clock. Every place where one could be found was secured in order to read the news from St. Domingo, which filled one entire page of interesting and important matter. In both Houses of Congress might be seen groups of members talking together upon the subject, perfectly amazed, and wondering at Bennett's industry in getting such information even in advance of the government. Nothing that has appeared on the tapis during the last ten years was calculated to cause more excitement than these letters. They give more than the information thrown before the public in those letters, respecting that island in your columns. Oregon and Texas are completely cast in the shade by them, and it would not surprise me much, were I to see 10,000 men in their way to that island before one month. They want such a force there at this time, in order to rescue the island from negro domination, and restore it to the white race, to whom it properly belongs. I have heard a gentleman say, who had just returned from there, that five thousand able-bodied men, in addition to the Dominican forces, would conquer, in forty-eight hours the whole of that part occupied by the blacks. There are no existing treaties between the United States and Hayti, to prevent our citizens from going there in any character they please, and I know from what I have learned on the subject, that assistance of this sort would be accepted by the Dominican government, and ample provision made for those who would emigrate there for the purpose of sustaining the white government and people against the black savages, with whom they are contending for liberty and independence.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
The cupidity of our slaveholding democracy, fattened on Texas, is already active to accomplish the acquisition of Cuba. Having at last in their hands, the 'valley of rascals,' an empty world, they burn to make the most of their opportunities. Hayti, that great black republic, so long an eye-sore to the slaveholders, must be put out of the way; it is a dangerous neighbor to our southern States. It must be re-subjugated; the attempt of Napoleon must be re-tried, and the white man again put in possession of the island, standard or no standard, slave or no slave. Bold as this project may seem, it is nevertheless in train, and active efforts are making towards its accomplishment. Read the Ledger of this city,—that willing tool of unprincipled men in power,—read the late letters of its Washington correspondent. In his letter of Monday last, he says that Mr. Hogan of New York, who, it will be remembered, was sent out to Hayti on a secret expedition by Mr. Tyler, has lately returned to Washington, and has made a luminous report on the subject of the annexation of Hayti to the United States. The object of his mission, this writer says, 'was to examine into the capacities of the Dominicans or white population in the Spanish part of the island, to sustain their independence against the Haytians; and his report, taken in connection with the known circumstances of the island, leaves no doubt that Hayti can be easily subjugated, or rather, leaves no doubt of the success of the Dominicans against the Haytians, and that, too, for the purpose of acquiring for itself ultimate possession of the whole island. It is now asserted that the Dominican republic is independent, and is suing to the government of the United States to acknowledge her independence! Another Texan affair precisely; Hayti is 'to be annexed to this country in the same manner as was the 'valley of rascals.' Emissaries are sent out to stir up malcontents to insurrection; proffers of sympathy and ultimate co-operation, and perhaps more substantial aid are offered; Hayti is to be weakened by the insurgents; their independence is declared; an army is sent out to fix the boundary, and all the rest is done; and, presto, the independent country is annexed. This is the way our Texan republicans and progressive Democrats do things.

From all the information which Mr. Hogan has communicated to the cabinet, he expresses that he is firmly of the opinion that the Dominican government will maintain itself, and that, eventually, all the Haytians are aided by some one of the European governments. The proportion of whites, Mr. Hogan considers, is sufficient to maintain their ground, but the condition of the Haytians is such that they cannot long remain to contend single-handed with the Dominicans.

In this view of the case, as the subject is properly understood, every friend of humanity will feel a deep interest. It can hardly be doubted, that if the Dominican government shall be extended over the whole island, that slavery, or at least the most cruel serfdom, will undoubtedly revert to their descendants as former colored masters. From what we know of the flock of French refugees, when the time comes—and it is not far distant—making it necessary that they return to the island of their fathers, will find an early entry with them American feelings and principles; and that such a state of things, as this Domingo will, from these causes, utterly become essential to slaveholders.

In a commercial point of view, the success of the Dominicans will be of no small advantage or importance to the United States. With a government firmly established in the island by white men, the sympathies of the people will naturally be with us—and our commercial relations with Santo Domingo will be vastly increased. In a military and naval point of view, the possession of the island or independence by the United States is equally important.

Was there ever a bolder or more villainously conceived scheme of wholesale plunder? Surely God will be avenged on such a nation as this.

records.full_text:
From the Boston Journal.
HAYTI.

MR. SLEEPER—Since the return of Mr. Hogan from his secret mission to St. Domingo, a strong disposition has been manifested to learn the real state of Hayti.

The Washington correspondents of several northern journals, with a view of gratifying curiosity, have drawn heavily upon what they represented to be the substance of his report. These communications have generally stated that a favorable arrangement for 'mutual benefit,' is nearly completed with the Eastern part of St. Domingo. One writer expresses surprise that Mr. Hogan should have found Hayti to contain a population of 190,000, including 130,000 whites.

His astonishment is certainly natural, for the population of Hayti is about 800,000—not 190,000—and Kendal green.

According to a census taken in 1825, the eastern division contained less than 65,000, all told : at this time, it is probably numbered 80,000, including 5 or 6,000 whites.

Another writer, in allusion to the question, luxuriates upon the idea of annexing the whole island. He considers it the most delightful country which the sun shines upon, which has for twenty-five years went out of cultivation, and descendants philosophically living upon plantains and wild cattle, from which he might wring out of its soil. But before we proceed to take possession of Hayti, it would be as well to consult the history of this country. It will be found in the pages of the checkered history of St. Domingo, and learn something of the relations which should exist between us.

Possibly nothing injurious may immediately grow out of an alliance between the Eastern section and a foreign power; but that an effort will be made hereafter to bring, with the views of the secret agent, there exists not a doubt.

The writer to whom we refer, (a Washington, perhaps, draw 'a shining robe for Greece,' but describe a cause not tinged with romance,) we dip our quill in ink of a darker color, and present briefly some of the peculiarities which mark this business, and which should be considered in any negotiations which have been circulated in relation to an independent government, and a harmless and afflicted people.

In the first place, there is no good reason for the opinion, that the Dominicans were originally annexed to the government of the French part—except their poverty. That they were conquered, beaten down, trampled upon, and crushed, is untrue; but the direct reverse of this was the case, as we shall attempt to show.

In 1821, at the time of Christophe's death, Boyer succeeded in uniting the whole island under the Haytians. At that period, the Spanish part of the island was independent, but its situation was very precarious. The success which attended the revolted provinces in South America was at its height; the privateers which thronged the waters of the Caribbean seas were continually plundering the Haytians; and as there was no naval force to protect them, there were many persons in that division of Hayti, who were desirous of placing it under the protection of the patriots of South America—but by far the greatest portion were desirous of continuing the existing state of things at the commencement of Boyer's government. After maturely reflecting upon the difficulties by which they were surrounded, the feeble government of the Spanish part sought protection from Hayti; and the Haytian President was formally solicited by them to grant his consent to the annexation of the Eastern part to the Republic of Hayti. The request was complied with, and the Eastern portion became a part and parcel of that Republic, as much so as Massachusetts now is of this Union. Thus it appears that the Dominicans entered the Haytian Government, voluntarily, if not gladly, but joyfully. Shortly after this, the French (with an overwhelming force in the harbor of Port au Prince) demanded an indemnity for the property sacrificed in the Revolution. The people of the country had 'supped full of horrors,' and Boyer, to prevent further bloodshed and destruction of property, agreed to the payment of 150,000,000 of francs; the independence of Hayti was then acknowledged by France and other European powers. A vigorous attempt was made to obtain a similar acknowledgement from the United States; but the advocates of slaveholders prevailed against it, and nothing was effected.

About three years since, Herard was elected President of the Island. This was the signal to the Spanish part for a separation from the legitimate Government, and they declared themselves independent of it. It does not appear that this movement was caused by the election of Herard, or from a conviction that his policy would be a bad one, for what his policy would be was not known. It cannot, however, be denied, that Mr. Boyer's later or his worst acts were consequent upon the rebel movement in the Spanish part; for it is maintained by many that Herard's impolitic course was the great cause of discontent. If it were so, it may be asked why Herard, and Boyer, and all others who have been in power, have been unable to induce the Dominicans to return to their allegiance?

About two years since, agents were despatched from St. Domingo to the United States to ask for some support. The application was coldly received by Mr. Tyler; but Mr. Calhoun, under the influence by which he was surrounded, was somewhat more remarkable. After the death of Mr. Upshur, the application was renewed, and the representative of the Spanish part found a kindred spirit in Mr. Calhoun, the secretary of state. The latter gentleman has attained the distinguished honor of sending a secret agent to a country with which we are on terms of peace, to ascertain whether the dissolution of an Union, constituted under such circumstances, and where the proportion to nine-tenths of its inhabitants, was an act which this Government ought to encourage, in order to give a small fraction of the population, to maintain their rights even in their own country, if indeed they were possessed of any right whatever. To be sure, we are told of the advantages to be derived by this country from the French part of the island, if we acknowledge her independence—but who believes that a fleet of French vessels, sent by a government in this movement? The commerce of our country in his long had little of its care—had it been otherwise, millions of dollars might have been saved in our trade by making the slight concession to the Haytians, which have been so often recommended by the administration of General Jackson. It is notorious that for the last twenty-four years, goods imported into Hayti in American vessels have been subject to and have actually paid an extra duty of ten per cent, beyond that charged by vessels of other nations. The interest of the country has been sacrificed to the real or fancied interests of our Southern brethren. 'Aristocratic England' could extend protection to the Spanish part of St. Domingo, encompass an immense trade, which naturally belonged to us—but 'Democratic America' for 'a peculiar institution,' to which the commerce of the country was made subservient. Does any one imagine the prospect of future business with eighty thousand Dominicans induced the secret mission? Why, an untrammeled trade with one million of Haytians, under a regular government, had not been deemed worthy of the slightest consideration. But we are told that the Haytians are cruel, blood-thirsty and barbarous—Christophe is held up as an evidence of the fact. It is true that the black chief was a great ruffian—so was Napoleon, in about the same way; the former, however, merely directed the avenue to his citadel with blood, to perpetuate his rule in his own country, whilst the latter waded through seas of slaughter to subjugate other nations. Napoleon was of course the most popular man, for it is a great and philanthropic truth that
'One murder makes a villain—
Millions a hero.'
The Haytians universally hold in utter detestation the memory of Christophe, whilst the refined French almost forget Napoleon in the remembrance of the past.

The successor of Christophe, as has been stated, was Boyer, the first President of the Island. It does seem to us to have required a degree of stupid anomaly, to speak of the Government of the Island. The truth is, that during his administration of twenty years, there was less taking of responsibility on the part of the Executive, fewer executions of criminals, less plundering of the treasury, and a more steady adherence to standard principles, than in any other country during the same period. Why, then, it may be asked, has not the island prospered in a higher degree? Why is not the French indemnity paid entirely? Let it be remembered, that the island was forced to pay millions to France, to meet its obligation to the French honorably. They did not repudiate as some states of the Union, the debt was contracted; but, since that period, the produce of Hayti has fallen off, it is said, one or two-thirds. Moreover, the losses, (both public and private,) by fires in the principal towns, have been immense. In Port au Prince, the late fires almost destroyed it, and completely destroyed the Cape, and if the whole island had been taxed to its utmost, it could not all have been avoided. The President might, perhaps, have avoided many of the evils brought upon the island, and preserved the finances, but he could not prevent the late fire.

On the score of indolence, the Haytians may be justly chargeable, but in no greater degree than the inhabitants of other tropical countries. If we look within the tropics, amongst the children of the sun, whether in Mexico, South America, or the East, and the Soolooan. It is very true that the capabilities of Hayti have not been developed, but if the resources of such countries are never fully developed except by foreign labor, why should we expect the Carolinians 'wring' from their swamps with their own hands?

There are, however, other, and more important attributes of the people, in the interior, (who have been represented as living on wild cattle,) which might safely be affirmed that the peasantry of the Island, (for the lower classes are peasantry) compare favorably with the cultivators of any country, for mildness, order, and quietness. They have not had the opportunities, however, for religious and moral teaching have been slender—circumstances beyond their control.

But our missionaries have gladened nearly every benighted spot,
'It is Greenland's icy mountains
To India's coral strand.'

But it is a melancholy fact that Hayti has been neglected by all. No less than seven missions at one time have been permitted to grope in comparative darkness. How far this neglect is to be attributed to the contemptuous tone of our Government towards them... we leave to those who are familiar with American missionaries.

If a missionary had been sent to Hayti, a disposition on the part of the United States to aid the Dominicans would lead to difficulty. Not only would such an act be wrong in itself, but on the miserable score of policy, it would provoke perversity and be dangerous in the extreme. It is well known that there has long existed a prejudice in the minds of the Haytians, and that the most liberal intention on the part of the United States would be lately been greeted with him, with the kindest expressions of good will. France will not allow us to interfere, and any attempt to do so, under an ill-timed, impertinent interference with another power, would subject us to a severe rebuke for our pains. A difference with the French, however, would be preferred to an alliance with the South, which would attach itself to the neck of a great portion of our citizens, to protect a very insignificant portion of its territory.
B. C. C.

records.full_text:
The New-York Express, edited by James Brooks, (formerly of Maine,) is one of the dirtiest, meanest and most villainous papers published in the nation. As a specimen of its villainous spirit, the following comments on the last letter published in the Liberator from the eloquent and gifted Douglass:—

"If this man Douglass had not run away from the South, the people there would tell him he would make a very good field hand, or 'he'd be worth a thousand dollars in here.' It is only in the free States, that this 'negro,' this 'nigger' Douglass, could create a stir among the abolitionists, as among any any people in the world. If Douglass had laid at home, in the position in which his Creator had placed him, he would have had the same privileges as any person that ever lived. But he was a king! The nobility of England—if the Lord Mayor of London divested himself of his robes of office, he was not equal to the white servant of his own miserable, poverty-stricken, ragged, starving country—sed de gustibus, &c. De gustibus non est disputandum. If Douglass will only travel among the 'peasantry' or the 'miner,' or the 'factory operative' among O'Connell's wretched tenants, whom the 'Time's' corresponds to, we think even the 'Express' itself will confess that the worst off slaves in this country are princes in comparison with them.

But there is, we imagine, something deeper in all this than the mere envy of the New-York Express of runaway negroes of America. 'Comparisons,' said Sage Dogberry, 'are odoriferous;' and this may be so; but it cannot be very pleasant for a representative to the Maryland refugee demonstrate rather the fact that his constituents have not so much a love for him as hate for the country and the institutions, which it is the special business of the fugitive to inspire them with. This glib-tongued scoundrel, (who is now in the U. S. Senate, to the shame and disgrace of Maryland, and a disgrace to the whole country,) is doing more to arouse the British people against this nation, than all the other causes combined. He is travelling through the length and breadth of Scotland, demagoguing through the cities and towns, vilifying his country, making himself a welcome guest with lords and ladies, and instilling his poison into their minds, that we have leagued with the United States for the perpetuation of slavery—that emissaries had been sent to Mexico for the purpose of creating divisions, and producing a revolution that will eventually result in the annexation of Mexico also—that efforts are now being made to purchase Cuba, and that persons have been sent to St. Domingo to array one party against another, to weaken their power, and that the South would never rest till that Republic is destroyed—

If the Tribune is pleased with the spectacle of the aristocracy of England embracing a runaway slave, he should be welcome to his own, & if we welcome the aristocracy of England to lend their aid abroad to the slavery of America ; for she forced the pest upon us, in spite of our will, and she herself sustains a state of society in which ten thousand times more suffering exists than that in which our slaves are in. Southern slavery is heaven compared with starving Ireland, or pale, haggard, wretched, sooty Birmingham. The 'liberty and equality' of the Southern master's slave is princely, compared with the degradation, powerlessness, and utter hopelessness of the Irish peasant, or the English workers in the mines and factories. Slavery is a terrible calamity, but it has no terrors of starvation, no frightful dread of the future, no unassuaged, unheeded, uncared-for death-bed—no parish prisons, no such awful scenes as Dickens describes, but hardly exaggerates. When England regards 'the rights of man,' she has a right to rebuke us, and not before."

Here we have accounts from St. Domingo, the city, to the 10th of February. The Dominicans were expecting the attack of the Haytiens, with good courage and preparations. There was a report current that Acaau had been playing again.

It was believed at St. Domingo that the U. S. Government had recognized the Dominican republic, and that a U. S. ship of war, with a consul on board, would soon arrive at St. Domingo.

The story prevailed, also, that a Spanish squadron from Cuba was coming to protect the Dominicans against the Haytiens.

records.headline: FROM HAYTI.
records.summary_en: The *New York Herald* reported that news reached Cape Haytien that the people of St. Mark's and Port-au-Prince, as well as the southern part of the island, had revolted against President Perriot and refused to march against the Spanish portion of the island. The populace chose General Rishere as the new President, who marched toward Port-au-Prince while it was believed President Perriot would resign. Additionally, a Spanish fleet that sailed from St. Domingo city to Cape Haytien had settled matters to its satisfaction and returned to St. Domingo city.
records.summary_es: El *New York Herald* notificó que llegaron noticias a Cabo Haitiano de que los habitantes de Saint-Marc y Puerto Príncipe, así como los de la banda meridional de la isla, se sublevaron contra el presidente Pierrot y rehusaron emprender marcha contra la demarcación española. El vecindario proclamó mandatario al general Riché, quien avanzó hacia Puerto Príncipe entre rumores fundados de la inminente renuncia de Pierrot. Asimismo, una escuadra española que zarpó de la ciudad de Santo Domingo con rumbo a Cabo Haitiano compuso las diferencias a su entera satisfacción y tornó a la capital dominicana.

records.headline: Affairs in Mexico and Texas.
records.summary_en: The general in chief of the Spanish naval forces in the Antilles requested that the Dominican Republic respect the Spanish and exempt them from a supposed blockade. The Dominican government replied that no such blockade had been decreed by them, clarifying that any blockade had been declared by the Haytiens, and that Dominican naval demonstrations were intended only to prevent Haytien depredations and protect commerce. Following these exchanges of amity, the Spanish commanders and officers were invited ashore the next day, where they were received with profuse hospitality and departed with feelings of the warmest friendship.
records.summary_es: El general en jefe de las fuerzas navales españolas en las Antillas solicitó a la República Dominicana que respetara a los españoles y los exonerara de un pretendido bloqueo. El gobierno dominicano replicó que jamás había dictado semejante medida, aclarando que cualquier bloqueo procedía exclusivamente de los haitianos y que sus evoluciones navales sólo procuraban contener las depredaciones de aquéllos y resguardar el tráfico mercantil. Tras estos testimonios de concordia, los comandantes y oficiales hispanos bajaron a tierra al día siguiente por invitación, siendo agasajados con esmerada hospitalidad y despidiéndose en un clima de la más cordial amistad.

records.full_text:
(From the New Orleans Bulletin, April 9.)

The news from the city of Mexico is to the 21st of March. It is of no importance. The only thing of interest is the arrival at the city of Mexico of a messenger from his excellency the general in chief of the Spanish naval forces in the Antilles, to reclaim and desire of the Dominican republic that the Spanish be respected, and also exempted from the blockade which had been, it was said, proclaimed by the Dominican government. In reply, the U. S. consul returned for answer, that no blockade whatever had been decreed by the Dominican government, as was supposed by the Spanish commander, and their excellencies the captain general of the Havana and the general in chief of the naval forces, were in error. The Dominican government, on the contrary, had opened all the ports of the republic to the commerce of all nations, and that the Spanish flag would be respected and protected as well as that of any other nation.

records.summary_en: The Liberator reprints an address to the colored people of the United States, dated Saint Domingo, July 10, 1847, from native Americans who had emigrated there in 1824, offering the emigration law passed by their House of Congress. The law invited strangers without distinction of color, paid passage at 14 dollars per head, and promised those coming as farmers fifty acres of land forever, farming implements and maintenance until they could support themselves, with exemption from military service for them and their offspring.
records.summary_es: The Liberator reproduce un llamamiento dirigido a la gente de color de los Estados Unidos, fechado en Santo Domingo el 10 de julio de 1847 y suscrito por estadounidenses de nacimiento que habían emigrado allí en 1824, que ofrecía la ley de emigración aprobada por su Cámara del Congreso. La ley invitaba a los extranjeros sin distinción de color, pagaba el pasaje a razón de 14 dólares por persona y prometía a quienes vinieran como agricultores cincuenta acres de tierra para siempre, aperos de labranza y manutención hasta que pudieran sostenerse, con exención del servicio militar para ellos y su descendencia.

records.full_text:
ADDRESS TO THE COLORED PEOPLE OF
THE U. S. OF NORTH AMERICA.

SAINT DOMINGO, July 10, 1847.
Dear Friends—We being native Americans who emigrated to this country in 1824, being now in body assembled, have resolved to offer to our brethren of the United States the law of emigration passed by our House of Congress, on the 5th inst. It invites all strangers here to participate in our glorious liberty, without distinction of color; and all who will come by this invitation, will have their passage paid at the rate of $14 per head; and those who will come with the avowed intention of becoming farmers will have, in addition to the payment of their passage, fifty acres of land, as a donation to them forever, together with the implements of husbandry, and a regular maintenance until they are able to maintain themselves; and they will be entirely exempt from military service, as also their offspring, in order that they may attend to the agricultural pursuits. We presume that this law can fully be depended on by all who may feel disposed to embrace its offers, as it is founded on necessity. As we have a very healthy climate, and perhaps one of the best soils in the world, with a generous population, all we stand in need of is American society—or in other words, tillers of the ground; in fact, by the aid of foreigners, this might be made a paradisiacal garden. We have the full right of the liberty of conscience. We have a Methodist church in the city of Port Plat; and in Samana, and one in this city, where we worship God according to the dictates of our consciences, without the least molestation. Our friends may depend on this information as being strictly true; and up to the present time we have a majority of colored population of more than two-thirds. We expect that many white people will accept this offer, as they seem generally more disposed for adventure than the colored. However, we hope that our friends will not let this fine opportunity pass, without embracing it.

There is a vessel engaged to bring out emigrants. She is consigned to the house of Messrs Amar & Co., New York. Persons interested will do well to call on the above gentlemen. Furthermore, should it become a general desire, any merchant who would choose to fit out a vessel, for the purpose of bringing out emigrants, will be sure to receive $14 a head, including all expenses, for as many as they will land here. If any merchant should like to have a guaranty, they could, by writing to our President on the subject. His name is ‘Pedro Santana,’ President of the Dominican Republic. It will not be as inconvenient to new comers hereafter as it was with us. We can give them all the necessary information how to conduct themselves in this country.

We remain, dear brethren, yours.
Signed in behalf of the meeting,
REV. JAMES FALLS, Chairman.
ELIJAH B. GROSS, Secretary.

records.summary_en: *The Liberator* reported that the deck of the vessel *Esturra* carried destitute refugees—some formerly wealthy—who had fled following a political confrontation in Port-au-Prince. According to the account, a deputation of influential men questioned President Soulouque regarding the reigning constitution, and upon being told the 1816 constitution was in effect, Senator Celigne Ardoin asserted that Soulouque was not president. When immediate orders were given for his arrest, Ardoin drew a pistol and fired at Soulouque, though the shot missed its mark.

Al dictarse su inmediata detención, Ardouin extrajo una pistola y descerrajó un tiro contra Soulouque, sin acertar en el blanco.

ject of my first letter. But on arriving and making various inquiries, relative thereto, and after carefully looking over the state of the country, I was thoroughly satisfied of the perfectly tranquilized state of this city and its inhabitants, which had been represented to me as being in a state of siege. A very intelligent merchant, and one who had a considerable stake in the issue of events, said to me, the plot did not give them four-and-twenty hours uneasiness.

The principal facts concerning it are briefly the following, which I have gathered on the spot, and from authentic sources. On the 21 of December last, the President, receiving information through several individuals, that a conspiracy was on foot in this city to throw off the Haitian yoke. He immediately summoned a cabinet council of the principal officers of state, to take measures to secure the city and put it in a state of defence; and measures were forthwith taken to disarm the troops and the citizens who volunteered with them, and a number of the principal citizens were arrested at the command of the military authorities.

On the morning of the 22d, on the reassembly of the cabinet, the officer in command of the garrison, the officer charged with making the inquiries, relative thereto, reported that no plot existed, as the result of them thus far, the discoveries made, showed that no plot existed. He then present in the council, and who had officially issued or countersigned the order for these very measures, and measures were forthwith taken which he had called for, was at the head of the conspiracy. He was immediately arrested, with several others, and conveyed away to prison. A brother of his, who was also arrested, and four or five several others, to the number of about nine, were brought to trial before a military commission, composed of members of congress, judges of the court, officers of the army, and private citizens; and four of the number, including the two brothers, were convicted of the crime of high treason, and condemned to death. They were accordingly executed on the morning of the 23d instant. Several of the others were subsequently banished the country.

Such was the end of the affair. The firmness, energy, and decision with which the government acted on the occasion, at their first discovery, and meeting the emergency, inspired all, I believe, and with good reason, with a thorough conviction of its ability to maintain its authority. Towards evening the consternation was great and universal. Every preparation had been made to resist an attack, which, in such cases, rumor, with its thousand surmises, had magnified into a formidable one. The foreign traders, merchants, all armed to sustain the government, and preserve their property from the plunder with which they were threatened. But the lapse of a very few hours brought back order and tranquility; and though business was somewhat paralyzed by the event, it soon recovered its former tone as far as these had disturbed it.

The effect of the plot, however, will still continue to be felt, and with for some time to come. Besides the cost of the military force, which had mostly been sent to the city, the government paper fell about fifty per cent. in value, causing a necessity, for apart for the purpose of encouraging and effecting foreign immigration, the withdrawal of much of the rural population--sparse and scanty at best--from their agricultural avocations, to serve as additions to the army, caused a necessity for the interruption to that branch of domestic industry, and a consequent diminution in the corresponding productions, together with a proportionate advance in the price of the necessaries of subsistence; a calamity, of course, to a country that imports a very large proportion of these necessaries.

As regards the state of the currency--which after all is the pulse of the political system--so far as affected by these disturbances, I will briefly refer to it. During the early part of the first two months of my absence, which included that in which the affair took place, the currency depreciated only about as much as it had done during the three preceding months, or about five per cent; and stayed there, and during the last two or three months has recovered its former position.

Thus much, by way of anticipation. The history, political organization, the condition and prospects of the Dominican Republic, will form the subject of the remainder of this letter, and of the succeeding ones.

For about a century and a half after the first discovery of Spanish colony, Columbus had founded the first settlement in the island, until the buccaneers--that hybrid race of adventurers, who have so often been written, and written about, but whom so little is correctly known--commenced their incursions into the north and west portions of the island in quest of the cattle which ran wild in immense herds over its rich plains; and finally formed settlements at the western end.

As these adventurers were mostly French, that nation began to regard them as a colony of her own; and in the treaty of Ryswick, she obtained from Spain, the cession of that portion of the island, comprising nearly one-third of its whole extent. The two colonies came thus to be posssessors, and at long intervals, and remained so separate and distinct, the one a dependence of Spain, the other of France, until 1795, which, so at the period of the memorable revolt of the blacks, and massacre of the whites, in the French part, in 1791. At that period, the latter colony had attained a high degree of prosperity, while the Spanish colony, of which this city was the capital, which had been languishing for nearly two centuries under a very partial and inefficient system of practiced agriculture. Slavery existed in this as well as in the French part of the island; but the condition of the slaves, towards the end of the present century, were there still existing in Spanish colony, was far different from the severe, forced labor, which in the other part produced those immense crops of sugar, coffee, and indigo, for the revolt which in the other part resulted in the independence of the black population, and white race, did not extend to this portion, or, at least, to any such extent or degree as to affect the relative position of the different races.

Meanwhile the year 1795, France, which was still at war with Spain, obtained by treaty the cession of the Spanish colony, on the island, by maintaining a desperate struggle to retain possession of her own colony in the island, obtained by cession from Spain the nominal possession of Spanish colony also. But, on the final triumph of the blacks in the former, and the establishment there of the Haitian governments (of which there were at first two), the Spanish population, who had ever preserved, as they still do, their separate position and ancient social and political institutions against the claims and attempts of the black governments of the west. With the loss of her own colony, France lost all foothold on the island thenceforward, with the exception of one or two years' occupation of this city in the early part of this century.

Here he remained until the winter of 1843-4, when the Spanish portion of the inhabitants of this city, who had often sought in vain for an opportunity to throw off the Haitian yoke, suddenly found a favorable one, on occasion of the main body of the Haitian troops being withdrawn for some domestic purpose to the other end of the island, only a few hundred being left in the fort to guard and hold the city. This juncture gert on the unsuspicious garrison, besieged it within the fort, after gaining possession of the city and which they compelled it to capitulate, allowing it to return home.

From this period, the existence of the republic, or, to speak more accurately, its style and duties were assumed by the central junta, or committee, of this city, consisting of its president, vice, president, and eight members, which had organized and nurtured the revolutionary movement. On the 16th of January, 1844, this body published a manifesto setting forth the grievances and oppressions they had suffered under the Haitian rule, they expressed their determination to submit to them no longer, incline their enemies to a just and reasonable settlement of the difficulty, but to avoid the effusion of blood and the horrors of a calamitous war, expressing their readiness to defend their rights, which, if begun, shall, if the case calls for it, be several of the succeeding ones.

On the 9th of March following, the same executive body, in an address to the inhabitants, accompanied with a respectful and dignified address, to the President of the republic of Haiti. In this address, they speak as the organs of the "people of the Spanish part of the island," and reiterate the sentiments of devotion to the existing mating that they thus notify him of their determination, so far as the Dominican people are concerned, that he may act as the occasion may seem to require. On the 15th of March, the junta, in the month, published an address to the resident foreigners, assuring them of their intention of respecting the inviolability of their persons and property, and assuring them of protection under the new government. These guarantees have never, I believe, been violated in the cast of their persons or legitimate rights.

In April, 1844, the Haitian government, disposed to relinquish their former possession without a struggle, sent a force of 15,000 to 20,000 men, an army to the frontier, where it found the Dominicans prepared for them, and eager to defend their presents to the foreign press. Towards the middle On the 11th of the month of March, in which the Dominicans were successful, and forced them to retreat against great numerical odds. The issue of these battles was so far satisfactory to them, and though the war still nominally continues, and has since that time, keeping a considerable force ment along the frontier, as a measure of security, very little fighting has occurred.

The independence, or separation, as it is more properly termed, took place on the 27th of February, 1844; and the name assumed by the new state was that of the Dominican Republic.

Subsequently to the victories which secured the quiet possession of the country, and after order had had been commanded on the frontier, and under whom the government had been conducted, the inhabitants, without distinction of color, had triumphed over their oppressors, sending out of a faction opposed to the Provisional government re-established the authority of the Republic.

The duty of drafting a constitution for the new state, was committed to a convention, which when completed, was published with great solemnity, and ceremony on the 24th of November, 1844.

Having thus brought down the history of the domination of Haitians, the people of the old Spanish part of St. Domingo, have asserted their independence, and sought to assume a place among nations. And as the political position of this island will, most assuredly, some day, and that, probably, not very distant, awaken the attention of our people and government, I shall, besides, in my next, give an outline of the Constitution, and of some of the organic laws enacted to carry out its provisions.

COUPEUR.

records.summary_en: *The New York Herald* detailed provisions of the Dominican constitution regarding foreigners, citizenship, and civil rights. Foreigners of non-hostile nations who practiced useful industries were granted civil rights and could gain residency, with requirements reduced for those marrying Dominican citizens or establishing agricultural estates worth at least $12,000. It also affirmed that Dominicans were born free and equal, abolished slavery forever, protected private property from confiscation, and guaranteed due process and the inviolability of citizens' homes.
