records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
Decree for Organizing the Civic Guard—Requisitions on Foreigners to Enroll themselves therein—Subsequent Modification of it in Regard to this Class of Residents—The Question of the Lawfulness of such a Requisition, under the Law of Nations, Briefly Considered—Steps taken to Obtain the Recognition of the Republic—A Ground of Difficulty in this Matter Stated.

A measure of some interest to foreigners residing here—and to foreign states, also, so far as their interests are concerned—and on which action has just now begun to be taken, seems to demand some notice at the hand of your correspondent, if from no other American quarter.

Acting under the general authority conferred upon him by the article of the constitution mentioned in my last letter, the President of this Republic promulgated on the 22d of February last, a decree for the organization, throughout all the provinces, of the civic guard, or militia, of the State. This decree, in substance, made it obligatory on all male persons who at the sound of the tocsin of alarm, should be found within the limits of any town or place, to take arms, shall be considered as forming part of the guard, and as subject to perform duty, as the law or circumstances shall require. It further declared that foreigners, long established in the country, shall also form part of the civic guard, and, on the same footing and under the same penalties as the citizens, are allowed to choose in what company they will enroll themselves, and shall be furnished at their own expense.

It is decreed that the civic guard shall appear under arms to pass review once every three months—namely on the third Sunday of each quarter, in January, April, July, and October respectively. And, on all other occasions of alarm or duty, which includes the obligatory liability to march to the frontier, or another cantonment, in case of threatened invasion; and, in short, to serve in any manner the public service may require.

After entering into some details, which are unimportant to a foreign reader, the decree proceeds to prescribe specific penalties for non-compliance with its provisions. Non-commissioned officers and privates of the guard who shall not appear at the prescribed review, are subjected to six days' imprisonment; non-commissioned officers and privates of the line to a fine of two dollars, and a very small pecuniary fine; and, for the second offence, to double these penalties, or being incorporated into the troops of the line. No distinction is made between foreign residents and citizens; but all are subjected to the same rule.

The promulgation of this decree caused great excitement among the foreign residents, who are almost exclusively of European origin; and the national representatives of France and Spain, the only European ones here, and under whose protection most of the foreign residents are placed, immediately protested against its provisions as inapplicable to them, and instructing their countrymen not to comply with the mandate. The United States have no representative here, but the consul at Puerto Plata, on the north side of the island, took part in the protest, and sent a copy to the U. S. deputy here, at the capital, for a list of whatever American citizens were resident here, to enable him to protest to the government of this Republic against its application to them, in case such an intention on the part of the authorities to enforce it against citizens of the United States, should be manifested.

The executive, standard of these protests, suspended this decree against foreign residents, made by the 24th of March last, and the decision of the President to modify its terms in reference to this class of foreigners, which resulted in a supplemental decree, dated the 29th of March. In this latter, he states that the same penalties are to be applied to foreigners who are required to enroll themselves in the civic guard as upon national citizens—inasmuch as by not being in the enjoyment of political rights, (which belong only to citizens) the former cannot be made to constitute part of the militia of the country. On the contrary, the penalty against them will be, for the first and second delinquencies, arrest and imprisonment in the Commissariat—and the small prescribed fines; and for the third delinquency, to pay a fine, which is to be double the former, and to lose their patents, that is, licence to trade, &c., and of the right to obtain one again for the space of two years. The foreigners are further exempted from all duty, except that of defending by themselves, which shall constitute part of a detachment or guard, their own residences, or not to march to the frontier, or other cantonment, or to serve in any case except on the occasion of invasion—or calling forth and marching—of the civic guard. Inside of the precincts of their residences only, to take arms in the place of their residence, and under the command of an officer of the government for the purpose of protecting their own property, and that of the place, where their language allows it with equal propriety to be stationed, though the word country is that used by the public here, is in accordance with the spirit and intention of the law, for the protection of property. But whenever any of this company become so required, they are to be subject to the same penalties of the civic guard.

These modifications, so far from satisfying the spirit of the original decree, in connection with that of the original law, and the treaty stipulated mandatory one, for the sake of preserving the historical sequence of these proceedings, to show the course of things here, and not for the purpose of casting blame on the president of this republic, between which, though a flagrant contravention of personal rights of foreigners, under the law of nations, was yet essentially modified on protest being made against it. He tried to do full justice to foreigners, and while preserving the spirit of the decree, having all the binding force of the law, made such modifications as placed all on the same ground.

It is a principle of well settled, undisputed jurisprudence, that what is called the private law of nations, that no state has the right of calling on foreigners, who have not acquired the rights and privileges of citizens, to march to its frontiers, or to perform the same obedience that natives do to the general sovereign power of the state; but foreigners are exempt from all militia duty, or any public service whatever; and that in all cases of public emergency or commotion—intestine or from without—they are only liable to be called on as a guard, in this character, to place themselves under the command of their respective consuls, or of their late or embassy, as the case may be. The decree of the President of Santo Domingo, as modified, this government has the right to say, that no foreigner residing within its territory shall be allowed to carry on trade or follow any occupation, who refuses to enroll himself in the militia. This is an act of sovereignty which, so far as I am aware, has never been brought in question, though its exercise is certainly contrary to the spirit, as well as the usages, of modern times. But to subject foreigners to penalties, which, though pecuniary and otherwise small, necessarily carries with it as a sanction the right to enforce them, by arrest, imprisonment, or the seizure and confiscation of property, is to assume and exercise over a foreigner by the State, the legality of which is altogether denied by the law of nations. The United States, right, under the law of nations, it I am right in my construction of it, to complain of this decree, though by no means to the same objectionable extent as under the first. The republic of Hayti seems to have acquiesced in the terms of the supplementary decree, and this morning there were eight or ten Haytians enrolled in a guard for the purpose of organizing their company by electing their officers. The protest of the French correspondent, Mr. Herald, of course looked at it in a very different light; and while it was signed by any of his legitimate subjects, whose number, at Puerto Plata, and in all parts of the republic, is sufficient to form a tribe. If, instead of the form of a protestation, the communication of that power upon the foreigners had been in the form of an instruction, to be followed by a manifestation of spirit, our venerable and beloved uncle would have found himself in a very different situation than by those of "his own flesh and blood." My opinion is, that if France had chosen to act with that worthy gentleman's male representatives, this republic would have been instantly driven into a thing which cannot be rightfully required of it, by the refusal to yield to any reasonable request or soberness. It is not by a parade of fleet, or of troops, that small powers are brought to their senses, but by acts that show that if they do not listen to reason, they will be made to feel the weight of power.

The subject of the recognition of this republic, to which I have given some attention, as I have been given to understand, as before stated, no official application for the recognition of this republic has yet been made here in behalf of the United States' government. A circumstance occurred, not long since, connected with this simple statement of the fact, that this republic was about to send an embassy, and its attendant circumstances in full, should occur to make it worthy of a brief notice.

The truth is, the United States ought to be represented here, at least by a consul, or rather by an agent appointed directly by the department of state, with a small salary, to act as commercial agent, and not by a deputy of the one as appointed and resident at Puerto Plata, which port, for all practical purposes, is farther removed from the capital than is Castine, in the State of Maine, from Corpus Christi, Texas. Nor are the facilities of communication or intelligence between these two points of Puerto Plata and Puerto Capital as great as those, for all practical purposes, between this and the port of New York. looked to by the United States government than that which this republic has had to offer from its own, or as it has had for several years. Several let U. S. President appoint such a commissioner or agent; let him instruct her commander to enquire after resident American citizens, and perform every service where American citizens are denied any rights or exemptions which the law and usage of nations guarantee to the foreign residents of a country. Such a step, with such instructions faithfully carried out—as they certainly would be, if committed to any officer of the American navy—would have a most beneficial effect, and, even if its visit, so far from creating ill feeling, the writer knows would be received with open arms, while it would show that the American government is jealous of the rights of its citizens, wherever situated, and visited to its citizens the code of nations, the republic itself would feel that it had no longer reason to be feared, the Spanish States of the new world had, by a single act, stepped into the light of day.

This republic, now—since the 27th of February last—in the 5th year of its existence, has not yet been recognized by any power. Soon after the establishment of the present government, a commission was sent to Washington for the purpose of obtaining its recognition by the United States. It did not, however, succeed in reaching the object of its mission.

Since that time this government has sent commissioners to Europe, to endeavor to obtain the recognition of the new republic by the powers of Spain, France, and Great Britain. The aim has been to obtain a joint or simultaneous recognition of these three powers. This is regarded as a measure of policy, and as being essentially necessary to obtaining that of the other two, on account of the old Spanish title, to the territory of the republic—a title which has been so long and so frequently over-ridden without protestation, by supervening ones, as to be now buried, one would suppose, almost beyond the power or reach of resurrectionary resuscitation. I have said, without protestation. That is not altogether correct for the whole of the above period, as will appear by the following historical anecdote, which I have from good authority, and repeat, partly to preserve a curious piece of history, and partly as a record existing, on this side of the ocean at least, of a piece of history nowhere else, I believe, to be met with. Soon after the arrival of Boyer at Port au Prince, and partly to illustrate the political condition of Santo Domingo, at that period, or in or about the year 1827, the King of Spain sent a commissioner, named Don Jose Maria de Caminero, to formally demand of President Boyer the surrender and restoration of the Spanish part of the island, at that time constituting, as has been seen, a part of the Republic of Hayti. Boyer, who made an interview with head for that purpose, after listening to the demand of Caminero for the possession of it, at the solicitation of its inhabitants, for a long series of years, put to Caminero the question back to them, whether they would remove to Spain, or become citizens of the Haytian republic, or return under the dominion of Hayti; and on Caminero replying, that was not their popular voice, in favor of the latter course, which was probably true, he added, that no decided offence could be taken at so seemingly fair an outcome of the question, as Caminero, as is well known as well as President Boyer did, what would be the result of a vote of the inhabitants upon this method of decision; for a large majority of the inhabitants of Santo Domingo were then of African origin, and those who sympathy with them from being free of color; while a very small proportion of these would, of course, have an equal voice with the rest, though of a different political disposition, which, to the emancipated portion of them, would be to forfeit their freedom of political existence, or return to servitude under Spanish masters. Caminero took his passports, took his leave, and the demand was prosecuted no further.

The first commission sent to Washington, I learn, was received by the government from their commissioner, or by the secretary of state, through a letter sent from Madrid, in which they express the intention of the Spanish government of entertaining the recognition of the republic. It had, in fact, been solicited by the Dominican agent, and by the Spanish minister; but his displacement from office, and the events in Spain, which have rapidly followed each other, of a similar kind, have put an end to, and prevented the termination of the negotiation.

My own impression is, and I know it to be the government of the United States, that a question for recognition must be determined, in their wisdom, to determine for themselves. I do not feel authorized, for reasons set forth in my last, to state what the opinion of so humble an individual as myself may be on the subject; I have thus far contented myself with mainly stating facts, and circumstances of various kinds, leaving those who read my communications, so far as I have attempted to draw their own conclusions on this as on other points. Here, at least, is my own impression, that whatever question, I shall stop for the present. Hereafter, if circumstances permit, and the subject, as it well may, be on the point in consideration, superinduced by any state of things sufficiently favorable and tolerably well improved opportunity for further consideration, I trust I will have enabled me to bring together.

The newspaper noted this action is motivated by principles of humanity and the general interests of commerce to help consolidate existing institutions under General Monagas. Additionally, the publication offered commentary praising the United States for the cheerful submission of the minority to their defeat.

El periódico remarcó que dicha determinación obedecía a razones de humanidad y a los intereses globales del comercio para afianzar la institucionalidad vigente bajo el general Monagas. Asimismo, la hoja vertió elogios hacia Estados Unidos enalteciendo el digno acatamiento de las minorías tras sus derrotas en los comicios.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
Intelligence from Venezuela. — We have before us files of the paper El Patriota, of the 11th November, published in Caraccas. This, we believe, is the latest intelligence received from this republic, and we regret to say that its contents do not throw any light on the state of affairs in this country. Since the arrival of the last news from Maracaibo (the seat of war) for the last four months, there have been no satisfactory accounts, and the various statements published have been so tinged with the partisan feelings of the writers, that we are absolutely in the dark as to what is going on. We do not know whether it is true that Monagas' fleet or Paez's troops are about to do something or go somewhere; but we have never heard of their doing anything of any importance, except cruise about and brag against one another, much after the fashion of that famous king of ancient story, who,
'With ten thousand men,
Went up the hill and then — came down again;'
— meantime keeping Venezuela in uproar, destroying her commerce, and paralyzing all the resources of the country, which, at the commencement of these movements, were just beginning to be developed. The only positive item which we notice for the first time, is one which indicates that the British government is inclined to interfere in the matter. The vast commercial interests which British subjects have in Venezuela, have probably induced their government to take the step which is mentioned in the following notice, which we translate literally from the Patriota: —
'We have been informed, in a most positive manner, that the British Minister of Foreign Affairs, Lord Palmerston, has given the British ministers in Holland, Denmark, New Granada, St. Domingo, and Haiti, special instructions to inform the respective governments to which they are accredited, that H. B. M. government, in view of the difficulties which exist, and which are so contrary to the general interests of commerce, will not countenance the existing government of Venezuela, but, on the contrary, by following the existing institutions of the country, they may be consolidated and general order and peace be re-established.'
It is to be hoped that this will put a stop to the fitting out of expeditions, on either side, at neutral ports. If either of the contending parties have the interests of their country really at heart, and personal ambition has no place in their hearts or actions, surely in this enlightened age, something might be done to settle differences. The trouble in the republics seems to be that the minority will not submit. Let them take a lesson from the United States in that particular. The cheerful submission of the minority to their defeat is one of the most striking features in the character of the masses in the United States.

records.full_text:
Late from St. Domingo.
The schooner Mary and Elizabeth arrived here yesterday afternoon from Mariagone, St. Domingo, which place she left the 7th instant. Capt. Smith informs us that President Soulouque had, after a severe battle, taken from the Dominicans the towns of Las Matas and St. John, in which a great many of the Dominicans were killed and taken prisoners. Many of them escaped, abandoning five large pieces of artillery and a 6-pounder.

The above attack took place on the morning of the 18th March. Gens. Bobo, Vincent and Michel were left in possession of the captured towns, and the President with his troops left on the 19th for Port au Prince.

Three hundred troops from Jeremie passed through Mariagone on the 2d inst., on their way to Port au Prince to join the President. Men were gathering from all directions to join the President, who would shortly make another attack on the Dominicans.—N. Y. Tribune.

records.headline: FROM HAYTI AND ST. DOMINGO.
records.summary_en: Based on the provided newspaper excerpt, the war between the Haytiens and the Dominicans intensified, leading the city of St. Domingo to be placed under martial law around April 22 while its president led men out to meet Haytien President Soulouque's advancing forces. Following a disastrous defeat for the Dominicans on March 18—where they lost many men and artillery, and the towns of Las Matas and St. John fell—Haytien forces continued to grow as a decisive battle was soon expected in their favor. Additionally, a Dominican flotilla of five war vessels carrying 500 troops departed for Azua, and the U.S. sloop-of-war *Albany* arrived in St. Domingo on the 10th before departing for Aux Cayes on the 13th.

Tras el descalabro dominicano del 18 de marzo —donde padecieron considerables pérdidas humanas y de artillería, cayendo las villas de Las Matas y San Juan—, los contingentes haitianos continuaban reforzándose en vísperas de un combate decisivo favorable a sus armas. Se añadía que una flotilla dominicana de cinco naves artilladas con quinientos soldados zarpó para Azua, mientras la balandra de guerra estadounidense *Albany* arribó a Santo Domingo el día 10 para continuar viaje hacia Aux Cayes el 13.

records.full_text:
FROM HAYTI AND ST. DOMINGO.—The Boston Traveller of the 28th ult. notices the arrival of the Mary Chilton, from Hayti. The accounts by the Chilton are up to the 29th of March; and her commander, Capt. Skirvan, states that Soulouque's army was at least 15,000 strong, and that he had taken measures to prevent the cowardice of his soldiers by ordering those who exhibited any signs of wavering to be instantly shot down. Some think that he will enter St. Domingo without the firing of a gun; others that a bloody battle will ensue. Capt. Balcom gives some curious statements in regard to the mortality of the new regiments, &c. He says that the government stores are opened twice a week, when the canaille is called in for their coffee, which should be, according to the law, equally divided. Many, however, in the rush die—as, in one case mentioned, one man got 15,000 pounds, another 2000, and a third 4000. The Haytien officers are, evidently, not averse to a bribe.
The New York Herald gives the news brought by the Sarah Jane and the Mary and Elizabeth, whose arrival is mentioned by our correspondent "Indicator." The Herald says:
'There were two arrivals at this port, yesterday, from the island of Hayti: the brig Sarah Jane, Capt. Washburn, with dates from the city of St. Domingo to the 29th of March; and the schooner Mary and Elizabeth, Capt. Smith, from Maragone, whence she sailed on the 7th of April. We are indebted to Captains Smith and Washburn for papers, and for verbal information in regard to the affairs of the island. It seems that the war between the Haytiens and the Dominicans has commenced right earnestly. The city of St. Domingo was placed under martial law, about the 22d ult., and all the men of the city who were capable of bearing arms were mustered and marched out, under their President, to meet the Haytien President Soulouque, who, with his black army, was supposed to be advancing towards the city. A battle took place on the 18th of March, which resulted disastrously to the Dominicans, they having lost 42 men killed, a great number wounded, and prisoners, and several pieces of artillery—the towns of San Juan and St. John falling into the hands of the Haytiens. The force of President Soulouque was constantly increasing; a body of 700, from Jacmel, passed through Maragone on the 2d inst., on their way to Port-au-Prince and head-quarters, while others were gathering from all quarters. A decisive battle was expected to take place soon; and the chances of success appear to be in favor of the Haytiens. A flotilla, consisting of five war-vessels, with 500 troops on board, recently left St. Domingo for Azua, where it was thought a severe battle would be fought.... The U. S. sloop-of-war Albany arrived at St. Domingo on the 10th, and left for Aux Cayes on the 13th; officers and crew all well. The U. S. sloop-of-war Germantown was daily expected at St. Domingo.'

records.headline: LATER FROM ST. DOMINGO.
records.summary_en: *The Daily Crescent* reported via arrivals from the brig *Stephen G. Ross* that Haitian President Soulouque was advancing within 16 miles of Santo Domingo City with an army of 30,000 troops. Residents were fleeing the anticipated attack, with British vessels crowded with refugees and valuables deposited with American and British consuls for safekeeping. The city was largely deserted by women and children, and it was feared that Soulouque had already captured it with significant bloodshed.
records.summary_es: *The Daily Crescent* comunicó, con base en despachos traídos por el bergantín *Stephen G. Ross*, que el presidente haitiano Soulouque marchaba a unas dieciséis millas de la ciudad de Santo Domingo con un ejército de treinta mil hombres. El vecindario huía ante el asalto inminente, abarrotándose las embarcaciones británicas de prófugos y confiándose caudales a la custodia de los cónsules norteamericano y británico. La población se hallaba desamparada en gran parte por mujeres y niños, temiéndose que Soulouque hubiese doblegado ya la plaza con profusión de sangre.

records.summary_en: The *Daily National Intelligencer* reported that the Haitian army under President Soulouque was completely routed in the Dominican Republic, leaving behind numerous dead, artillery, munitions, and captured battle flags. Dominican forces recaptured Azua on April 21, with General Santana advancing across the border in aggressive pursuit. The report also reprinted a proclamation from Soulouque urging the eastern inhabitants to submit to the Haitian republic.

Las fuerzas dominicanas recuperaron Azua el 21 de abril, avanzando el general Santana a través de la frontera en decidida persecución. La reseña reprodujo asimismo una proclama de Soulouque exhortando a los habitantes del Este a someterse a la república de Haití.

Los dominicanos los atacaron entonces, matando a muchos y tomando muchos prisioneros; Soulouque escapó por poco de ser capturado, y su ejército fue puesto en fuga el día 21.

records.summary_en: According to the *Arkansas State Gazette* reporting on information from the *Evening Post*, Dominican General Santa Anna defeated Haitian President Soulouque and his forces in a severe contest at the town of Azera, driving the Haitians completely out of Dominican territory. The report noted that the retreating Haitians burned Azera and suffered the loss of 500 troops and two principal generals, Geffrad and Paul Jean Jacque. records.full_text:
By Captain McIntyre, of the schooner Enterprise, arrived on Monday night, in eleven days, from Cape Haytien, we have been furnished with the following items of news:—

The Emperor of the Republic of Hayti had issued an edict, to take effect on the 5th instant, that no foreign merchant should be permitted to do any business under $1800, Spanish, per year, in place of $600, as heretofore; or any foreign clerk, unless he paid $1000. No vessel will allowed to take more than five tons of wood per ton her cargo at the port. The export duty on coffee and logwood was 150 Haytien per cent, or 1 1-2 per cent instead of 50, as heretofore; and in the same ratio on all articles. He had fixed a price on all goods imported and exported. He was adding 50 more St. Domingo troops to those already in the island. Business was very dull.

We learn from Capt. McIntyre, that schooners Jane and Eliza, which arrived yesterday week from Port au Prince, confirm the late news of the total defeat of Soulouque; the news had just reached Port au Prince when the schooner left.

A meeting was about to take place, to take into consideration the better mode of defending the country against the Haytians. Logwood, American provisions are getting scarce. The Emperor of Hayti was expected on the 20th, destination supposed to be for Jacmel.

Orders had been given that the Emperor was to march on St. Domingo on the 20th, with the whole army, for the Spanish part of the island.

The United States frigate St. Lawrence was at St. Thomas waiting orders. The British brig of war Persian, was at Jacmel on the 24th, looking after British property.

PROCLAMATION.
Buenaventura Baez, President of the Dominican Republic, to the Haytians.
HAYTIENS!—The fleet belonging to the Republic of Dominica addresses you, in the name of his fellow-citizens, and in the solemn conduct of an act of war, which for nearly six years ago that we separated from you, and built up a separate government, you have constantly made war against us, pretending to force us again to be united to one. We may yet live as good neighbors, though two distinct nations. We have invited you to do this, by proposing a peace, which is necessary to us, as well as to you; but, up to this time, you have rather preferred to force you to leave your country to go into exile, or to be slaughtered, as so many of you as were unwilling. Recollect your suffering in the march through our desert, and the terrible disaster at Ocoa; re-enter into yourselves, for what can you achieve in a war where you have gained no glory, and where you have only spent your resources? We have always contented ourselves with defending ourselves against aggression; this is the first time that we have taken the offensive to make war upon you, and to show you that we can hurt you in your own homes. We make war upon you on your own soil—on your properties—on your persons; without a fleet, without any defence, offering yourselves an easy prey to flames and pillage. Our cities are going to disappear, and their inhabitants to be driven into the woods.
Haytiens! Our fleet, well armed, well equipped, well commanded, having numerous troops on board, has set sail to cruise on your coast and intercept your shipping. Watch, then, night and day, on the North, on the West, on the South. Drive your wives and children into the morasses, abandon your towns to the power of the flames and the rain—and then when you go into the woods to perish of hunger and misery, you may accuse your leaders, whose insane policy has brought all these sufferings already upon you. You suffer already, dreadfully, by the war; you have lost your resources, the country is in ruins through the tyranny you labor under. See, then, whether you will suffer this to continue, or whether you will not have peace; we wish to live in peace and happiness, each in his own territory, each under his own laws, under the government of his own choice; but if your rulers will not have it so, Well, then, be it so! Let all the blood that will be spilt fall upon those who cause it—not upon us, who will not force them to better measures.
By the President, BUENAVENTURA BAEZ.
Minister of War, J. E. AYBAR.
St. Domingo, Oct. 19, 1849.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
HAYTIENS!—The new President of the republic of Dominica addresses you, in the name of his fellow-citizens, and in the common interest of all. It is now nearly six years ago that we separated from you, and declared ourselves independent; and this separation, in spite of false assurances to the contrary, is destined to be an eternal one. We may yet live as good neighbors, though under different banners. We have treated you as brothers, proposing a peace, which is necessary to all our interests; but those who rule over you have always preferred a state of war; they have armed you against us, and doomed you to be shot, as many of you as were willing. You know what you suffered in the last campaign, which our brave Santana terminated so gloriously, and what is more, what confidence you have in men who could not deliver your territory. We have never attacked your independence; you can have no doubt of our feelings towards you; we have given you too many proofs of our moderation. But patience becomes sometimes exhaustion; and since you would not have peace, you, then, in your turn, support all the sufferings of war—a war that we will carry into your territory, because it is there only that we can make you feel our advantages and your weakness. We can hurt you without sacrificing our men or exhausting our riches. While we have only three cities on our coast, (and within sight of a fleet of thirty vessels, all well fortified and secure from attack,) your shores are covered with defenceless villages, small habitations, towns and cities, built of wood, without any defence, offering themselves an easy prey to flames and pillage. Your cities are going to disappear, and your mountains to be filled with the woods. Haytiens! Our fleet, well-armed, well-victualled, well-commanded, having numerous troops on board, has set sail to pillage your coast and intercept your shipping. Watch, then, night and day. Watch on the north, on the west, and on the south. Drive your wives and children into the morasses; abandon your fields to keep guard on the tops of the rocks—your guns in your hands in the wind and the rain—and then when you go home you will find your houses burnt down. You know all these sufferings already. You suffer them still, and you will continue to suffer them, really, dreadfully, by this war. To it you owe the misery with which you are overwhelmed, and you will suffer if you continue this war. Haytiens! We offer you peace; we offer you to live as neighbors, each in his own territory, making a mutual exchange of our commerce. If you wish for peace, you have it; if you will not have it, so be it. Let all the burden of the war rest on those, and those only, who will not force them to better measures.
By the President:
BUENAVENTURA BAEZ.
Minister of War, J. E. AYBAR.
ST. DOMINGO, November 16, 1849.

records.full_text:
ST. DOMINGO.—Capt. Ogler, of the schooner Cabot, from the city of St: Domingo, the capital of the Dominican republic, April 14th, reports affairs there tranquil. Apprehension was entertained of further invasion from the blacks of the West End, which keeps the Dominicans in a constant attitude of defence and uncertainty, preventing productive labor, and destroying commerce.

The United States steamer Vixen, Lieutenant Commanding Ward, arrived at the city of St. Domingo on the 28th of March—all well. The Vixen was to sail for Washington in a few days with the United States chargé, Mr. Green. The Vixen takes home a magnificent altar, highly wrought with carved work, in solid mahogany—a present, through Mr. Green, from the Archbishop of St. Domingo to the Archbishop of Baltimore. It is in size 44 by 26 feet, weighs ten tons, and belonged to the ruined chapel of the Jesuit college. The Vixen has also a superb painting, a Magdalen, by “Murillo”—a present, from an ancient but decayed Castilian family, to the surgeon of the vessel, “Dr. Bell,” in token of gratitude for the numerous delicate and skilful professional operations performed among all classes of inhabitants who have come to him from various parts of the island.—New York Journal of Commerce.

records.full_text:
[Correspondence of the Journal of Commerce.]
Military Preparations in Hayti.
PORT AU PRINCE, July —, 1850.
The most prominent item of news, in public affairs here, for the last few months, is the rumor of another onset by Soulouque upon the Dominicans. As far as any foreigner, or native even, can consult, to prevent the march of the emperor against the Dominicans, and bring about a treaty between the two parties, no move has been known in relation to this matter; but the consuls of Great Britain and France have sent a joint note to the emperor; and it is reported that they have each, in the name of their governments, remonstrated with the emperor against his contemplated march against St. Domingo.

As it is only moral force that these consuls use, it is uncertain how their labors will result. The emperor has seemed madly bent upon subduing the Dominicans, and the past few months have been one scene of preparation for another onset. When crowned, he was declared emperor of the entire island; and at that time, and since, the Dominicans retained possession of their territory, which is about two-thirds of the island. None of Soulouque's predecessors, since Boyer's reign, have reigned over the Spanish part. When the Haytians revolted against Boyer, and he was compelled to fly from the island, the Dominicans declared themselves independent, and have maintained their independence ever since. The route from Port-au-Prince to St. Domingo is not comparatively smooth. I have several times seen a young Dominican woman, taken prisoner last march, and dragged to a cannon over the entire route to Azua, and the river a few miles beyond, where they met with their defeat, and then marched back again through the desert to Port-au-Prince. In this march they took two days to reach River de las Damas, 21 leagues, and then marched upon Azua, which they took after a three days' fight. In marching this far, Soulouque's army was so short of food that what they could carry in their knapsacks was soon exhausted; and then, in that extreme distress, they had to satisfy their hunger for the time, and also to march on to subduing the Spanish side. But St. Domingo was yet a long way off, and the intermediate town of Azua, the only one of note that was taken, and his reign over the Dominican thus rendered short.

The flour they had here was baked, and one biscuit given to each soldier; and thus provided, away went the army, three to four miles an hour.

To reach and cross the river Ocoa, the emperor had built, with great labor, a wooden bridge. The only route to the river was by a narrow pass between two hills of high elevation, and immediately upon the edge of the sea. The Dominicans, knowing that this was their only route, had stationed two or three of their small war-vessels immediately abreast this passage, and were able to pour upon them a fire so destructive, that Soulouque's army was checked. However, with great loss of life, they succeeded in reaching the banks of the river Ocoa. This, as I have already hinted, proved to be the fatal step for them. On the bank of the river which they occupied was a level plain, but the opposite side was a high cliff, which the Dominicans held; and a few pieces posted upon this eminence, were enabled successfully to resist all their efforts to cross the river. Here the army remained for five days broiling in a hot sun, without an ounce of provision, or a drop of water, from its intensity, and the great body of them were on the point of starvation. The emperor himself (from what those who have spoken to him told me) that he was obliged to eat raw beef, without salt, to keep his mouth damp, as his comrades did theirs, by holding a lead bullet in it. Wells were dug, but salt water only was obtained; and while the men were thus suffering, and the horses upon which the officers rode were dying from thirst, the river Ocoa rolled immediately before them! and the starved soldiers, in their ecstacies at their distress, would go down to the edge to drink, and then, mad with the salt water, jump into the river before them! Yet every man and company of men, who undertook to cross the river, paid for his temerity with his life.

Desperate as affairs were, Soulouque seemed determined not to abandon his cherished purpose. When his under officers came to remonstrate with him on the distress of the troops, and their consequent insubordination, he reproached them with want of bravery; and beat them from his presence with his cane. At length he was compelled to desist.

Since that signal defeat the emperor seems conscious of the great mistake it was to undertake this march without the aid of war-vessels, to enable him to effect this pass; consequently, he has been making great efforts to increase his navy, which he has a good deal more than doubled within the last few months. These additions consist of an Austrian ship of about 900 tons, at the rumored price of $150,000; two Danish brigs, which, together, are said to have cost them $40,000; and a Curacoa schooner, for $12,000. Besides these, it is said that a steamer is being built for him in England, and a vessel of war.

I need hardly say that these vessels have paid "somebody" a good round profit. It has been most painful to be upon the island for the last twelve months, and witness the distress that has been occasioned by the preparations that have been made to carry on war against the Dominicans. Merchants, mechanics, school teachers, young men from stores, and indeed nearly every possible class and condition of the people, have been drafted by force to form an army, and sent to join the army. Some of these have been taken away from their business, which has been left to suffer, and perhaps they are completely ruined. Others have been taken from large families, who depend upon them for their daily bread; others have been taken from school, which have been thereby broken up. It does not matter much though a man's private fortune is ruined, though a wife and large family of children are left to beggary and starvation, though mothers and sisters suffer the agonies of a thousand deaths, when sons and brothers are torn away from them. Soldiers must be had; the Dominicans must be conquered. "Vive l'indivisibilite du territoire!" So says Faustin, and so it must be.

records.full_text: A treaty between St. Domingo and Great Britain has been signed, to endure for ten years, which permits the right of search for the prevention of the slave trade. Dominican vessels suspected of being engaged in the traffic may be searched by British cruisers, and, if found with slaves on board, or equipped for the trade, they are to be sent to the nearest Dominican port for adjudication by the Dominican authorities. The treaty also contains a provision for the mutual surrender of criminals.

The Republic of St. Domingo also celebrated the ratification of a treaty in which England acknowledged its independence from Hayti, during which the British Consul stated that England would not interfere in the coming contest and noted that British vessels would pay fifty cents less tonnage duty than American vessels. records.full_text:
The Dominican Republic.

TREATY OF PEACE, COMMERCE AND NAVIGATION, BETWEEN HER BRITANNIC MAJESTY AND THE DOMINICAN REPUBLIC.

IN THE NAME OF THE MOST HOLY TRINITY.
Her Majesty the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, and the President of the Dominican republic, being desirous to maintain and strengthen the relations of friendship, and to secure and extend the commercial intercourse between their respective dominions and territories, have resolved to conclude a treaty of peace, commerce and navigation, and have named as their respective Plenipotentiaries, that is to say:
Her Majesty the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, Sir Robert Hermann Schomburgk, Doctor of Philosophy, Knight of the Royal Prussian Order of the Red Eagle, of the Royal Saxon Order of Merit, of the Legion of Honor of the French Republic, her Consul to the Dominican republic;
And the President of the Dominican republic, Senor Jose Maria Medrano, Minister Secretary of State for the Department of Grace and Justice, Public Instruction, and Foreign Affairs;
Who, after having communicated to each other their respective full powers, found in good and due form, have agreed upon and concluded the following articles:—
Art. 1. There shall be perpetual peace and friendship between her Majesty the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, her heirs and successors, and the Dominican republic, and between their respective subjects and Citizens.
Art. 2. There shall be reciprocal freedom of commerce between the British dominions and the Dominican republic. The subjects of her Britannic Majesty may reside in and trade to any part of the territories of the republic, to which any other foreigners are or shall be admitted. They shall enjoy full protection for their persons and properties. They shall be allowed to buy from and sell to whom they like without being restrained or affected by any monopoly, contract, or exclusive privilege of sale or purchase whatever; and as her disposition is, moreover, enjoy all other rights and privileges which are or may be granted to any other foreigners, subjects or citizens of the most favored nation.
Art. 3. No tonnage, import or other duties or charges shall be levied in the Dominican republic on British vessels, or on goods imported or exported in British vessels, beyond what are or may be levied on national vessels, or on the goods imported or exported in national vessels, to and from the open ports; and, in like manner, no tonnage, import, or other duties or charges shall be levied in the British dominions on vessels of the republic, or on goods imported or exported in those vessels, beyond what are or may be levied on national vessels, or on the like goods imported or exported in national vessels to or from the ports open to commerce, without prejudice whatever to the stipulations contained in the fifth article with regard to national vessels of each of the two contracting parties.
Art 4 Merchandise or goods coming from the British dominions or any other foreign country in British vessels from any country, shall not be subjected in the Dominican republic, to other or to higher duties than are levied on the same kinds of merchandise or goods, coming from any other foreign country, or imported in any other vessels.
Art 5. Goods, the produce of the republic, when exported therefrom by British subjects and British vessels, or to British ports, shall not be subjected to higher duties than are levied on the same kinds of goods when exported in Dominican vessels or the vessels and citizens of any other foreign country.
Art 6. The protection of the government of the republic shall be afforded to all British vessels, their officers and crews, in case any wreck should be wrecked on the coast of the republic, the local authorities of the place shall use their utmost endeavors to save the property, and protect it from plunder, and shall cause all articles saved to be delivered up to their respective lawful owners. The amount of salvage dues in such cases shall, if a dispute arise, be settled by arbitrators chosen by both parties.
Art 7. Furthermore, the two contracting parties bind to themselves by the present treaty, that if either grant to any foreign or the most favored nation, it is hereby agreed between them, that the favors, privileges, or immunities in matters of commerce and navigation, which either contracting party may hereafter grant, to the subjects or citizens of any other state, shall be extended to the subjects or citizens of the other contracting party, gratuitously, if the concession in favor of that other state shall have been gratuitous, or in return for a compensation equal as possible in effectiveness, value and effect, to be adjusted by mutual agreement if the concession shall have been conditional.
Art 7. Each contracting party may appoint Consuls for the protection of trade, to reside in the dominions or territories of the other; but no such Consul shall enter upon the exercise of his functions until he shall have been admitted and approved, in the usual form, by the government of the country to which he is sent.
The commerce, navigation and subjects of each of the two contracting parties residing within the territories or dominions of the other, shall enjoy the same rights, immunities, privileges and exemptions, which are or may be granted to the diplomatic agents or Consuls of equal rank, of the most favored nation.
Art 8. The subjects of her Britannic Majesty residing in the Dominican republic shall not be disturbed, persecuted, or annoyed on account of their religion, or their religious worship, but in conscience therein, and exercise their creed either within their own domestic dwellings, or in the particular chapels. Liberty shall also be granted to bury the subjects of her Britannic Majesty who may die within the Dominican republic, in the manner, they may freely establish and maintain, in convenient places, which for that purpose they may set apart, in any part of the Dominican republic in the territories of the said republic. In like manner, the citizens of the Dominican republic shall enjoy, within all the dominions of Her Britannic Majesty, a full and exact freedom of conscience, and shall be allowed to exercise their religion publicly or privately, within their own dwelling houses, or in the chapels and places of worship appointed for that purpose.
Art 9. Slavery being perpetually abolished in the Dominican republic, and having been recently declared by her an act of piracy punishable with the pain of death, the Dominican republic engages to permit any British vessel of war, which may be furnished with special instructions, to search any Dominican vessel which may be suspected of being engaged in this vile trade in human beings; and the distances and places between which the right of search may be exercised, shall be governed by the treaties with other powers, for Cuba and Porto Rico, within the distance of twenty leagues from the coasts of the Dominican republic. In case it should appear to the officer in command of such British vessel of war, that the suspicions of his being engaged are well grounded, the vessel shall be sent, without delay, to the port of Santo Domingo, in the Dominican republic, and shall be delivered up to the Dominican authorities to be tried according to the laws of the republic.
It is understood that the present article shall not be extended to other cases, which might occasion vexatious search of Dominican merchant vessels in their voyages and commercial enterprise; but for preventing all abuse, the officers authorized to expect protection and assistance; and if, in the case of such search, it should turn out not to be as supposed, that the Dominican republic should suffer any damage from such search or vexatious molestation, it rests with her to withdraw the concession made in the present article, or to modify it.
Art 10. In order that the two contracting parties may have the opportunity of thereafter treating and agreeing upon any other terms which may be useful to their commercial relations, and to give greater stability to the present treaty, the contracting parties shall have the right of giving to each other notice of their intention to modify it at the expiration of said ten years the stipulations of the present treaty relative to commerce and navigation shall cease to be binding after ten years, and all the terms of peace and friendship shall remain obligatory to both nations.
Art 11. The present treaty shall be ratified, and the ratifications shall be exchanged at Santo Domingo within twelve months from the date of this treaty, or sooner, if possible.
In witness whereof, the respective plenipotentiaries have signed the same, and affixed thereto the seals of their arms.
Done at Santo Domingo, the sixth day of March, in the year of our Lord eighteen hundred and fifty.
(L. S.) ROBERT H. SCHOMBURGK.
(L. S.) JOSE MARIA MEDRANO.

ADDITIONAL ARTICLES.
As the citizens of the Dominican republic and of the Haytian nation might oblige the Dominican republic to modify the stipulations of article 2, it is specially understood and agreed between the two contracting parties, that the Dominican republic shall have perfect liberty of making the duration of the 2d article shorter than ten years, or to reduce the defence, notwithstanding the stipulations of article 2; provided that the subjects of her Britannic Majesty shall not be restricted or affected by any monopoly, contract or exclusive privilege of purchase or sale; and as her disposition is consistent, to permit any foreign merchant or trader to enter in her views to adopt any measures of limitation, except in the case that Haytians should also continue.

The present additional article shall have the same force and validity as if it were inserted, word for word, in the treaty signed this day. It shall be ratified at the same time. And in case Hayti should resume or continue, it is understood that the sanction or disapprobation of the present article by either of the two contracting parties shall not affect the validity of the main treaty.

In testimony whereof the undersigned have, in virtue of their full powers, signed and sealed the present article.

Done at Santo Domingo, the sixth day of March, in the year of our Lord eighteen hundred and fifty.
(L. S) ROBERT H. SCHOMBURGK.
(L. S.) JOSE MARIA MEDRANO.

Ratified in the city of St. Domingo, September 10, 1850.
BUENAVENTURA BAEZ.
Dr. JOSE MARIA CAMINERO.

records.summary_en: The *New York Herald* reported that the Dominican Republic declared the slave trade to be an act of piracy punishable by death. To help prevent this trade, the republic agreed to permit British warships—acting under specific treaty instructions—to visit vessels sailing under the Dominican flag that are reasonably suspected of slave trading within twenty leagues of the Dominican coast. If suspicions are confirmed, the detained vessel is to be sent to Santo Domingo and delivered to local authorities for prosecution under Dominican law.
records.summary_es: El *New York Herald* informó que la República Dominicana declaró la trata de esclavos crimen de piratería conminado con pena capital. A fin de coadyuvar a su erradicación, la república consintió en facultar a los cruceros de guerra británicos —conforme a instrucciones capitulares precisas— para inspeccionar embarcaciones que arbolasen insignia dominicana bajo fundada sospecha de tráfico de esclavos en un radio de veinte leguas de las costas dominicanas. De comprobarse el delito, la presa sería remitida a Santo Domingo y consignada a los tribunales de la República para su procesamiento conforme al derecho patrio.

records.full_text:
IN THE NAME OF THE MOST HOLY TRINITY.
Her Majesty the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, and the President of the Dominican Republic, being desirous to consecrate the formal recognition of the independence of the same, and to conclude a treaty of peace and friendship, and to regulate thereby the commercial intercourse between the dominions and subjects of her Majesty, and the territories and citizens of the Republic, they have for this purpose named as their respective Plenipotentiaries, that is to say:—
Her Majesty the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, Sir Robert Hermann Schomburgk, Doctor of Philosophy, Knight of the Royal Prussian Order of the Red Eagle, of the Royal Saxon Order of Merit; of the Legion of Honor of the French Republic; Her Consul to the Dominican Republic;
And the President of the Dominican republic, Senor Jose Maria Medrano, Minister Secretary of State for the departments of police and the interior, and charged with those of Justice, Public Instruction, and Foreign Affairs;
Who, after having communicated to each other their respective full powers, found in good and due form, have agreed upon and concluded the following articles:—
Art. 1. There shall be perpetual peace and friendship between her Majesty the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, her heirs and successors, and the Dominican republic, and between their respective subjects and citizens.
Art. 2. There shall be reciprocal freedom of commerce between the British dominions and the Dominican republic. The subjects of her Britannic Majesty may reside in and trade to any part of the territories of the republic, to which any other foreigners are or shall be admitted. They shall enjoy full protection for their persons and properties. They shall be allowed to buy from and sell to whom they like without being restrained or affected by any monopoly, contract, or exclusive privilege of sale or purchase whatever; and they shall moreover enjoy all other rights and privileges which are or may be granted to any other foreigners, subjects or citizens of the most favored nation.
The citizens of the Dominican republic shall, in return, enjoy similar protection and privileges in the dominions of Her Britannic Majesty.
Art. 3. No tonnage, import or other duties or charges shall be levied in the Dominican republic on British vessels, or on goods imported or exported in British vessels, than are or may be provided to be levied on national vessels, or on the like goods imported or exported in national vessels; and in the same manner, no tonnage, import, or other duties or charges shall be levied in the British dominions on vessels of the republic, or on goods imported or exported in those vessels, beyond what are or may be levied on national vessels, or on the like goods imported or exported in national vessels; or from the ports upon the commerce, without prejudice whatever to the provisions of the fourth article, exclusively reserved to national vessels of each of the the two countries respectively.
Art. 4. Merchandise or goods coming from the British dominions in any vessels, or coming from British vessels from any country, shall not be prohibited in the Dominican republic, nor be subjected to higher duties than are levied on the same kinds of merchandise or goods, coming from any other foreign country, or imported in any other vessels.
All articles, the produce of the republic, may be exported therefrom by British subjects and British vessels, on as favorable terms as by the subjects and citizens and vessels of any other foreign country.
Art. 5. The protection of the government of the republic shall be afforded to all British vessels, their crews and goods. If any British vessel should be wrecked on the coast of the republic, the local authorities shall afford them aid, and secure them from plunder, and shall cause all articles saved from the wreck to be restored to their lawful owners. The amount of salvage dues in such cases shall be settled, in case of dispute, by arbitrators chosen by both parties.
Art. 6. It being the intention of the two contracting parties to bind themselves by the present treaty, to treat each other on the footing of the most favored nation, it is hereby agreed between them, that any favor, privilege, or immunity whatever in matters of commerce and navigation, which either contracting party has actually granted, or may hereafter grant, to the subjects or citizens of any other State, shall be extended to the subjects or citizens of the other contracting party, gratuitously, if the concession in favor of that other State shall have been gratuitous, or in return for a compensation as nearly as possible of proportionate value and effect, to be adjusted by mutual agreement if the concession shall have been conditional.
Art. 7. Each contracting party may appoint Consuls for the protection of its trade, in the dominions or territories of the other; but no such Consul shall enter upon the exercise of his functions until he shall have been admitted and approved, in the usual form, by the government of the country to which he is sent.
The respective agents and Consuls of each of the two contracting parties residing within the dominions or territories of the other, shall enjoy the same rights, immunities, privileges and exemptions which are or may be granted to the diplomatic agents or Consuls of equal rank, of the most favored nation.
Art. 8. The subjects of her Britannic Majesty residing in the Dominican republic shall not be disturbed, persecuted, or annoyed on account of their religion, but they shall have perfect liberty of conscience therein, and exercise their creed either within their own private houses, or in the said or particular chapels. Liberty shall also be granted to them to bury in the Dominican republic, in the manner, they may freely establish and maintain, their subjects who may die in the territories of the said republic. In like manner, the citizens of the Dominican republic shall enjoy, within all the dominions of Her Britannic Majesty, a perfect and entire liberty of conscience, and shall be allowed to exercise their religion publicly or privately, within their own dwelling houses, or in the chapels and places of worship appointed for that purpose.
Art. 9. Slavery being perpetually abolished in the Dominican republic, and having been already declared by her an act of piracy punishable with the pain of death, the Dominican republic engages to permit any British vessel of war, which may be furnished with special instructions under the treaties between Great Britain and foreign powers, and with the formalities as are provided for in such cases by the said treaties relative to the prevention of the infamous slave trade, to visit any vessels sailing under the Dominican flag, which may, upon reasonable grounds, be suspected of being engaged in this vile trade in slaves; it being understood that the distances and places between which the right of visit shall be exercised as restricted as they are in the treaties with other powers, for Cuba and Porto Rico, shall likewise refer to the same distance of twenty leagues from the coasts of the Dominican republic; and if, by the result of the visit, it shall appear to the officer in command of such British vessel of war that the suspicions of the commander are well grounded, the vessel shall be sent, without delay, to the port of Santo Domingo, in the Dominican republic, and shall be delivered up to the local authorities, to be proceeded against according to the laws of the republic.
It is understood that the present article shall not be extended to other cases, which might occasion a vexatious and unnecessary visit to the Dominican vessels in their voyages and commercial enterprises; but that, with the aid of the Dominican authorities, authorized to expect protection and assistance; and, if the case should arise, which, however, is not to be supposed, that the Dominican republic should receive a conviction of having suffered a vexatious molestation, it rests with her to withdraw it, after having given a year's previous notice thereof.
Art. 10. In order that the two contracting parties may have the opportunity of hereafter treating and agreeing upon such other arrangements as may tend still further to the improvement of their mutual interests, and to the promotion of the commerce of their respective subjects and citizens, it is agreed that the present treaty shall remain in force for the term of ten years from the date of the exchange of the ratifications, and either of the contracting parties shall have the right of giving to the other party notice of its intention to terminate at the expiration of the said ten years the stipulations of the present treaty; and the present treaty shall cease to be binding after ten years, and all notice that might be given and amity shall remain obligatory to both nations.
Art. 11. The present treaty shall be ratified, and the ratifications shall be exchanged at Santo Domingo, within the space of eight months, or sooner, if possible, counted from the date of this treaty, or sooner, if shall be possible.
In witness whereof, the respective plenipotentiaries have signed the same, and affixed thereto the seals of their arms.
Done at Santo Domingo, the sixth day of March, in the year of our Lord eighteen hundred and fifty.
(L. S.) ROBERT H. SCHOMBURGK.
(L. S.) JOSE MARIA MEDRANO.

ADDITIONAL ARTICLES.
As the circumstances of the Dominican with the Haytien nation might oblige the Dominican republic to modify the third article, it is hereby especially understood and agreed between the two contracting parties, that the Dominican republic shall have perfect liberty of making during the space of ten years such changes as she may think fit in her duties, notwithstanding the stipulation of article 3 aforesaid; but the subjects of her Britannic Majesty shall not be restrained or affected by any monopoly, contract or exclusive privilege of purchase or sale; and as her disposition is constant to afford and protect commerce, it should enter in her views to adopt any measures of limited or except in the case that the existing laws should continue.
The present additional article shall have the same force and validity as if it were inserted, word for word, in the treaty signed this day. It shall be ratified at the same time. And in consequence of the exception in article 3, it is to be understood that the sanction or disapprobation of the treaty is naturally reserved to Her Britannic Majesty.
In testimony whereof the undersigned have, in virtue of their full powers, signed and sealed the present article.
Done at Santo Domingo, the sixth day of March, in the year of our Lord eighteen hundred and fifty.
(L. S.) ROBERT H. SCHOMBURGK.
(L. S.) JOSE MARIA MEDRANO.
Ratified in the city of St. Domingo, September 27, 1850. BUENAVENTURA BAEZ.
DR. JOSE MARIA CAMINERO.

records.summary_en: According to an account from St. Domingo City received via the brig *George Otis* and reported from Boston on November 30, 1850, a treaty of peace between the Haytiens and Dominicans had been concluded through the intervention of the English and Americans, following some brief fighting that caused no serious loss. records.full_text: A late arrival from St. Domingo announced that the Dominican government was making great preparations to repel the expected invasion by Haytiens under the black Emperor Faustin I. The Dominican fleet, consisting of one ship, one bark, three brigs and a large number of schooners, was being put in order; the fortifications were undergoing repairs, and every male inhabitant capable of bearing arms had been enrolled. Santa Ana has been placed in chief command of the army. The ratification of a treaty with England, in which that nation acknowledges the independence from Hayti of the Republic of St. Domingo, was celebrated by a public dinner, at which the President of the Republic presided, and the British Consul was present. The latter made a speech, in which he said that the English would not interfere in the coming contest between them and Hayti. Neither the American Consul nor any of the American shipmasters were present at the dinner.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
The Commissioners on Mexican Claims have this morning completed their awards. They amount to forty thousand dollars less than the sum appropriated to meet them, of one million and a quarter of dollars.

Major Donelson publishes a letter in the Union this morning, three columns and a half long, to the editor of the Union, upon assuming the editorial control of that journal. The Major endeavors to make the compromise a tower of patriotism above the ordinary spirit of party; but says that 'if the ultra Democratic party of this nation can be brought together in no other way than by an abandonment of the Union, or a compromise with the enemies of the compromise, we can never consent to buy peace on such terms.' He thinks the Democratic party, nevertheless, will unite on a constitutional basis, and elect the next President.

The intelligence brought by the last arrival from England, relative to the movement of British naval force, is considered to have a direct bearing upon the movements of Southern adventurers. It is supposed that the British vessels which have been dispatched may first meet the West India fleet somewhere near the shores of St. Domingo, for the purpose of obtaining redress, instant and immediate, from the Emperor of the black republic; while the adventurers from the Southern States may effect a landing on Dominica, and unite with those forces to assault the black republic in the flank. It is very true that our government at Washington can't declare war, or commence hostilities, without an act of Congress, but it can connive at the movement of a body of armed men, who may choose to emigrate to Dominica.

The intelligence brought by a letter from Mr. Riddle, United States Commissioner to the World's Fair, relative to the space allotted to the United States, is believed to be very onerous and expensive. The custom house commission on each package amounted to nearly $2, besides which, all the duties, tares, draperies, &c., for the display of goods, have to be provided by each nation, and those of other countries are very brilliant. He has had to employ a number of clerks to make out a descriptive catalog. Among these, he says, he is behind hand, owing to the late hour at which goods arrived.

The charge against Collector Lewis, of Philadelphia, after a full investigation by the President and Secretary of the Treasury, has been dismissed.

The Hon. John M. Clayton arrived here yesterday.

records.summary_en: The *Wilmington Journal* reported on April 25, 1851, that because St. Domingo (the Dominican Republic) was unrecognized by the United States, it was regarded as a piratical government rather than a nation requiring an act of Congress for military action. The newspaper suggested that U.S. vessels fitted out at Norfolk and New York could join other American ships to demand redress from the "emperor" of Hayti or demolish his regime. Additionally, it noted rumors that expeditions from the Southern States purportedly bound for Cuba were likely intended to land on the Dominican part of the island to assist the Dominicans and revolutionize the social and political condition of the blacks.
records.summary_es: El *Wilmington Journal* comunicó el 25 de abril de 1851 que, por carecer de reconocimiento oficial por parte de Estados Unidos, Santo Domingo (la República Dominicana) era conceptuado más bien como un gobierno pirático que como una nación formal que demandase una ley del Congreso para emprender acciones militares. La hoja apuntaba que buques de guerra estadounidenses alistados en Norfolk y Nueva York podrían concurrir con otras unidades navales para exigir satisfacciones al «emperador» de Haití o derribar su régimen. Recogía además comentarios de que expediciones armadas procedentes de los estados del Sur, supuestamente destinadas a Cuba, tendrían por objeto desembarcar en la parte dominicana para auxiliar a los naturales y trastocar el ordenamiento político y social de las poblaciones negras.

records.full_text:
ONE DAY LATER FROM HAYTI.—A letter from Porte-au-Prince, dated April 10, published in the New York Journal of Commerce, says that the Haytien Congress have not yet made a decision on the offer of mediation between the Haytiens and Dominicans, by the three commercial powers. This is one day later than the report that the offered mediation had been rejected. A Boston dispatch of the 1st inst. has the following:
The schooner October, from Porte-au-Prince, with advices to April 13, arrived here to-day. It is currently reported at St. Domingo that the Chambers had refused to comply with the demands of the American Commissioner, or to make peace. Emperor Soulouque was preparing to march on St. Domingo with all his forces. He had dismissed his Cabinet, and replaced them with men who were in favor of war.
The steamboat General Taylor arrived at Port-au-Prince on the 10th April, and was offered for sale.

records.full_text:
THE INTERNATIONAL MAGAZINE FOR JUNE. Price 25 cents.
This number is one of the best and most attractive yet issued. It contains a great variety of interesting and valuable matter, among which we notice a very interesting and well-written account of the mission of Mr. Robert M. Walsh to Hayti, as Special Agent of the United States. Mr. Walsh's instructions were to act in concert with the agents of France and Great Britain in an endeavor to induce the Emperor Soulouque to recognize the independence of the Dominican Republic. The writer gives a very graphic description of the character and court of the sable monarch, and of the progress and results of the mission. He represents Mr. Walsh as having acted with great energy and decision, and at various places in Hayti, as threatening to blockade and bombard Port-au-Prince in case Soulouque should still refuse to recognize the eastern part of the island as separate and independent. Armed coercion was apparently as familiar to him as his own title of "Special Agent," and his dreams by night and his talk by day seem to have been mainly of seventy-fours, frigates, paixhans, bomb-shells, rockets and thirty-two pounders. An inexorable and most unmitigated "interventionist" was Mr. Walsh, and if his advice had been followed, the "Napoleon of the West" would have been taught a lesson which he would not soon have forgotten. The Magazine contains also a great variety of other interesting matter, including several original stories and poems, and a large number of well-executed wood-cuts.

records.headline: The idea and the wish to dissolve the com pulsory union
records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that after the expulsion of Boyer in 1843 and the accession of Gen. Riviere, the Dominicans seized an opportunity while the garrison was reduced to capture the remaining troops, proclaim a provisional independent government in early January 1844, and issue a revolutionary manifesto on January 16, 1844. It described the Dominican population as consisting of pure whites—who were the intellectually predominant and ruling class—and mixed races of various colors, all of whom were constitutionally declared equal citizens before the law. Additionally, the excerpt noted that Santana, the Dominican liberator and first President, resigned in 1848 and was succeeded by Jimenez, who was described as a traitor.
records.summary_es: El periódico relató que tras el derrocamiento de Boyer en 1843 y la exaltación del general Rivière, los dominicanos aprovecharon la mengua de la guarnición para reducir a las tropas restantes, proclamar un gobierno provisional independiente a principios de enero de 1844 y promulgar una manifestación revolucionaria el 16 de enero de 1844. Describía a la población dominicana integrada por blancos puros —que constituían la clase intelectualmente rectora y gobernante— y razas mixtas de diversos matices, proclamados todos constitucionalmente ciudadanos iguales ante la ley. Añadía el extracto que Santana, libertador dominicano y primer presidente, renunció en 1848 y fue sucedido por Jimenes, a quien se tildaba de traidor.

records.headline: HOW THEY DO IT.
records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that after being left to themselves by Colombia and Spain, the Dominicans were invaded and subjugated by Haytian President Boyer under the pretext of aid. Under Haytian rule, local institutions and the University of Santo Tomas de Aquinas were destroyed, public edifices were dismantled, and property was confiscated due to constitutional laws forbidding white property ownership. Consequently, many Dominicans fled the country while the rest remained stripped of their means to leave.
records.summary_es: El diario relató que, tras quedar desamparados por Colombia y España, los dominicanos fueron invadidos y sojuzgados por el mandatario haitiano Boyer so pretexto de auxilio. Bajo la dominación haitiana, las instituciones vernáculas y la Universidad de Santo Tomás de Aquino fueron desmanteladas, los edificios públicos arruinados y los bienes confiscados en virtud de preceptos constitucionales que vedaban a los blancos el derecho de propiedad. En consecuencia, numerosos dominicanos huyeron de la patria, en tanto los restantes quedaron desprovistos de recursos para emigrar.

records.full_text: HOW THEY DO IT.—Some time in 1849, Mr. King, of Georgia, then a member of the House of Representatives, made a speech on the subject of the recognition of the independence of Hayti, in which he gave a brief history of the manner in which the Dominicans were brought under the yoke of the Haytians. In 1821, the Spanish part of the island of St. Domingo declared its independence of Spain, and sent commissioners to ask admission as one of the States of that republic. The Colombians were then too much engaged with their own affairs to undertake the defence of the Dominicans. Spain, engaged in the vain effort of reclaiming her other more populous and valuable colonies, left the Dominicans to themselves. Boyer, then president of Hayti, called out his whole military force, and passing the frontier, under pretence of aiding the Dominicans, took possession of the country, and annexed it to Hayti.

records.headline: The Dominican Loan in London.
records.summary_en: The *New York Herald* reported that the Dominican Republic comprises about two-thirds of the island of Hayti and occupies a position of significant commercial importance, though its ability to meet the annual interest on a £760,000 loan was doubted. The article noted that the Dominican population is estimated at 200,000 of Spanish origin (including whites, blacks, and a mixed race), contrasting it with Hayti proper, which was under the despotic rule of Emperor Soulouque, possessed a population of 700,000 all-black citizens, and barred white persons from holding property. Furthermore, the excerpt stated that the entire island had been united under the Haytien government from 1821 until 1844, when Dominica separated due to Haytien violations of annexation terms and a refusal to permit white immigration.
records.summary_es: El *New York Herald* expuso que la República Dominicana abarca cerca de dos tercios de la isla de Haití y goza de una ventajosa posición mercantil, si bien se ponía en duda su solvencia para satisfacer los réditos anuales de un empréstito de 760.000 libras esterlinas. El escrito consignaba que la población dominicana se estimaba en 200.000 almas de origen español (comprendiendo blancos, negros y razas mixtas), contrastándola con Haití propiamente dicho, sometido al mando tiránico del emperador Soulouque, con un censo de 700.000 habitantes exclusivamente de raza negra y con leyes que prohibían a los blancos poseer bienes raíces. Asentaba por añadidura que toda la isla permaneció unida bajo la potestad haitiana desde 1821 hasta 1844, año en que la parte dominicana proclamó su separación a causa de las transgresiones de Haití a las condiciones pactadas y su veto a la inmigración blanca.

At the same time, it is impossible to comprehend the purpose for which it can be required. The depreciated paper circulation might be bought up for £30,000, and the idea of a State with only 200,000 inhabitants, and scarcely yet sure of its independence, or secure from the domestic intrigues peculiar to all races of Spanish origin, taking upon itself a debt of £760,000 simply to promote enterprise and immigration, is preposterous. The interest and sinking fund upon this would be nearly £60,000 per annum, and the entire revenue of the republic is supposed not to exceed £60,000. Raybaud as the French Consul General at Hayti, while the French war steamer *L'Ardent* departed St. Domingo on July 14 for Puerto-Plata carrying the resident French Consul. American, French, and Spanish Views of the Question.
