records.summary_en: The *New York Herald* reported that France allegedly intended to take control of the Dominican Republic to subsequently conquer the western part under the black regime and restore French dominion over the island. According to the excerpt, these secret machinations—initially pursued under Louis Philippe and later renewed under Louis Napoleon—found a warm supporter in Dominican President Buenaventura Baez, who was educated in France and held French notions.
records.summary_es: El *New York Herald* refirió que Francia pretendía supuestamente asumir el señorío de la República Dominicana para sojuzgar ulteriormente la sección occidental gobernada por el régimen negro y restablecer el dominio imperial sobre la isla. A juicio del extracto, semejantes maquinaciones secretas —fraguadas inicialmente bajo Luis Felipe y reactivadas luego con Luis Napoleón— hallaron un decidido valedor en el presidente dominicano Buenaventura Báez, instruido en Francia e imbuido de ideas francesas.

records.full_text:
THE FRENCH MOVEMENT IN ST. DOMINGO.

American, French, and Spanish Views of the Question.

THE NEW CASUS BELLI.

[From the New York Herald of April 21, 1852.]
OUR PORT-AU-PLAT CORRESPONDENCE.
PORT-AU-PLAT, Dominican Republic, February, 1852.
I have on former occasions addressed a word to you, to draw the attention of the public of the republic, respecting what it pleases our present administration to throw dust into the eyes of the United States citizens. I mean the false information which the President officially stated in his message, that the differences between the Dominican republic and the Haytian empire were arranged, while such a desirable event is as far off as ever—thanks to the intrigue of public agents.

I may as well advise; for if you will refer to the Revue des Deux Mondes, for May, 1851, its pages corporate more than a sentiment, since Mr. M. Barrot, a member of the Assembly, contains an article on the empire of Hayti and the Dominican republic, which, it is confidently reported, has the French Consul in Port au Prince for author. Now, for its author, and is so filled up with misstatements that it is impossible that the reviewer in Paris could assemble a print contained therein to insert similar stuff it is clumsily attempted, in these pages, to make it appear that the Dominican republic desires a French protectorate over St. Domingo, is the most ardent desire of the Dominican population, who would see with pleasure their President, Senor Baez, (who, to his shame be it said is more Frenchman than Dominican,) and a small clique of French partisans, surrender the republic, although the inhabitants utterly despise Johnny Crapaud with as deep a hatred as ever did their Haytian neighbors.

I am now resident here for some years, during which time I have studied the character of the Haytians, and remarkably; and I must confess that the steady exercise of French diplomatic agents in Hayti, for some years past, inspires me with a suspicion that those agents have only had one aim—namely, to get hold under some plausible appearance of the Dominican republic and to conquer afterwards the western part, under the black ribbon, with comparative facility, thereby restoring the 'Queen of the Antilles' to the dominion of France; or, if you will, since the Dictator has restored 'the eagles' of Napoleon to the French army, to the claws of the rapacious bird, which, although it may resemble ours in form, has no relationship with it in character.

The supposition of an intended protectorate in St. Domingo is further strengthened by the arrival of the Prince de Joinville and the Duke d'Aumale in Hayti, during the presidency of General Guerrier. The children of Louis Philippe, the late King of the French, came to Hayti under the pretext of paying the Montalais their legacy, which was left by the late King of Hayti to the widow of Prince de Joinville's brother, the late Prince of Joinville, and to her sister-in-law, the Duchess of Orleans; but the real object of their visit was to prepare the way for the French fleet to come and occupy Cuba and Porto Rico to her sister, bidding the young princes a very cool adieu, and telling them they had better turn back, as they would find nothing there to do, and to render it in time the stronghold of these seas, and to conquer the rest of Hayti.

The Emperor's downfall and the revolution interrupted the intrigue, but scarcely had Louis Napoleon reached the presidency than the old schemes of Louis Philippe's agent were recommendations, and found a warm supporter in a French agent, named Mr. Raybaud, who was sent to the Dominican republic, clever, educated and French in heart, although a Dominican citizen.

The Revue des Deux Mondes tells us that this patriotic citizen had proposed to Mr. M. Barrot, the French Consul in Port au Prince—'You have only to give us your support, or a company of 2,000 men, to convince France of our sincere desire to place ourselves under her protectorate.' But Mr. Raybaud, although a Dominican citizen, was so far from having the modesty to refuse the proposal, that he had even the face to ask for more—namely, that 5,000 French troops should be sent to occupy the republic of Dominica.

So far from having the modesty, or to make statements from the executive of the Dominican republic, will be still more surprised if they continue to deny them for a short distance. They will find that Mr. Senor Baez, the President of Dominica, actually sent Mr. Raybaud to induce the acceptance of the young republic, foot and arm, of the French flag, and to place it under the protectorate of France; and that, at this moment, Mr. Raybaud (Mr. Green)—sent to St. Domingo with full powers from President Baez, to treat on this subject; so that, as long as there is a spark of hope that France will accept my proposals, I will wait with resignation.'

The author of these precious state papers from St. Domingo sent to Paris, where he went to further the object of his mission to produce the annexation of St. Domingo to the French empire, was Mr. Raybaud, although it is well known that another agent, whose name was kept secret, while the English cabinet employed only intrigue, which altogether failed.

The objects of Mr. Green's mission are well-known to the public of Dominica, although it was stated by the president's partisans that he was merely sent to Paris to purchase arms, &c. But Mr. Raybaud (Green), whose real name was known, selected young Green, who by the situation he had formerly held in Mexico, seemed to be a proper person for the mission to Paris; and his brother, who is now in his cabinet, although he never affirmed his connection with it.

I need not tell you how Mr. Green succeeded in his cabinet at Aranjuez. I never heard of any; but I can tell you what he did in Paris, and also what Mr. Baez's Carminero, then Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Dominican republic, did in London. Mr. Carminero was offered him the protectorate, promising that the British flag should be hoisted in St. Domingo; but Mr. Carminero refused it in the name of his government, and that the same Mr. Carminero, as soon as he found that Mr. Green was sent to London, sent the British Cabinet a diplomatic note, in which he declined to accept any such proposals.

The intention of Mr. Raybaud was not to produce an aggrandizement, but desired merely the prosperity of Dominica, and to avoid the trouble of getting a new prince to govern the republic. He added however, should France reject the offer, that if the Dominican republic can flag, it would be the sign to him to strike the British flag. Now, is it not surprising that after such facts, the city of a person who fabricates falsehoods in his message to Congress, in the manner of Mr. Fillmore, could assert such fables?

To show how far he abuses the Ministers of France and England, he says, 'We have offered to the United States to place ourselves under her protection, but no answer was given.' Now, no such proposal was ever made by Mr. Baez to the United States. He also says, 'We have offered to the Dominican flag to be hoisted in St. Domingo.' Now, this is another falsehood of Mr. Fillmore. Mr. Fillmore says, 'We have offered the Dominican flag to be hoisted in St. Domingo.' He says, 'We are forced by the French to consent.' This is another falsehood of Mr. Fillmore. Now, this is another falsehood of Mr. Fillmore, who says, 'We are forced by the French to consent.' Our lethargy, he says, 'has prevented us from accepting the offer, or the financial obstacles that might be given as an excuse to us for not having accepted it.' Now, no such excuse can be made, for no offer was ever made to us. We have not even the trouble to carry it there—it is all a invention of Mr. Fillmore; and we are sure that, if such a proposal had been made to the Dominican republic, the New World the future entrepot of the two hemispheres would not have been rejected. But Mr. Fillmore, it is openly, may be objected to us: 'Good God! because it is a secret.' If it is a secret, how does Mr. Fillmore and his friends know of it? because it such a legitimate and honorable mission that it must be kept secret. Yes, because others already dispute themselves publicly for the Dominican republic; and Mr. Fillmore, who has done so far for the eight years has answered to the gut vice of the cabinet of Paris.

Answer to Mr. Green: But if Mr. Green might succeed under such circumstances, the diplomatic tendency of the British cabinet, although it may seem so, is entirely different; how different with the Dictator, Louis Napoleon at the head of the French army, and the article of the Revue des Deux Mondes, written by Mr. Raybaud, is still more surprising. If we look at the article in the Revue des Deux Mondes, written by Mr. Raybaud, we find that the writer, after describing the state of Hayti, says that the French flag, hoisted in Dominica, would be a strong inducement for France to accept the proposal; and he adds that the French government ought to accept it, because it would give France the key of the Gulf of Mexico, and enable her to conquer Hayti, and to regain the control of the Queen of the Antilles. Now, it is well known that Mr. Raybaud was the principal agent of Louis Philippe in Hayti, and that he directed all the intrigue which led to the overthrow of General Guerrier; that he was the person who persuaded Prince de Joinville and the Duke d'Aumale to visit Hayti, and that he accompanied them when they returned to France. This is the man who has now been sent by Mr. Baez to Paris on the mission of annexation. On his arrival, he was received by Louis Napoleon, and received the cross of the Legion of Honor, and the rank of colonel. The article of the Revue des Deux Mondes, which was written by him, shows that he still continues to entertain the same views; and he has now been sent to Paris to finish what he commenced in Hayti.

The cabinet of the Tuileries hesitated to assume the responsibility which was offered to it, and the news of the expedition might have been prevented to it, that excess of timidity which formed the base of French diplomacy under the republic, until the 2d of December, 1843, a treaty was signed upon the following bases:—
First. France should send an effective support to the Dominican republic to protect it against Haiti, until peace should be firmly established.
Second. The Dominican republic should yield to France the peninsula of Samana, to found a permanent establishment there.
It was added that the Dominican republic, under these conditions should be the direct personification of the protectorate; that the governor of the island should be named by France and he should be invested with full powers to this effect.

This treaty, accepted by M. Ferdinand Barrot, was modified by M. de Trobriand, who, finding it contained an engagement which it had assumed, had causing the modified treaty to be signed by Mr. Baez and the Rear Admiral de Mogen, Commander of the West India squadron.
By this new arrangement, which is an amendment, France officially proclaimed the independence of St. Domingo and promised it her moral protection, reserving to the French government to install at Samana the effective force necessary for its defense; while the Dominican republic requests her prayers, nor even the threat of throwing herself into the arms of the United States. It was, besides, a question of a protectorate, an eclipse to a measure which might involve some diplomatic complications, but simply an intervention of humanity, which French diplomacy, with its usual dexterity, did not fail to reveal. The revolution of February, which overthrew the Orleans dynasty, came to produce an absolute change in this state of things, forcing the republic to seek an offset, and finding it in the peninsula of Samana, which her former government had found the means of possessing, and to which the present government appears attached.

records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that correspondence between the State Department and its agent, Mr. Hubert M. Walsh, has been made public, clearly setting forth the administration's motives in offering its good offices to the Dominican Republic. According to the excerpt, the Spanish portion of St. Domingo voluntarily subjected itself to Hayti in 1821, but later established an independent republic out of self-preservation due to the invasion of their rights, liberties, and threats of extermination under Haytien rule. Although the negroes of Hayti regarded this separation as a revolt and attempted to reduce the Dominicans to subjection by force, all efforts by the Haytien government to reconquer the territory proved unequal.
records.summary_es: El diario notificó que se dio a la estampa la correspondencia cursada entre el Departamento de Estado y su comisionado, Sr. Hubert M. Walsh, esclareciendo los móviles del gobierno al brindar sus buenos oficios a la República Dominicana. Según el extracto, la comarca española de Santo Domingo se acogió espontáneamente a Haití en 1821, pero constituyó luego una república independiente por imperativo de propia conservación ante la vulneración de sus prerrogativas, libertades y fundados temores de exterminio bajo el dominio haitiano. Pese a que los negros de Haití juzgaron dicha separación como sedición y procuraron someter por la fuerza a los dominicanos, cuantas tentativas desplegó el gobierno haitiano para reconquistar el suelo patrio resultaron estériles.

records.headline: HAYTI AND ST. DOMINGO.
records.summary_en: The *Weekly National Intelligencer* described Dominican efforts following the February 1844 declaration of independence to obtain an official French protectorate at Samaná. Despite repeated Dominican overtures offering protectorate status, ownership, or complete sovereignty to France, King Louis Philippe and later the French Provisional Government declined to assume the role due to diplomatic concerns.
records.summary_es: El *Weekly National Intelligencer* reseñó las gestiones entabladas por los dominicanos con posterioridad a la proclamación de independencia de febrero de 1844 para recabar de Francia un protectorado formal sobre Samaná. records.full_text:
HAYTI AND ST. DOMINGO.

The official paper of France (the Moniteur) lately contained an article from which we translate the following paragraphs:

“The Emperor Faustin I, immediately upon his accession to power, manifested his hostile views against the people of the eastern part of the island of Hayti, who, after the fall of the President Boyer, in 1844, had proclaimed their independence and established the Dominican Republic.

“The first essay of the Haitien Emperor, however, was not fortunate; defeated at the battle of the Ocoa, in 1849, his armies were entirely broken up, and he was obliged to retire, followed by the Dominicans, who would have carried their successes much further had it not been for the friendly mediation of the Powers which intervened in the conflict.

“On this occasion France was naturally called upon to act the first part. In 1843, in fact, before the division of the island had taken place, and when the eastern part was yet under the Haytien yoke, the inhabitants of the province of St. Domingo had, of their own accord, invoked the protection of the King of the French, and offered, on this condition, to deliver up to him the peninsula and bay of Samana.

“This treaty, accepted by M. Ferdinand Barrot, was ratified at Paris early in 1844. Soon after France fulfilled the first engagement it had assumed, by causing the Dominican movement to be supported by Vice Admiral de Moges, commander of the West India squadron. Strong in this support, the Dominicans were enabled to maintain their separation, and on the 27th February, 1844, hoisted the national flag.

“When, however, the French Government came to be called upon to carry out the conditions of the treaty of 1843, the Chamber of Deputies was not favorably inclined to it; they found that it would be dangerous to accept a military post in the proximity of a colony which had so cruelly escaped from us, and in the possession of which an attempt might be made to establish ourselves; moreover, and above all, the Chamber did not like to take up a position which seemed to engage us to assume in future the permanent protectorate of the Dominican Republic.

“These considerations prevailed: the treaty of 1843 was abandoned; the peninsula of Samana was not occupied; but France, nevertheless, remained the declared protectress of the new State, and it was in this capacity that she afterwards offered her mediation to put an end to the contest between the Haitiens and the Dominicans.”

The readers of the Intelligencer will not have forgotten that this was the project which was defeated by the unremitted vigilance and resolute conduct of the lamented Commodore Knox. The scheme is far from being abandoned, as the public may soon have occasion to perceive. England has already secured an island (the island of Alta Vela) in the same quarter, but having an eye to an establishment on that very point of Samana.

records.headline: OUR NATIONAL REPUTATION.
records.summary_en: The *West-Jersey pioneer* reported on December 18, 1852, that recurring American expeditions against Cuba and the Rio Grande caused neighboring regions—including St. Domingo, which barred its doors against foreigners—to view American commercial enterprises with extreme suspicion as disguised filibuster incursions. The newspaper lamented that these actions damaged the reputation of the United States, causing foreign nations to regard the American government as a piratical force rather than an honorable republic.
records.summary_es: El *West-Jersey pioneer* expuso el 18 de diciembre de 1852 que las recurrentes intentonas expedicionarias estadounidenses contra Cuba y el río Bravo suscitaron que los territorios colindantes —incluido Santo Domingo, que cerró sus accesos a los forasteros— contemplasen los tratos mercantiles norteamericanos con hondo recelo, teniéndolos por desembarcos filibusteros solapados. El periódico deploraba que tales desafueros menoscabaran el crédito de Estados Unidos, incitando a las potencias extranjeras a considerar al gobierno estadounidense como una potencia corsaria antes que como una república honorable.

records.full_text: From the Saturday Gazette. OUR NATIONAL REPUTATION. The United States is rapidly becoming the terror of the world. We are a nation of filibusters and colonizers of weaker nations, whose territories lie within range of our commerce or speculation. New Grenada is alarmed at the infusion of our population into her territories, and last, of all, the little republic of St. Domingo has been in a panic about a report, received by way of Turks Island, to the effect that an American steamer had put into Puerto Plata, but had fled on sight of an English steamer, and that this solitary steamer was bound to land a force that would take possession of the Dominican Republic and straightway annex it to the dominions of Uncle Sam. However absurd such a report might be made, it is wild to suppose that the government of the United States would sanction it, or shoulder the responsibility of it. It would rather have declared the whole affair illegal and outrageous, and done every thing to give up the lawless invaders to the justice of the injured government. That such would have been the result, we have an assurance in the policy laid down by our government, in various administrations, when similar troubles have been menacing us with Canada, Cuba and Mexico. But neither the declared policy nor the actual practice of a government can give confidence to foreign powers, so long as the shameless spirit of encroachment, annexation and revolution exists as it does among so large a portion of the American people. The lawlessness of a class inspires more faith than the promises of a President, and the reputation of the nation suffers for the shamelessness of a faction. Thus it is that every commercial enterprise that is set on foot in an American port is at once looked upon as a Fillibuster expedition in disguise. Cuba shakes in her shores at the sight of an American steamer; St. Domingo bars her doors on all foreigners, lest a stray American invader may come in and upset her government, and we shall next hear that Soulouque, the supreme, the Emperor of Hayti, drawing a cordon across his land frontier and fortifying his ports, to prevent his Imperial domains from being carried off bodily to be annexed to the great American Republic. While we can laugh at the folly of these foreign fears, we cannot help lamenting that the name of the United States should have fallen into such an odium as to justify, in the slightest degree, such absurd alarms. But, thanks to the oft-repeated and shameless enterprises upon cuba and the Rio Grande, the government of the republic fought for by the fathers, and identified in all honor by Washington and those around him, has now come to be looked on as a species of piratical craft cruising in all seas, and ready to plunder and capture all foreign property. It is beginning to be a sort of national Rob Roy, whose policy is '—the simple plan, That they shall take who have the power, And they shall keep who can.' Right-minded citizens, who respect national honesty and deem acts of national wrong as shameful as pocket-picking, should set their faces against all movements that may tend to strengthen the opprobrium into which we have fallen among foreign governments. The mere fact of our being a nation of unexampled prosperity, and rapidly growing in wealth and power, should not satisfy us, so long as we are looked upon abroad as a lawless people, with a government incapable of checking the growing popular frenzy for annexation. There is something more than mere power and wealth to be attained by a nation—and that is the reputation as well as the fact of national integrity.

records.summary_en: The editorial calls it preposterous for The Union to talk of the United States assuming a protectorate over the Dominican Republic, or over any of the republics south of the United States, and says the true American policy is to keep clear of all protectorates. It argues that the Dominicans themselves would refuse and repudiate such protection, having instead solicited France for eight years, so that an American protectorate would have to be enforced at the cannon's mouth while France's would be welcomed.
records.summary_es: El editorial califica de absurdo que The Union hable de que los Estados Unidos asuman un protectorado sobre la República Dominicana, o sobre cualquiera de las repúblicas al sur de los Estados Unidos, y sostiene que la verdadera política estadounidense es mantenerse alejada de todo protectorado. Argumenta que los propios dominicanos rechazarían y repudiarían tal protección, pues en cambio la han solicitado a Francia durante ocho años, de modo que un protectorado estadounidense tendría que imponerse a cañonazos, mientras que el de Francia sería bien recibido.

records.summary_en: The *Daily National Intelligencer* reported that a mission by the Creole Minister of Foreign Affairs failed to persuade the Haitian Emperor Soulouque to sign a peace treaty or a ten-year truce with St. Domingo. Soulouque argued that the island was naturally one and indivisible, viewing the Dominicans as rebels who had no right to secede, and therefore peremptorily declined the propositions through his Senate. However, the Emperor's Minister of Foreign Affairs subsequently volunteered a positive assurance that hostilities against the Dominicans would not be renewed.
records.summary_es: El *Daily National Intelligencer* refirió que la legación encabezada por el canciller de origen criollo no logró inducir al emperador haitiano Soulouque a pactar un tratado de paz ni una tregua decenal con Santo Domingo. Soulouque adujo que la isla era indivisible por naturaleza, conceptuando a los dominicanos como facciosos sin potestad para segregarse, por cuya causa desestimó rotundamente las proposiciones ante su Senado. Con todo, el ministro de Negocios Extranjeros imperial brindó ulteriormente seguridades formales de que no se reanudarían las hostilidades contra los dominicanos.

The December number, for January, 1853, will be the first of the forty-first volume of the Knickerbocker Magazine.
Since the price of subscription has been reduced from five to three dollars a year, the circulation of the Knickerbocker has been increased nearly four to one. In many places ten are sold where there was but one before, and through the year it has been steadily increasing. It is now offered as cheap as any of the Magazines, all things considered. Instead of making new and prodigious promises, we submit a few extracts from notices of late numbers, which we might extend to a number of pages.
Those familiar with the Editor's monthly "gossip" with his readers have, doubtless, with ourselves, admired the taste and judgment displayed in the selection of articles that adorn its pages. It is a sufficient guarantee that no contribution is admitted to its pages that is not in every way worthy of his perusal. When storms and wild tempests are abroad, and the "stormy spirit of the storm" is out, and all is drear and desolate without, ask for no more agreeable companion than the KNICKERBOCKER. Its contents impart valuable information, its sallies of genuine wit are a sovereign specific for all the "ills that flesh is heir to," and it never fails to drive away the "blue devils" of the horrors, and time passes merrily on.—[Courier, Burlington, Vermont.]
[National Intelligencer, Washington.]
'The December number of the Knickerbocker is a capital one. It contains a very interesting article on "The Creole Minister of Foreign Affairs," which gives a graphic account of the mission of the late Mr. Walsh to the Court of the Emperor of Hayti. Mr. Walsh was sent by the United States Government to negotiate a treaty of peace between the Emperor and the Government of St. Domingo. He had several interviews with the Creole Minister of Foreign Affairs, but failed to accomplish the object of the mission. Neither persuasion nor argument could induce the Emperor to make a definite treaty of peace, or a truce of ten years, with the Government of St. Domingo, which he regarded as a rebel whose subjection was necessary to the maintenance of his own authority. He argued that nature had designed the whole island to be under one Government, that the constitution of Hayti so declared it, and that he was bound to maintain the integrity of his empire. The article is well written, and contains much interesting information.'
'The Knickerbocker has been and will be a fact of its own: it is a sort of "institution." We never yet took up a new number of its pages, filled with articles not printed from English authors, but we felt a sort of "home-feeling" in its company and welcome.'—New York Christian Inquirer.

records.summary_en: The newspaper criticizes United States policy toward Hayti, attributing it to slavery-dominated diplomacy and the failure to recognize Hayti's independence. It reports that, following domestic interference and joint bullying with foreign governments, the French have taken possession of Samana as a naval station under the pretext of intervening for Dominica. The publication warns that this acquisition will allow France to monitor American commerce and facilitate hostile actions against the United States in the event of war.
records.summary_es: El periódico desaprueba la directriz diplomática de Estados Unidos hacia Haití, imputándola a la servidumbre de intereses proesclavistas y al desconocimiento de su independencia. La publicación previene que dicho enclave consentirá a Francia vigilar las rutas mercantiles norteamericanas y propiciar acometidas bélicas contra Estados Unidos en coyunturas de guerra.

records.summary_en: The *Wilmington Journal* reported on December 24, 1852, that the Dominican Republic had long sought French protection and offered annexation, a step the current French Emperor was taking to secure a strategic point for monitoring American movements regarding Cuba under existing treaties. The newspaper contrasted the history of the former Spanish portion—which achieved independence without a servile insurrection and retained a white and mixed population superior in society and education—with the former French portion (Hayti), where a violent slave uprising had occurred.
records.summary_es: El *Wilmington Journal* comunicó el 24 de diciembre de 1852 que la República Dominicana procuró largamente el patronato de Francia y propuso su anexión, resolución que el actual soberano galo aprovechaba para guarecer un apostadero estratégico desde el cual observar las maniobras norteamericanas respecto a Cuba al amparo de las convenciones vigentes. El diario contrastaba los antecedentes de la antigua sección española —que conquistó su autonomía sin insurrecciones de esclavos y preservó un vecindario blanco y mestizo más encumbrado en cultura y letras— con la antigua colonia francesa (Haití), teatro de un sangriento levantamiento servil.

records.summary_en: The *Pawtucket Gazette and Chronicle* reported that Haitian Emperor Soulouque rejected Dominican independence, insisting the island was indivisible, though he offered assurances that hostilities would not resume. The ongoing truce was attributed in part to the depletion of the Haitian treasury following Soulouque’s lavish coronation ceremonies. An observer, Mr. Walsh, concluded that Dominican independence could ultimately only be maintained by force of arms against Haiti.

La subsistencia del armisticio obedecía en grado sumo a la ruina del erario haitiano provocada por los suntuosos fastos de coronación del monarca. Un observador, el comisionado Walsh, dedujo que la independencia dominicana sólo podría asegurarse a la postre por la vía de las armas contra Haití.

records.summary_en: On January 19, 1853, *The Republic* reported that Mr. Soulé submitted a resolution requesting the President to provide the Senate with State Department information concerning American citizens' claims against Hayti and correspondence from the 1849 special agent who reported on the condition of the Island of St. Domingo. The newspaper also noted that Mr. Brooke withdrew a resolution regarding the suspension of official relations with Nicaragua's minister for later introduction in Executive session. Additionally, the Senate considered Mr. Cass's joint resolutions reaffirming the Monroe Doctrine and applying it to Cuba.

La gaceta registró asimismo que el Sr. Brooke retiró una moción tendiente a interrumpir los lazos diplomáticos con el ministro de Nicaragua a fin de someterla en sesión secreta. El Senado atendió además las resoluciones conjuntas del senador Cass que revalidaban la Doctrina Monroe aplicándola a Cuba.

records.summary_en: The *New-York Daily Tribune* reported on January 19, 1853, that a treaty with France involved aiding individuals to dismember Haytian territory and establish a new government through a revolutionary conspiracy. The article compared this French action to supporting South Carolina in seceding from the Federal Union and suggested that the Emperor of Hayti would be justified in considering the French debt cancelled if France does not disclaim the acts. Finally, the excerpt questions whether the Emperor of Hayti will dare to challenge Emperor Napoleon III and the power of France.

records.headline: FROM OUR PARIS CORRESPONDENT.
records.summary_en: The *Daily National Intelligencer* reported on foreign newspaper discussions regarding rumored French acquisitions, specifically the alleged occupation of the Samana peninsula by French forces and a possible French protectorate over the Dominican Republic. French sources, such as *La Patrie* and the *Journal des Débats*, dismissed reports of a territorial seizure, attributing the presence of the French frigate *la Sibylle* to a routine cruise following an epidemic in Martinique. Additionally, the *Journal des Débats* recalled that a decade prior, the Dominican Republic had offered a protectorate to Louis Philippe to protect against western neighbors, which was interrupted by the 1848 revolution.
records.summary_es: El *Daily National Intelligencer* resumió el debate en diarios del exterior respecto a supuestas anexiones francesas, singularmente la alegada ocupación de la península de Samaná por destacamentos galos y un previsible protectorado sobre la República Dominicana. Fuentes de prensa francesas como *La Patrie* y el *Journal des Débats* descartaron una usurpación de tierras, explicando que la navegación de la fragata gala *la Sibylle* obedecía a un crucero ordinario tras una epidemia sufrida en Martinica. El *Journal des Débats* rememoró además que diez años atrás la República Dominicana brindó el protectorado a Luis Felipe para guarecerse de sus convecinos occidentales, proyecto truncado por la revolución de 1848.

records.full_text:
All the news from France seems to-day to confirm the story of the imperial programme announced in the Moniteur on the 1st of January. Indeed, the French have the few words uttered by the Emperor himself at the Tuileries on the 1st January, in reply to felicitations of the Diplomatic Corps, at the head of the few members of the diplomatic corps whom the official sheet represents as having been present to present themselves, had repaired to the palace to offer to the Emperor the compliments of the season. He said:
"I trust, with the Divine protection, to be enabled to maintain the prosperity of France, and assure the peace of Europe."
Then we have a little note in the official Moniteur, which was no sooner inserted in the official sheet than it formed part of NAPOLEON III. to the odious treaties of 1815, which it was the ambition of his life to undo, as ruinous and degrading to France. This curious note was elicited by the evident sensation produced in the political circles (if there can be said to be political circles now in France) by the appearance of a pamphlet entitled Limites de la France, the object of which was to indicate the tendency of the new Government to total conquest, or at least the absorption of all nations and fractions of nations west of the Alps and the Rhine. This publication was so identified in style and arguments with those which preceded and pamphlets which occur instantly to every one's mind as issuing from the highest source, as preceded the advent of the empire, that, of course, the bare announcement of the title caused all ears to prick up and all eyes to open wide. The author of Limites de la France published, it was asked, if it were not approved of? It would have been so easy to prevent it—to refuse the Government imprint. Sensation becoming so deep, the pamphlet in question was really intended to indicate the line of policy intended to sound public opinion upon the subject. The Government, soliciting this impression, and innocent of preparing, seeing that its silence was being interpreted in a manner dangerous, deemed it best—as Government is bound to do under such circumstances—instantly did, what it had formerly done in relation to the pamphlet which preceded the Empire, and which was used under its cover for the preparation of the empire; and what it did, not with regard to a compromising document upon Swiss affairs, published by a member of the Government, came out and repudiated all connection with the document, in the Moniteur of yesterday, the 5th of January, in the French, following and satisfactory terms:
"There have appeared recently several works, one among others under a title which seems calculated to excite—they seem to be intended to flatter tendencies which are supposed to exist in the French nation. The Moniteur repels all connection with the authors of these works, of which the spirit is as far removed from the intentions of the Emperor as from his loudly-declared policy."
After this, it is to be hoped that the most suspicious and incredulous as to the origin and intent of Limites de la France will submit his error, and abandon his apprehensions. To be sure, the Empire has come, as predicted by the pamphleteers of two and three years ago, and the said pamphleteers are now high in imperial favor. But that I don't pretend to be any thing more than a remarkable coincidence, which if I were a French writer it would be very indiscreet to remark upon. To be sure, the document on Swiss affairs, of which the existence was so positively denied, was afterwards published, in totidem verbis. That was certainly unlucky; but it does not authorize the suspicion, and still less the plain charge, that the disclaimer above quoted from the Moniteur is not irreproachably sincere and correct.
Extraordinary movement in the high functionary world has taken place in France upon the occasion of the new year. A decree of the 31st December nominated thirty-three new Senators. This body may now consist of 150 members, besides the ex-officio members, i. e. the French princes, the cardinals, marshals, and admirals of France. Six seats, original creation, by the decree of 1852, still remain, therefore, yet unfilled, in order to complete the Senate, forty-four nominations to make. These will doubtlessly be held back, only to be used to reward possible future exigencies. I must mention some of the names of the new Senators. The MARQUIS DE DAMPIN, the MARQUIS DE LAROCHEJAQUELIN, and the DUKE DE MOUCHY. These are three Legitimists, who have rallied to the Empire. In the Senate, M. DUPIN (ainé) has been replaced by Henry V. upon whom they wished to impose their own peculiar views as to the political course he should pursue. Legitimism has lost almost from history one of its most illustrious names, which he inherited, coming with all the luster that approved devotion to a principle, loyal fidelity to the King, and chivalric heroism could cast upon it, of which he never had any thing to bestow upon a cause, but which he has to-day honored by the connection with it in his person of the Senatorial dignity under an imperial Bonaparte. We have also M. DE HEECKEREN, late Baron DE ANTHES. This is the person who went to England to arrange Sir HUDSON LOWE after the death of Napoleon I, and who went to Russia, who was so grossly and publicly insulted the keeper of the Emperor. Beside these three, we have in the Senate three names of note: then M. FIALIN DE PERSIGNY, the devoted Minister of Louis Napoleon on 2d December, 1851; CLARY; SANTOUR DE LA TRESSONIER; MARSHAL VAILLANT; LUGUI; LUCIEN BONAPARTE, cousin of the Emperor Napoleon III, and son of Lucien Bonaparte; the DUKE DE BASSANO, and TASSCHER DE LA PAGERIE, cousin of the Empress.
The military enterprise of Count G. DE RAOUSSET-BOULBON in Northern Mexico, has, as might be expected, excite here a marked interest. The Paris papers give a large share in their columns to the latest news from the scene of operations. The Assemblée Nationale publishes the following letter from the French adventurer, written, it would seem, when just upon the eve of starting upon his expedition. If it has not yet appeared in print in the United States, it will be read with interest:
"I have for a year devoted my whole life, all my resources, all my exertions to the realization of a colossal enterprise, one of the boldest which has been witnessed for a long time. I have fully succeeded in my combinations, and I am now about to put my projects into execution. I start with two hundred men, adventurous, resolute, and full of faith. I shall find reinforcements in the country. I have foot soldiers, horsemen, and cannon, and I am about to put my project into execution..."
The Moniteur, among its foreign items, has merely stated the fact of the conquest of Count RAOUSSET-BOULBON—but the semi-official comments, in a tone, however, which would indicate a thorough consciousness of the danger of the ground they were treading on, and of the immenseness of collision with the United States, if this Government should give the slightest intimation of an intention to profit by the victory of the French band of adventurers in Northern Mexico, for the establishment of "a nascent colony" or by asserting the protectorate of an independent State upon the North American continent or on the borders of the United States. But I apprehend no such result. Whatever may be his personal instincts, by those of a victorious, NAPOLEON III. will seek other vent for his lust of enlarged dominion. He meditates other conquests; for the success of which he desires, IF NOT WINS THE AID, AT LEAST THE NEUTRALITY OF THE UNITED STATES. He is conscious, moreover, of many reasons not to provoke us by assuming a sovereignty or a protectorate in defiance with the policy loudly proclaimed by the United States for the last thirty years, and which no European State has dared to contest for the space of even one year. The Count, would-be imitator of Cortez, must therefore, in spite of himself, remain a buccaneer with the products of his enterprise, unless the Mexicans should succeed in repelling him, or unless we should nip his "nascent" glories in the bud by purchase from Santa Anna, and Santa Anna should not succeed to become a citizen of our Republic, or seek his ancient leader, Santa Anna, to the conquest of yet another province from Mexico. The Constitutionnel, I say, in putting allusions to the same subject, before summing up her article, as follows: "This column, which left California to seek its fortune in Mexico, is acting, be it well understood, on its own account, on its own risk and responsibility. It is a romantic episode, but one of an exclusively private character, to which, as between State and State, no importance attaches except as a matter of curiosity. It is strictly for the satisfaction of that word which we borrow from the Courrier des Etats Unis all the new details with which here column is filled..."
This Journal, I remember, has found phrases much less academic than "romantic episode," "column of adventurous spirit," "enterprising spirit," when it attempted to stigmatize the very similar, and certainly equally excuseable, invasions of American citizens into neighboring countries by citizens of our own "enterprising" population. Far be it from me to justify or even to palliate those invasions; but I dislike to see France engaging in these culpable adventures. The French journals have found no terms too severe by which to stigmatize them. I only insist that equal justice be rendered to all, and that an act be not qualified as enterprising, admirable, romantic, chivalrous, or heroic, when it happens to be French or American origin.
The occupation of Samana, in the Dominican Republic, by a portion of the French fleet in the West Indies, has been matter of lively interest here during the last week. What appeared in the official Journal, but—we well understand—La Patrie, a more or less semi-official sheet, thus explains the fact, which it seems has been sadly exaggerated and misinterpreted in the United States. It would certainly add something to the value of this explanation if it had appeared in the official journal; but we well understand how the official would seem not too anxious to show that this Government has avoided interference with the well-known American policy touching European acquisitions of territory or influence on our side of the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. La Patrie would have hardly ventured the following explanation of the Samana affairs if it were not true:
"English and American papers speak of an occupation by the French forces of the peninsula Samana. This news is like all those of the same sort (a very profound invention of the same sort), destitute of all foundation. A mark that the French semi-official) which many foreign sheets, and among them those of the United States, have given to the corvette La Silphide, which had remained in the West Indies, had no other purpose than a change of air. It proceeded upon a cruise in the seas of the Dominican Republic to give a passage to the French Consul, who had previously requested to report upon the news given to him in that country."
The Journal des Débats, alluding to the same report, had previously rated as quite unworthy of credit the supposition that the French Government had seized upon, with intention to appropriate, the eastern portion of the Island or St. Domingo; but regarded as at any rate less improbable than the news that Louis III. had accepted the protectorate of the Dominican Republic. And it calls to mind, in this connection, the fact that ten years ago the Republic offered the protectorate to Louis Philippe, in order to secure it from hostile invasion by its neighbors of the West end. Before Louis Philippe had positively accepted or refused the protectorate, a revolution broke out in Paris and led to negotiations. They were afterwards renewed, and the proposition was finally rejected by France under the Republic. It was apprehended that NAPOLEON III, so solicitous to increase the influence, and especially the maritime force of France in the West Indies, had reviewed and reversed the decision of the statesmen of the Republic. But I feel sure that NAPOLEON III. will commit no such folly; that he has too lively a sense of the "reproach of humiliation and effacement," which he says rests upon France, to seek glory for her at St. Domingo, when opportunities near home, of more facile execution, of better promise; opportunities in which he would be better supported by the strong national instincts, by the fierce, inextinguishable antipathies of his subjects, than he would be were he to throw down his glove to the young giant of America. Selfish, doubtless, and unjust those instincts and evoke those antipathies, and it will require the supreme efforts of all Europe to stay the deluge which may be made to pour upon it from France. A war with the United States would not stir up in France and array for action those terrible elements which would constitute the force of NAPOLEON III, and make him almost invincible if he sagaciously chooses the moment and the occasion for foreign war. Court proceedings revealed a questionable letter involving Senor Jose Maria Pando, the Spanish commercial agent at Curacao, regarding instructions and financial advances for the ship via a merchant in Porto Plata. Additionally, the Dominican Republic celebrated the February 15 inauguration of General Santana as president.

records.full_text:
We have received files of El Progreso, published in Saint Domingo, extending up to the 1st of May. It seems that the Dominicans are making preparations for war, as it is feared that Soulouque might meditate an invasion of their territory. El Progreso says:—

Last week a vessel of war left our port for Azua, loaded with troops; and to-day another goes to the same destination, taking provisions for the army. The Dominican President had already left for that town, where he is organizing a powerful army, capable of supplying the northern frontiers with whatever may be necessary to repel an invasion. Up to the present, no hostile activity on the part of Hayti has been observed; but it is known that Soulouque has assembled a considerable force in the Canton of Maissade, and that a single caprice of the Emperor of Hayti, is sufficient to draw us into an unexpected conflict. Up to the present, the Dominicans have accepted the mediation of the three powers; but we want peace, not a truce, and if Hayti will not make peace, we feel confident that above all the conduct of the Liberator is guided by wisdom and prudence.

The most conclusive argument against force is force itself. We have, besides, an army in the field; and we should not, therefore, be surprised if our liberty is protected by our troops. In the mean time, a Spanish vessel of war, the Cortes, and an English vessel of war, the Cormorant, are in the Canton of Guayubin, as has been reported, to protect their respective subjects; but we are assured that, on the contrary, the intervention of the Spanish vessel, through its captain, has brought about a reconciliation between the two parties.

The Spanish brig of war, Veloz, under the command of Don Carlos Valcarcel, had arrived at Saint Domingo on the 26th of April, bringing on board the envoy of the President of the republic in the name of Her Catholic Majesty. On coming into port, the Veloz saluted the Dominican flag with twenty-one guns, which were returned by the fort. The Spanish captain and officers were received at the house of the President of the Republic with the highest honors, and were entertained at a banquet given in their honor.

On Sunday, the 17th of April, the ratification of the treaty of peace, navigation and commerce between France and the Dominican Republic was celebrated in Saint Domingo with great pomp. The day was announced by the firing of cannon and the ringing of the cathedral bells. Three high masses were celebrated in the cathedral, after each of which off went a broadside from the French vessel of war, Iphigenie, which was lying in port; after which the French flag was hoisted on the cathedral, and the French consul was received at the portal by the President of the Republic. In the evening a grand ball was given by the President, at which all the authorities, civil and military, were present. The festivities were concluded on the 18th, when the treaty was solemnly ratified with a salvo of twenty-one guns.

records.summary_en: The *Port Gibson Reveille* reported the arrival of a Spanish brigantine under Don Carlos Valcarcel from Puerto Rico to congratulate the President of the Dominican Republic on behalf of her Catholic Majesty. Additionally, the newspaper covered the grand celebration in St. Domingo on Sunday, April 17, marking the ratification of a treaty between the French Empire and the Dominican Republic with music, fireworks, balloons representing friendly nations, and a solemn church service accompanied by military salutes.

El periódico reseñó asimismo las solemnidades cívicas celebradas en Santo Domingo el domingo 17 de abril para festejar la ratificación del tratado entre el Imperio francés y la República Dominicana, concurridas con acordes marciales, fuegos de artificio, globos alegóricos a potencias amigas y una misa de acción de gracias con salvas de ordenanza.

records.headline: The revision of the Dominican Cogstitution, for which an extreordinary session
records.summary_en: According to the *New-York daily tribune* on April 21, 1854, martial law was declared in Santiago following a conspiracy, with five ringleaders before the court and over forty persons under arrest. Meanwhile, the revision of the Dominican Constitution was completed, featuring an increased number of representatives and senators, the creation of a vice president, and changes reducing the naturalization time periods required for foreigners to become eligible as representatives and senators. Additionally, while the standard presidential and vice-presidential term was set at four years, actual President General Santana was granted two terms in office, allowing him to hold the chair until February 1861.
records.summary_es: Con arreglo al *New-York daily tribune* del 21 de abril de 1854, se declaró el estado de sitio en Santiago a raíz de una conspiración, encausándose ante los jueces a cinco cabecillas y permaneciendo más de cuarenta sujetos en prisión. Entre tanto, concluyó la reforma de la Constitución dominicana, elevándose la representación en el cuerpo legislativo con mayor número de diputados y senadores, estableciéndose la magistratura de vicepresidente y abreviándose los plazos de avecindamiento para que los forasteros optasen a ser elegidos representantes y senadores. Asimismo, fijándose en cuatro años el mandato ordinario del presidente y vicepresidente, al actual mandatario, general Santana, se le concedieron dos períodos sucesivos, autorizándosele a regir la presidencia hasta febrero de 1861.

records.full_text:
TO THE EDITOR OF THE NEW YORK HERALD.

The Evening Post, in an article so maliciously and contemptibly false that it could not possibly be written by a gentleman, and to which no gentleman would condescend a written answer, accuses me of playing a very secondary part in what he calls the "St. Domingo intrigue." My whole course in the matter of a Dominican treaty, from the first moment of her revolution to and since annexation, will answer for me; nor did I ever speak or think of influencing any man's party or acting on any man's dictation.

By one accident, has happened one truth: I do feel a deep sympathy for the brave Dominicans, and I shall not be driven by the tricks of any anti-American clique, or partisan who prostitute their cause until the Dominican republic obtains its deserved and honored place in the family of free American States. I protest against the insolence of the Post in abandoning my principles whenever the popular tide sets against them, or fleeing my colors from newspaper warfare.

I could not descend to reply to the Post—for my way—but it is my duty as an American citizen to throw light on the subject of the Dominican treaty.

I charge the New York Evening Post with working—at standard prices—for His Imperial Majesty Faustin I., Emperor of Hayti, for the destruction of the white population of that island.

I charge it—in its capacity of organ and co-laborer of the imperial government of Faustin I.—with habitually garbling and suppressing the news from St. Domingo, for the purpose of keeping people from turning their attention and sympathy to that brave struggle of the Dominicans for liberty and self-government. It has aimed to sustain Hayti in its anti-American system for the exclusion of whites, and as such, has denied the right to carry into their territory an army of invasion for the purpose of destroying her sovereignty.

I charge it with asserting disgraceful ignorance or wilful falsehood, in asserting that the Dominican is not an independent state, and that there is not a negro in the Dominican territory, while the fact is that the number of pure black Haytien inhabitants in this small American State is smaller than of any other.

I charge it with attempting to deceive and mislead the American people by fabricating, under the form of Post editorials, the fabulous bulletins of Soulouque, written by his own tools; of glossing over the invasion of the Dominican republic in 1849; and of glossing over, and indirectly justifying, the burning of whole villages, and the indiscriminate slaughter of women, children, and even domestic animals, on his savage march. Faustin and the Post say he marched an army into the Spanish portion of the island, "with the intention of restoring the integrity of the republic." They suppress the history of Soulouque's humiliating defeat at Las Carracas, by a small force of Dominicans, and his retreat—or rather his covered retreat by stating that, "in consequence of the mutual distress of the troops, and the impossibility of getting food for his horses, he was obliged to return;" but "gave notice that he intended to renew hostilities the following year—1850"

The Post says, Mr. Pierce ought not to send Mr. Fillmore "to prevent Soulouque's executing his purpose of subduing Hispaniola to his government and territory," and is as indignant as his friend Faustin can be at Mr. Fillmore's threat to check these wholesale butcheries. It regrets that "this absurd pretension directly led to a second attempt by Soulouque with more respect than it deserved—for he did not make it until the Dominicans refused to give any pledges for the future;" and then this false organ of Hayti adds, "the President could not put it hard in so publishing the affair as to make it appear that the threats of the United States had any effect, for the simple reason that these things are taken from its own open and glorified in-structions to the French commander." This was a significant visit of one of the concern to Hayti! and the author of the article above quoted was sent to learn what reward for past service, or what pay for future exertion, was then arranged with Faustin.

Finally, I charge the Post with wilfully misrepresenting the Dominican government and people, in order to discourage the American government and people, in order to prevent a treaty between them... and turn it, if possible, into Haytien channels, to carry out their plan of Haytien policy, which is already enjoying the best of the St. Domingo trade, through secret pay with the Haytien government. This young, enlightened and pro-gressive people, with a debt of not a dollar in their treasury, has ably sustained its domestic government for ten years, and is as free to form alliance and make treaties with other nations as any nation on earth, and far more worthy of American sympathy.

I finally charge the Post with subterfuge in in-sinuating that the President is attempting by these in-trigues to frighten weaker children than itself—if it refers to the Dominican people as symptoms of new slave States and future annexations. I have had no interest, directly or indirectly, in the Dominican treaty, nothing to hide, deny or conceal in my plans, princi-ples or conduct.

Whatever I have done in the matter of Dominican independence, has been because I thought it right, necessary and beneficial to both countries; and while life lasts, my whole influence, so far as it extends, shall be used to preserve the white race from Haytien supremacy.

WILLIAM L. CAZNEAU.

records.full_text:
It would hardly seem possible to deny, in a formal manner, the ridiculous stories put in circulation by the New York Evening Post respecting Gen. Cazneau's mission last winter to St. Domingo. His honorable career as a public officer, his high standing in Texas as head of the State Department, attest his character and capacity in a sufficient manner; but the letter we give below is the most complete refutation that could be given to the unmerited attacks of the Evening Post. It tells its own story, and we think our New York contemporary will find it no easy matter to extricate itself from its false position—never so satisfactorily as Gen. Cazneau does his with the Dominican and the Dominican republic.

To the Editor of the Union:
The Evening Post persists in grossly misrepresenting the Dominican people, and even goes so far in its spirit of Haytien partisanship as to deny that I desire the white or mixed race to be dominant. It branded that article as "so malicious and false that it could not possibly be written by a gentleman;" and if that is what the editor of the Post calls an admission of the truth, he is welcome to all the benefit of it. I ask no authority for its assertions, and I most emphatically deny, so far as I am concerned, all knowledge, past or present, of any "conspiracy" or "design," on my part for the acquisition of Domingo.

I do know, however, that the people of the Dominican republic, are anxious for the recognition of their independence, and of public justice. It has a right to expect this from our government; and its recognition as an act of justice and public faith. It has a right to expect this from our government; and its recognition and application as will secure that promising young State from the aggressions of Hayti.

It is the duty of the United States government to carefully promote our commerce with all the Republics on this continent.

Our ships are in a position to do their carrying-trade, and we should encourage and facilitate them in every way for the requirements of their people. It is our interest to cherish the peace of the world, and expand our commerce with all the American States, for their wealth and strength contribute to our own. It is our duty to maintain our peace with all European powers, in opposition to the present and future pretensions of European discussion. This is the principle of the American Monroe doctrine. The recognition of Dominica has long been urged upon my friends the propriety of giving it our warmest support. Generals Cass, Douglas, Houston, Rusk, and many other distinguished members of both houses of Congress, have advocated it with success, and their authority should be as good authority with an enlightened people as that of the Evening Post.

"We infer," says the Post, coming at last to the real question, "that it is the intention of the Dominican party to claim that Dominicans and Hayti are two different races; and that it is the interest of the whites for which they contend."

This is precisely the issue; they are different races: Dominicans are white and mixed, the Haytiens are black; and I repeat, and, a white government. I repeat, Mr. Editor, what I said, that, "since the late peace congress, or the convention, that has just adjourned, who has no sympathy with the color of his line. Hayti is an intolerant, irresponsible, stubborn negro despotism, without a language, though their tongue assimilates to the French.

They are governed throughout by men of pure African race. In their wars, they are as merciless as savages; and it has been, on more than one occasion, their declared intention to wholly annihilate the white and mixed race on this island. The Post is extremely unfortunate in taking into its service "rights of Hayti," which the Post's editorials maintain in terms remarkably like the official bulletins of Soulouque.

The Dominican people, on the contrary, are brave, orderly, and peaceful. Their long conflict, "sustained by their own courage," is proved by the manner in which they have successfully maintained their independence since the expulsion of the Haytien government in 1844. They have been victorious in every battle with the Haytiens; and always against great odds. In the battle of Las Carreras, Faustin had five hundred men, (and three pieces of artillery,) killed; yet the Dominicans had the character and courage to cut off his retreat, taking several pieces of artillery. His retreat across the frontier was characterized by Haytien cruelties, by the sacrifice of blood and ashes, by the destruction of property and the cruel slaughter of women and children.

Haytien atrocities cause among the colored Dominicans that horror which I take to be common to their race, to torture and murder the whites in the interior districts. They were used until the Dominicans were compelled to make slaves of them—in the style of the Post planters, which they "succeeded in doing;" but the Dominican blacks were not ignorant enough to believe those white men were their enemies; and, if the Post's editorial does not cause distress, and should fail to shake them, American slavery would be more tolerable than the Haytien, which alarms and excites the blacks into insurrection, while it defends the "rights of Hayti," to make a general destruction of the white race.

The editor of the Post may keep his eyes on the white race of the world, but he cannot see that a white-black war in Dominica would not destroy the line of white people, as it does in some of our southern States—but it is surprising that he, on the contrary, insists that we are doing nothing to promote peace and harmony between the white and black populations.

I not only "pretend to believe," but positively assert, that there are African fringe in that brave soldier and patriot statesman, President Santana. Look at the president of Hayti, Faustin, and at President Santana, educated in Louisiana, and Senior Baez, a quadroon—and compare the former monster in the South upon that accomplished gentleman as a "full-blooded white man." The American consul, or commercial agent, at Santo Domingo may inform the Post whether he considers his father-in-law, the dignified Don Domingo de la Roca, a white man. He is the minister said to be now in charge of the government, while Santana heads the army. Baez was a quadroon, but he owed his short-lived elevation to European intrigues, which are always at work in the Antilles to elevate the African, and harass and subdue the white race. He attempted, with their aid, to fraternize with Hayti, and was banished from the country in consequence.

The editor of the Post probably met some of the Baez party last winter, in the select circles of the negro nobility, during his stay of about six months ago. This is very natural, considering some of his extraordinary information in regard to Santo Domingo; for example—"that there are not two hundred whites, all told, sailors and diplomats included," in the republic of Santo Domingo.

The editor of the Post informs his readers that he knew nothing about me six months ago. This is very natural, considering the difference in our tastes and associations; but there is no occasion for the rancorous violence he exhibits because I prefer the free, permanent and intelligent white society of Dominica to the attractions of his Haytien circle. He may don a coat of mail, if he choose, and present a breastwork to Hayti; but I did not thereupon write home slanderous attacks upon the character of a citizen who was doing no wrong to his family. Men do not engage in work like this. My own character is above the reach of those mischievous misrepresentations which are calculated to lead to the wholesale murder of the white race in the island of Santo Domingo.
WM. L. CAZNEAU.

records.full_text:
It was hardly worth the trouble to deny, in a formal manner, the ridiculous stories put in circulation by the New York Evening Post respecting Gen. Cazneau's business last winter in St. Domingo. His honorable career as a [illegible] of their people. It is our interest to cherish the power, production, and general welfare of all these American States, and build up a strength to contribute to our own. It is so much strength added to the American force, in opposition to the present and future pretensions of European dictation. This is the principle of the American system, or it has none. In accordance with that principle, I have been urging upon my friends the propriety of giving to the Dominican republic the encouragement of a friendly recognition, as long and as earnestly as I have opposed it in the service of the black Emperor Faustin Soulouque.

The only plan I have ever heard of, or advocated, in connection with Gen. Cazneau, or any successor of his in office, was to strengthen the country relation with all the Spanish American States, and to establish them where they did not exist, as in the case of Dominica. It was only on this principle of American policy, that the recognition of Dominica was discussed with Senators Rusk, Douglas, Mason, Slidell, and many other distinguished members of the Senate, prior to Gen. Cazneau's connection with them; and those gentlemen should be as little suspected of a scheme of "filibustering" as the allies of Faustin.

We infer, says the Post, coming at last to the real question, "that it is the intention of the Post's editorial friends to show that Dominica and Hayti are under the control of different races, and that it is the interest of the whites for which they show such an anxiety."

This is precisely the issue; they are different races. Dominica is governed by civilized white manners, with a democratic constitution, and, obedient to the laws of nations. There is not, to name one man, either in the cabinet, Congress, or the Dominican forces, that has a drop of African blood in his veins. Hayti is an ignorant, barbarous, stubborn negro despotism, without a legal code, and obedient to no laws, unanalogous to the French.

They are governed throughout by men of negro blood and negro ideas. In their wars, they are as merciless enemies to quadroons as to whites, for they audaciously proclaim their intention to wholly annihilate the white and mixed race on the island. This creed of extermination is the leading point in those "rights of Hayti," which the Post's editorials maintain in terms so remarkably like the official bulletins of Soulouque.

The Dominican people, on the contrary, are from Spanish stock, and their character is not "without character and courage," as the Post says. As a matter of history, having sustained themselves since the establishment of their republic, they have been victorious in every battle with the Haytians. Under Santana, as well as under Santana's predecessors—at the battle of Las Carreras, Faustin had five times their force, and yet victory was with the Dominicans. Have the Dominicans had the "character and courage" to put him to flight, with the loss of thousands of his troops? He escaped, and the frontier was characteristic of Haytian warfare, and marked by blood and ashes, by the destruction of property and the cruel slaughter of women and children.

Haytian emissaries came among the colored population in Dominica, and tried to set the country on fire, to incite them to rise and murder the whites in the interior districts. They asserted that the Americans were coming to make slaves of them—in the style of the Post's phraseology about "the extension of slavery;" but the Dominican blacks were not ignorant enough to believe these monstrous absurdities. Their prudence does not excuse, and should put to shame an American journal in continually presenting the case in a shape to alarm and excite the blacks into insurrection, while it defends the "rights of Hayti" to make a general destruction of the white race.

El editorial describe en detalle la bahía de Samaná, su entrada, sus islas y su puerto, y denuncia la adquisición como un punto de apoyo para un gobierno empeñado en extender la esclavitud y como un primer paso hacia la anexión de la isla.

records.headline: From the Boston Commonwealth.
records.summary_en: The *Liberator* reported that the Boston Post defended the United States government's disposition to recognize the independence of Dominica while ignoring the absence of any proposed recognition for Hayti and Liberia, despite stronger commercial and historical reasons to do so. The article argued that Dominica is of little commercial importance and would be politically united with Hayti—from which it rebelled due to religious differences—were it not for outside intrigues. Furthermore, the newspaper claimed that the American "Slave Power" has decided that the prosperity of Dominicans and Haytiens of African descent would injure its "peculiar institution."

La columna aducía que Santo Domingo poseía escaso relieve mercantil y permanecería unido políticamente a Haití —de donde se desgajó por disidencias religiosas— de no mediar intrigas foráneas. Aseveraba además el periódico que el «Poder Esclavista» norteamericano determinó que el florecimiento de dominicanos y haitianos de ascendencia africana perjudicaría a su «peculiar institución».

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
From the Boston Commonwealth.
THE SLAVE POWER AND ST. DOMINGO.

Filibustering Manifest Destiny has proclaimed that the Slave Power must have ‘our Southern islands,’ and that the negroes of Cuba, Hayti, &c., must be doomed to perpetual slavery, and ‘kept at work under white republican masters.’ When this language was used in the Democratic Review, Hayti was named particularly, and it expressed no more than the Slave Power actually means and is now planning to accomplish. The purpose is to get possession of Hayti by means of filibusterism cunningly introduced into Dominica. One insidious attempt has been made upon Dominica, but failed. Duff Green was concerned in that affair, and his son was the agent employed in Dominica by our government. The conspirators sought to make an arrangement with the Dominican authorities, which should secure filibusters the privilege of ‘colonizing’ on that part of the island, with a separate and independent military organization of their own. Ostensibly, they were to be cutters of mahogony and dye woods, but really a filibustering army designed for the subjugation of the island when strong enough in numbers. But the Dominicans were suspicious, and the negotiation fell through.

Recently, Mrs. Cazneau, the ‘Cora Montgomery’ of some of the newspapers, and Gen. Cazneau, her husband, have been sent to Dominica to negotiate, plot, and intrigue, in behalf of this scheme of the Slave Power; and ‘Cora,’ it is said, has far more genius for the business than the General. It is reported that they have made some progress, that our Government will make a formal treaty with Dominica, and recognize its independence as a nation, and that the matter will soon be in shape to come before Congress. Of course, all this will not be done without such provisions in the treaty as will give our Slave Power that foothold in the island which it seeks. The whole purpose, on the part of our Government, is a filibustering invasion of both Dominica and Hayti. It means nothing else. It is seeking to execute that decree which says the African race in that island must be reduced to slavery, and ‘kept at work under white republican masters.’ If what is reported is true, (and it is fully credited by those likely to be best informed on the subject,) this is one of the next forms in which the slavery question is to be presented to the country, and the people should take it to their thoughts and feelings. The following statement in regard to this Cazneau treaty shows what is on foot:—

‘As far as could be collected from the first proceedings, the treaty is to have for one of its various ostensible objects, to stipulate for certain rights in the ports of the Republic, and especially in the spacious and secure bay of Samana, for the armed vessels of the United States, in case of war, and in time of peace, for the establishment of a kind of colonization, black or white, of individuals from the United States, in some part of the Dominican Republic.’

The Boston Post has already begun its defence of this villany, in a characteristic parrgraph of three or four lines, full of hypocritical wonder that anti-slavery men should put forth hostile criticism on the disposition of our government to recognize the independence of Dominica. Of course, that paper will never intimate to its readers, that, if this disposition of our Government were honest—if it is not, in fact, full of plotting piracy—it would also propose a recognition of the independence of Hayti and Liberia. There are more and stronger reasons for recognizing either of these gevernments than can be invented for this negotiation with Dominica. We have a large commerce with Hayti, and Liberia has grown up under American influences. Dominica is of little or no importance commercially, and would now be politically united with Hayti, if it had not rebelled and withdrawn, because that government proclaimed free toleration of all religious sects. The Dominicans have the religious training and bigotry of Spanish Catholics. They occupy what was the Spanish portion of the island, and the Haytiens that part which was held by the French. But they are all of African descent, and would constitute but one people, if not interfered with by the rascally intrigues of outsiders.

Our Slave Power has decided that it will injure the peculiar institution to allow the Dominicans and Haytiens, whose parents were slaves, to realize a prosperous and happy fortune. It will not do to let the world see them work out for themselves such a fortune; and, moreover, the slaveholders hope to prepare that island for annexation to the Union as a slave State. ‘Our Southern islands,’ they say; and how much that signifies!

records.headline: PARTIES IN THE ISLAND—CAZNEAU'S NEGOTIATIONS.
records.summary_en: The *New-York Daily Tribune* reported on political maneuvering in the Dominican Republic, including past appeals to the United States for annexation or protection against Haitian incursions. President Santana and the Cibao region strongly rejected diplomatic advice to adopt the Haitian flag, threatening instead to invite American forces to assist in conquering Haiti. The report noted that while territory was divided between opposing factions, Haiti contained roughly two-thirds of the island's population.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Daily Tribune* reseñó las maniobras diplomáticas en la República Dominicana, comprendidas las pasadas solicitudes formuladas a Estados Unidos en pos de anexión o resguardo ante las acometidas haitianas. El presidente Santana y los pueblos del Cibao repudiaron categóricamente el consejo diplomático de enarbolar la enseña haitiana, amenazando en su lugar con impetrar el concurso de fuerzas estadounidenses para acometer la conquista de Haití. La crónica hacía notar que, si bien el suelo insular se hallaba escindido entre bandos contrapuestos, Haití concentraba cerca de dos tercios del censo de la isla.
