records.full_text:
Interesting from Santo Domingo.

THE BAEZ PARTY REDUCED TO THE LAST STRAITS—POSITION OF HIS FORCES AT SAN DOMINGO CITY AND SAMANA—WANT OF PROVISIONS—GENERAL PALMANAT AT POINT DE SAMANA—NAVAL NEWS—GERMAN IMMIGRANTS DYING OF HUNGER, ETC.

By the schooner Brenton, from Puerto Plata, we have received files of the Gaceta Oficial of the Dominican republic, from Santiago de los Caballeros, and the following correspondence:

OUR DOMINICAN CORRESPONDENCE.
ST. DOMINGO, Jan. 19, 1858.
Return of the Exiled Correspondent—Position of the Besieging Armies—Surrender of the Baez Steamers—Hopes of Recognition by Foreign Governments—War Vessels Arrived—Naval News, &c.

It is a long time since I had the pleasure to address you, but it has been owing to the political affairs of this country, in consequence of which I have been to exile, residing in Curacoa and Turks' Islands. But now that I am back again, you will receive my letters as regularly as before.

Enclosed you will find a file of the Official Gazette, by which you will perceive that Baez is strictly confined to the city of St. Domingo, and Baez's general at Samana, Gen. Suero, in the city of Samana, by the forces of a large army, besieging said city, where foreign provisions are very scarce, and none at all of the domestic. Produce, also, is very scarce, and the provisions brought by a very few traders, are very small, and sold at exorbitant prices.

According to that account, which confirms the reports brought by the different assemblies of all the communes of the republic, Baez has sent his commissioners to all the towns and villages twelve miles from this city, in order to make a new levy, which has produced a very poor result. Baez's position is very critical. The people are very tired of him, and there is every reason to expect that the new political state of things will soon commence, as Baez suffers the penalty of death for political faults being forever abolished, the right of trial by jury established, harmonizing the democratic principles with the strength of the government. The constitution is favorable to foreigners; not only to those belonging to friendly nations, but to all nations and states of the world that enter into Santo Domingo.

We entertain the hope that as soon as the new authorities take the helm of state we shall see a large number of nations which have representatives in this country take part in it, and we shall see trade again flourishing and concord with international respect, not forgetting that the soil of Santo Domingo is full of resources to be developed by enterprise; and that the whole population of this country, having lost all hope of Baez, expects the new government to expect from every civilized nation that their new rulers will be recognized by the different powers. We have already seen two small sailing vessels of our own fitting for war at Samana, and now there is on the stock at the shipyard of this place three small ones that Baez has on the waters of Samana.

Trade here is getting somewhat better, although money is scarce, and business goes straight and lively, the tobacco crop having been a very large one this year.

[Translated for the New York Herald from La Gaceta Oficial of Santiago de los Caballeros, Jan. 17.]

The facts which the Generals commanding the besieging armies of St. Domingo and Samana, with all their details, have officially communicated to the government, as well as the letters written by private persons from the first of these two places, both to us and to other persons, fully confirm our prediction, that within a very short time we should see the complete downfall of Baez. Such is the inference naturally drawn from the relation made by Gen. Baez at the head of the army besieging the city of St. Domingo, as well as that of Gen. Suero, who commands the troops at Samana, of the loss experienced by them over the troops of Palmanat. No other reason than that he has in advance imposed silence with regard to the siege of Samana could have induced Baez to repeat the repeated defeats our valiant troops caused to him, and it is for this reason that he tries to sustain himself by force of that place is inevitable. It is for this reason that he in advance imposed silence with regard to the war which Generals Puello and Mella are carrying on against the troops of Baez, and prints only reports of the defeats of the enemy, as if a body of troops, residing on that point, has in advance put a curb on Baez's power to corrupt, and monopolized the bad news he is receiving from Samana.

Be this as it may, our predictions receive every day new confirmation relative to the speedy termination of the existence of Baez, whose forces are diminishing every day. As our readers will learn from the communication addressed by Gen. Bide, under date of the 7th inst., to the provisional government, the spirit of revolt against Baez, which is everywhere, and more particularly among the inhabitants of the communes of the south, both on the coast and in the interior, is going on increasing. When Santana left that place it was with no other view than to go to the different communes of St. Domingo, such as San Cristobal, Los Banos and Pajarito, who, unfortunately for them, since the war began, had given their assistance to the faction of Baez, and the troops of the race, who, although small in number, have done great hurt to the provinces. We must, in consequence of this move, expect Baez to invite the population of St. Domingo to surrender within two or three days. It is impossible, besides, the great majority of the population, that Baez has gathered inside the two localities above mentioned, are composed of very poor people, who can produce no bread (nor produce what they did not find) and any others on their small farms which they leave to take up arms; they cannot even eat a little cocoa nut, what kind of food can they get out of them? We do not see how Baez can sustain himself in those two places, both to us and to other persons.

To the above must be added those military persons who, in consequence of their not having received their pay, and idea that our flotilla might cut off their retreat. Poor wretches, they say, 'Baez promises them to-day and to-morrow to pay for their experience, and takes them on board his vessels, and what sort of treatment does he give them?'—they ask—'he leaves them to die of hunger!'

It is known, besides, that the Baez ships sent by Baez to Samana he has not had any news, although they left St. Domingo since the 1st inst. He expects the Baez ship, the Baxe, every moment, but she does not appear. Thus Baez has at present no slip left at his disposal, since those three carry on trade, create no end of trouble, named El Liberador, la Australia and El Cirus, 19 de Julio, having been given up or taken by the forces of the Dominican government, as well as the flotilla of Baez, and the government by Her Commander, and la Merced having been run on shore by a merchant vessel; and as to the former left that place that he was not even able to speak.

According to that account, which confirms the reports, the soldiers who form the battalion under the command of General Palmanat, which has arrived at Samana, have experienced a series of bad treatment and hardships, as is confirmed by the commander of Puerto Plata in his despatch of the 13th instant to the government, in which he states that the former left that place that he was not even able to speak; and to these must be added that the remaining of the peninsula find themselves in a very very bad situation as far as food is concerned, being reduced to eat cocoa nuts and palmae, as stated by the same individual.

What must be added to all these facts is, a sincere sympathy, adds of that his companions act like him, and have fled to St. Domingo and to Samana, for wickedness and crimes, and have made their submission. Only two days ago two or three of them had asked from us their pardon, which we granted them, on condition to the contract on the stipulation of which they had left their work; and to these must be added that their intention, and kept even for some days in the neighborhood of St. Domingo, is to make their submission, as it is intended to send them to the provisional government, to be released by the government, if they have not committed crimes. Why have they not accepted the benevolent offer of Gen. Santana? Because they know, as it is said in the contract, that they would be punished; and those who were under those unfortunate persons had been taken by Gen. Santana with military measures to prevent them from perishing by hunger.

records.summary_en: According to *The New York Herald* on March 4, 1858, French immigrants in Samaná and St. Domingo suffered from severe provisions shortages, resulting in deaths from sickness and famine. The report notes that General Santana had offered to have them provided with land to work in the fields, but questions why the offer was not accepted and criticizes the French Consul for failing to prevent their starvation. Additionally, the newspaper reported on personal intelligence, noting the presence of Judge Bourdier, commissioner to the Sandwich Islands, and Admiral Forrest in town.

La crónica hacía constar que el general Santana se brindó a adjudicarles terrenos de labor, preguntándose por qué no se acogieron a tal providencia y censurando al cónsul galo por no conjurar la hambruna de sus connacionales. El diario consignaba por añadidura notas de sociedad dando cuenta de la estancia en la ciudad del juez Bourdier, comisionado en las islas Sandwich, y del almirante Forrest.

By the schooner Brentea, from Puerto Plata, we have received files of the Gaceta Oficial of the Dominican republic to the 31st January, and a letter from our correspondent at St. Jago de los Caballeros, the provisional seat of government.

OUR DOMINICAN CORRESPONDENCE.
ST. JAGO DE LOS CABALLEROS, }
Jan. 19, 1858. }
Return of the Exiled Correspondent—Position of the Contending Parties—Sufferings of the Baez Partisans—Hopes of Recognition by Foreign Governments—War Vessels Fitting Out—Lack of Provisions—&c.

It is a long time since I had the pleasure to address you, but it has been owing to the political affairs of this country, in consequence of which I have been in exile, residing in Curaçoa and Turks' Islands. But now that I am in freedom again, you will receive my letters as regularly as before.

Enclosed you will find a file of the Official Gazette, by which you will perceive that Baez is confined to the city of St. Domingo, and that the provisional government, heading it in the form of a large army, besieging said city, where foreign provisions are very scarce, and none at all of the domestic. Cattle, equal to $4 to $5 per head produce, &c. are very few, and these destroyed almost daily, three by three and five by five, and sometimes in larger numbers.

The government, as shown by its decree, has appointed by the different conventions of all the communes of the republic, to meet on the 1st of February, at Moca, a town about twelve miles from this city, in order to make a new constitution, reform many of the old laws, and reorganize the republic on a firm and stable basis; and there is every reason to expect that the new political code will be fully adequate to prevent the repetition of the penalty of death for political faults being forever banished; taking a step forward in civilization, and harmonizing the democratic principles with the strength of the executive power, and granting broader security to foreigners; not only to those belonging to friendly nations, but to all, without exception, who may choose to come to the republic.

We entertain the hope that as soon as the new authorities take the helm of the state, foreign nations—such as those which have representatives in this country—will recognize it as a government, which, as it is strictly conformable to the national will, ought not to be delayed. Up to the present, trade has been at a total stand-still, and the entire population of the country are waiting for the extraordinary production of coffee and cocoa to commence, which will give life to business again. We have two small sailing vessels of our own fitting for war at Puerto Plata, and two others at St. Jago, besides three or four small ones that Baez has on the waters of Samana.

According to that account, which confirms us in our opinion that trade has already commenced again at Puerto Plata, and business goes straight and lively, the tobacco crop coming into a very large figure.

[Translated for the NEW YORK HERALD from the Gaceta Oficial, January 31.]

The facts which the Generals commanding the besieging army of the South, as well as those of the North, have officially communicated to the government as to the situation of the forces of the enemy inside the first of these two places, both as to us and other persons, give, week to week, the same idea as to their complete state of distress, and their utter inability to move. Such is the inference naturally drawn from the relation made by an individual who left Samana on the 7th inst., who states that at that date Baez had only sixty men in that peninsula, under the command of General Juan Esteban Francis, who had replaced the expelled Captain Baldomero Victorino.

According to that account, Baez prohibited that the condition which Samana at present is in be spoken of, or the number of his troops there; and brave Generals at the head of the army besieging that place, for the purpose of removing all suspicion on the part of the enemy, had permitted some thirty persons to be taken up by them over the troops of Palmerino. No other reason can be assigned for the extraordinary prohibition. In consequence of the official communications, in which General Juan Esteban Francis speaks of Samana, Baez repeated the default regarding various troops he had in Samana, and by force the fall of that place is inevitable. It is for this reason that he has taken the resolution to enter into a naval war which Generals Puelio and Mella are carrying on with some success in those seas, who have captured two small vessels and burnt two others in Samana, since on that point, Baez having in advance put a curb on the trade of the coasts and monopolized the bad news he is receiving from Samana.

But this is not the only reason which confirms us in our conviction relative to the speedy termination of the blockade of Samana, which was established by General Francis. As our readers will learn from the communication addressed by Gen. Bide, under date of the 7th inst., to the provisional government, the population of that peninsula, which is at present, and more particularly among the inhabitants who have taken up arms for the cause of the city, is going on increasing. When the Arriano left that bay, there were 100 head of cattle, a number not sufficient to provide the entire population of St. Domingo with meat, which is also wanted by the inhabitants of San Carlos and Pajarito, who, unfortunately for them, since the 21st of July, have taken the side of Baez; to say nothing of the troops, and the garrison of the race, who, although small in number, have been made one of the provisions. The stock of taro, planted by the force of Baez, has lasted for about two weeks; but will the poor be able to buy this crop at a cost of 24$ the quintal? This is impossible. Besides, the great majority of the population who inhabit the localities above mentioned, are composed of very poor people, who can find no work at present (since they can find not any) and others on their small farms which do not yield at this season of the year, or on small cocoa nuts, what kind of food can they get out of them? We do not see that there can be any other resource for them than to suffer the consequences of their temerity and folly.

To the above must be added three hundred military persons, who, in consequence of their not having provisions, came to the conclusion that their situation was not good, and left the peninsula on the 7th inst. under the command of Gen. Bide. Thus Baez has at present no sloop left at his disposal, since he can no longer use the three vessels he named the Liberador, the Australia and El Cirus, 19 of January, to carry provisions and troops to Samana, as, by the government, he is restricted from sending any more to the peninsula. This result is further confirmed by the directed balls of the besieging army before Pajarito.

As regards Samana, the capture of General Francis by the besiegers under the command of General Palmero, is confirmed, who, after having taken up his position at the point of the peninsula, has been reinforced by the governor of Puerto Plata in his dispatch of the 23d inst., in which he states that he had seen a foreigner left that place that he was not even able to speak; and there is no doubt but that the population of that peninsula find themselves in a very bad situation as far as provisions are concerned, a chicken bringing gold for five pesos, as is stated by the same individual.

This latter, with whose misfortunes we sincerely sympathize, adds that of his companions immigrants like himself, eight died in St. Domingo and six in Samana, one of sickness and the others by famine. The unfortunates, in September last, left Hamburg for Santo Domingo, with the intention of establishing themselves as agriculturalists, and have ended their career in the manner above mentioned. We hope that the government will take the necessary measures to prevent them from perishing by hunger.

records.summary_en: Following the expiration of a deadline, a bombardment of Port au Plate commenced, though fire from the fort forced the attackers out of range. The St. Jago government stated it would seek foreign aid before yielding to Baez, whose fleet's movements were favored by English and French consuls, leaving the United States as the sole government to depend upon. Additionally, the American schooner *Wing of the Wind* successfully ran the blockade with a cargo from New York on the 27th, while the U.S. Consul at St. Domingo, Mr. Elliott, remained imprisoned in his house for fear of his life without the presence of U.S. warships.

records.full_text:
The steamship Moses Taylor, has arrived from California, with one million eight hundred thousand dollars in specie.
The Moses Taylor left at Aspinwal, the U. S. steamer Colorado, which arrived on the 17th from San Domingo.
The Powhatan was at Hong Kong. It is rumored that the Chinese intend to destroy all the European dwellings on the Hong Kong river.
The Emperor of Russia has invited the French Ambassador to accompany him on a tour through the Southern Provinces.
The Colorado brought intelligence that President Baez, of the Dominican Republic, had capitulated to Santa Anna, and was to leave San Domingo on the 12th for Curacoa. The most of his adherents left the day previous.
Santa Anna had given Commodore McIntosh the strongest assurances of the protection of American citizens and desired him to express to his government his wish to maintain the most amicable relations. It is said that the Commodore succeeded in obtaining from President Baez all the documents for which he was sent.
The Colorado was to sail on the 21st for Havana.
The U. S. steamer Saranac and the Vandalia, were lying at Panama.
The Decatur sailed on the 13th, and the Merrimack on the 19th.
The excitement in California in relation to the Frazier river gold mines continues. Three thousand persons have already left San Francisco for that region.
The California mines are yielding largely and accounts from every section are highly favorable. The agricultural prospects were never brighter, and a full harvest is confidently anticipated.
The California papers contain more than the usual amount of murders, assassinations, casualties, etc.
The advices from Oregon are to the 24th of May, they announce a general Indian outbreak there. Col. Stevens' command on Snake river was attacked on the 16th of May and forced to retreat with the loss of fifty privates, three officers, two howitzers, baggage wagons, and nearly all the animals.
Three companies of dragoons and one of infantry were engaged with one thousand five hundred Indians. The names of the officers killed are Capt. Winder and Lieut. Gaxen, the name of the third is not given.
A fire in Nevada on the 23d of May, destroyed nearly all the business portion of the city.
The town of San Andreas, Calveras county was entirely destroyed by fire on the 2d of June.
The U. S. surveying steamer, Shubrick, arrived from Philadelphia, via Panama, at San Francisco, May 27th.

records.headline: The editorial looks back on the eleven-month civil war just ended in the Republic of San Domingo, describing it as…
records.summary_en: The editorial looks back on the eleven-month civil war just ended in the Republic of San Domingo, describing it as largely a geographical contest between the northern and southern sections, led by the rival cities of Santiago and San Domingo under Pedro Santana. It sketches the two cities and the republic's history: independence declared in 1821, twenty-two years united with Haiti under Boyer, the proclamation of the Dominican Republic in 1844, Haitian invasions beaten back by Santana, who received the title of Liberator, and the dissatisfaction that followed under President Jimenez.
records.summary_es: El editorial repasa la guerra civil de once meses que acaba de terminar en la República de Santo Domingo, describiéndola como en gran parte una contienda geográfica entre las secciones norte y sur, encabezada por las ciudades rivales de Santiago y Santo Domingo bajo Pedro Santana. Esboza las dos ciudades y la historia de la república: la independencia declarada en 1821, veintidós años unida a Haití bajo Boyer, la proclamación de la República Dominicana en 1844, las invasiones haitianas rechazadas por Santana, quien recibió el título de Libertador, y el descontento que siguió bajo el presidente Jiménez.

records.summary_en: The *New-York daily tribune* reported that the cultivation of tobacco had stimulated industry in Santiago, a city with a fine climate and a larger population than its southern rival, which the prevailing party in the late civil war—led by Pedro Santana—sought to make the seat of government. Historically, the territory acknowledged Spanish authority until declaring independence as the Republic of Spanish Haiti in 1821, though the inhabitants soon united with the western Haitian Republic under President Boyer. Following the fall of Boyer twenty-one years later, the people of San Domingo seized the opportunity to regain their independence.

Tras el derrocamiento de Boyer veintiún años después, el pueblo dominicano aprovechó la coyuntura para reconquistar su libertad política.

records.summary_en: The *New-York daily tribune* reported that Baez has been overthrown and Santana has taken power in the Republic of Dominica. While Southern journals view this as a triumph of the white over the black race and urge the U.S. government to formally recognize the Dominican Republic, the newspaper supports recognition regardless of racial distinctions. However, the publication questions whether the U.S. government and its Washington court circle would tolerate diplomats or future presidents of darker complexions in a country where the vast majority of the population is of African lineage.
records.summary_es: El *New-York daily tribune* notificó que Báez fue derribado y Santana asumió el timón de la República Dominicana. Si bien los periódicos sudistas conciben esta mutación como un triunfo de la raza blanca sobre la de color e instan a Washington a convalidar a la república, la publicación respalda el reconocimiento con prescindencia de castas. Con todo, la hoja se pregunta si el gabinete estadounidense y las tertulias de Washington consentirían a diplomáticos o futuros mandatarios de tez morena oriundos de una nación cuya gran mayoría desciende de linaje africano.

records.summary_en: The *Wilmington Journal* reported on October 1, 1858, that a French, English, and Haytian protocol from December 14, 1854, constituted an attack on the Monroe Doctrine by establishing an Africo-European protectorate and interdicting the island to American people and enterprise. The newspaper stated that the protocol was prepared to cancel an American treaty and prohibit the future admission of American depots, factories, and emigrants. Additionally, the excerpt details the draft of the protocol involving English and French consuls aiming to secure engagements from the Dominican Government regarding a truce with Hayti.
records.summary_es: El *Wilmington Journal* aseveró el 1 de octubre de 1858 que un protocolo suscrito por Francia, Inglaterra y Haití el 14 de diciembre de 1854 vulneraba frontalmente la Doctrina Monroe al instaurar un protectorado colombo-europeo y vedar el suelo insular a la estirpe y las empresas estadounidenses. El diario señalaba que dicho instrumento se fraguó para dejar sin efecto un tratado con Estados Unidos y proscribir el futuro establecimiento de factorías, almacenes e inmigrantes norteamericanos. El texto desglosa las minutas de aquel protocolo en las que los cónsules de Londres y París procuraban recabar compromisos del gobierno dominicano respecto a una tregua con Haití.

records.summary_en: The *Wilmington Journal* reviewed the history of Hispaniola, explaining the division between the western French colony of Haiti and the eastern Spanish colony of Santo Domingo. It recounted that Santo Domingo declared independence in 1821, was subjugated by Haiti, and subsequently expelled Haitian forces in 1844 to establish a republic under General Santana. The article noted ongoing tensions between the two governments and criticized the political instability of the region.
records.summary_es: El *Wilmington Journal* repasó los anales de La Española, dilucidando la partición entre la antigua colonia francesa occidental de Haití y la demarcación hispana oriental de Santo Domingo. Rememoró que Santo Domingo proclamó su independencia en 1821, fue sojuzgado por Haití y expulsó finalmente a las tropas haitianas en 1844 para erigir una república acaudillada por el general Santana. El escrito destacaba las continuas tiranteces sostenidas entre ambos regímenes y afeaba la crónica inestabilidad política de la zona.

records.headline: A political history of the republic traces the rivalry of Baez and Santana, beginning with Baez, twice called to the…
records.summary_en: A political history of the republic traces the rivalry of Baez and Santana, beginning with Baez, twice called to the presidency, as Santana's intimate friend and able co-operator in securing independence after Soulouque, the Emperor of Haiti, twice invaded and was beaten back. It recounts an embassy to Port au Prince that found Soulouque would accept nothing but the complete subjugation of Dominica and produced only an exchange of prisoners, the fight over ratifying a treaty with the United States, Santana's election and the friendship turning to bitter hostility, and Baez being sworn in again amid the demands of the naturalization party.
records.summary_es: Una historia política de la república recorre la rivalidad de Baez y Santana, comenzando con Baez, llamado dos veces a la presidencia, como amigo íntimo y capaz colaborador de Santana en asegurar la independencia después de que Soulouque, el emperador de Haití, invadiera dos veces y fuera rechazado. Relata una embajada a Port au Prince que descubrió que Soulouque no aceptaría nada más que la completa subyugación de Dominica y que solo produjo un intercambio de prisioneros, la lucha por la ratificación de un tratado con los Estados Unidos, la elección de Santana y cómo la amistad se convirtió en hostilidad amarga, y la nueva juramentación de Baez en medio de las exigencias del partido de la naturalización.

records.summary_en: Forty-five Dominican officers and civilians signed a manifesto from Baní on October 27, 1858, expressing indignation over a memoir by Senor Maximo Reybaud that proposed sacrificing their nationality to Hayti. The signatories declared that patriotism among Dominicans remains strong, asserting their readiness to defend the freedom and independence won in 1844 rather than submit again to Hayti.
records.summary_es: Cuarenta y cinco jefes militares y próceres civiles dominicanos estamparon su firma en un manifiesto fechado en Baní el 27 de octubre de 1858, exteriorizando su viva indignación ante una memoria de Maxime Raybaud que proponía el sacrificio de la nacionalidad patria en provecho de Haití. Los signatarios proclamaban que el sentimiento patrio permanecía inalterable entre los dominicanos, jurando hallarse resueltos a empuñar las armas para defender la libertad e independencia conquistadas en 1844 antes que someterse de nuevo a la servidumbre haitiana.

News from St. Domingo.
ARRIVAL OF GENERAL BUENAVENTURA BAEZ—RESULT OF THE ELECTIONS—BALDORAGE ABOUT THE UNITED STATES, &C.
[From our own Correspondent.]
St. Thomas, Jan. 12, 1859.
General Buenaventura Baez, ex-President of the Dominican republic, was among the number of passengers that came from St. Thomas to St. Thomas, on the 10th inst., from Southampton.
The Prensa del Comercio, of Habana, of January 12, says:—
The Viajero del Ozeano has brought us newspapers from Santo Domingo to the 22d ult. They announced the arrival in the Republic, of Santiago de los Caballeros, in his number of the 3d ult., of General Buenaventura Baez. Everything took place in a quiet way, giving the following result:—
President of the Republic—General Buenaventura Baez.
Vice President—General Juan Esteban Aybar.
Seven Senators were also elected.
In the same city of Santiago, on the 4th, General Domingo Ceara, and new plankings of tobacco, the greater part of them damaged, that the high water of the River Yaque del Norte, had been made, thanks to the activity of D. Juan Aibar, who had succeeded in saving them.

ST. DOMINGO AND THE UNITED STATES—THE IMPORTANT DISCOVERIES OF MONSIEUR REYBAUD BALDORDAGE.
[Translated from La Patria, of January 8, for the NEW YORK HERALD.]
The United States want the island of St. Domingo, say the tidings. They dream of possessing Cuba, and are endeavoring to establish themselves in the republic of Dominican Republic. General Baez is going to lend his aid to their designs, or at least he has never ceased up to the present time to favor their pretensions. It would there be question of an absolute or partial cession, or at least of a protectorate, wholly in the hands of the blacks, whose antipathy for everything that is white or of the color of slavery—would offer the most sure guaranty.
Such is the opinion that we set forth in our number of the 4th of January. La Patria takes another view of things. It has the right to do so; but she has sought to sustain that upon positive facts, which is the error committed. We shall prove it:—
1. We are in a position to establish in a positive manner, says that journal, that far from being disposed to enter into negotiations with the United States, the Dominican government has just formally refused to receive an envoy sent to Santo Domingo with a mission to negotiate a treaty.
We will observe that this fact, far from diminishing, rather gives strength to the Dominican question; for it proves that the cabinet at Washington continues to pursue the scheme of its designs upon St. Domingo. Nothing can be more insignificant than the pretext under which the agent was sent to Santo Domingo; and it is surprising to see how easily public opinion lets itself be abused in France on the subject of the United States. No, a thousand time no. Even when we cannot doubt that the cabinets of London and Paris will find means to overcome, or at least recriminate which the moral world concedes to those who feel themselves to be the strongest; but, what cannot be prevented, is the first effect of the stroke—the blow—the terrible stroke which falls upon it when it shamefully accepts a role which it ought never to play.
And can a popular corporation, that makes such an evil use of the influence it possesses, call itself, with impunity, a power? It is foolishness. Is there, perchance, any nation in Europe so blind as not to see that the time has come when it must show that the prestige and the credit of a chamber is perverted when it lends itself to the furtherance of such intrigues? It is a spectacle as sad as it is unpleasing to see how easily are sacrificed the philanthropic designs of Washington?
To come back, however, to the opinion of La Patria; this latter is somewhat bold, we confess, but it is not the less absurd—we mean to say that what she has written serves only to comprehend the truth of this proposition; in a word, she has fallen into a trap.
We take from the Feuille du Commerce, one of the Port-au-Prince journals, under the title of "An Unfortunate Proposition:"—
It is nothing more than a mournful observation which is made, but it is unfortunately true, that our country does not hold the rank which it held in former times. It is not respected as it was in former times. If it was respected, for its glory, if it was feared for its military power, if its ships of war carried everywhere the Dominican colors, it is no longer so. Unhappily for the country, there are found two class of men who have caused all this disgrace—class no. 1, who are filled with a spirit of discord, and class no. 2, who bear the virulence of a spirit as fatal as fierce. The right of Santo Domingo to be free and independent has been recognized by a solemn treaty. In spite of the prestige of Washington, we have the great historical facts of the past; we have the rights of humanity, and the rights of justice; and if the cabinet of Washington thinks itself entitled to be considered as superior in wisdom and wisdom, we possess the right to oppose the cabinet at Washington.
A great people, that respects the dignity of the first forum of the world, can never be made to suffer what we have suffered. Washington has abused its power; its policy is degraded, it has humiliated so profound, that it was which caused the revolt of the Dominican people against the authority of Hayti; and now that the Republic of Hayti is so weakened, it is found necessary to order that the protector, shall far exceed in power that of Washington.
With these facts before us, it is surprising that the Haytian government has been able to take no step to prevent the cabinet of Washington from intervening in Dominican affairs. We have seen, on two or three occasions, the discussion renewed on the subject of the annexation of Santo Domingo to the United States. We have seen that the Haytian government has been silent on all these questions. It is not necessary to say, for instance, that the Haytian government has made any protest against the project of the Dominican government, because it has been silent; and it is because it has been silent, that it has been possible to entertain the idea that the Dominican government could be brought to consent to such a step.
In this manner has the NEW YORK HERALD referred to the subject of the Dominican question, and the intrigues of the cabinet of the Union.
It was to be hoped that from this extraordinary correspondence, the Haytian government would learn that its attention should have been gone forth the defaming thought that Santo Domingo is about to fall into the power of the cabinet at Washington. We have no desire to make a passing observation on the North American mission to St. Domingo. It is a matter of detail. The Commander Page who is to come heading the invasion, is a prudence and daring man; if his mission fails, he brings to provoke us to hostilities, he brings another which he brought back when sent to Saint Thomas on his way to Paraguay. It is probable, we repeat, that he will return to the purpose of his mission to St. Domingo. He is an agent whose instructions are to provoke a conflict, and he will do so; all know he had prepared from the moment in which he prepared his instructions at Washington.
It is known that before this unlucky discord, Page wrote to Baez; and he had taken no steps to know whether he was in the same course when he wrote to Santana. Baez has answered the Commander Page; he refused to treat with him, as well as the Minister of Foreign Affairs, of all of which the cabinet of Washington could not fail to have notice.
Who knows if the same thing will not occur with any other mission? Whatever may be the events that may happen, it is impossible that the ministry and the mission can fail to understand that a great door has been open to the creation of serious difficulties that the world of the cabinet of Washington would have avoided if it had been represented to the person of a person sufficiently versed in the Haytian idiom to explain the real sentiments of the Dominican people.
Diplomats, in their notes, have special terms which it is proper to express in a manner clear, so that there can be no doubt; and equivocal interpretations to which the cabinet of Washington is accustomed, are not at all applicable, particularly for those who have not been born English. We have seen in the notes which the Haytian agent at Saint Thomas has adopted, in their diplomatic correspondence, the use of terms which could not be understood by any American.
It is pain itself, which has no counsel, had the manners of Hayti been represented to the Haytian agent at Saint Thomas by our minister in the English idiom; and the same error has been committed at Washington, for if there had been a minister, the cabinet of Washington would not have acted as it has.
We will accept, therefore, all notes that come in future; and if the Haytian agent at Saint Thomas is not in a position to convince the minister of the Union, who came to treat with the government of Santo Domingo or Hayti, we are in a position to show that there is no Dominican agent to preserve the honor of Santo Domingo. We believe that full justice will be done to the Haytian agent, and it is which we had to add to these brave remarks.

records.full_text:
To the Editor of the Anti-Slavery Reporter.'

SIR,—The island of St. Domingo, once united under the firm administration of Boyer for a period of twenty-two years, is now divided into two parts; the East, or Spanish part, forming the Dominican Republic, and the West, or French part, being constituted into the empire of Soulouque. It is not, at present, my intention to enter into the history of the civil war in the eastern province which led to the separation, nor is it necessary to show to any one who has studied the recent history of the country, that this separation has occasioned much present weakness and past ruin to both, and surrounded both with perils of incalculable magnitude. The existence of two independent states on so small an island, necessarily influenced by mutual jealousies and hatreds, and each looking to foreign aid for protection against a foreign power and a revolted province, could not fail to invite foreign aggression and intrigue. The great representatives of England, France, Spain, and the United States, have, in turn, taken advantage of the weakness of the local governments to play the game of their respective countries, but the aggressions of the latter power appear to have been influenced by the most evil motives, and to have a direct tendency to encourage new attacks on the liberty and independence of the island. These intrigues doubtless form a part of a systematic plan of American encroaching policy, holding propaganda, which aims to extend the ‘blessings of the peculiar institution’ over Hayti, Central America, and Cuba. The first-fruits of American diplomacy in the Dominican Republic were gathered in 1854, when, by dint of intrigues with Santana, the President, and, as it is asserted, heavy bribes to the petty representatives of the Dominican Republic, the United States’ Commissioner, General Cazneau, obtained the cession of Navaza, in the splendid peninsula bay of Samana, together with other privileges to which I need not more particularly allude, further than to say that they included a right to establish factories on land and to construct railways to the interior, and, in short, to work mines. This object of this treaty was, doubtless, to allure large numbers of American adventurers into the country, who, dazzled by the certainty of immediate profit and the prospect of far more substantial rewards, would form a powerful nucleus. Fortunately, this plot was not carried out, owing, in a great measure, to the exertions of the French and English Consuls, who, by showing to the Dominican Congress the danger of making such important concessions to the United States, prevented its ratification. The agent of General Santana, however, still refused to encourage American interests, and shortly afterwards the invasion of Dominican territory in 1855 by the Emperor Soulouque, whose fears were not unnaturally excited by the prospect of an American occupation of St. Domingo. This war turned out to be disastrous to Santana, however, which took place in 1856, when he was compelled to resign the presidential office amid the execrations of his countrymen. In his flight through the streets of San Domingo, *A bas le tyran! A bas les Americains!* rang from every lip. Baez, the former President, was compelled to leave the country; but he returned after a short absence, and by decree of the Senate succeeded in capturing the city of San Domingo, and restoring himself to power.

It is not difficult to discover what political advantages the possession of territorial rights in the Dominican Republic, together with the important bay of Samana, would have conferred upon the Americans; nor is it more difficult to see that, had it come to pass, they would have been able to prevent that union of the two sections of the island which alone can give a fair chance of success to the great experiment of negro self-government, and thereby prove the falseness of those theories of the natural and inherent inferiority of the African race, which form the sole justification for American slavery. This would have given them a pretext, of which they would not have been slow to avail themselves, to interfere by force in the domestic affairs of the whole island; and if no worse result happened, they would, at least, have placed the Haytian Government and Dominican President in a position of abject dependence upon the United States; while the bay of Samana might have formed a point from which to carry on filibustering operations against Cuba, and even our West India possessions; thus giving a new lease of life to slavery, if not a new field of action. No doubt all these considerations were well weighed by the Cabinet of Washington in instructions to their commissioners, and by Santana and his confederates bought with American gold, and to whose standard every enemy of his country seemed by destiny to rally. Happily, however, the temporary overthrow of Santana put an end to these projects, or at least suspended their execution; but their revival is not unlikely, now that Santana, by the defeat of Baez, has been restored to power. General Cazneau, it is true, has retired from the scene, but his party still continues in the ascendant at Washington, and Mr. Buchanan, like his predecessor, is its creature and instrument, rather than its director.

That a change of Presidents in the United States has produced no change of policy is but too evident from the proceeding of Mr. Buchanan in regard to the island of Navaza. This island, which forms a part of the Dominican territory, is small and uninhabited, situated between the south-western extremity of Hayti and the island of Jamaica, and is about thirty miles from Cape Tiburon. That the island belongs to Hayti is proved by incontrovertible historical evidence. A French authority, Moreau de St. Mery, is agreed on this point. Herrera says, in his ‘Descripcion de las Occidentales,’ chap. vi. p. 7, Madrid, 1730:—‘The harbors, &c., and the isles belonging to the coast of that island (Hispaniola) are found several small isles that are annexed to her, and that may still be very useful to her. The most considerable are the Saona besides Navaza and Mona, the first being ten leagues from Cape Tiburon towards Jamaica.’ Several months ago the Haytian Government learnt that this island, which contains extensive deposits of guano, had been invaded by a party of American adventurers, who had established themselves there for the purpose of digging and exporting the guano, without making any attempt to obtain the permission of the authorities at Port-au-Prince. The Haytian Government immediately forwarded a statement of the facts of the case to the Cabinet at Washington, soliciting their intervention as a medium of communication with the American adventurers occupying Navaza, because, up to the present time, no diplomatic relations had been established between the two countries. They also dispatched two Commissioners to Navaza to report upon the actual state of affairs in the island. The Commissioners, on their return, reported that they discovered on the northern side of the island three distinct establishments for the exportation of guano. This establishment consisted of about fifty persons, together with a wharf, boats, and houses, and two four-pounders. The whole party was under the management of Mr. John L. Frazier, who acted as agent for the officers of an association at Baltimore which had entered into a treaty with the leaders of the pirate party in the Caribbean Sea, for the exportation of guano from such of them as might be found to contain that valuable manure. It is scarcely necessary to say that no such treaty had ever been made with the Haytian Government, and that Mr. Frazier’s statement was an invention of his own.

As might be expected, the remonstrances of the Haytian Government have failed to produce any effect upon the American Cabinet. The protest sent through the American commercial agent was answered by Mr. Cass to the effect that the President had ordered the appearance, at Port au Prince, of two American men-of-war. The American commodore notified to the Haytian Government that he had not come to vindicate the sovereign rights of Hayti, but to raise the flag of the United States, and protect the intruders at Navaza, who, he alleged, had a clear right by virtue of an Act of Congress passed on the 18th of August, 1856, which authorized the President to protect American citizens who may discover guano on any island not within the lawful jurisdiction of any other Government. The Haytian commodore, not being empowered to discuss the question,—for in all likelihood, the very size of his vessel formed the principal reason why he was susceptible of too easy a proof—sailed off without making any reply. The Haytian Government have addressed a new protest to Washington, and there, for the present, the matter rests. It will be remembered that this is not the first case of a similar difficulty that arose between the United States and Peru, when the island of Lobos was invaded by a party of American citizens. Then the Cabinet at Washington was compelled, after a brief show of bluster, to respect the rights of Peru. Why, then, should America treat Peru with respect, and refuse to render equal justice towards Hayti? The reason would certainly appear to be, either that she cares no longer to recognize the rights of weak nations, or that, in the particular case of Hayti, she has ulterior designs to accomplish. It is certainly more than probable that this aggression, like most others of a similar character, has for its ultimate object, not the mere possession of guano, which, according to report, is of such an inferior quality, that it was impossible to find a market, and the vessel in which it was loaded was compelled to take it back again, thereby involving the speculators in a serious loss. But although America may not be able to turn the guano of Navaza to profitable account, she may, nevertheless, retain possession of the island for more important purposes. What could be easier than for her to erect on the island a small fort, and garrison it with soldiers? or to use it as a coaling station for American steamers? But whether the act of 1856 be made by America or not, the principle involved in the question remains precisely the same: If an American is allowed to retain possession of Navaza without protest, what is to prevent him from seizing on the numerous other islands which dot the Haytian coast, and, under similar pretexts, erect a fort upon such of them as he may please to occupy?

Clearly it is the duty of England to interpose her powerful influence, and to exert all the influence she can exert, to protect the rights of a feeble ally. St. Domingo may have fallen, and Hayti may have fallen, under the hand of Lord Malmesbury; but as this is necessarily a matter of truth and importance to humanity, we cannot but hope that the influence of Lord Brougham and of other distinguished friends of the negro in both Houses of Parliament, will be exercised to accomplish this most desirable object.

With your permission, in a future communication I shall call attention to another and a later phase which American designs against St. Domingo have assumed.

I am, Sir, your obedient servant,
F. W. CHESSON.

records.full_text:
There are now two regular packet brigs running between New York and Puerto Plata, one of which arrived yesterday, bringing advices from Dominica to the 12th instant.
The sixteenth anniversary of the separation of Dominica from the Haitien rule was celebrated at Puerto Plata and at Santiago de los Caballeros in a very spirited and joyous manner. On the evening preceding there were splendid displays of fireworks, balls, dances and entertainments of every kind. On the morning of the 27th ult. there was a solemn thanksgiving service, when a Te Deum was sung amid the distant roar of deafening cannon. At a later hour their Excellencies, the President and Vice President of the republic, the Council of Ministers, Senators and the Judicial and Consular bodies assembled at the Palace, where speeches were delivered and the utmost enthusiasm prevailed.
OUR PUERTO PLATA CORRESPONDENCE.
ST. DOMINGO, RIVER PUERTO PLATA, March 12, 1859.
Accompanying this please find a file of Santiago and St. Domingo papers, and I will from time to time forward you our latest papers, as there are now two packets (the New York and brig Puerto Plata) running between this and your port.
I can say of this government, it is in a bankrupt state.
Reports are current here of another revolution in St. Domingo city, and I learn that President Santana has expelled four or five of the parties concerned.
Mr. Lassen, Danish and Swedish Consul at, and has been for some time at St. Domingo city, to settle a claim for the destruction of the Danish schooner Ida (capturing two Danish schooners and cargoes during the blockade of this place in April last, and for other losses incurred at that time), have proposed to the Commodore of the Danish fleet to leave the question to some foreign nation or will arbitrate.
The Haitiens have sent a commission to St. Domingo city to treat for peace for ten years, and also to settle all previous hostilities and territory, and apparently for a final peace. It is the public opinion that the Dominicans will accept.
The tobacco crop, which was expected to be one of the inducements to the business community, will fall far short of what was anticipated, on account of the drought for three months. Should it still continue the crop must be a total failure.
No cargos of wood can be shipped at present, as there is no water for rafting.
The thermometer at this season of the year ranges from 84 to 89 degrees.

records.summary_en: The New York Herald reported on the formal opening of the fourth session of the Dominican Congress following addresses by President Santana and the Senate President, with festivities concluding in fireworks and balls. A communication in the *Gaceta* recommended building a turnpike between Santiago and Puerto Plata instead of a railroad due to the country's exhausted means, while suggesting improvements to the Yuna river and Samana bay, including establishing a central station for British West India mail steamers at Angalina. Additionally, Don Juan N. Riveiri was recognized as Consul for the Republic of New Granada, and the government committee established the official value of the paper currency for the ensuing month at the rate of 3.50 on March 1st.
records.summary_es: *The New York Herald* informó sobre la apertura solemne de la cuarta legislatura del Congreso dominicano tras los discursos del presidente Santana y del presidente del Senado, cuyas festividades concluyeron con fuegos artificiales y bailes. Un comunicado en la *Gaceta* recomendó construir una carretera de peaje entre Santiago y Puerto Plata en lugar de un ferrocarril debido a los agotados recursos del país, a la vez que sugirió mejoras en el río Yuna y la bahía de Samaná, incluido el establecimiento en Angalina de una estación central para los vapores correos británicos de las Indias Occidentales. Además, don Juan N. Riveiri fue reconocido como cónsul de la República de la Nueva Granada, y la comisión gubernamental fijó el 1 de marzo el valor oficial del papel moneda para el mes siguiente a una tasa de 3,50.

Additionally, private advices from Washington stated that the French commander had previously demanded the concession of all Dominican gold, silver, copper, and coal mines, and that Santana might dispatch a commissioner to the United States to grant privateer commissions.

records.summary_en: According to the *New-York daily tribune* of August 1, 1859, the Dominicans (described as Spanish negroes and mulattoes) seceded from the government of Boyer's successor. While their manifesto listed the new constitution's establishment of religious toleration as the chief grievance, the real reason for secession was reportedly that Boyer treated them unequally by sending Haytians to rule them and spending their tax proceeds in Western cities rather than their own division. Additionally, they were rejoicing at the success of President Geffrard, anticipating that a treaty of peace and commerce would soon be made.
records.summary_es: Según el *New-York daily tribune* del 1 de agosto de 1859, los dominicanos (descritos como negros y mulatos españoles) se separaron del gobierno del sucesor de Boyer. Aunque su manifiesto señalaba el establecimiento de la tolerancia religiosa en la nueva constitución como el principal agravio, se afirmaba que la verdadera razón de la secesión era que Boyer los trataba desigualmente enviando a haitianos a gobernarlos y gastando la recaudación de sus impuestos en las ciudades occidentales en lugar de en su propio departamento. Además, se regocijaban por el éxito del presidente Geffrard, anticipando que pronto se concertaría un tratado de paz y comercio.

records.full_text:
AT GONAIVES.

My last letter, I believe, descriptive of the country, left me, knapsack on back, tired and indisposed to walk, at a distance of several leagues from this ancient town. The hour was sunset—a season here of truly celestial splendor; for the clouds and scenery at this time, as elsewhere at the same hour in the tropics, are indescribably and inconceivably beautiful. Neither the poet's pen, in my opinion, nor the brush of the divinest painter, could do the vaguest justice to a sunset in the tropics: and far from me be that too common profanity which attempts, with flippant phrase, to attempt what Genius could never fully achieve.

We walked on, traversing a wide sandy plain nearly all of it uncultivated, and occasionally showing symptoms of the violence of earthquakes, and along through sections of well-tended gardens to the house of a friend—a gentleman whose knowledge of the country and whose familiarity with their history—for his actions, I find, are extensively written—may be of service to the student and philanthropist; to his topics of the characteristics of the historical Haytians he added:

Toussaint L'Ouverture, he said, was a great man—for a slave—a great man for the Times: he was the first to conceive the idea of Independence, but he feared the power of France; he had not the energy, being then an old man, to achieve it by force of arms, he sought to secure it by a treaty. The Constitution he drew up was a marvel: Franklin was as great a politician as Toussaint was for war; perhaps was naturally not inferior to Napoleon. The other Haytian generals had not the clear ideas of liberty that they so often dedicated the general of Napoleon. If Hayti had possessed a larger field of action, they would have equalled the best generals in Europe. Christophe was a brave soldier, but a cruel tyrant—Toussaint was not cruel. Toussaint he was my peer of Peter the Great—only a savage instead of a Christian ruler. Petion he regarded as the greatest man that Hayti had produced; he was the greatest in peace. I neglected to put down what he said of Boyer.

He had read Franklin's Hayti—the work of an intelligent traveler, but full of errors. Franklin said that extreme old age was very unusual here. He branded it rather briefly as a lie. He offered to conduct me to a Congo woman, of the ripe age of one hundred and twenty; and stated that not long ago Gen. Apollon—one of Toussaint's generals—died, in his one hundred and thirtieth year. (Of this Franklin, I afterward heard, that he was accused while in Hayti of a very grave crime. What it was, however, I could not discover. His book is sufficient to make any Haytian hate him.)

A RELIC OF SLAVERY.

I spoke of the slave-necked women that we had seen at the streams.

He said that in the days of Slavery the female slaves were prohibited by law from wearing shoes and dresses; they were only allowed to have a petticoat and chemise. Hence, the habit of exposing the upper part of the body had originated; and it still continued in the rural districts when they washed in the streams. Travelers seldom passed; the natives thought nothing of it.

It is only just to add here (so that chicken-limbed modesty may not say that this proves the natural inferiority and degradation of the negro), that the habit of exposing the upper part of the body is characteristic of all the Central American, Mexican and South American communities.

On the other hand, after reading the above note to an English missionary, he said that in his opinion the immorality of the people and the indecent exposure of the person in the interior, proceeded from a lack of an innate sense of modesty and decency—not from the habits of slave life or the laws of the Colonists. "I have often traveled," he said, "from Cape Haytian to this place, and yet, in all my trips, I have seen only one woman who exhibited, when seen in her washing path, any sense of modesty. She had only a cloth around her loins, as usual, and when she saw me she tried to conceal herself. Often, when crossing rivers and seeing them in that state, I have turned my eyes away out of shame for them; but they never exhibited any delicacy about it—they would continue to stare at me without a particle of shame."

I agree with both of these opinions. Doubtless the slave code, and their life as slaves, did not tend to civilize them—but it must also be remembered that previous to their being slaves they were savages. Savages have no scruples about the exposure of their persons: the negro women, there, fore, never knew, and were never taught, the requirements of civilization in that respect. Yet, while they seemed to be without shame, to my English friend, and it would be unjust to believe that they were shameless in the sense of willfully immodest. They deem it, doubtless—their actions proved it—no more immodest to expose their bodies, from the loins upward, than our belles—when the fashion says so—consider it indecent to have arms and necks uncovered. I doubt whether they are no less conscious of any wrong in doing so.

DISPROPORTION OF THE SEXES.

My molestous friend did not think that the disproportion of the sexes was considerable in the Republic, although it might appear to be so, because the women visited the cities only. It was apparent in the cities rather than real, because so many men were all ordinary laborers.

THE CATHOLIC PRIESTS.

It was true, he said, that the Catholic clergy in Hayti were immoral—so true—that they lived in concubinage openly, and even legally recognized their illegitimate offspring. It was true, also, that polygamy prevailed among the lower class, but a sentiment, he said, was daily extending in favor of legalized marriages. There are no Protestant missionaries in the interior, he said, although they are not only tolerated, but protected in the cities, and preaching everywhere in the Republic.

AFRICAN RITES.

We spoke of the traces of African worship that still linger in the mountains of Hayti. He said that these Pagan rites were sometimes performed at funerals in the interior, but secretly, and by natives of Africa chiefly, of whom there is still a considerable number living. Dessalines whipped every one detected in practicing these rites. Petion and Boyer passed laws against them, and their rural police strictly enforced the penalties prescribed for them. The French Célestine were never bigots in religion; hence, in ever green, they never showed bigotry or hatred toward other creeds and races; were of all nations the most tolerant; and they succeeded, in the Eastern division of the island, in ingrafting this sentiment into the creed of their bondmen. You see how the better nature of Christianity will show itself even in Romanism "in the abstract and principle," but in their life they encourage it and give it every protection.

WHITE LAW.

I think I have already mentioned that in Hayti there is no white race; the color of a white man is black; there, the testimony of a black man against a white is good, while the testimony of a white against a black is void! There, a slave state, being himself a black—or, rather, a free negro—possesses no rights; there, the Constitution—which is the law—says: "henceforward no white shall ever set his foot in this island in the capacity of a master or proprietor." Here, in our Southern States, a marriage between a black and a white is illegal; so antagonistical are the races, that, if a native woman at old marry a foreign white, she would instantly lose her nationality and be regarded in future as a foreigner; also: "To one who has never lived where the prejudices of color, to use a common phrase, are 'on the boot,' where the whites are the subjects and the blacks are masters—where the capacity of the negro for self government and self sustenance is no more a problem than the similar capacity of the Saxon race, where the color of the skin is neither the index of nobility nor the measure of intellect, it is difficult to conceive how exceedingly ludicrous these Pagan Black Laws of America appear. Our Slave Code, and its appendices in the Northern States are worse than the Haytian White Laws, for they were the offspring of an indubitable necessity, and were provoked by fourteen years of slaughter and two centuries of the foulest oppression. But what has the negro ever done to us, that, except to labor untiringly for our pecuniary interest, as contrasted with his own, that we should manifest such fear and hatred of him as the Slave Code of the South displays in every page?"

THE MASONIC ORDER IN HAYTI.

The Masonic Order in Hayti is very popular, numerous and influential. In 1851, Mr. D. informed us, there were thirty-nine lodges, thirty-four chapters, and three Areopagiti, in the Empire. He did not know the number of brothers. It must be very great; for one sees the symbols of the fratemity wherever he goes. "S. M. Faustin the first," I noted on the Report, held the honorable office of Grand Protector, Emperor, Pope, Grand Protector of the Masons, leading officer in the heathen Vandoux Order—important positions for a man born a slave, not long ago an overseer, and now, in his old age, an imperial exile! Let us live in hope. If we could not well mount higher than he—the Emperor of an Empire which he called into existence—surely, also, we could not well wish for an humbler starting point.

COMMERCE OF HAYTI.

He furnished me with a published statement, which, as he has made the subject his special study, is certainly deserving of consideration:

In the last days of French slavery and under the severest forms of slavery, St. Domingo furnished annually to the mother country not less than 150,000,000 pounds of frane (upward of $20,000,000 American) in the amount of producers which it produced for exportation, and its ports contained a considerable number of foreign ships. At present 400 vessels have been counted at once in the harbor of Cape Haytien, and 90 at that of Port-de-Paix, one of the most contracted. But, when these terrible catastrophes which were introductory to the liberty and independence of the Island, took place, plantations have been destroyed by fire, the fields laid waste, and the population disorganized and transformed into soldiers, it is obvious, then, that the same result can no longer be obtained. Afterward, the intestine wars, waged for the purpose of humbling or of maintaining the pride of chiefs, dispute among themselves the supreme power, completed the ruin of this once beautiful territory, reducing every day its population; for there, where on the field of battle and by emigration to other countries, a modern population had lived, for there, where former ly stretched out, as far as the eye could reach, vast plantations of sugar-cane, with their white plumes; where stood those superb sugar-houses, whose smoke ascended into the air in lofty cone-like columns, and where the measured song of a thousand male and female laborers, under the whip of the overseer, filled the air day and night with harsh accents, now extend thick forests, where the eye of the traveler sees only ruins and rubbish, a chapless mixture of walls, ponds and aqueducts, utensils broken to pieces, and aqueducts on beautiful arches, speaking witnesses everywhere of the opulence of colonial times.

"During the ten years of the peace of the adminis-tration of Toussaint, the revenue of Hayti was $4,000,000. In 1842, it had dropped to $2,000,000, and now it does not exceed $1,000,000. The weight of the indemnity—$12,000,000 to be paid to France by Boyer's imbecility—has already been paid, he says, four times over, in the shape of a bonus. In 1820, the statel that installed was regularly paid every year, but Boyer pocketed the money.

"The Haytian dollar has fluctuated during residence in Hayti, from 174 to 154 to the Spanish dollar. It is gradually appreciating. January and February last year, one gentleman informed me, the value of the gourde was equal to 67 cents net.

"Coffee," said a merchant, "is the real currency of the country. For example: During the month of November, December, January and February—it sells at $100 to $108 (Haytian dollars per cwt.); with the interior of the country in June, July and August, at from $160 to $180; by December, January and February, the exchanger will receive 16 Haytian for one Spanish dollar; during June, July and August it will run from eighteen to twenty. Thus, therefore, in consequence of these fluctuations, an exporter may lose by the coffee but gain upon the currency.

Here is an average of the value of the gourds or dollars for a number of years past; never hitherto, nor any similar statement, published. There are about 300 commercial days in the year, Sundays and fest days bearing no quotations, although the principal days for the retail trade:

At the average rate of last year, the paper money of Hayti, 3 single gourde or dollar bills, is worth somewhere between $5,000 and $5,500 (American currency) per acre! Some of them are nearly 7x9 inches in size! They are nearly all in two-dollar bills—that is, worth 12 American cents. A few hundred dollars' worth of this money I fear would break down a first-rate mule.

JAMES REDPATH.

Much of this letter has been revised, since it was written with special reference to recent events, and with information which I gathered at Port-au-Prince during a second visit which I gathered subsequent to my visit to that city.

records.headline: INTERESTING FROM ST. DOMINGO.
records.summary_en: According to *The New York Herald* on January 14, 1860, Hayti's consuls returned with new demands amounting to an unconditional surrender of the Dominican Republic's independence, backed by a quadruple alliance of France, England, Spain, and Hayti. The newspaper reported that these demands seek to forbid American commerce, enterprise, and citizens from Dominican territory and force submission to Hayti, arguing that this situation will persist until the republic is recognized by the United States or Hayti takes full possession of the island.

El diario reportó que estas exigencias buscaban prohibir el comercio, las empresas y los ciudadanos estadounidenses en territorio dominicano y forzar la sumisión a Haití, sosteniendo que esta situación persistiría hasta que la república fuera reconocida por los Estados Unidos o Haití tomara posesión total de la isla.

records.full_text:
INTERESTING FROM ST. DOMINGO.

Our St. Domingo Correspondence.
ST. DOMINGO, Dec. 13, 1859.
A French and English Squadron Before the City—Peremptory Demands—The Depreciated Paper Currency—Requisition for Its Redemption at Extravagant Rates—History of Its Issue—Venality of European Consuls—Their Efforts to Crush the Liberal Government—Probable Ultimate Designs of the Present Demonstration, &c.

We have now four European ships of war on parade before this city. They have come to St. Domingo on a mission so strange and scandalous that it almost staggers belief. There are two French vessels, one English and one Spanish steamer engaged in bullying this government into sanctioning a stupendous swindling operation, but the moneyed profits of the speculation will remain to the exclusive benefit of two or three British officials.

To begin at the beginning, and make a clear statement, we must go back to 1857-8, when—thanks to European intervention—Baez became the despotic ruler of the Dominican republic. Baez has the warm support of a large portion of the negroes, who wish to unite with Hayti on the basis of holding the white race in absolute subjection to the black; but when left to themselves, this party is much the weaker, and can only keep the control while European vessels of war are on hand to sustain them in the possession of the capital and other seaports.

Baez, with his staff of ministers and officers, being thus backed, were disposed to shear as large a fleece as the closest cutting could collect from the backs of the poor Dominicans while he had them in hand. They had many ways of fleecing the people, but the one in which they operated the most extensively was in the issue of paper money. During the whole of his administration, Baez kept the government press hotly at work manufacturing paper dollars, until the whole country was swamped with it. Millions of it was employed by Baez and his agents in buying up property of every kind on speculation? Among other friends and partners in these operations, some members of the British consular corps became deeply interested in the Baez money, or as the people here call it, “Mangolino papeletes.”

There are limits to everything, and the issue of forty or fifty millions of “papeletes” banished specie circulation to such a degree that not even a copper coin was visible in trade—necessarily the Baez paper went down to nothing. The poor people who had received it for their rice, sugar and tobacco; for their corn, cattle, wax, honey, yams, cocoanuts, &c., were dismayed to see their little all melting away into bits of waste paper. They had sold the fruits of their labor for this “government currency,” because it was the only circulating medium of the country, and there was no help.

While Baez yet held the supreme power in St. Domingo, his “Mangolino papeletes” sunk down to the rate of two thousand to the dollar under his own eyes; yet he went on printing it off by millions, and sent it into the interior to buy up produce for shipment to Europe on his own account.

At last the whole country rose against the Baez government and his iniquitous nest of money-makers. The whole concern, except the foreign consuls, were forced to leave the Dominican territory, but not without the “spoils,” for the European consuls used their official position to cover their own and their partners’ ill-gotten wealth. The French Consul, who governs the other consuls here just as his master—Napoleon—governs their masters at home, abetted and sustained Baez and all his corruptions in their most offensive forms, although no one accuses him of any personal interest in the papelete speculation.

This may be perhaps explained by considering this support the reward of Baez’s disposition to carry out the Anglo-French plan of annexing this republic to Hayti.

When General Santana succeeded to the Presidency this proposition of accepting the negro rule of Hayti, was pressed upon the Dominican Cabinet with such disrespectful urgency that the Executive sent Mr. Raybaud his passports. This gentleman was the late Charge d’Affairs of France at the court of Soulouque, but is now the special annexation agent of France, England and Hayti. While Santana was battling with the European scheme of Haytien supremacy, the Consular speculators in Baez’s paper were pressing him to recognise the “Mangolino papeletes” as government currency. This Santana had no right to do, for, by an act of Congress, provision had already been made to call in and cancel this paper at a fixed price. This was at the highest rate at which it was circulating before Baez went out of power—that is, at 2,000 papeletes to the dollar. But this liberal law did not satisfy the demands of the European Consuls, and they officially informed the government that they would be “treated as null and void.” None of them pretend that a rag of the millions of it they have on hand cost either of them more than the government offers to allow and it is known that they have bought nine-tenths of it at 3,500 and 4,000 “papeletes” to the dollar. Yet, in the face of these admitted facts, they have brought a fleet to “insist” upon this poor and friendless government allowing them twenty times as much as they paid for their 18,000,000 mangolino papeletes.

After an official correspondence full of dictatorial arrogance on the part of the French, English, and Spanish Consuls, these gentlemen informed the Dominican government that they would close their consulates and leave the country in a body if their demands were not acceded to at once. They were answered that the Dominican executive had not the right or power to annul an act of Congress, and they were reminded that the act was in itself most just and liberal, as it provided for the acceptance of the Mangolino papaletes at a much better rate than its makers had left it in circulation; the government therefore could do no more in the premises.

On this the Consuls of France, Spain and England struck their flags with a great deal of parade, and left the country. The Dominican government despatched agents to Paris, London and Madrid, with full statements of the case, but all those courts have united in the plan of suppressing—that is, of crushing out the Dominican republic—and refused to entertain the question.

This republic has not an ally on this continent, and the European Powers take advantage of its friendless, unsupported position to oppress it outrageously. Revenons a nos moutons. The French, English, and Spanish squadron now pointing its guns on our city, has brought back our consular masters with a list of new demands, amounting in fact to an unconditional surrender of the independence of the Dominican republic.

Some of these demands are secret, but there is scarcely room for a doubt that it is a repetition of the old alternative—negro rule or ruin. Be certain that American commerce, American enterprise and American citizens must be forbidden the Dominican territory, or the Dominican republic must be “suppressed,” and the white race driven out if it does not yield submission to Hayti.

This is the sum and substance of the old quadruple alliance of France, England, Spain and Hayti, and it will not be changed until this republic is recognized by the United States, or the negroes of Hayti are put in full possession of the whole island.

It is the cue of the consuls to let the Dominicans understand that the Anglo-French alliance no longer consider it an independent nationality. Spain and Hayti are but passive tails to this kite, although they are counted in as equal Powers in the quadruple alliance. Since Faustin has dropped out of the square, his imperial brother, Napoleon, and his august sisters, Victoria and Isabella, may only stand for a triangle, though it is very far from a right angled triangle. The square of the French base is a good deal more than equal to the square of the British and Spanish sides which Napoleon subtends, and, what is more than Euclid knew how to reduce to geometry, extends at his pleasure without increasing their power. Before they landed the consuls sent a note to the Dominican Executive ordering that a salute of twenty-one guns should be given within twenty-four hours to each of their flags. The Dominican Cabinet felt and said that such an order would only be issued to a dependent, or in chastisement of some wrong inflicted, and outside of the “Mangolino Papelete question” no offence had been alleged. The consuls only replied by commanding the salutes to be given within six hours.

The Dominican government complied, though under protest that it yielded to force, for they could not expose the city to the horrors of a bombardment for a form. After this preliminary the French consul carried his British colleague to the palace, that he might repeat after him, and endorse in the name of the English government, the recent orders of the Emperor Napoleon. What these are no one knows positively, but enough has leaked out to justify the belief that they relate to Hayti, and contain a death blow to this republic.

After this was attended to, the British consul had his turn, and was let loose on his Papelete business. John Bull is not to be balked of his pennies, and the allied squadron is here to see everything settled to their mind.

John Bull’s fight for the opium smugglers was a noble and honest war by the side of this bullying a weak republic into bankruptcy in support of a fraudulent paper issue; and the Anglo-French exploits in doctoring “sick Turkeys” to death and robbing bits of “broken China,” become in comparison fair business transactions.

POSTSCRIPT.
DECEMBER 14.
The government has surrendered to the consuls at discretion. It agrees to redeem all the Mangolino papelites at 500 to the Spanish dollar, and pledges the custom house and all other resources for principal and interest. The eighteen or twenty millions of it stored at the British consulate was bought at 2,500, 3,000 and 4,000 to the dollar. To buy 18,000,000 papelites at an average of 3,500 to the dollar and sell them off at 500 is a very good spec for a couple of these consular worthies; but that is the way John Bull uses his navy to take care of his children.
