records.full_text: THE DOMINICAN REPUBLIC.—We learn from the Gaceta Oficial, of San Domingo city, that the Dominican government has published a protest in regard to the recent ceremony of taking possession of the island of Alta Vela by the United States. The protest is dated the 13th of November last, and is addressed to the United States Consul at San Domingo. It sets forth that the island of Alta Vela is an integral part of the Dominican territory, and that the act of taking possession of it by the United States is a violation of the sovereignty of the Republic.

records.full_text: The political horizon of this republic is at present very dark. The government of Santana is entirely under the control of Spain. Santana is a mere tool in the hands of the Spanish agent here. He is a most faithful and submissive knight; he does nothing in his political government without previously informing his sovereign, the Queen, and receiving the consent of her ministers. This may read to you like an exaggerated statement, but it is only the smallest part of the degrading sycophancy of the Dominican Cabinet to Spain. Although the Dominican Minister was a long time treated like a dog by the Spanish Court, he waited at the Queen's back door until he obtained a hearing. He has at last succeeded in his mission. Spain has promised her protection to the Santana government, and a Spanish vessel of war is now at the city of Santo Domingo to protect Santana against any attempt that may be made to overthrow his government. The people are very much dissatisfied with the present state of things, and a revolution is expected at any moment. The Santana government is very unpopular, and it is only by the help of Spain that it is able to maintain itself in power. The Dominican people are in favor of a republic, and they will never submit to be ruled by Spain.

records.summary_en: The *Holmes County Republican* reported on May 31, 1860, that a coalition of French, Spanish, and English diplomats was conspiring to force the Dominican Republic to unite with Haiti. According to the article, England sought to prevent white emigration to stop American progress, Spain desired to keep Americans away from Cuba, and France aimed to extend its 100-million-franc mortgage over the entire island to eventually colonize it using coolie labor.

records.summary_en: The Dominican Senate requested the President to demand explanations and immediate reparation from Venezuela regarding the shooting of several Dominicans, warning that recourse would otherwise be taken. The President replied that no expostulations or reprisals were warranted because the individuals had abandoned their nationality and entered the enemy's ranks, noting further that letters from Venezuela asserted those men had actually been killed in battle rather than executed. Additionally, the press advocated for establishing a bank to suppress paper money, and the value of the gold ounce was fixed at 4,000 national dollars.

To the Militiamen of the State of Arkansas.
Executive Office,
Little Rock, Ark.,
Sept. 22, 1860.

I have caused to be published, the foregoing laws of his State and of the United States, on the Subject of the militia, for the information, observance and government.

The constitution of our State declares "that the military shall be kept in strict subordination to the civil power." The constitution of the United States declares "that a well regulated militia is necessary to the security of a free State."

I appeal to you to remember that it is the duty of every good citizen to yield to his country such services as the law requires of him. You cannot perform those duties without a knowledge of them, nor can officers without being thoroughly organized. "To keep the military in strict subordination, and a well regulated militia," to be such security as is meant in the constitution declares to be necessary.

I point you to the State of Arkansas: I point you to the laws of the United States, and appeal to you to prompt, zealous and active duty. In doing so, I would remind you that those who continue to hold office, and who shall be elected or appointed to perform, as far as possible, the duties of their respective offices, as well as those who are different on the subject of organizing the militia, are mistaken. We do not know how soon the strong arm of the military may be needed. Then, if we have any State pride, let us be prepared, and let us work together, and have the returns made as required by law. By the laws of this State and of the United States, each officer is required to furnish his own arms and equipments. The State has a quantity of arms, such as muskets, pistols and carbines on deposit, at the U. S. arsenal, at Little Rock.

The State of Arkansas is entitled to receive, under the acts of Congress, seven hundred and ninety-four muskets, at an aggregate valuation of thirteen dollars for each musket. If armed with artillery, or cavalry accoutrements, the State is entitled to but three hundred and forty-seven muskets. Let arms be applied, the number of them will be according to their value and cost. There has no law of this State authorized the Governor to receive this or any other company of militia with arms. In 1856, the quota was 1,172 muskets. The General Assembly has not yet passed any law to distribute these arms to the militia. But the whole amount of arms due from the United States to the State of Arkansas, would be sufficient to arm all the militiamen in the State. In 1856, the quota was 1,494 muskets now due from the United States, or an aggregate valuation of $21,169. It is therefore manifest that the militia, to be armed and equipped, must first be fully armed by the State, nor by the United States, until the volunteer companies are called into actual service of the United States. The expense of arming all the volunteer companies of the State, or of the United States and of this State require that each company shall be furnished with such arms and equipments as the law prescribes; and the volunteer companies authorized by law in every county in the State should be organized and thoroughly organized and disciplined, and bearing the state flag or national banner as soon as possible. The only mode, as I conceive, for the volunteer companies, there is one mode by which the State or county could procure them and have them placed under the control of the proper authorities of the State, for the use of the State, when in use by the volunteer companies.—That is, for the county court to levy a tax, or by voluntary subscription, to raise money to buy arms and equipments to arm all the volunteer companies in the county; or a portion of these companies may be organized in each county in the State, as a company of cavalry, or infantry, one of light infantry or riflemen, or a company of artillery. This company shall be wholly independent of the militia regiments, except at battalion and regimental parades.

Were the whole of the volunteer companies in the State, organized and armed as they should be, each composed of fifty men, including officers, making the amount in the aggregate to twenty-two hundred men, well disciplined, equipped, and at all times ready for service, in addition to the volunteer companies, we should now have six-two regiments, and which will soon be organized.

Under the provisions of chapter 112, provides that volunteer companies "shall elect their own officers," and the place to be ordered by the colonel of the regiment, and the certificate of election commissions shall issue.

The law in section 20 of chapter 113, that "out of the militia enrolled, there shall be formed for each battalion, at least one company of light infantry, or one of riflemen, and that to each division there shall be at least one company of artillery, and one troop of horse." These volunteer companies are to be formed as part of the regiments of the regular militia.

Under section 22, a volunteer company shall consist of not less than thirty-four nor more than one hundred non-commissioned officers and privates. Section 23, each company may have not less than three commission officers—a captain, first lieutenant, and second lieutenant.

A battalion cannot consist of less than three companies.

No regiment shall consist of more than two battalions. All volunteer companies in a regiment are designated by the letters of the alphabet.

Volunteer companies are designated by proper terms indicating the character of troops—infantry, riflemen, or cavalry. Each volunteer company is entitled to three officers, and the colonel of the regiment of the regular militia is entitled to but two—a colonel and lieutenant colonel.

It devolves upon each colonel commandant to organize his regiment, but he is also to have formed within the bounds of his regiment these volunteer companies, independent of his regiment, as well as the required quotas, and the number of militiamen will not exceed forty or fifty men to a company, in the bounds of any regiment than necessary to form three volunteer companies, containing one hundred non-commissioned officers and privates each. If there are an excess of the militiamen, all the volunteer companies are formed, and there should still be a surplus, the colonel would have to apply to the brigadier general of the brigade to divide the regiment and make a new regiment out of part of it.

The law in section 20 of chapter 113, prescribes that "it shall be the duty of the colonels, at all times, to keep the vacancies of all officers in their regiments filled."

Every officer will promptly comply with the important and solemn duty so positively and clearly enjoined upon him by the laws of his State, and he will feel himself in conscience and law bound to obey as long as he holds the office of colonel commandant of a regiment, the militia of our State will be organized, and will be kept continually organized.

Let every officer remember that the chief honor derived from holding an office, is that which an honest and intelligent community will ever accord to an officer who promptly, faithfully and efficiently performs his duties. To know "what these duties are," he must read the law. He must study to understand the laws and the duties required of him, and he will then be prepared to act, and if he have pride and energy of character, he will promptly and efficiently discharge the public trust reposed in him.

I have prepared and had published with the militia laws, a register of the divisions, brigades, regiments and companies, with the names of the major generals, brigadier generals, colonels, and lieutenant colonels. If these officers will go to work in earnest, as they ought to do, under the law, they will acquire credit and distinction for themselves, and put the militia to be such to the security of the State as the constitution declares to be necessary.

While the constitution declares to be necessary to the security of a free State; and while I urge the militia by preparing and organizing under the law, to avert coming danger;

It is for no purpose for trouble or danger, which can certainly be brought upon our borders, that I would move you to less and indifferent the security of the people of Arkansas and their property. The dangers which threaten the political status of the people of Arkansas are of such a character that no patriot, however he may hope, will be willing, calmly to encounter them. He will be willing, nay, anxious to exert his influence in favor of raising money in the county where he resides, to buy arms to arm and equip the volunteer companies of his county. He will take hold of this matter and petition the General Assembly, at its coming session, to pass such a law as I have suggested, to enable every county may be enabled to have its volunteer companies fully armed and equipped, so that they would afford ample protection to the people of the county, in their persons and property. Is there any reason to doubt that the British government, or her abolition emissaries, or the non-slaveholding States, or the unconstitutional acts of our government shall have placed her armed forces or her political mercenary agents stationed in our midst, or in our neighborhood, in every county in our State, and near every slaveholder's house, and that things ready at the appointed time, to incite and encourage slave insurrection? The open and notorious acts of the British government, the long continued, deep-laid and settled secret policy of the British government to destroy the supremacy and equality of the United States. That it is her object to break up and destroy our government, and establish her own power and supremacy over the whole of the British possessions on this continent, and then establish her own power in America.

In 1850, the British, French and United States governments entered into a truce, for ten years, between the Empire of Hayti and the Dominican Republic. That truce has expired. The British government has entered into a treaty with the Dominican Republic, by which the Dominican Republic gives its adhesion to the said truce under the guaranties of the same powers: 1st. Not to alienate, lease, hypothecate, or cede gratuitously, either temporarily or permanently, any portion of the Dominican territory, particularly in the Bay of Samana, to any government whatever. 2d. Not to contract any engagement with any foreign State; not to accept any subsidy from a foreign company; not to hypothecate much of the revenues of the Dominican Republic to any foreign State; 3d. Not to accept any protectorate, nor to submit to any foreign intervention, or any other act contrary to her independence.

The political status of the slaveholding States is now such that no reflecting man, who was fully aware that the British government was acting in concert with the abolitionists of the non-slaveholding States, in a policy that disturbed the domestic tranquility of the United States, but must admit that there is an "irrepressible conflict" between the free States and the slave States. Is it not a fact known to all men, that British gold have been and will be spent in multiplying abolition emissaries in the United States to stir up and intensify this "irrepressible conflict" between the free States and slave States. That the policy of the British government has been to use all her efforts to overthrow our government, (by using her abolition emissaries and domestic emissaries,) that the mischiefs and outrages of the non-slaveholding States would seem to have been prompted by the British government for the purpose of destroying the States. It is my opinion that the British government has been at the bottom of all of the mischiefs and outrages perpetrated against the slave States, and that the identity of one federal government, and of the domestic policies of the United States to hold the British government in check, and preserve the domestic tranquility of the United States. It is my opinion that the British government has determined that, as long as the federal government exists, that she henceforth has no domestic tranquility in the United States, and that British gold has been and will be used to hire unprincipled abolitionists in the free States, and send them into the slave States, with a view to excite or encourage that the people of the South will become weary of the Union, and the north, and the aggressions and outrages perpetrated upon the slave States, and those hired abolition British emissaries, prompts the people, in 1860, to elect, and it is voted that civil war will be produced, the Union dissolved, the non-slaveholding States left with domestic evils and deeds of plunder, robbery, arson and murder, and under prevailing.

I believe that such a conspiracy exists against our federal government, and that, if successful, it will be carried into execution, as above indicated, and the names of the secret agents and emissaries of the British government, distributed throughout the United States, to stir up abolitionism, were detected and made public, the patriotic people of the United States, when he announced with astonishment; and having that disclosed, every honest author and instigator of the mischief, all anti-slavery men in both free and slave States would at once be dismayed.

It would then be seen that abolitionism would become formally and more firmly united with the British government, and that the patriotic citizens of the whole Union would unite, as one man, against those agents and emissaries, would be so completely unmasked and declared against the British government for her interference of months.

In conclusion, in making these statements, I my duty to the people of the State of Arkansas to urge them to organize, and arm, and equip themselves, and thoroughly prepare themselves, for any emergency, to be ready to protect themselves and our State against all foes, and to be satisfied that our government intends shall not be violated, and that the "irrepressible conflict" is indeed "irrepressible" and terrible.

Every county in the State of Arkansas should have at least one or two volunteer companies, well armed with arms; and that every citizen who has a gun, should keep it in repair and unmolested, and that volunteer companies should be ready at all times to defend the State.

Let these important matters not be lightly considered, but promptly and maturely considered. We must look as far as human foresight can reach, and prepare to guard against evil before it is too late to prevent it.

Then as wise men and prudent, as men who feel a deep interest in the welfare of the militiamen of the State of Arkansas, let us put our shoulders to the wheel, and emergency which shall call for their strong arms in defense of our rights and our country.

HENRY M. RECTOR, Governor of the State of Arkansas, and Commander in chief of the militia thereof.

Additional naval and military forces, along with approximately 5,000 regular troops on the *Petronila* and *Derenguela* and about 10,000 more from Spain, were reported to be following. Meanwhile, business on the island remained depressed, and passengers traveling on the *Quaker City* included ex-President Miramon of Mexico and Major Patterson, a bearer of dispatches from St. Domingo to Spain.

Entretanto, el comercio en la isla continuaba deprimido, y entre los pasajeros que viajaban en el *Quaker City* figuraban el expresidente Miramón de México y el mayor Patterson, portador de pliegos oficiales desde Santo Domingo hacia España.

records.chapter_en: Annexation to Spain and the Restoration War
records.chapter_es: La anexión a España y la Guerra de la Restauración
records.full_text:
The Spanish steam frigate Blanca, with a full complement of troops, and the steam sloop Isabel, left our anchorage in our harbor Saturday evening last for St. Domingo, having in view a mission of an aggressive policy and to defeat any opposition that might be made by the government or people of the Dominican Republic to the proposed annexation of Spain. Many thousands of people were upon the wharf to cheer this enterprise for the restoration of the banner of the old and haughty Spanish power upon their ancient domain, where were impressed almost the first footsteps of the pioneers of Spanish civilization. In the wake of the ships above mentioned the steam frigate Berenguela and Petronila, also heavily armed and with many hundred men drawn from the army, to compel respect for Spanish power and to enforce obedience, it is said that five or six thousand soldiers are to be sent to St. Domingo to be distributed as may be signified by the Spanish government, by a quiet introduction of the people, ostensibly as the home and field for their services by grants of lands which were to be given to them, but in reality to be distributed at government where they pretend to seek homes and prosperity.
Every demonstration tending to territorial acquisition on the part of Spain in St. Domingo, from the reports of those who have recently returned from the city of St. Domingo, to defeat the policy of the United States—the Monroe doctrine—is being carried out with every good faith with the Dominican republic, through their agents here. It is said that the terms of annexation and support, after the same had been thoroughly discussed and agreed upon by the high contracting parties—the one to surrender and the other to receive—have been made to include the following:—To recognize the Spanish officers of high rank in the army and navy, and to continue them in their respective positions, as heretofore, for the purpose of future action to construct a case against the republic of Hayti to be followed by annexation.
Through the facts, views and deductions of your correspondent have been subsequently fully verified and confirmed, and the arrangements, although not officially made public, are known to be the current news. Effectual steps have been taken to check or prevent the slightest opposition on the part of the people to this change of jurisdiction. These demonstrations of a Power you have so often and so justly characterized as a "dying" country by their own assertions are of great importance at this time, as they are to share the island of Hayti between an upstart and a throne. The Dominican republic, it is said, is to be the share of Spain, and the republic of Hayti is to share the fate of her sister republic under the wake of Spanish policy, by previous understanding with the French government.
England is not, under this view of advantage for Spain, to be an idle spectator, but she is under the influence of her yarns, when a free people pass under the yoke of a power where the most cruel and unmitigated power, where slavery and slave traffic are to be found in their most hideous forms. She will not, she cannot, interfere with the policy of Spain, because her England is, still, with folded arms, and says nothing against the policy of Spain, because she is the principal consumer of the world, for none of which can be substituted for the southern products of your heritage. How will it be with the growing prosperity and power of the people of the United States? Spain sees her opportunity, and she will not only take St. Domingo, but her designs to annex Mexico she only held in restraint until she saw your internal difficulties, and then her subsequent movements would flow towards the shores of Mexico.
The political disturbances in the United States showed that the time was ripe for the aggrandizement of Spain, and hence the prompt action she has taken of it. But what will be the result hereafter? Are not all the people, in or out of the Union, interested in the cause of liberty—in political and social rights? and is there not some power to check the aggressive policy of Spain and compel the respect of foreign Powers?
The future is soon to show us these things. Who is to control? The colored race will cry aloud if Spain controls the island of Hayti, for they know that their freedom will not be likely to receive any recognition from Spanish power.
The United States war steamer Mohawk, Lieutenant Commanding T. A. Craven, arrived here on the 20th inst. from Key West.
The health of the eminent merchant, Mr. Drake, is said to be somewhat improved.
The suicides of the coolies continue to be of frequent occurrence, and it is said that no less than seven or eight have occurred within the last few days.
The steamship Panama, from New York, arrived here on the 21st inst.
General Miramon, ex-President of Mexico, and family, left here on the 22d inst. in the Spanish mail steamer for Cadiz, via New York.
The news of the political sentiments and action of the new President of the United States of America has been received here with much interest, and the dark dreams of fanatical raids upon our peaceful domain have passed with the shadows of the night. Circumstances have occurred in the last few years to leave a very deep and many painful shadows following in the trail of more than one of your expeditions, and they were not likely to wind up a good many more on the same string; yet there is now room to hope for the better and we will take it. The business circle among those interested in the sugar market is not as active as it has been for some time, and the prices have not been as well sustained as they were at our last advice. The sugar market at the close of the week is very dull, and the prices are as follows for sugar:—No. 12, 4 1/2 rs.; No. 11, 4 1/4 rs.; No. 10, 4 rs.; No. 9, 3 3/4 rs.
Molasses in net tierces demand at 1 3/4 a 2 reals per keg of 5 1/2 gallons. Exchange on London, 14 1/2 a 15 per cent premium; on New York, 2 1/2 a 3 per cent discount. The shipments of sugars and molasses to a considerable extent have been made to the United States during the last few weeks. Freights—Demand on declining, but will probably be better as the season advances.

records.summary_en: Following years of division and subsequent unification under Boyer, the Dominican population rose in insurrection against Haytian ascendancy and chose Pedro Santana as president. After Santana's term expired in 1849, Jimenes was elected Chief Magistrate while Santana was banished due to suspicions of intriguing with Madrid; however, Jimenes soon conspired with Hayti's Emperor Soulouque to unite the island, prompting the Dominicans to recall Santana from exile and invest him with dictatorial power.

Al concluir el mandato de Santana en 1849, Jimenes fue elegido primer mandatario mientras que Santana fue desterrado por sospechas de intrigas con Madrid; sin embargo, Jimenes pronto conspiró con el emperador Soulouque de Haití para unificar la isla, lo que impulsó a los dominicanos a llamar a Santana del exilio e investirlo de poderes dictatoriales.

records.chapter_es: La anexión a España y la Guerra de la Restauración
records.full_text: If any one will take the trouble to draw, on any good map of the United States, a line due South from the extreme point of the Peninsula of Florida, it will be found—after crossing the inlet, sixty miles wide, from the Atlantic Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico—to intersect the Island of Cuba at a point about one-third of its length. The Northern shore of the remaining two-thirds of that Island winds in a gentle curve, in a South-Easterly direction; finally terminating at Cape Maysi, which is nearly on the "Windward Passage"—a strait which connects the Atlantic Ocean with the Caribbean Sea—separated there from Hayti—the distance between Cape Maysi, the Eastern terminus of the former Island, and Port St. Nicholas, the Western terminus of the latter, being not more than twenty-five miles. In the Western portion of Hayti, covering about one-third of the area of the Island, is situated the Republic of Hayti, Port au Prince being its Capital. The Eastern division of the same Island, and by far the most mountainous, constitutes the Republic of Dominica, of which San Domingo is the Capital. The Mona Passage, another entrance from the Atlantic to the Caribbean Sea, separates on that side Hayti from the Island of Porto Rico, the distance between them being about the same breadth as the Windward Passage—twenty-five miles. It will thus be seen that Hayti occupies the midway between Cuba and Porto Rico both of which are Spanish dependencies, and that if that territory, these three islands would be in possession of the same power, and would command all the entrances to the Caribbean Sea, and all the States of Central America. We have from the latest advices from St. Thomas, the geographical situation of these Islands, and their relative positions to each other, and to us, because intelligence reaches us from Havana to the effect that Spain has accepted the surrender of the Island of Hayti which is known to us as the Dominican Republic, or more popularly still as San Domingo, and is about to re-annex it to the Spanish Crown. There is nothing at all improbable in this report, though it is not unlikely—if it should turn out to be true—that the fact of this reassertion of an authority which had been abandoned for nearly half a century, will lead to grave complications with this government. The history of San Domingo is the history of nearly all the Spanish possessions on this continent. Discovered by COLUMBUS in 1492, and claimed and held by right of discovery, Hispaniola, San Domingo, or Hayti, which are the names by which the Island has been known, continued under the exclusive dominion of Spain until 1697, when the Western part of it—that which is now styled Hayti—was ceded by the treaty of Ryswick to France. The remaining part, known as the Dominican Republic, continued a Spanish colony until 1795, when it too was ceded by the treaty of Basle to France, who thus acquired possession of the whole Island. It did not long remain under French rule. Shortly after the annexation, the negroes of the Western part rose in insurrection under TOUSSAINT L'OUVERTURE, and after a long and bloody war, and a series of massacres, scarcely paralleled anywhere, succeeded in either murdering or expelling all the white population, and in establishing a monarchy in that which then became, of the Island, under CHRISTOPHE, and a Republic in the South-West, under PETION. In 1808 the Dominicans, oppressed by the tyranny of DESSALINES, called upon Spain for assistance, who seized upon the opportunity which was thus presented to her, to regain possession of her former territory, but held it but for a brief period. The following year the Dominicans, again rising against the Spanish, declared their independence, expelled the Spanish Governor, General REAL, and established a republican form of government. The Island continued divided, for some years, into three separate and distinct principalities—a Republic, under PETION, in the South-West; the monarchy, under CHRISTOPHE, in the North-West, and the Dominican Republic, under various chiefs, in the East. This distinction was kept up until after the death of PETION, in 1818, when the popularity of BOYER enabled him to unite all the governments under one rule, for which himself being chosen President of the Republic for life. In 1844 the negroes of what is now the Republic of Hayti, obtaining the ascendancy, condemned the President to exile, and established a Republic of their own, fearing the expulsion or utter extermination of the Spanish population, which had so long existed, and, succeeding in maintaining their independence, chose GUERRIER, and, shortly after, PIERROT, for their President. His term of office expiring in 1846, RICHE was elected, but died, and SOULOUQUE, in 1847, was chosen to fill the vacant seat. It was not long after he had attained to power, before he began to manifest his hostility to the Dominicans, and in 1849 he led an army of 10,000 men against them, but was again encountered and defeated by SANTANA, in a well-pitched battle. The independence of San Domingo was thus secured, and SOULOUQUE, having assigned his Dictatorship in favor of BAEZ, retired from the field. In 1853, however, BAEZ becoming unpopular, by reason of his favoritism, was forced to leave the country, and SANTANA was elected to the Presidency in 1853; but, four years after, BAEZ returned, and SANTANA was in his turn exiled. BAEZ, however, had not been more than six months in power, before the general dissatisfaction with his policy led, in 1858, to a popular rising against him, and SANTANA, who had become the leader of the movement, was again restored to power. Theoretically, the Dominicans are as free as the people of the United States, with whose Constitution that of San Domingo is modeled. The laws in relation to the administration of justice are singularly liberal. "Free farms, farming utensils, and provisions for six months," are offered to settlers, and no distinction, as in Hayti, is made in favor of colored persons. These laws, it is now alleged, Spain has, for some years past, been taking advantage of, to introduce, under the auspices of President SANTANA, large bodies of persons from Cuba, who, with the view of promoting Spanish interests, and of "preparing the way of the Spanish dominion," on the first sign of resistance on the part of the "native population." The plan is said to have succeeded. This disaffection of the mixed breeds, we are told, became gradually so menacing, that, on the 16th of last month, Spanish troops from Porto Rico were on board the vessels of war in the harbor; the Spanish flag was hoisted on the fortress of the Capital, and, at the last advices from Havana, the details of the formal surrender, and reinforcements of troops, had been despatched to support the movement which has so successfully inaugurated, and which, if report speaks true, is designed to re-establish the authority of Spain in Hispaniola, the most ancient of all her South American dependencies. We forbear from making any comment, at this time, upon a movement which may have been misunderstood, and concerning which we have as yet but imperfect details. Until we know more with regard to the matter, the foregoing résumé of the history of the Island will serve, perhaps, to enlighten some of our readers, and will certainly enable us, on any further occasion, to render better understood such remarks as we may have occasion to make upon the subject.

records.full_text:
James Redpath, whose knowledge of the condition of affairs in the island of Hayti is as comprehensive as that of any other man in America, and who, in his various social and political organizations, addresses a letter to the New York Tribune in relation to the alleged Spanish attempt upon the independence of St. Domingo, from which letter we take the most interesting and valuable part. Within the last two years Redpath has made several voyages to Hayti, in connection with the colored emigration movement, and he speaks from personal and recent observation.

To the Editor of the N. Y. Tribune:
In common with the majority of our fellow citizens who know little or nothing of the island of Hispaniola, or of the two nations which inhabit it, except as a people of African descent, it may be necessary to say that the whole island is not governed by Haytians, or Hayti, it is held by two independent nationalities—that of the eastern and larger portion, the Dominican Republic, often called St. Domingo, or more frequently the Spanish part; and that of the Republic of Hayti (the French part,) being known as the Republic of Hayti. In the Dominican Republic (which has a population of 150,000 souls, who are chiefly mulattoes, talk Spanish and are a primitive children of nature,) there lives at San Domingo City, a man nearly white, whose sympathies, ideas and interests are with the old Spanish Monarchy, and who is his country's to the immemory Empire of Spain. Santana (Pedro) has a reputation for bravery and some ability, but he is hated by the people he governs. He is the President of the Dominican Republic.
The Republic of Hayti, on the other hand, was, as is well known, founded by the blacks, who, led on by Toussaint L'Ouverture, Dessalines and Christophe, drove the whites out of the island. In 1822, the Spanish part was formally delivered over to that power. It remained under their protection for twenty-two years, until 1844, when a revolution overthrew its authority.
Since then the Spanish part was united to Hayti, then governed by President Boyer. In 1844, however, the Spanish part asserted its independence and influence indicate their respect as yet been effected.
Since the independence of the Dominican Republic, two parties have divided and alternately governed it, whose respective leaders—Baez and Santana—have each sought to induce and independence indicate their respect as yet been effected.
Santana, it is said, Santana would rather be a little man in a great nation than a great man in a little one. He has formally offered to place the Dominican Republic under the Spanish crown, and, failing in those efforts, he has sought for a similar purpose with France and Spain, and Venezuela, and even the United States. But none of these Powers would accept his proposals. France and Spain had been bitten once, and were satisfied with that experience, and Venezuela did not want to be bitten at all. His last desperate effort was to induce a white emigration from the United States, but, although seconded by our Consuls there, (whose longer continuance in office will be disgraceful to our Republican Administration), he signally failed to interest either our capitalists or laborers in the project.
Some years ago—and I say now is drawn from the Spanish Government—Santana borrowed a million of dollars from Spain, failing to pay the interest on which, he has now offered to place it with a mortgage on the custom-house. Last summer, however, a movement of the people, including the blacks, in all—at St. Domingo, and the three other provinces, took place, and Santana was forced to fly to the mountains, where his last rest were mechanics. That is all the "emigration" that has been sent to the Dominican Republic by Spain. There has been a small increase in the Spanish population, but this is due to the fact that many of the old families, the descendants of the Spanish Colonies; for, when the island was ceded to France, many of the old Spanish families, numbers of the best and most respectable, left the island.
The spirit of the people is now as much as ever for an effective union among the people of the island. The President of Hayti, Geffrard, who succeeded the Emperor Soulouque, early last December, revolutionary circulars were distributed, and a copy of the proof, I know, were sent to the Dominican Government at Santo Domingo. He is still in the exiles. The intrigues of the Spanish Government are now being used as the call for aid—first, in order to secure a protectorate, which may eventually lead to a return to the Spanish Government.
This, I venture to say, is the "sum total" of the whole matter, and we have from the official reports of the Associated Press and the New York journals, it is not improbable that this should occur (for it is given only as a supposition) that the Spanish Government will take possession of the Dominican Republic. The notion that the Haytians would ever be reconciled to the Spanish Republic if it was not quite absurd.
Spain has never recognized the independence of the Dominican Republic.
She has recognized the independence of Hayti.
The Dominican Republic from Hayti, payment for recognizing that independence.
But it is said by those in power—Hayti against all foreign attacks; and—lastly
Hayti would not allow of any alliance that would be detrimental to herself.
I might add to these reasons two others: First, that the experience of Napoleon, called the Great, conclusively proves that France could not conquer Hayti if she were to try; and, secondly, that the Haytians would not be too slow to announce a voluntary alliance with any other powerful nation. If the whole physical power of England combined, when, with the aid of the climate, it would not begin to balance the expenses of conquering it. And, thirdly, the Haytians are now better prepared to defend their rights for his ambition than Hayti, the common enemy of the island.
I have also official authority for stating that the Haytian Government has already taken measures to prevent any such alliance as that between Hayti and the Dominican Republic. The Haytian Government has already notified the Spanish Government that any interference by any foreign power is guarded. The position of the Haytian Government is this: If the Dominican Republic is what it is signed, France and England should be notified of the fact.
But, even if France and England were pledged, it is likely that England would permit the Spanish Government to take possession of Santana and her own treaty stipulations?
England has a mortgage on the island of St. Domingo, and she has a naval station at Mole St. Nicholas, by the expenditure of £10,000 per annum, as a naval station. It is not likely that England would not permit her trade with Hayti to be interfered with.
Hayti, then, is not to be conquered by Santana or a sighted leader. He knows, too, that the Dominican Republic is a part of the island of Hayti, and that it is, and must be, tied by the Constitution, and independent of any foreign power. Any other measures may compel him to appeal to the United States for protection. If the Spanish Government should attempt to bring the States into the Gulf, at a quicker rate than it has done, the result may be easily seen.
Respectfully, JAMES REDPATH.
FREDERICK, Maryland, March 30, 1861.

records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that the Dominican Republic, covering an area of 1,000 square miles with a population of 136,000, declared its complete independence from the French portion, though Spain had never formally admitted its independence after forty years out of its possession. According to Mr. James Redpath, officially connected with the Republic of Hayti, the Dominican Republic has been divided between two alternating parties represented by Santana and Baez, whose policies indicate re-union and independence. Redpath explained that after Santana failed to repay a million-dollar loan borrowed from Spain and offered a mortgage on the custom-houses, a small band of eighty Spaniards arrived in St. Domingo last summer to work as custom collectors and mechanics, which fueled the opposition's revolutionary claims that Santana was selling the country.
records.summary_es: El periódico informó que la República Dominicana, con una superficie de 1.000 millas cuadradas y una población de 136.000 habitantes, declaró su completa independencia de la porción francesa, aunque España nunca había reconocido formalmente su independencia tras cuarenta años fuera de su dominio. Según el Sr. James Redpath, vinculado oficialmente a la República de Haití, la República Dominicana ha estado dividida entre dos facciones alternantes representadas por Santana y Báez, cuyas directrices apuntaban respectivamente a la anexión y a la independencia. records.full_text:
A Washington dispatch to the New York Tribune, Thursday, says:

The Dominican Republic, which has an area of 18,000 square miles, and a population of 136,000, had declared its complete independence of the French portion. Spain, however, has never, it seems, formally admitted its independence of herself. It has been forty years out of her possession.

Mr. James Redpath, who is officially connected with the Republic of Hayti, gives the following explanation of the reported usurpation:

"Since the independence of the Dominican Republic, there has always been a Spanish party in it, who have desired to return to their old allegiance. This party has been led by Santana, the present President. He has long been in negotiation with the Spanish Government for the purpose of bringing about the present result. The people of the Republic, however, are almost to a man opposed to the change, and will resist it to the last. The movement is a most important one, as it is the first step towards the re-establishment of the Spanish power in the West Indies, and the ultimate recovery of the whole island of St. Domingo. It is also a direct violation of the Monroe doctrine, and will, no doubt, lead to a protest from the United States Government."

records.summary_en: Following the 1844 secession of the Dominican Republic, two alternating political parties led by Santana and Baez emerged, representing reunion and independence policies respectively. Santana repeatedly and unsuccessfully sought to place the republic under the control of Spain, France, or Venezuela, and also failed in his efforts to induce white emigration from the United States.

records.full_text:
The Dominican republic committed suicide yesterday. I was one of the witnesses of the act, and can testify that it was a very discreditable affair. Never was there seen a more grotesque corpse or a more ridiculous funeral. Santana, the President, has sold the republic to the dead republic, in an honest old fool, and accepted the Spanish knife to cut his country's throat, under the delusion that he was performing a specially religious operation. He is no coward, but as stubborn as a mule, and about as well learned in the grammar of nations as the average of those useful animals. It is impossible to explain his astounding stupidities without this insight into his mental calibre. The Haytiens were always threatening to reconquer the Dominican territory, and he was as mad as those well informed people in seeking Spain to assert a protectorate over this, her former colony of St. Domingo. His best counsellors advised him to form a treaty with the United States, and, by opening the magnificent resources of the island to American enterprise, create in a few years the capital and the interests which would force the Union to protect its own. Unfortunately England and France would not permit this, and as the republic was a necessity to her existence, they compelled this government to cancel a treaty it had just concluded with the United States. Ever since then Spain has been coquetting with the Dominican government for this surrender, body and soul, to the service of Spain, from whence she expects for a cheap penny her own she has it.

The Santana's Cabinet are pure Spaniards, and every one of them would rather wear a gold coat to-day—with a neat pension tacked to it—from the chaste hand of Isabella Segunda, than live the plain citizen, or even first minister, of a simple republic. They are dogs for the chase, and they have scented the Spanish bounty to run down the prey, and bring their country to the feet of Spain. The prime movers—outside of the Cabinet—were the brothers Felipe and Juan Alfau, one a Spanish General, and the other the Vice President of the republic. Santana himself was born in the Spanish portion of the Dominican republic, and was at first treated with the most cutting disdain by the grandees of the court; but when he asserted his power the cooling luxury prevailed; but, then, what to do with the Dominican people? Three members of the Cabinet took charge of that. The transfer was to be effected by a coup de main, and after that, the resistance of the people could be crushed out by Spanish artillery in legal form, and, as General Scott would say, 'According to the science of war.' The war steamer Don Juan de Austria was despatched from Cadiz early last summer to begin the game by landing at St. Domingo no less than ninety secret agents to hunt up proselytes, help set them at work, and report progress to the Spanish government. Spanish steamers of war were continually coming and going between Cuba, St. Domingo and Porto Rico, and their many visits and unusual movements the Cabinet manifested an increased taste and means for the costly luxuries of life. Priests from Spain came as agents with Spanish subjects, their passage and three months' provisions being paid by government. This set the Dominicans wondering, and the local authorities ventured to inquire, but they were told that the Spanish officers and soldiers landed by their war ships, were a few friends from the coast of Spain. Half the time, indeed, they—the officers and soldiers had come to instruct the Dominicans and assist them to repel Haytien invasions, and the other half—why, they were simple visitors to till the ground and develop the stagnant resources of the country! As soon as these visits were without any further movement, the people began to believe that their Cabinet told the truth, and that after all there was no fear of a Spanish protectorate, and for a while there was a general repose throughout the land.

It was during this interval that the Dominicans asked what was done for a treaty with the United States, and had it been accorded to them the destruction of this American State, and all the horrors of a bloody war of races, would have been avoided. Why was it refused? That no one understands.

When all was ready for the treaty with the United States, then, given up, Santana became as anxious as the most Spanish of his friends to be accepted a person beyond redemption. Nothing short of annexation would satisfy him any more. Many times, during this, were emissaries from Cuba to buy up the willing, and plenty of wine and aguardiente were dispensed with the doubloons to silence the refractory; but it was managed so cunningly that everything was kept secret, and when the people made inquiry of, they were even led to suspect they were actually sold to Spain.

A small party of troops was sent, under disguised Spanish officers, to each leading town—at least, thirty, and between five and ten thousand men in all—to shout with them at the same time, 'Long live our mother country!' and plant the Spanish flag in a conspicuous place. When the people assembled, as they naturally would, to inquire into the meaning of this proceeding, a speech was made to the effect that the Queen of Spain, having learned the ferocious determination of the Haytiens to invade their villages with fire and sword, she resolved to protect them from all these evils and all the horrors of war; that it wasn't their liberties, but, on the contrary, she yearned to shower upon them all the blessings of peace and prosperity, and as a first evidence of it she proposed to exchange their depreciated paper money for gold, gold and silver. Some of the local magistrates were hesitant to have tested this last promise, and found it true in their own cases. They touched Spanish gold for their paper, but on condition that they added their official signature to the request written for them at St. Domingo, that their districts had pronounced for annexation to Spain.

A powerful and fast steam fleet of vessels came in together about the 18th and 20th of March, and on them it was reported to everyone that 'Dominican republic' is province of Spain, by the act of the people; but the presence of the war vessels was so many symbols of the Spanish power that it was useless to attempt to protest. Instead of waiting until the 25th inst., as originally intended, Santana hastily threw up the Spanish flag on the 18th, in order to employ the Spanish troops in crushing out whatever resistance was shown by the pride of their 'tender mother country.' Santana made short work of it. He told the people that their country was now 'the province of St. Domingo and a part of the kingdom of Spain,' and on the 18th he showed himself on the balcony of the national palace and raised the Spanish flag amid the roar of Spanish artillery and the music of the Spanish bands, without even a cheer. Even the Dominican traitors, who have made their own fortunes by selling their country, could not hide the grim grief of the citizens present by lending their voices to this shameful act of treason—not even! The citizens were ordered to assemble in the Plaza to hear the decree of the sale of the republic to Spain, but hardly one went that was not specially ordered to be present under pain of imprisonment. Such was poor Santo Domingo, while Santana gave in his allegiance to Queen Isabella, and Dominican gold—no, the gold that was offered by Spaniards—and, each of the double traitors was to have his reward. Is there no hope for traitors? Yes; even that will not keep down the people.

The following is the

Protest of the Foreign Consuls—Feeling in the Country—Dominican Currency, &c., &c.

Of course it will be made to appear that this conquest is the will of the nation; that, tired of internal dissensions and dreading an invasion from Hayti, the young republic, like a wayward and weary child, has sought to repose again in the arms of its old mother. This is all false. Fear alone of the power of the sword prevents a [illegible] speak openly denouncing the treason, and in the province, I am told, there is a determination not to submit to the annexation without a struggle. All the people's eyes are turned anxiously to the United States. There they believe they may expect some sympathy. It is true, the French and English Consuls have protested, struck their flags, &c., but the people here have no faith in these gentry. They say it is not in the order of things for monarchies to protect republics, except with the ulterior design of swallowing them. Gen. Cazneau, our diplomatic agent here, has been strongly appealed to to protest against this usurpation of Old Spain but, although I believe the Texan hero has no particular affection for the flag which his friend Quitman styled 'the Pirate Flag of Blood and Gold,' I have not heard that he has acted in the matter as yet. records.summary_en: Based on the provided newspaper excerpt, forty-three notable persons from Cibao were arrested and sent under escort to St. Domingo, while Padre Moya hoisted the Spanish flag in Vega despite public opposition and subsequently escaped the pursuing populace. The nation is described as indignant over being sold and betrayed through annexation, with unarmed citizens struggling in Moca following disarmament, a movement resulting in seven persons being shot in Azua, and reinforcements requested from Porto Rico. Consequently, Spain finds herself engaged in an unforeseen labyrinth of trouble stemming from the annexation.
records.summary_es: A tenor del extracto de prensa, cuarenta y tres personalidades destacadas del Cibao fueron arrestadas y enviadas bajo escolta a Santo Domingo, mientras que el padre Moya izó el pabellón español en La Vega a pesar del rechazo popular y luego logró huir de la multitud que lo perseguía. La nación se describe consternada e indignada por verse vendida y traicionada mediante la anexión, con ciudadanos desarmados resistiendo en Moca tras el desarme forzoso, un estallido que dejó siete personas fusiladas en Azua y peticiones de refuerzos a Puerto Rico. Por consiguiente, España se encuentra atrapada en un imprevisto laberinto de dificultades derivado de la anexión.

records.full_text: Important Movements of British Naval Vessels, &c. The business of transferring vessels from the American to the British flag is proceeding with alacrity and despatch. Quite a number have availed themselves of the time allowed by the ample provisions of the British law for this purpose. The British war steamer Jason, and several other frigates in the British navy, arrived here yesterday on her way to the mouth of the Mississippi river, for the purpose of seeing that the blockade is effectively maintained. It is expected that the blockade is carried on in Spanish style. She is to be further reinforced, to be followed by a number of other first class frigates, with smaller vessels, which will be distributed all along the blockaded coast, with instructions to break the blockade wherever it may be found unprovided by a sufficient naval force to make it effective. This is the report current among those whom the writer of this is what communications such instructions would lead to lead. The Sickles leaves to-day, with Messrs. Wilder and Mathew, late of the American army in Mexico. Mr. Mathew is in a very critical state, being very much frightened ahead by the yellow fever, which is very fatal. General Ampudia and his wife, together with Mrs. Arista and lady, late of New Orleans, are the guests of B. J. de Aldama, Esq. It is thought that Mexico will become a resident of this island. The weather is hot and sultry, with daily showers. The extreme dulness of the city is to be enlivened the week by a ball at the Spanish Governor's newly opened. Five or six Spanish men-of-war, with several thousand troops, left this port for St. Domingo on the 14th inst. The news from St. Domingo is very unfavorable to the Spaniards. In the town of Moca the people rose against the Spanish authorities, and after a short struggle the Spaniards were driven out of the town. In consequence of this forty-three persons of note of Cibao have been arrested and sent under a strong escort to the city of St. Domingo. In spite of the opposition of the people Padre Moya, sold to the Spaniards, caused the Spanish flag to be hoisted in Vega. The people are pursuing him, to put him under arrest, but he appears to have made his escape. In Cibao they do not wish to have the Spaniards at any price. Serious conflicts will take place, as the people are determined to resist the Spanish rule.

records.summary_en: A report from Cadiz dated the 6th states that exiled Dominican generals—including Cabral, Sanchez, Valentine, and Baez—joined disaffected populations to lead a serious insurrection against the Spanish occupation, raising the Dominican flag in La motta, Ney be, Cerca, and San Juan. The insurgents declared that if they could not remain independent, they would prefer incorporation with the Haytien Republic, while the Haytien Government maintained an attitude of observation with only a few prudent frontier troops stationed near the border.
records.summary_es: Un informe desde Cádiz fechado el día 6 señala que generales dominicanos desterrados —entre ellos Cabral, Sánchez, Valentine y Báez— se unieron a sectores descontentos de la población para encabezar una seria insurrección contra la dominación española, enarbolando la bandera dominicana en La motta, Ney be, Cerca y San Juan. Los insurrectos manifestaron que, de no poder preservar la independencia, preferirían la unión con la República de Haití, en tanto que el gobierno haitiano guardaba una postura de observación destacando únicamente escasas y prudentes tropas de frontera en las inmediaciones del límite limítrofe.

records.full_text:
HAYTI AS A COTTON COUNTRY.
This island, situated in the very heart of the cotton belt, has a climate unsurpassed for its culture, and untold acres waiting the hands of industry, a Government eager to promote enterprise, and a geographical-commercial position which renders it more easily accessible than the Central American to the mercantile navy of this or any other country. All the evidence proves conclusively that this island is admirably adapted to the raising of this staple. The writers upon this country speak enthusiastically of the quality of the cotton grown there. It is said to be of a very long and silky fibre, and to be even superior to the best Sea Island cotton. The soil is of the most fertile character, and the climate is such that the cotton plant becomes a perennial tree, producing two crops a year for many years without replanting. The Government of Hayti is offering every inducement to emigrants to settle in the country and engage in the cultivation of cotton. They offer free grants of land, exemption from taxes for a term of years, and other advantages. There is no doubt that Hayti is destined to become one of the great cotton-producing countries of the world.

records.headline: The republic was virtually dead, and the island was openly presented
records.summary_en: According to a January 13 dispatch reported by *The New York Herald* correspondent in San Domingo, the Dominican Republic was virtually dead and openly presented to the world as a Spanish province ruled by General Santana as the commissioned Captain-General for Queen Isabella. Spain promised numerous reforms as part of its policy of absorption—including declaring Samana a free port, inviting universal emigration, reducing tariffs on foreign-imported goods, proclaiming full religious toleration, and abolishing slavery—while it was also thought Queen Isabella would invite President Lincoln to send surplus negroes and contrabands to San Domingo. Additionally, the city's streets were enlivened with foreign carriages, buggies, drays, and new toilets, and the new United States Consul had not held any official intercourse with the government.
records.summary_es: Según un despacho del 13 de enero remitido por el corresponsal de *The New York Herald* en Santo Domingo, la República Dominicana había prácticamente dejado de existir, mostrándose abiertamente al mundo como provincia española gobernada por el general Santana como capitán general comisionado de la reina Isabel. España prometía múltiples reformas como parte de su política de absorción —incluida la declaración de Samaná como puerto libre, la invitación a la inmigración general, la rebaja de aranceles a las importaciones foráneas, la proclamación de una entera libertad de cultos y la abolición formal de la esclavitud—, al tiempo que se suponía que la reina Isabel cursaría una invitación al presidente Lincoln para asentar en Santo Domingo a los libertos negros rescatados de la Confederación («contrabands»). Asimismo, las calles de la capital se veían animadas con carruajes, calesas y carretas foráneas y novedades en el vestir, mientras que el nuevo cónsul de los Estados Unidos se abstenía de mantener trato oficial alguno con las autoridades.

Our San Domingo City Correspondence.

SAN DOMINGO CITY, Jan. 12, 1862.

Termination of the Republic and Commencement of the Provinciature of the Country—Non-Recognition of the New Government by the Great Powers—What Spain Has Accomplished and Promises—A Splendid Location for the Negroes and the Outcasts of the United States—How the City Has Improved in Dashing "Turnouts," Toilets, Crinoline and House Decorations—War News from America—Theatricals, &c.

We are mulling along here in a kind of "cucumber time" between hay and grass.

The poor old Dominican republic has breathed its last. It died, too, without even the usual amount of howling; but Spain still sits awkwardly in the new saddle. She finds it not a triumphal opportunity to invest the reals she got from Morocco, and those she expects to get from time to time from Hayti and Mexico (D. V.) She does not think she has got such an almighty bargain in San Domingo after all. Still her old Castilian pride will not permit her to back out without a first rate excuse.

As yet none of the great Powers have recognized this island as a Spanish province, and the several consulates of France, England and the United States present a singularly modest and "attendant" aspect.

Spain, however, has begun well—she is on her good behavior.

A new tariff is proposed, reducing duties on merchandise in foreign bottoms from 30 to 20 per cent.

A decree grants permission to whalers to make Samana a free port for all nations, and it is darkly hinted that President Lincoln will be invited by his august cousin, Isabella II., to send his "contrabands" to our fertile (not sacred) soil.

The most entire religious toleration will be exercised.

Emigration from every land under the sun, including coolies and the "rest lying east of Chinese Tartary," will be encouraged.

Our coasting trade is thrown open to all flags, and last, but by no means least, that nation whose name for centuries has been the synonym of tyranny and oppression, has begun a march with the progressive people of the earth; and here, on the spot where African slavery was first planted, and whence it spread its poisonous branches like a blighting curse over the surrounding countries; here her first act after annexation has been to declare the chains of the slave broken, and broken forever.

Materially the city at least has been benefitted by the change of government. Carriages that have seen service in the continental or insular world in the days of the puff and toupee of Havana, begin to show themselves in our unaccustomed streets. Spanish thoroughbreds, English, American and other high breds do their duty, whilst "Jack-ass-dom" is scorned and disgusted. Several fine horses from Cuba and Porto Rico have been imported, and gayly caparisoned, bear their creole masters right proudly.

Toilets are more dashing, if not more distingue than formerly. Less of the eternal and dreary black mantilla, but pretentious crinolines flaunt their voluptuous curves in our breeze.

Houses, too, are catching a fresh coat of plaster or paint, and shops and tiendas innumerable meet the eye in our streets.

Meantime traders are not frequent, but loafers abound.

I have little of importance to send you, being, like yourselves in political circles, confused in our notions of things. There are big stories afloat, of course.

One report was, that in consequence of the blunder made by John Bull upon the arrest of Mason and Slidell, the French Emperor has called upon John to account for the disposition made of his uncle, who placed himself as a refugee (not in act of war) on board a British craft; also that the Southern confederacy had declared war against Spain, and that a French and Spanish fleet had been seen off Charleston.

Nature, too, has not yet owned the culture of the husbandman. The island is the same wilderness as when Columbus gazed with rapture upon its green clad hills and magnificent prairies. Vast herds roam at will over the savannas, but the herdsmen are few. Its mines, that once yielded so fast to the conqueror, and, rich as the pockets of Spain, are unworked; its teeming valleys are unbroken by the plough, and its woods contain towering timbers to shelter navies. What a glorious field to try the experiment of your new freed or discarded black population.

General Santana is still Captain General. He is an exemplary gentleman, but slow. Affairs are managed pretty much by his Excellency, the Superintendente and the Governor General, who are both men of a high order of intelligence and of extremely liberal views. The Dominican party, though shorn of all their power, are reconciled, and Spaniards occupy their places and pocket their emoluments.

Mr. Jaeger, our new Consul, is at his post, but, like his predecessors, holds no official intercourse with the government.

We have at the theatre a prestigitateur. The feats, however, do not astonish the natives, since Santana changed a republic into a monarchical province by a dash of his pen.

The bark Harvest Queen, which sails to-morrow for New York, carries a sample of native cotton which grows here abundantly, and can doubtless be cultivated to advantage. It appears to be of the same species as the Peruvian tree cotton, and bears four crops in three years. It can probably be raised in our Northern and Middle

records.summary_en: According to the *New York Herald* on February 25, 1862, Spanish forces in the Dominican Republic maintained social distance from natives while leasing land, driving up rents and creating a strong market for duty-free wooden houses from Baltimore and ship bread. The newspaper also reported that local copper ore contained gold, Samana coal beds showed promise for miners, and suggestions were made to relocate four million American "contrabands" to the island to develop its wealth. Additionally, correspondence from Trujillo, Honduras, dated February 5, reported that a recent revolution had culminated in the assassination of President Guardiola following a conspiracy sanctioned by Colonel Agurcia.
records.summary_es: Según *The New York Herald* del 25 de febrero de 1862, las fuerzas españolas en la República Dominicana mantenían un distanciamiento social con los nativos al tiempo que arrendaban terrenos, encareciendo los alquileres y creando un floreciente mercado libre de derechos para casas de madera procedentes de Baltimore y pan de barco. El diario también señaló que el mineral de cobre local contenía oro, que los yacimientos de carbón de Samaná resultaban prometedores para los mineros y que se sugería asentar en la isla a cuatro millones de «contrabands» (libertos) estadounidenses para explotar sus riquezas. Por otra parte, correspondencia desde Trujillo, Honduras, con fecha del 5 de febrero, dio cuenta de que una reciente revolución culminó con el asesinato del presidente Guardiola tras una conspiración autorizada por el coronel Agurcia.

records.full_text: Our correspondent in St. Domingo City writes, under date of the 31st of January, that the Spaniards still held apart from intimate social intercourse with the native Dominicans. They had rented or leased lots of land on which to erect aristocratic mansions for their families. House rents had advanced considerably. In the meantime wooden houses, ready fitted for construction, found a good market—a lot just landed, from Baltimore, commanding profitable prices. A government decree admits such material free of duty. Ship bread is also ordered for free entry into the ports. Copper ore taken from mines near St. Domingo City was found to be strongly impregnated with gold. The coal beds of Samana promised a rich return to experienced miners. Napoleon had not yet appointed a French Consul in the city, or committed himself in any recognition of the new rule of Spain. The American “contrabands” left on Mr. Lincoln’s hands after the war can be taken, it is said, to the extent of four millions, on the island. They would be set to work, and really develope the wealth of the country. There was no American vessel in port.

records.full_text:
Increase of Union Feeling—Success of the Federal Officials—Revival of Trade—The Military Governor a Great Favorite with the People—Success of the New Daily Paper—The Norfolk Herald—Change in the Provost Marshal's Office, &c.
It will afford a sincere gratification to all well wishers of the Union cause to notice the gradual, steady return to a healthy state of public sentiment that is now in progress at Norfolk. But a few weeks ago it was difficult for an officer to pass one block and not meet with some expression of disrespect from the citizens, especially the women; but now they seem to take the presence of the federal authorities as a matter of course, and to prefer the good order now reigning in the city, the military occupation has, indeed, been a source of blessing to the people. Under the rebel rule everything was stagnant, and disorders were every day occurrences, and the most arbitrary and cruel persecutions were dealt out to all such as had moral courage enough to stand up for the right, and speak the truth and truth amidst the clamor of lawlessness and traitors.
Business is now fairly opening with northern traders and purchasers; the stores, one by one, begin to show signs of life, and the people are now gradually returning to habits of trade, which may soon be expected, and a large number of the citizens are deploring the folly of the secessionists who have so long persisted and will certainly find that the days of the rebellion are numbered and gone forever.
The manner in which General Viele, the Military Governor, conducts his department, has met with the highest words of the highest praise, and even the secession citizens of the bitterest stamp frankly admit that, while he deals out the strictest justice to all, his deportment is at all times courteous and characteristic of the perfect gentleman.
The weather, which during the early part of last week was extremely hot and oppressive, took a sudden turn on Wednesday night, and, with the exception of the dust, nothing could be more delicious than the climate we are now enjoying. The health of the citizens and the military is excellent.
The new Union paper meets with general favor, and is productive of good. It is called the New Regime, and the kind tone in which the claims of the Union and the dear old flag are presented is well calculated to win over the malcontents. The Dominicans have certainly no reason to complain of her occupation. Indeed, the benefits bestowed have been thus far like the jug handle—all on one side—for poor St. Domingo has had nothing but humble acquiescence and gratitude to render on its part. The officials of her Majesty's government are free to express their avowed desire to foster enterprise, and especially to welcome and protect foreign capital and labor. There will be plenty of room for all, and the field is a wide and inviting one. The climate is not more unhealthy than that of our Southern States, and the soil is of unsurpassed fertility. The city of St. Domingo is being rapidly improved, and the health of the Spanish troops is excellent. The most perfect order and security prevail throughout the island.

records.summary_en: A correspondent writing from St. Domingo City on May 17 reports that Spain is making its mark under the new rule, silencing the remaining malcontents and welcoming foreign capital and labour. A railroad from Santiago to Angelina on the Yuna has been decided upon, giving the Vega Real valley an outlet to the Bay of Samana, an American company has proposed navigating the Yuna, and a new tariff cutting duties from thirty to twenty per cent is expected to take effect in July.

records.headline: The wishes of the people were not consulted, and how large
records.summary_en: According to the *New-York daily tribune*, the Dominican Republic was unexpectedly annexed to Spain on March 12, 1861, through the treason of President Santana without consulting the public, and the annexation was formally accepted by the Queen of Spain on May 20, 1861. While resident Spaniards and their descendants favored the change, citizens of African or mixed descent opposed it and desired to retain a republican form of government. Cuban papers report that the national party subsequently made an attempt to regain their independence.
records.summary_es: Según el *New-York daily tribune*, la República Dominicana fue anexionada inesperadamente a España el 12 de marzo de 1861 debido a la traición del presidente Santana sin consultar a la ciudadanía, y dicha anexión fue aceptada formalmente por la reina de España el 20 de mayo de 1861. Aunque los españoles residentes y sus descendientes favorecieron el cambio, los ciudadanos de ascendencia africana o mestiza se opusieron y desearon conservar la forma de gobierno republicana. Los diarios cubanos señalan que el partido nacionalista intentó posteriormente recuperar la independencia.

records.headline: THE INSURRECTION IN SANTO DOMINGO.
records.summary_en: The *New-York Daily Tribune* reported that an attempted insurrection by the small population of Santo Domingo against Spanish rule was speedily put down, resulting in the population having to succumb to the overwhelming power of Spain. Following this triumph, Spanish officers and the *Diario de la Marina* accused the Haytian government of instigating the movement, renewing threats against Hayti's independence and prompting the newspaper to warn of European encroachments upon American independence.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Daily Tribune* informó que un intento de sublevación de la escasa población de Santo Domingo contra la dominación española fue sofocado rápidamente, debiendo la población sucumbir ante el poderío abrumador de España. Tras este triunfo, oficiales españoles y el *Diario de la Marina* acusaron al gobierno haitiano de instigar la insurrección, renovando las amenazas contra la independencia de Haití y llevando al periódico a advertir contra los avances europeos sobre la soberanía en el continente americano.

records.chapter_es: La anexión a España y la Guerra de la Restauración
records.full_text:
Two years ago the eastern portion of the island of Hayti, constituting the Dominican Republic, was quite unexpectedly, by the treason of its President, Santana, deprived of its independence, and annexed to Spain. The wishes of the people were not consulted, and how large a portion of the population was in favor of annexation has never been made known. Immediately after the proclamation of the President, dated March 18, 1861, Spanish troops landed, and took possession of the Republic in the name of the Spanish Government. On May 20, 1861, the Queen of Spain formally accepted the annexation, and the Dominican Republic was reduced from the condition of a free State to that of a Spanish colony.
That a great many Dominicans from the beginning protested against this change of government has never been denied; and according to the best accounts, it appears probable that only the resident Spaniards and the descendants of Spanish families, who form but a small part of the population, were favorable to the sale of their independence, while the citizens of African or mixed European and African descent wished to retain a republican form of government.
Spain has never allowed them a free expression of their preference, and it was therefore both natural and justifiable that the national party should make an attempt to regain their independence. This attempt, we learn from the Cuban papers, was actually made during the past month of February. A General Mella, who, previous to the time of annexation, had been exiled from the Dominican Republic, and who with many other opponents of the annexation has found an asylum in Hayti, is reported to have been at the head of the movement which, on Feb. 21, broke out in the towns of San Lorenzo de Guayubin, Las Matas, Dajabon, Sabaneta and Monte-Christi, and later also in the provincial capital of Santiago, having, besides, numerous sympathizers in all the other parts of the former republic. Of course, such an attempt, made by a population not numbering more than 200,000 souls, had no chance of success, and, as was to be expected, it was speedily put down. The reports of the victories claimed by the Spanish troops are unmistakably gross exaggerations, but about the final result there could be no doubt. As Poland was unable to cope, unaided by foreign nations, with the combined forces of Russia, Prussia and Austria, so the small population of Santo Domingo have had to succumb to the overwhelming power of Spain.
The Spanish officers are not satisfied with their easy triumph, but, charging the Haytians with having instigated the insurrectionary movement, they renew the threats which have frequently been made against the independence of Hayti. The Diario de la Marina declares that, inasmuch as the Haytian Government was cognizant of the insurrection, the Government of Her Catholic Majesty will at once take measures for preventing the repetition of such interference.
Spain should not assume any arrogant attitude toward an independent American State such as that France displays toward Mexico and England toward Brazil. The time must come when the governments and nations of North, Central, and South America will be compelled to take into common and serious consideration what means will be best suited to prevent the further encroachments of Europe upon American independence.
