records.full_text:
By the arrival of the steamship Eagle, Captain Adams, at this port yesterday from Havana, we have news to the 12th inst., which will be found detailed in the letter of our correspondent.

Our Havana Correspondence.
Havana, Sept. 12, 1863.
Relations of Spain with Hayti—Probability of War—Another Fire in Havana—Murder of an Editor—An Elopement—Arrival of the Anglo-Saxon, &c., &c.
During the three days which have elapsed since my last letter, nothing of real importance has transpired anywhere. Troops continue to be sent from here to St. Domingo, and other garrisons in the island are also further decimated, although it might be said for certain that the insurrection in the latter colony was regarded as a very serious affair by the authorities. Whether it be really so or not we have no means of judging; for no intelligence from the disturbed regions has been published for several days, and the space between the different points of infection has shown itself at other points. If I might venture on an opinion, I would say that the insurrection amounts to nothing, and that the great number of troops which have been despatched are not sent simply to crush out a movement, but because a war with Hayti is not far from probable. Spanish feeling towards that republic is not the most friendly, as I have frequently had occasion to mention before, and in the present instance, if the slightest pretext be found, the slightest proof afforded, that Haytian hands have been implicated in the present insurrection, I think war is imminent. The news that there was not only an insurrection, but the rebellion of the province of Cibao last spring, and now, for the second time, the same province is in revolt, giving rise to the same suspicions and a renewal of the threats that were then made. I do not pretend to pronounce one way or the other on the question whether Hayti is innocent; but I would remind you of the fact that the capture of Geffrard's vessel gave the highest degree of satisfaction to Spain. The Haytien general was forced to fly for his life, and the members of his government became aware that he had encouraged the insurrection of 1861; and now that they know that the Spaniards know anything of his criminality—in fact, if they do find out—after they had told him and other Haytian official had been guilty of any such conduct. This should have been sufficient to keep him from a second illegal attempt, but there would be no reason for a war. In such a case what can Hayti do? She is not a military power, and her people are not a bit more sensitive than her interest is. In the matter of St. Domingo, Spain will be her conqueror, and the frequently recurring difficulties that must arise as long as Hayti remains an independent republic, will be swept away forever. Hayti is now regarded as the nest wherein Dominican insurrections are hatched, and Spain concludes that she must either destroy the nest or abandon the island altogether. Which alternative do you think she will adopt? To answer this question we must understand Spanish nature and temper—a not very difficult matter. In some respects the same people that they were in the days of Ferdinand and Isabella. The Spanish spirit is much more like an Englishman or an American. Passion governs him more than judgment, and his honor is much more sensitive than his interest is. In the matter of St. Domingo, Spain has spent a weight worth her gold, and she will ruin herself rather than throw it away. Worthy of saving, people will say; it is surely worthy the cost. It is not for a moment to be doubted, especially when the finances and patience of the mother country are exhausted, that her statesmen will begin to think it might be wiser to let Dominicans go to the devil by some other way. But until that time shall have arrived, and, to avoid it, Spain will tighten her grip on the island more and more. She will do everything to avoid the humiliation of being obliged to abandon St. Domingo, and, if the possession of the whole island will prolong her rule there, she will annex Hayti. This is my conviction. It is the opinion of everyone in Havana, and the annexation, or bestowal of populous countries, goes on. It is the old way the crowns had, and they cannot help the force of habit.
Our quiet in Havana has been disturbed by fire and blood. A cruel and mysterious murder has been perpetrated on the person of the editor of the Revista Militar, by whom is not yet known. The case is at present involved in mystery.
Fires here are not known, unusual, but it will sometimes wipe out a house or two. Night before last, a good many citizens alike were aroused by the usual fire signals, and those who chose rushed out to see all about it. It proved to be the residence of the Conde de la Reunion, a very fine house on the corner of the streets Aguiar and Sol. Nothing could save it—that is to say, nothing was to be had there—none save a few buckets, in a country provided with fire engines, the consequence of which in this instance was that the house was destroyed. Another fire occurred last night. To one who has seen the splendid fire engines of New York and Philadelphia, nothing can be more ridiculous than the absurd machines we have here; and it will only be when some disastrous fire occurs that the authorities will begin to think of it. A stone wall, as a rule, never is touched till the horse has been stolen.
Since Matanzas has built her new theatre there is no standing the city. Just think of the Matanzeros calling it their city by so many names, while we in Havana must do without one or be contented with the musical crumbs that may fall from the table—we well say the table of our country sister. It is too bad. In fact it would be unendurable did not the news that the impresario, Signor Albertazzi, takes his departure for that purpose to day. He intends getting the very cream of the Italian opera singers. All right. Let him have it; but when it is all gone I wish somebody would furnish us with some for some time.
A steamer arrived this morning from Nassau with news that Charleston is not yet taken. Exchange on New York about 26. Weather quite pleasant.

records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that after President Santana betrayed the Dominican people by annexing them to Spain, the Dominicans launched a unanimous rebellion marked by fierce fighting and atrocities on both sides. Recent reports indicated that Spanish troops suffered heavy losses, including a division of 2,000 men that was forced to capitulate after Santiago was burned, while another division of 1,600 men was repulsed. Additionally, the town of San Carlos near Santo Domingo city was reportedly burned by the rebels.
records.summary_es: El diario informó que, luego de que el presidente Santana traicionara al pueblo dominicano anexionándolo a España, los dominicanos emprendieron una rebelión unánime caracterizada por encarnizados combates y atrocidades de ambos bandos. Informes recientes indicaban que las tropas españolas sufrieron severas bajas, incluida una división de 2.000 soldados obligada a capitular tras el incendio de Santiago, al tiempo que otra división de 1.600 hombres fue rechazada. Además, se comunicó que el poblado de San Carlos, cercano a la ciudad de Santo Domingo, fue incendiado por los insurrectos.

records.summary_en: According to the *Chicago Daily Tribune* of October 10, 1863, the Dominican people are fiercely rebelling against Spanish rule following President Santana's annexation of the country to Spain. The newspaper reports that Spanish forces have suffered significant defeats—including a routed division of 3,000 men with over 1,000 casualties and the capitulation and retreat from Santiago—amid a conflict marked by mutual atrocities and the burning of towns such as San Carlos. Additionally, while the Dominicans reportedly receive sympathy and support from neighboring islands and the Unitedest States, the article questions their capacity for self-government due to past deficiencies in vigor and cohesion.
records.summary_es: Según el *Chicago Daily Tribune* del 10 de octubre de 1863, el pueblo dominicano se subleva con ferocidad contra el dominio español tras la anexión del país a España efectuada por el presidente Santana. El periódico consigna que las tropas españolas han sufrido considerables reveses —entre ellos una división dispersada de 3.000 hombres con más de 1.000 bajas, así como la capitulación y evacuación de Santiago— en el curso de una contienda signada por atrocidades recíprocas y el incendio de poblaciones como San Carlos. Además, si bien se señala que los dominicanos reciben la simpatía y el respaldo de islas vecinas y de los Estados Unidos, el artículo pone en duda su capacidad de autogobierno debido a su pasada falta de vigor y cohesión.

records.full_text: The New York Tribune's Washington special says: The Herald's statement that a proposition has been made to Spain for the purchase of St. Domingo, is denied by the very highest authority. The Tribune also says: If we may trust the intelligence from St. Domingo, the people of that island can not only maintain their independence against Spain, but drive her troops entirely from the island. Their independence was recognized by Hayti in 1844. With France, a treaty with that power was concluded in 1848, and with Great Britain two years later. For a time they enjoyed a considerable degree of prosperity, but through the treachery of President Santana the rights and liberties of the people were sold to Spain and the act of annexation consummated. Against Spain they now rebel, the Dominicans displaying an earnestness and unanimity which gives promise of a long and desperate struggle before Spain regains her former ascendancy, if indeed she ever succeeds in doing so.

records.summary_en: According to *The Lancaster gazette* on November 5, 1863, fighting and fires in the Dominican Republic resulted in the destruction of the Government House, the Roman Catholic Church, and the American and British Consuls' residences, the latter of whom arrived at Grand Turk. Reports indicated that the entire south side of the island was in actual rebellion with 40,000 Dominicans in the neighborhood, and that Spanish soldiers pillaged the town before 600 Spaniards sortied from the fort and drove the Dominicans away with the aid of the fort's guns. The resulting fires destroyed numerous stores and properties belonging to foreign merchants, with losses in Santiago and Port-au-Platte expected to reach several millions of dollars.
records.summary_es: Según *The Lancaster Gazette* del 5 de noviembre de 1863, los combates e incendios en la República Dominicana ocasionaron la destrucción de la Casa de Gobierno, la iglesia católica y las residencias de los cónsules británico y estadounidense, habiendo llegado este último a Gran Turca. Los informes indicaban que toda la vertiente sur del territorio se hallaba en rebelión abierta con unos 40.000 dominicanos en las proximidades, y que la soldadesca española saqueó la población antes de que 600 peninsulares salieran de la fortaleza y rechazaran a los dominicanos con el auxilio de los cañones del fuerte. Los incendios resultantes destruyeron numerosos comercios y propiedades de comerciantes extranjeros, previéndose pérdidas millonarias en Santiago y Puerto Plata.

records.full_text: NEW YORK, Nov. 1.—The Grand Turk has arrived. She carried one hundred passengers. At Port au Plata, on the 4th, the Spaniards attacked the Dominicans, but were repulsed, and retreated to the fort, with the loss of four hundred and fifty men. A brisk fire from the fort compelled the Dominicans to leave the town. The Government House, American and British Consuls' residences, and the Roman Catholic Church were among the houses burned. The Spanish soldiers were seen going about with fire brands in their hands when the fight was progressing. A report said the Spaniards would evacuate the fort, as they cannot retain it against the Dominicans. The whole town except the Wesleyan mission house and a few small buildings, was burnt, and it was believed the rest of the town would be destroyed. The losses by the two fires, at Santiago and Port au Plata will reach several millions of dollars.

records.headline: FRENCH REPORTS FROM SAN DOMINGO.
records.summary_en: *The New York Herald* reported, based on accounts from Port-au-Prince, that Dominican insurgents had established a provisional government in Santiago and chosen a native leader to head the republic. Fierce fighting in Santiago between Dominican forces and the Spanish garrison resulted in hundreds of casualties, forcing Spanish ally General Santana to flee into the woods near Azua. The report observed that Dominican enthusiasm for Spanish rule had collapsed, forcing Madrid to send costly military reinforcements.
records.summary_es: *The New York Herald* informó, basándose en despachos de Puerto Príncipe, que los insurrectos dominicanos habían constituido un gobierno provisional en Santiago eligiendo a un líder del país para presidir la república. Cruentos combates librados en Santiago entre las tropas dominicanas y la guarnición española dejaron cientos de bajas, forzando al general Santana, aliado de España, a refugiarse en los bosques cercanos a Azua. El reporte destacaba que el entusiasmo dominicano por la soberanía española se había desvanecido por completo, constriñendo a Madrid a despachar costosos contingentes militares de refuerzo.

records.full_text: The Paris Moniteur of October 23, publishes news from St. Domingo to the 27th of September. It states that the insurgents had suffered a defeat, that a provisional government had established itself in San Jago and, finally, that a native Chief, named Polengo, had been chosen head of the republic of St. Domingo. The town of St. Domingo surrendered, it is said, without striking a blow, which would show that the Spaniards had before them an overwhelming force. Resistance was, however, offered at St. Jago. A combat ensued between the native troops and the Spanish garrison, which continued for three days, and ended in one hundred of the latter being killed. The insurgents, who numbered four thousand men, then set fire to the town, leaving only a few houses standing, and fled to the mountains.

records.full_text:
The annexed important correspondence from St. Domingo reached us by the steamship Tubal Cain in addition to that published in the HERALD yesterday:—

Our St. Domingo Correspondence.
ST. DOMINGO CITY, Oct. 27, 1863.
Influencing Causes of the Revolution—Not a War of Races—Abolitionist Stories to the Negroes—Pay of General Santana from Spain—Foreigners in a State of Starvation—Rumor of American Intervention, by Recognition of the Republic—The Reward of the Lincoln Government—The Blockade, &c.
The Spanish portion of St. Domingo is at the present writing the theatre of one of the most flagrant revolutions of this age of topsy-turvy revolutions. It is not a war of races. Remember that. I have been among these people long enough to know what I am saying when I assure you that there is not on this continent, nor any of the islands thereof, a population more exceedingly mixed up in color or more happily mellowed down to a consensus than is to be found on this island. The whites lift their eyebrows with a mild expression of contemptuous surprise when some daring Yankee emits the idea that it would be a favor to everybody to force the idle blacks into some system of industry. They see no reason why they may not, laughing, take their coffee with their darkey neighbors, who have in their easy, irregular way, worked themselves into positions, and their fathers for them for two generations, should be molested in their little ways. It is true they are not hard and steady workers, but they are fed and paid accordingly, and it is the settled custom among Dominicans of all shades to take care of and be that same. But the "abolitionist" is active—the black Dominicans jealous of, or in a hurry to get rid of, the whites. They provide a great deal of very combustible stuff to lay on the [illegible] and [illegible] of the servant class on their plantations, in their mahogany "cuts," and, where a white man makes himself "no better than a nigger" by his bad habits or incorrigible stupidity, he is at once made a target of the black press.
Some amiable foreign abolitionists of the Congo-Sumner school tried to get up a war of races by furnishing arms to a few of the most desperate characters in Hayti, and teaching them how to take an unbefriended hospital and cut the throats of the sick and wounded. These simple people were also told that the murder of white women and children would be very agreeable to the "king of the United States," and that the "great Lincoln" and the "great Seward" would come with a great army and help the blacks to destroy the Spaniards the very minute he saw his dear children—the real negroes—had given him this proof that they were determined to have no more to do with the white race.
This abominable story, coming to them in company with the fact of several hundred fine guns and pistols—all gratis, free love offerings—wherewith to slaughter the "white devils" so designated by the "friends of the United States," had the effect of stimulating the border negroes to frenzy and some revolting atrocities among the struggling, half savage towns along the frontiers of Hayti. The object of the planner of this movement was to initiate a war of extermination by throwing away the scabbard when the sword was drawn; but after the first burst was over, and the masses of the Dominicans were lured into the conflict, there was no longer a question of races.
It is simply and entirely an uprising of the native Dominicans against the Spanish military officers. What is the basis of the difficulty? Of what do the Dominicans complain? you will naturally ask. That it is impossible to say. Nobody knows what the fight is about; and, what is funnier still, nearly all the mischief done by either party is done to themselves. There is any amount of large talk about victories on both sides, but the fact is there have been no effective battles fought, except on paper. Some contemptible skirmishing, in which certain Spanish officers took commendable care that nobody should be hurt, is all that is doing here. General Pedro Santana, the former President of the republic, and the man who made a present of this fine country to Spain, commands the Spanish forces, and he will do his best to win the day for Spain, as he will be the loser, if he don't win, of the comfortable pension of two thousand hard dollars every month of his natural life for the job, if any such favor an American President has a province to sell he knows where to find a market and his fee. Isabella pays like a lady for this kind of merchandise, when she finds that the article is worth.
The Dominicans knew nothing of this transaction until the Spanish flag actually floated over their heads, and the petty outbreak on the border, touching this prepared material like a match to tinder, lighted up a rather offensive blaze. There are eight or ten thousand Dominicans in arms, equally ready to form guerillas and take care of the border parties, or condense into brigades to oppose the advance of the Spanish troops into the interior. At Santiago—the loveliest city of the plain—the Dominicans burned up their beautiful town to dislodge the Spaniards; and at the seaport of Puerto Plata the same thing was done. In fact, they are burning the quarters to prevent the natives who were unhoused at La Vega from returning to their homes. It is a bad job for all the business for both sides, and are likely to be the most costly of all the Spanish wars. "I wish to God I could see how this thing is going to end" or "where it will end" asked one of another in my hearing this morning. "I wish I could see where it is in our way," was the reply.
It will end in the Spaniards taking the country—no doubt. The Dominicans will restore their old white and yellow and black mixture of government; that is all.
It is reported that the United States Consul has a document in his pocket from Washington recognizing the shattered old cage of Uncle Sam's. That is, it was so reported to me; but I should as soon expect to see the "great and good" Lincoln as he looked after a "decisive military movement," although everything that looks ugly for us is none. The Spanish "occupying force" heard on the road that the treaty was "concluded and signed," and some of them who were on the "neutral" board the Spaniards were "accumulating" to take them and their baggage back too. I heard that the American Consul had received orders from his government to recognize the revived Dominican republic forthwith, and obtain the cession of a free port on the great bay of Samana, as the reward of a little word of encouragement at the critical time; and on the whole I think the cat is out. Find nothing new at St. Domingo to justify any great stroke of statesmanship; (and when did Washington and Jefferson ever hatch a phoenix like that?) I turned my face in the opposite direction in search of more exciting signs of war.
I sailed up the Ozama in the wake of a little government which had agitated the whole district; returned to the "dead city," and took passage on a dirty little Spanish steamer, with a lively crowd of passengers, if it can be said that any Spanish crowd can be anything but monotonous. Business is dead here, and three-fourths of the people are in a state of starvation. All the work is done by foreigners, who have no interest in the country, and who are only waiting for a chance to leave. "Whose vocation is to feed men, not to kill them," and who, if they could only find a way to get away, would succeed much better than the natives. If I have written anything that looks like a joke, it is because I think the revolution itself is, in this respect at least, a joke. There are eight or ten thousand men on each side of the island they say; but they are so scattered that they can do nothing of to do. The military commanders on both sides are afraid to fight, and each tried to take the city by getting in a panic himself; but the enemy was too quick for him.
The weather is splendid. I think the mornings and evenings are the most beautiful I have ever seen or experienced. We have had but little sickness of a fatal stamp, and no yellow fever.

Another Letter from St. Domingo.
ST. DOMINGO CITY, Oct. 18, 1863.
The Spanish Blockade of the Coast—What is Required of Vessels—The Spanish Forces—The Insurrection—The Evacuation of the City of the Ozama by the Republic—Active Operations of the Spanish Troops—The Situation at San Cristobal—Haitien Help from the Island—Position of Santana—What Will the Issue Be?
The Spanish government has officially notified the blockade of the coast of St. Domingo by Spain. This does not include the ports in the actual possession of her Catholic Majesty. Vessels arriving here will, however, be subject to a rigorous examination. It will be well for vessels clearing from New York for this port to see that their papers are correctly filled up and properly certified by the Spanish Consul.
The insurrection still appears to be making headway. General Santana is in command of the Spanish forces in the Captain Generalcy. His successor, General Vargas, is daily looked for, and then, it is said, important movements will be made to develop the colony and to finally exterminate the handful of marauders now in arms against the authority of her Catholic Majesty. It is more than whispered that she contemplates retiring from the island altogether, after having expended some millions here upon these "wayward children," and with but small prospect of return. Last year the revenue of the island, after paying for the construction of internal improvements, amounted to one million eight hundred thousand dollars; the revenues, all told, only reached four hundred thousand.
On the 11th inst. the garrison at Agua, fifteen hundred strong, were withdrawn and brought by steamer to this city. All the loyal portion of the inhabitants came up with them. The city is now filled with these miserable subjects, some three hundred strong, marched in and provided for by the government.
At San Cristobal, which was pronounced for the republic on the 8th, it is said that there has been a counter proclamation.
An expedition left here on the 15th for the latter place, under command of General Santana and General Alfau, numbering three thousand men. They were obliged to take the beach, as the insurgents had felled trees and other obstacles on the road being in the hands of the rebels. We are very anxious to hear the result of this movement, as it is the first of any importance that we can afford to list.
The families of the loyal rebels have been reported at Fort St. Geronimo, three miles distant from this city. Fatigue parties and convicts are employed continually in clearing away the brush and trees for the distance of three miles from the walls, that no harbor may be left for the enemy. Many of the beautiful country seats which have felt the devastating axe is the lamented General Santana's, at the "Quinta de Santa Anna," which was the model residence of the neighborhood, and embellished to an extent that years cannot replace.
The families of the prominent officials are leaving for Porto Rico and Cuba. On the 15th inst. the wife and children of the Captain General embarked on the "Santa Lucia" for Havana. The Captain General's family left on the West India Company's steamer "Tubal Cain" for New York, on the 20th inst.
General Santana remains at San Pedro with two thousand men. He is said to be in a very bad way. The Soyo Indians, it will be a hard matter to bring any such race to reason. A regiment of Spaniards in so many years were taught to regard him as the father of their country. The insurgents are said to be concentrating their forces at San Pedro, and it is expected that they will attack the enemy near Monte Plato, and defended him with great bravery.
Communication remains open with Azua, where the theatre of the American West India Company's cotton operations, and accounts from there report matters as progressing as well as could be expected.
At first blush one would say No. The native population appears thoroughly aroused against her, although on what grounds it is hard to say, and these natives are a hard race to subdue. A regiment of Spaniards in an open field would put to rout their entire army. But it is not in the open field that they fight. They are in the woods, and at this, they are expert. They know the country, every mountain path is familiar to them. They have followed the mountain hog to his farthest recesses, and tracked the wild bee through its densest wilds, living on pork, honey, and the spontaneous fruits of the earth. The Spaniards cannot do this. They must take their provisions with them. It was the remark of a former age observed with regard to an invasion of Spain, "if a small force is sent there it will be defeated, if a large one, it will starve." It will be a question whether that Spanish coast cannot meet the expenses of a protracted war, such as this is likely to be. It is a bad job for Spain at St. Domingo; that already the state of things there is very bad. The Spaniards are withdrawing from the towns already withdrawn from those islands and concentrating their forces at the capital, and the loyal portions of her Majesty's domain.
The Spanish government has entered upon the subjugation of St. Domingo, not without mature deliberation. She has counted the cost, and she has conducted herself in such a manner since the annexation as to command the respect of all the foreign residents. The Dominicans are not a people to govern themselves; they are a degraded, ignorant and decaying race. That after forty years of independence they were unable to maintain their territory without a protest, is evidence of the low state of their civilization and their unfitness for self-governance. Foreigners were looked upon with suspicion and their property was not safe. Now, under the Spanish rule, life and property are respected, and with the liberties [illegible] foreign enterprise, labor and capital, [illegible] is able to develop the resources of this most beautiful and fertile pieces of earth, is, in my humble judgment, destined to become one of the most prosperous of the Antilles, and gladdening it with the triumphs of science, industry and art.

The Spanish Blockade of the Coast of St. Domingo.
ST. DOMINGO CITY, Oct. 18, 1863.
The following is a list of the ports of the island of St. Domingo now in the possession of the Spanish government:—
St. Domingo City,
Samana,
Puerto Plata,
Monte Christi,
Azua,
Neyba,
Barahona.
All other ports are declared to be in a state of blockade.

records.headline: BLOCKADE RUNNING.
records.summary_en: The *Wilmington Journal* reported that Dominicans took up arms against Spanish troops in San Domingo, claiming that President Pedro Santana's invitation of the Spaniards was an unauthorized and treacherous surrender of their rights. An issued manifesto from Santiago declared the country's independence, denounced Santana's power to deliver the country to Spain, and appealed against the injustices and oppression of Spanish representatives. Additionally, the newspaper reported that General Trim, the Spanish commander, sought permission from Hayti to cross 6,000 troops over its territory to act against the Dominicans, but was refused.
records.summary_es: El *Wilmington Journal* informó que los dominicanos se levantaron en armas contra las tropas españolas en Santo Domingo, sosteniendo que la convocatoria de los españoles por parte del presidente Pedro Santana constituyó una entrega inconsulta y traicionera de sus libertades. Un manifiesto promulgado en Santiago proclamó la independencia patria, negó a Santana toda facultad para entregar el país a España y clamó contra los desafueros y la opresión de las autoridades peninsulares. Asimismo, el rotativo refirió que el general Prim [Trim en el texto], comandante español, solicitó autorización a Haití para cruzar con 6.000 soldados por su territorio a fin de combatir a los dominicanos, petición que le fue denegada.

records.full_text: BLOCKADE RUNNING. -- A letter received in Polkton, Anson county, N. C., says that about the 20th October three vessels arrived with safety on a salt water river in Santo Domingo with cargoes of dry goods, coffee, &c. They found the Spaniards treating the Dominicans as a conquered people, proceeding to oppress them without measure. The Dominicans, claiming that the act of their President PEDRO SANTANA, in inviting in the Spaniards, was not the act of, or authorized by the people, but on the contrary a treacherous surrender of their rights and liberties, have taken up arms and have hemmed in the Spanish troops in the city of San Domingo. An ACT OF INDEPENDENCE has been issued by the Dominicans, and the Spaniards are in a very critical condition. So says our informant.

records.headline: On the 'Jtn to capture 8t Lhrtstabal, but were harrassed terribly
records.summary_en: Based on the provided excerpt, Spanish forces attempting to capture St. Christabal were harassed by Dominican guerrillas and driven back in confusion at the river Jaina with a loss of 200 casualties. The Dominicans also captured supplies, rifles, ammunition, a field piece, and a cannon at Santa Anna's supply depot, and defeated the Spaniards in a battle at Purata Plata on December 20th. Consequently, the Spaniards are reportedly confined only to the ground they stand upon, prompting a resume in *The Standard* to suggest that Spain should withdraw from the contest.

The report noted that Dominicans held St. Christobal, cut off Spanish land communications, captured various supplies and equipment, and placed Santanna in a critical position. records.headline: From San Domingo—Critical Position of the Spanish Army—Victories of the Dominicans.
records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that Dominicans captured Spanish supplies and a field piece at Yabacoa, while Spanish forces under Santana remained unable to move forward near San Guino due to reinforcements of 700 men being offset by over 700 sick in camp. Additionally, a severe battle occurred on December 20th at Puerto Plata, resulting in the defeat of the Spaniards, who lost 100 out of 600 men and a cannon to the gallantly fighting Dominicans. The *Standard* characterized the contest as unprofitable and dishonorable for Spain, noting that the Spaniards only hold the ground they stand on, while a separate weather report from Toronto noted a fierce snowstorm stopping railroad trains.
records.summary_es: El diario consignó que los dominicanos capturaron suministros y una pieza de campaña española en Yabacoa, mientras que las columnas peninsulares al mando de Santana permanecían inmovilizadas cerca de San Guino, toda vez que la llegada de 700 hombres de refuerzo quedó neutralizada por más de 700 enfermos en el campamento. Además, el 20 de diciembre se libró una cruenta batalla en Puerto Plata que concluyó con la derrota de los españoles, quienes perdieron 100 de sus 600 efectivos y un cañón ante el denodado arrojo dominicano. El *Standard* describió la lucha como estéril y deshonrosa para España, señalando que los españoles solo dominan el terreno que pisan, al tiempo que un parte meteorológico independiente desde Toronto daba cuenta de una feroz tormenta de nieve que paralizó los trenes.

The Turk's Island Standard of the 2d inst. has intelligence from the city of St. Domingo of Dec. 14th and Puerto Plata of the 24th. The capture of Azua by the Spaniards under Gualier is confirmed, but the Dominicans claim that although it has cost two months' fighting and many lives, its possession is of little real value to the Spaniards.

A train of eighty mules laden with ammunition for Santana's army was captured Dec. 9th by the Dominicans.

Twelve hundred Spaniards left St. Domingo city Dec. 6th to capture St. Christobal, but were harassed terribly by the Dominican guerrillas, and on reaching a defile at the river Jaina were driven back hilter skelter to the city, losing some 300 in killed and wounded. The Dominicans still hold St. Christobal, thus preventing all land communication with places occupied by the Spaniards.

Some 20 Spaniards, 300 rifles, 4000 rounds of cartridges and a field piece had been captured by the Dominicans at Yabacoa, Santana's army supply depot. The Spaniards are strengthening the fortifications of St. Domingo by two redoubts. Santana is near San Juan, and has been lately reinforced by 1000 men, but there were more than 700 sick in his camp. He is unable to move.

records.headline: Assisted by the artful management of his Secretaries of War and
records.summary_en: According to the newspaper, a leader deceived the Dominican people by inviting in Spanish forces under the guise of assistance and instruction, subsequently collecting their arms, declaring the Republic extinct, and proclaiming the Queen of Spain as ruler. After being oppressed by Spanish officials and failing twice in armed resistance, the Dominicans achieved victory on their third attempt, restoring their free constitution while retreating Spanish forces burned towns in vengeance. The report notes that the Spanish navy subsequently maintained a strict blockade of most of the seaboard with six thousand Spanish soldiers.
records.summary_es: Según el periódico, un caudillo engañó al pueblo dominicano llamando a las fuerzas españolas con el pretexto de ayuda e instrucción militar, para luego confiscarles el armamento, declarar extinguida la República y proclamar soberana a la reina de España. Tras padecer la opresión de los funcionarios coloniales y sucumbir en dos tentativas armadas, los dominicanos alcanzaron la victoria en su tercer alzamiento, restableciendo su constitución libre mientras las tropas españolas en retirada quemaban poblados por venganza. El informe agrega que la escuadra española impuso subsiguientemente un riguroso bloqueo sobre la mayor parte del litoral apoyada por seis mil soldados peninsulares.

records.full_text: The New York paper, whose love for gossip has evidenced some information that is particularly valuable, as showing the spirit which animates the insurgents of St. Domingo in their war with Spain. In payment for giving the Government a world of trouble, and insuring its uncomfortable demise, the rebels are committing all sorts of atrocities. Every Spaniard who falls into their hands is caught and butchered and treated as a wild beast. All the towns in the interior have been given to the flames, and the insurgent leaders have sworn to lay waste the whole island, with its magnificent cacao plantations, its noble forests and rich sugar lands, leaving to the Spaniards a desert to run the spring campaign upon. Each rebel soldier has sworn to this, and if he fails, he has agreed that his brother, wife or child, shall be butchered and his house burned. A case of a similar character has been reported, where a rebel leader gave his own father up to be butchered; and especially is evidence to this effect presented by the Diario, which says that the rebels are determined that if the latter succeed in getting possession of the country, it shall profit them but little. The Diario contrasts with this the mild and exemplary conduct of the Spanish troops, who take pains not to seize or injure private property, do all they can to help the people of the country, and manifest no disposition to despoil them. It thinks that the course of the rebels will alienate from their cause the majority of the people.

The news from St. Domingo is to the 18th ult. The Spanish troops had been successful in several small encounters with the Dominicans.
The news from Venezuela is to the 14th ult. The country was quiet.
The markets at Havana were dull. Exchange on London, 14 a 15 per cent premium; on New York, 1 a 2 per cent discount.

records.full_text: The Spanish government, it would appear, are at last becoming convinced of the impossibility of resubjugating St. Domingo, or rather of the uselessness of any further effort to accomplish that object. The Spanish press, which is usually the reflex of public opinion, if not of the government, seems now to be unanimous in advocating the abandonment of the struggle. It is urged that the island is of no real value to Spain; that its possession, so far from adding to her strength, is a source of weakness, and that it is better to withdraw her troops at once than to continue a war which is both costly and disastrous. The Diario Español, an influential organ, says that Spain has done enough to prove her power and to satisfy her honor, and that she can now abandon the enterprise without any loss of prestige. But the truth is that Spanish prestige in America has received a blow from which it will not easily recover. It has been shown that Spain is no longer capable of sustaining any but the very feeblest struggle on this side the Atlantic. This has been shown in the St. Domingo war. However we may rate Spanish power in Europe, Spanish power in America has been proved, by the power of the Dominicans, to be contemptible. Spain, after much effort, has not been able to overcome the resistance of these islanders to her dominion, and her inability to achieve that conquest is admitted in Spain. A Madrid paper urges the Spanish government to make peace at once with the Dominicans on the best terms they can obtain, and to withdraw their troops without delay. This advice will probably be followed, as the Spanish government must be glad of any excuse for putting an end to a war which has cost so many lives and so much money, with no prospect of any beneficial result.

records.full_text:
Extract of a letter from a gentleman recently returned from the Island of St. Domingo and Port-au-Prince to the Editor of the Dispatch, dated at Sea, on board the steamship Golden Gate, off Cape Haytien, Dec. 1, 1864.

DEAR SIR: After a long silence and many painful vicissitudes, I am again on my way to New York, and write to you of the news—the old and faithful friend of the White Cross banner.

I have seen the end of the Dominican Spanish War, for at this moment the scene of one of the most remarkable negotiations in history is being enacted at Port-au-Prince. The Territory of Hayti, but it is also a point of communication between St. Domingo and Europe, and therefore the common ground on which the subjects of the Spanish crown and the Dominican envoys could meet, to adjust their differences and agree upon terms of peace. It is for the restoration of peace and independence to the suffering and ruined people of St. Domingo, after a three years war, and thousands of valuable lives and millions of treasure, sacrificed in vain by Spain, in her attempt to re-establish her power and re-assert her domination over the land, that her General and Commissioner, General de la Gandara, has abdicated his position as President of the Republic, and left St. Domingo without a Spanish soldier or a Spanish flag.

The struggle has been one between the united and disunited Dominicans of the past of a re-conquest and powerful Spanish force of occupation. The heroic perseverance of the Dominican people were continued to this day; though betrayed by those who should have protected, they armed, they fought, they endeavoring to save their country, and through all the trial and misery they have endured alone, unassisted, save by God's protecting hand, against the number and resources of their enemy, their cause has prevailed; and now, to crown their triumph and rescue is drawing at last. Spain has parted at last by the broad concession of her supremacy; for since it is evident that the subjugation of the Dominican territory is a work beyond her power to accomplish, it is not worth her while to prolong the war for a piece of soil, and her garrisons are now withdrawing from the horrors of a Dominican war into any terms that standard may fall into, and now it remains for her commissioners to try and cover her retreat by saving the pride of a Spanish General, who gladly accepts the terms of a total evacuation of St. Domingo, free of charge, without fruits, or even the hope of fruits, in place of total destruction, if they do not escape from the disposable condition of peace. Salnave, the Dominican General, whose forces are around the remaining Spanish posts, means to make their conception a more tense and painful business, while the Commissioners of Spain treat for terms of peace.

In this dilemma, a private individual, having friendly relations with both parties, has proposed to the Commissioners for their consideration a plan that has so far been favorably received by both, and seems likely at this point to reduce the conditions to a diplomatic basis which will be acceptable to the Dominican government as well as the Spaniards of Jamaica. This secret confidential meeting will be held at Port-au-Prince on the 26th of November, at which line it was agreed: First. A full recognition of the sovereign rights and dominion over St. Domingo, and recognition of the non-interference treaty of the Dominican Republic. 2. The Dominican Republic grants in perpetuity any and all claims for indemnity for damages or losses. Mean ports in Spanish vessels shall be received as a duty-free port for all nations, and any Dominican port, or any Dominican territory, and lower if by law or treaty lower terms are given, and that no nation or powers shall be admitted to lower terms, but all nations shall be admitted into Spanish ports on the same terms with the protective clause in favor of the United States.

By this arrangement, the Dominicans have little to do but wait, and while they retain all the real material advantages which she could derive from the possession of St. Domingo, Spain saves her prestige by avoiding the responsibility of maintaining and defending it.

But the most critical point for Santo Domingo is a name special item for which provisions must be made in this treaty. Spain demanded to recognize the struggling Republic, and granted to it the same favor she granted to Mexico when it was writing for life in the agonizing grasp of Spain.

A matter of general interest, for about the time of the contest, the protest trumpeted out of an American republic about St. Domingo, in the name of the Monroe doctrine, sent a message of remonstrance to the Spanish Minister at Washington, which the Dominican envoys were informed was a mere empty paper, and contained no pledge of a determined plan. Said he done this much for Mexico, why does not the Cabinet at Washington send a message on the American Maximilian in Mexico to-day; laughing to scorn the proud boast of Monroe, and America's dominant position over the new republics in Republican America.

The grand Dominican envoy, Gen. Cazneau, a distinguished diplomatist and an ex-Secretary of State of the Dominican Republic, went to Washington to ask aid, and to present the position to the notice of the American government. These three gentlemen had a very early interview with the President, Mr. Lincoln. Their hands were clasped together all day, just as the very good public of America would have expected. But when the Dominican sailing rock is steaming in the bay, ready to raise force, equipment and ammunition for their war against the Dominicans, to meet the steamer Menemousa—as I may call it, which carried standard, ammunition, and men for the Spanish Navy to St. Domingo, is reported, is not far from Washington about this time.

Whatever may be the course of policy pursued by the peace councils of Spain and Dominica, it is not for me to express an opinion. But it is important that it should be known to the United States Government very soon that the territory of Samana—which is the chief basis, believing it to be the true interest of republican principles to have the facts known to the American people, I transmit them to you so far as they have assumed a definite shape.

Spain demands, as the price of withdrawing her arms from the Dominican soil, the cession of the magnificent bay and peninsula of Samana as a price, but always to remain under Spanish rule and protection. Samana is the priceless gem of the American seas, and, with its bold heights crowned and garrisoned by Spanish arms, the rest of St. Domingo would always hold a weak and painful tenure of independence. It cannot be left in the hands of Spain, though the Dominicans would not object to make it a privileged port for all nations—as indeed they consented to do in 1854, in the Cazneau Tijera treaty, when the United States proposed to make Samana a common and mail mated depot for all flags having trade an for all nations—as indeed they consented to do in 1854, in the Cazneau Tijera treaty, when the United States proposed to make Samana a common and mail mated depot for all flags having trade in the West Indies; but to cede it into a mere American center, entirely controlled by Spanish ideas or policy, which have not yet emancipated themselves from the iron fetters of the dark ages, do it the Dominicans will not, for they know it would only keep open another pathway of future troubles, and leave opened another and better path of deliverance. Samana is the true key of St. Domingo, and it must be retained as an absolutely free port, together with a neutral frontier around it, or it will be a source of future wars, line after line of division with Hayti. They put off another war only to start another. In the event of peace, Spain should a suitable place be given for coal depot, for it has an ocean steamer line corresponding with the harbor of Samana; but the Dominicans should be united with them in furnishing and guaranteeing the absolute neutrality of Samana; for in that way, and that way only, can peace between the two countries creating it, and in that way only can peace between the Dominican Republic and Hayti, if Hayti will unite in making the Bay of Samana a common refuge and common safeguard to both.

If the United States does not lose her opportunity, now is the open and secure way to her midway between her islands of the West Indies. But if Samana is ceded to Spain, or left to her real misrule, the free section of the island of St. Domingo will be a continuous prey to foreign ambition.

This island with its mines, fisheries and guano islands, contains resources of wealth for an immense population. No monopoly of mining rights are to be conceded to any standard company; no exclusive privileges to foreign nations; for Dominican ports are opened to free to buy, discover, announce and work any mines of coal, copper or silver, that they may choose; while in the St. Domingo bays free access to all traders or importers, if they choose to pay the simple standard duty—which is far from extraordinary, paying only ten percent of the value as an export duty on copper, and forty percent on silver; while on guano there is no export tax at all. Under the maintenance of free schools, which schools are to be established by the government, for the instruction of all, from either country, without distinction of race, lineage or condition.

I indulge the belief that the presence in St. Domingo of a diplomat so experienced as General Cazneau, who has taken such a broad interest in the preservation of free and neutral ports and an enlarged traffic.

Our own commercial interest in Samana ought to cause our Cabinet to take up and work in their own direction for its neutralisation, and Samana will be for the West Indies what the central ridges of the Isthmus are for Central America, and what Gibraltar and Aden have ever been to Britain. But all the cases that country can present, or any other part of the world, can never equal in value or strategic importance the bay of Samana to us, whenever we wish to open a communication between the East and the West, or whenever we would establish our power and protect our trade against the aggressions of European nations. It is the key of the West India seas, and the nation that holds it holds the trade of all the West Indies. We have no interest or right to prevent Spain from obtaining a foothold in Santo Domingo, or any other part of the West Indies, by fair purchase or conquest, but if she is driven to yield the prize by the bravery of the people, let her not take from them the key of their independence, but let Samana be left as it was in 1854, a free and neutral port for all nations, and we shall receive our share of its advantages.
United States.

records.full_text:
ENGLAND’S RECOGNITION OF THE DOMINICANS.
[From the Madrid Epoca, Dec. 18.]
In consequence of the effect produced upon the public mind by this announcement, Sir John Crampton, the English Ambassador at this Court, felt bound to request explanations from his government upon a matter in which he was without official instructions. Earl Russell lost no time in replying, and his despatch reached the English representatives yesterday evening, at the same time that the First Secretary of State received the despatches from our Minister Plenipotentiary in London, previously announced by telegraph to the Spanish Cabinet. These despatches contained ample details of all that had occurred. On account of certain questions arising from events that have taken place in consequence of the blockade of the Dominican coasts by the Spanish squadron, the English government considered it necessary to take the opinion of the legal advisers of the crown, following its practice in all matters of this kind. Their opinion was favorable in a certain manner to the recognition of the Dominicans as belligerents—Spain being bound, according to their view, by the maritime law laid down in the treaty of Paris, to maintain a real and effective blockade of all the points of the island where she undertook to prevent the entry of supplies destined for the rebels. Earl Russell communicated this opinion to our representative in London, who in his turn considered it urgently necessary to acquaint the Spanish government with the same. Hence the origin of a news which, having come to the knowledge of the telegraphic agents of various periodicals in this city, was transmitted by them with the urgency which its importance dictated, although the want of the details above mentioned caused some exaggeration in their communications. The reply of Earl Russell to the English Ambassador could not be expressed in more satisfactory terms. The English Minister confirmed the explanations given by Senor Comyn, and, wishing to afford a proof of the friendly attitude of England in questions so greatly affecting the prestige of our country, he authorized the English Ambassador to acquaint the Spanish Cabinet with his determination to indefinitely postpone any act which might be considered hostile, or as tending to exercise any sort of influence in the settlement of our internal affairs. We, who cannot be accused of being ardent admirers of the English policy, have satisfaction in declaring that its conduct in the present circumstances has been worthy of a great Power, and therefore merits our most sincere eulogies.

records.summary_en: According to *The New York Herald* on April 30, 1865, European monarchies were described as quaking with fear over the growing strength of the United States and its potential impact on Spanish possessions like Cuba and Porto Rico. The article specifically cited a fearful argument presented by the "Conqueror of Africa," which claimed the United States planned to send thousands of freed colored people to St. Domingo to form a negro nationality and army to ultimately attack and destroy Cuba. The newspaper dismissed this theory as a "raving of an imagination entirely possessed by fear," asserting that no dilatory measures would be needed if the United States truly intended to conquer European possessions.

El artículo citó en particular un medroso alegato esgrimido por el «Conquistador de África», quien aseguraba que los Estados Unidos proyectaban enviar a miles de libertos de color a Santo Domingo a fin de constituir una nacionalidad y un ejército negros con el propósito final de asaltar y arrasar a Cuba. El diario desestimó dicha teoría como el «desvarío de una imaginación presa del pánico», asegurando que los Estados Unidos no necesitarían recurrir a maniobras indirectas si de veras abrigaran el propósito de conquistar posesiones europeas.

records.full_text:
Permit one who has been no inactive spectator of the events described to offer to the American people in what way your Monroe doctrine has been attacked and defended at St. Domingo.
It is a matter of history that Spain, taking advantage of the internal troubles of the United States, made an ostentatious parade of her contempt for the Monroe doctrine by taking possession of the territory of the Dominican republic in May, 1861. Pedro Santana, then President of the republic, in conjunction with the Minister of State, War and Marine and two leading generals, had managed to collect the public seals in the city of St. Domingo, into which were privately introduced bodies of Spanish soldiers; and, so prepared, the authority of the Queen of Spain was declared by a royal edict.
The members of the Dominican Senate and Judiciary lodged a protest in the hands of the Governor; but the document was afterwards withdrawn from a fear that it might reach the hands of the Spanish Minister at Washington. Spain rewarded Santana with the title of Marquis, and a pension of $25,000 a year for life, which was cut down to $12,000 after two years.
Two or three attempts were made to revolt during the very first year of Spanish domination, but they were promptly quelled, and about fifteen months passed in apparent calm; but beneath it the old officials of the Dominican republic were busy in secret preparations.
THE DOMINICANS CAST OFF THE SPANISH YOKE.
The people bought arms, formed into bands, had their first success in an ambush in August, 1862, displayed the White Cross of the republic near the Haytien frontier, and declared war on their Spanish invaders. The Spanish affected to treat it as a mere tumultuous uprising of a few border villages of blacks; but there was no distinction of color in the united Dominican opposition to Spanish rule. The insolence and exactions of the Spanish officials were equally unendurable to blacks and whites; and before 1863 had well set in it was evident that Spain could only retain the Dominican territory by the wholesale extermination of the Dominican people. At first the leading Spaniards were pleased with the prospect of a general confiscation of Dominican estates in their favor; but the capture of Santiago, Moca, and San Cristoval aroused them to the fact that the entire country was held by the rebels. With the exception of four fortified camps, the citadel of Puerto Plata, and the walled city of St. Domingo, Spain had no longer a square league of Dominican soil under her jurisdiction. The republic had its seat of government at Santiago, from which it had expelled the Spanish garrison at the painful cost of laying their own beautiful homes in ashes. Samana, the finest harbor in the West Indies, which ought to be, and some day will be, the great mail and naval centre of the American tropics—Samana, I say, was strongly fortified, and in these fortifications the Spanish garrisons were kept enclosed for two years. They are but now leaving the country they failed to subjugate.
THE DOMINICAN MISSION TO WASHINGTON.
When the Dominican government found itself restored to the possession of its entire territory—except the fortified camps and a small portion of the coast—and in the full exercise of its rightful supremacy over the whole body of the Dominican people, except those which Spain held and punished, or was within her fortified lines and covered by the guns of her war ships, then a Dominican envoy was sent to the United States on a mission of the highest importance to both countries. This mission related to the protection due the citizens of the United States who had the misfortune to find their persons and interests included within the Spanish lines, where they were suffering ruthless persecutions. This mission also related to a friendly arrangement, by which the destruction of American property by rebel privateers might have been stayed, and is related finally to the honorable recognition of the republic; toward the support of which objects could have been secured by the simple recognition of the potent, undeniable fact that the Dominican republic existed, and that the drawing away of the United States ships-of-war cruising about Havana to look after St. Domingo was because they had no other interest. The Dominican envoy, after three visits to their almost continual presence at Havana, and had they been paid, and they had the same citizens of the United States have escaped the persecutions of Spanish governors, for the rebel privateers would have been found perhaps with her British coal-tenders at Samana. But faithfulness toward the people on account of filial devotion to the American name and cause, could not obtain from the official quarters of a hearing at Washington, and he returned to us at Santiago with the report that "the United States at this time only recognized the Spanish government."
THE MONROE DOCTRINE ADHERED TO BY THE REPUBLICANS.
We were wounded to the heart by this cold neglect of the dearest traditions of republican America; but still we vowed before the altar of God, our country and liberty, that though the powerful republic of the North might forget the great doctrine it had blazoned so proudly to the world, we, poor, friendless, forsaken Dominicans, would prove true to it. We continued to suffer and to bleed until we had forced Spain to confess, on our soil at least, that America belongs to the Americans. No nation united upon us. No people extended to us material aid. Greece, Hungary, Poland and Italy have each received the generous sympathy of the American people; but the Dominican republic, which has fought for the same principles, and which has triumphed over a first class European Power, has not yet received a word of recognition from the government of the United States.
THE TREATY REGARDING THE EVACUATION.
The Spanish government, finding that the war was a failure, and that the Dominican people were determined to be free, at last proposed a treaty of evacuation. The following are the principal articles of the treaty:—
First—The Spanish government will evacuate the territory of the Dominican republic.
Second—The Dominican republic will pay to the Spanish government the sum of $1,000,000, as an indemnity for the expenses of the war.
Third—The Dominican republic will not cede any portion of its territory to any foreign Power.
Fourth—A treaty of peace, amity and commerce should be established between the two countries on terms compatible with the honor of both parties.
Fifth—The questions arising out of the late events should be afterwards settled by special commissioners, to meet either at Madrid or St. Domingo for that purpose.
Fourth—If so mutually agreed, the original treaty of amity, commerce, &c., made in 1855, between Spain and the Dominican republic, to be declared in full force.
Fifth—Dominicans, who had been taken into the military service of Spain, to be amnestied for leaving the same, and vice versa.
Sixth—A formal exchange of military and political prisoners of war.
Seventh—The amount of arms and munitions of war belonging to the Dominican republic, and which Spain forced to be left in them, and also the national edifice and property, to be restored to the republic in good condition.
Eighth—That the final delivery of the fortified city of St. Domingo and the other fortified places should be effected with due international courtesies, both parties taking measures to preserve perfect order and tranquility.
General Gandara accepted the substance of all these conditions, though he insisted on phrases that would give Spain the air of granting favors rather than of acknowledging a defeat; and of course the treaty, first, and above all things, he demanded exactly what the conditions we were already agreed on, to be on their guard against admitting the idea that Spain, in the presence of the spontaneous and urgent petition of the Dominican people, accepted the territory for her own free will, purely and solely because she had learned that the majority of the Dominicans desired an independent nationality, and that the war she had made on them was against this spirit, although at the last moment she believes the majority of the Dominicans were attached to the Spanish rule. The commissioners accepted, for they knew the object in forcing them to put this false and humiliating statement on record was to enable Spanish pride to retire without a surrender, by taking the responsibility of this striking violation of the Monroe doctrine. But now it came, the war is an end here, and that the Spanish navy in the Antilles would maintain a "rigorous blockade of all the Dominican coasts and harbors" until this final declaration was subscribed and ratified. In their retreat it remains to see the Spaniards leave their land in peace, the commissioners were induced to sign it. They did so June 7, 1865, and the treaty with this humiliating preamble has been since submitted to the Dominican Executive. It was at once indignantly and publicly rejected by the Dominican Cabinet. The commissioners who acceded to it were removed and officially censured; and others appointed to negotiate a new treaty; though, with the exception of the preamble, the general conditions of that of June 7 were accepted. But General Gandara, having to a certain degree bound his word, refused to receive the new commissioners, and declared that the Dominican people must abide as shall be maintained until the Dominicans accept and sign the treaty of June 7. We are looking for friends in the United States—if we have any—to believe that, however we are, we will endure years more of blockade and suffering before we will falsely declare to the world that we voluntarily invited Spain here, or that we invited Spain to accept us as slaves, or that we owe our independence to her royal mercy, and not to our own arms and our own efforts.

records.summary_en: According to the *New-York Daily Tribune* of August 22, 1865, the *Boletin Oficial* of Santiago reported on July 7 that departing Spanish troops were taking Dominican cannon and property, while a few Spanish troops still lingered in St. Domingo because Gen. Gándara and the Dominicans had not agreed on a final evacuation treaty. The Dominican government rejected a drafted treaty because Gándara's preferred language made the agreement appear to be a Spanish concession rather than a surrender, and Gándara subsequently refused to receive new commissioners unless they confirmed the objectionable treaty. Consequently, the Dominican government officially expressed its determination not to yield, signifying that the war had not ceased.
records.summary_es: Según el *New-York Daily Tribune* del 22 de agosto de 1865, el *Boletín Oficial* de Santiago denunció el 7 de julio que las tropas españolas en retirada se llevaban cañones y propiedades dominicanas, quedando aún remanentes peninsulares en Santo Domingo debido a desacuerdos entre el general Gándara y los dominicanos sobre el tratado definitivo de evacuación. El gobierno dominicano rechazó el borrador del convenio porque los términos exigidos por Gándara hacían figurar el acuerdo como una concesión graciosa de España y no como una capitulación en regla, negándose luego Gándara a recibir nuevos comisionados si no convalidaban dicho documento objetado. Por consiguiente, el gobierno dominicano ratificó oficialmente su firme decisión de no transigir, lo que evidenciaba que las hostilidades no habían concluido.

records.headline: ST. DOMINGO AFFAIRS.
records.summary_en: The Spanish Cortes decreed in May that Spain's attempt to subjugate St. Domingo should be abandoned and its forces evacuated, but the evacuation has dragged slowly because Gen. Gandara insists on inserting a treaty clause stating the invasion was undertaken at the people's desire and given up voluntarily. The Dominican Government opposes this clause, leading Gandara to declare that the war must be resumed. Additionally, advices from Hayti report that rebels continue to hold Cape Haytien despite a continual cannonade and blockade by national troops.
records.summary_es: Las Cortes españolas decretaron en mayo el abandono del intento de sojuzgar a Santo Domingo y la evacuación de sus tropas, pero la retirada se ha demorado con lentitud debido a que el general Gándara insistió en consignar una cláusula estipulando que la anexión se efectuó por deseo popular y se abandonaba voluntariamente. El gobierno dominicano rechazó tajantemente dicha cláusula, lo que indujo a Gándara a proclamar la reanudación de la guerra. Además, despachos procedentes de Haití daban cuenta de que los facciosos conservaban el dominio de Cabo Haitiano a pesar del incesante cañoneo y del bloqueo impuesto por las tropas del gobierno.

records.full_text: NEW YORK, August 22.—The August 2d St. Thomas advice gives further particulars of the matter heretofore mentioned, regarding the new issue raised by General Gandara, the commander of the Spanish troops, with the Dominican Government, apparently only for the purpose of having a pretext to maintain a foothold with his forces in the republic. The Spanish Cortes, in May last, decreed that the attempt by Spain to subjugate St. Domingo should be abandoned, and that the island should be immediately evacuated by their military forces. The evacuation soon after commenced, but has since dragged along so slowly that it is not yet nearly completed. It appears that Gen. Gandara does not intend it shall be, since he insists on an insertion in the treaty of peace of a clause securing protection to Spanish sympathizers in the Dominican Republic. This the Dominicans naturally refused to grant, and Gen. Gandara now threatens to attack them if they do not agree to the proposed terms.

records.summary_en: The *New York Herald* reported that Spanish commander General Gandam blockaded the principal ports of the Dominican Republic after the Dominican government refused his peace treaty demands, preventing the exportation of American and European tobacco. In response, the Dominicans resolved to commission privateers against Spanish commerce, sending an authorized agent to the United States and Europe to issue letters of marque. Additionally, the newspaper reported that a severe summer drought, heavy taxes, and poverty left thousands of negro laborers in Jamaica on the verge of starvation, creating fears of a local outbreak against the Governor and his officers.

Como réplica, los dominicanos resolvieron armar corsarios contra el tráfico mercante español, enviando un agente facultado a los Estados Unidos y a Europa para conceder patentes de corso. Por otra parte, el periódico comunicó que una persistente sequía estival, tributos gravosos y la miseria general tenían a miles de trabajadores negros en Jamaica al borde de la inanición, desatando temores de un levantamiento popular contra el gobernador colonial y sus subordinados.

records.summary_en: The *Daily Ohio Statesman* reported on September 2, 1865, that Spanish commander General Gandara withdrew troops from the interior and blockaded the principal ports of the Dominican Republic after the Dominican government refused unreasonable peace treaty demands, prompting Dominicans to commission privateers against Spanish commerce. Additionally, a Kingston, Jamaica correspondent reported that revolutionists were making alarming headway, causing President Geffrard to charter a mail steamer to prepare for his escape, while severe drought and heavy taxes left Jamaican negro laborers in abject poverty and near starvation.

records.full_text:
The Herald's Kingston, Jamaica, correspondent says the progress the Haytian revolutionists are making in Hayti, has been deemed by President Geffrard as sufficiently alarming to induce him to make preparations for flight from the island. A small steamer has therefore been chartered by Geffrard to convey him to Port au Prince and there remain till the final action, when he is to take steam in flight or till the danger of such outbreak has passed.

Owing to the severe drought of the present season on the Island of Jamaica, the heavy taxes and other causes, the negro inhabitants have been reduced to the most abject poverty and great suffering, and thousands of them are on the verge of starvation. They blame the government for all this, as the cause of their afflictions, and so strong and bitter is their feeling against the local government that an outbreak on their part is feared in the western part of the Island, in consequence of which two gunboats have been dispatched to that locality.

The Herald's Santiago correspondent says, notwithstanding the havoc and destruction of the Spaniards during their invasion of San Domingo, the crops are now coming forward which promise ample subsistence for the inhabitants, and the war which has compelled the people to utilize their resources has united and determined them to maintain their independence. The Spanish forces have hardly borne out by reports which we have received, as to the resumption of hostilities between two native chiefs, but it has been ascertained beyond doubt that the Spaniards stole and destroyed property on the island, especially the property of American merchants. Geffrard has sent commissioners to different places, and now Gen. Gandara, the Spanish commander, having withdrawn his troops from the interior, has blockaded the principal ports of San Domingo, because the Dominican Government will not accede to his haughty and unreasonable demands in the peace treaty now pending. He has seized two large stocks of tobacco belonging to Americans as well as Dominicans. To offset this blockade the Dominicans have determined to commission privateers to prey on Spanish commerce and so far as reported one American merchant vessel has already left for the United States and Europe.

records.headline: THE REPUBLIC OF SAN DOMINGO.
records.summary_en: The *Daily National Intelligencer* reported on November 13, 1865, that Don Pedro Valverde, a member of the "Yankee party," supports opening Dominican gold mines, mahogany forests, and pearl fisheries to immigrants under a liberal colonization law, and proposes establishing free and neutral ports jointly with President Geffrard of Hayti. In contrast, the newspaper noted that General Cabral has intimate relations with European consuls while the United States is unrepresented, and suggested that Cabral might pursue a close union with Hayti that could threaten the white race in the eastern part of the island. Additionally, the article stated that if Valverde is elected, the Dominican Republic would respond to Spanish demands for the repayment of conquest costs with a counter-demand.
records.summary_es: El *Daily National Intelligencer* dio cuenta el 13 de noviembre de 1865 de que don Pedro Valverde, miembro del «partido pro-yanqui», promovía abrir las minas auríferas dominicanas, los bosques de caoba y los placeres de perlas a colonos extranjeros al amparo de una liberal ley de inmigración, proponiendo asimismo la habilitación de puertos francos y neutrales en concierto con el presidente Geffrard de Haití. Por el contrario, el rotativo señalaba que el general Cabral cultivaba estrechos nexos con los cónsules europeos mientras los Estados Unidos carecían de legación oficial, insinuando que Cabral podría propiciar una federación estrecha con Haití susceptible de comprometer a la población blanca de la parte oriental. El reporte concluía que, de resultar elegido Valverde, la República Dominicana ripostaría a las exigencias españolas de indemnización bélica con una enérgica contrademanda.

records.chapter_es: La lucha por la anexión estadounidense
records.full_text:
The Dominican Republic has arisen! No more will she be the prey to the great mother of republics. Should the Republic of Washington now turn her back, or refuse to unite the lot of this loyal American Republic, the white race will soon be extinguished in the Antilles. It was a cruel mistake in President Lincoln to receive Geffrard to his arms, and at the same moment reject the alliance of the Dominican Republic, offering us as a sacrifice to the dark race, as if no race but the negroes had the sympathy of the United States.

Only yesterday the mulatto came in from Petit Trou, on the coast of Hayti, with a stolen steamer, to stir up again the blacks of Jamaica, and now a new attempt of the negroes of Jacmel to exterminate the mixed bloods "between two fires"—mulattoes and whites.

President Geffrard, of Hayti, is a great and good patriot. All the negroes here have joined the color-line, and, after exterminating the mulattoes and quadroons, try to reduce the whites to the level of the Dominican blacks. It is a war of races; were it not that French, English, and Spanish vessels of war have arrived, Jacmel had been a port of Hayti. These naval vessels are to protect the citizens that have power to protect or avenge the citizens of their respective nations, and keep in check the Haytian throne by the insurgent negroes.

The President of the Dominican Republic will be elected on the 24th instant, and the choice seems to be between Pedro Valverde and General Cabral. Don Pedro Valverde is a noble soldier, and a finished gentleman of pure white stock. He is of the "Yankee party," and is openly pledged to sustain the course of policy inaugurated in June and July. This is to open the Dominican gold mines, mahogany forests, and pearl fisheries to all immigrants who have the means and disposition to develop the vast natural resources of the Republic, under a general colonization law. Don Pedro Valverde also would give President Geffrard no peace until the ports of Hayti were thrown open, and neutral ports where the elements of the two republics meet; which free ports should be placed under the commercial control of white agents or men who represent Dominican Republic. Free trade and a neutral line, if Hayti will accept it, would, he thinks, preserve it from obliteration.

General Cabral will go further than that with Hayti if he is elected, and if the United States Government refuses to co-operate and join hands with us. Cabral has a slight tinge of Indian blood in his system, and he may be inclined to enter into a union with Hayti so close as to blur the distinct line which separates them from each other. He has most intimate relations with the European Powers; while Don Pedro Valverde is a pure American or Yankee in his feelings, and we should be desolated if, again, Don Pedro Valverde is rejected. The foreign element in the government he will have created here in trying to conquer us will be met by a force of 15,000 men on the border to defend a neutral border line of division, with free ports on each end to keep up the peace, and preserve the Dominican Republic. If Spain insists on keeping Santo Domingo, or a pecuniary indemnity for the immense amount of property which she would have lost if your Government at Washington had simply recognized the existence of the Dominican Republic, the San Domingo question would be settled.

The election of Cabral will give a more European character to the government of San Domingo; and as to the white element everywhere in the Antilles, it may lead to the total extinction of the white race in the Antilles.

CARLOS MELLA.

records.summary_en: An armed man abruptly entered a session of the Dominican Congress to announce the impending arrival of revolutionary forces and proclaim General Baez as president, causing the ministers to flee in terror. Following this confusion, General Pedro Guillermo was appointed dictator until Baez could arrive, and an election on December 14th unanimously named Buenaventura Baez President of the Dominican Republic. Meanwhile, Cabral accepted a military position under the new government, which Guillermo practically headed.

Entretanto, Cabral aceptó un cargo militar bajo el nuevo régimen, que de facto encabezaba Guillermo.
