records.headline: This convention, in order to pnt tho contract beyond the risk
records.summary_en: According to the Burlington weekly free press on January 31, 1873, U.S. Commissioners reported that a convention regarding a contract in the Dominican Republic was submitted to a public vote to prevent future administrative interference, with voting underway on the 9th inst. The Commissioners expressed confidence that the popular vote would be nearly or quite unanimous for ratification, making the convention part of the Republic's fundamental law. Additionally, they noted receiving good wishes from leading foreign merchants and European consular representatives, along with assurances that the free port and city of Samana could quickly attract a large population from various West Indian islands.
records.summary_es: Según el *Burlington Weekly Free Press* del 31 de enero de 1873, los comisionados de los Estados Unidos informaron que la convención relativa a un contrato en la República Dominicana se sometió a plebiscito popular para conjurar futuras injerencias de gobiernos venideros, habiéndose iniciado la votación el día 9 del corriente. Los delegados manifestaron su certidumbre de que el sufragio popular respaldaría casi unánimemente la ratificación, elevando la convención a rango de ley fundamental de la república. Añadieron haber recibido parabienes de los principales mercaderes foráneos y agentes consulares europeos, junto con el augurio de que la ciudad y puerto franco de Samaná atraerían prontamente una copiosa corriente inmigratoria proveniente de diversas islas antillanas.

records.headline: Dr.
records.summary_en: Dr. Samuel G. Howe writes that he and Benjamin F. Wade, as United States Commissioners to Santo Domingo, favored political annexation, and that after annexation was rejected he worked for a commercial company to lease the peninsula and bay of Samana for ninety-nine years. He describes negotiating the terms with President Baez and his cabinet, consulting the Dominican Senate of Seven, and organizing the company, with the first year's rent of $150,000 to be paid in advance.
records.summary_es: El doctor Samuel G. Howe escribe que él y Benjamin F. Wade, como Comisionados de los Estados Unidos a Santo Domingo, favorecieron la anexión política, y que tras ser rechazada la anexión trabajó por una compañía comercial que arrendara la península y la bahía de Samaná por noventa y nueve años. Describe la negociación de los términos con el presidente Báez y su gabinete, la consulta al Senado dominicano de los Siete, y la organización de la compañía, con el primer año de renta de 150.000 dólares a pagar por adelantado.

records.headline: A proclamation issued at headquarters on January 10, 1873, and signed by Dominican leaders including Gregorio…
records.summary_en: A proclamation issued at headquarters on January 10, 1873, and signed by Dominican leaders including Gregorio Luperon and Jose Maria Cabral, calls on Dominicans in this hour of sorrow to come as brethren and array themselves under the banner of liberty. It declares that the land must be rid now and forever of traitors and of the burning disgrace that has fallen upon it, and gives the rallying cry of liberty and independence, and down with Baez, their perpetual enemy.
records.summary_es: Una proclama emitida en el cuartel general el 10 de enero de 1873, y firmada por líderes dominicanos, entre ellos Gregorio Luperón y José María Cabral, llama a los dominicanos en esta hora de dolor a acudir como hermanos y formarse bajo la bandera de la libertad. Declara que la patria debe librarse ahora y para siempre de los traidores y de la ardiente vergüenza que ha caído sobre ella, y da como grito de unión libertad e independencia, y abajo Báez, su enemigo perpetuo.

records.headline: A dispatch from New York confirms that the revolutionary chiefs in San Domingo have allied against Baez, in a…
records.summary_en: A dispatch from New York confirms that the revolutionary chiefs in San Domingo have allied against Baez, in a pronunciamiento by Luperon, Cabral and twelve other leaders issued a few days after the sale of the Samana Peninsula. The proclamation protests the sale of Samana to an American company that will transfer its powers to the United States Government, denies that the Dominican Senate has power to grant such a commission to a foreign nation, and concludes with an appeal to all Dominicans to rally and wage a vigorous war against Baez.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de Nueva York confirma que los jefes revolucionarios de Santo Domingo se han aliado contra Báez, en un pronunciamiento de Luperón, Cabral y otros doce líderes emitido pocos días después de la venta de la península de Samaná. La proclama protesta por la venta de Samaná a una compañía americana que transferirá sus poderes al Gobierno de los Estados Unidos, niega que el Senado dominicano tenga facultad para otorgar semejante comisión a una nación extranjera, y concluye con un llamado a todos los dominicanos a unirse y hacer una guerra vigorosa contra Báez.

records.headline: A Herald correspondent traveling in the Samana country reports that the Dominicans he meets are all for renting…
records.summary_en: A Herald correspondent traveling in the Samana country reports that the Dominicans he meets are all for renting Samana Bay to an American company, expecting American capital and colonization to make their lives more prosperous; on the road he falls in with a party of Americans, one of them sketching with a banana stick a diagram of the country of La Vega and the course of the Yuna River.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del Herald que viaja por la región de Samaná informa que los dominicanos que encuentra están todos a favor de alquilar la bahía de Samaná a una compañía americana, esperando que el capital y la colonización americanos hagan sus vidas más prósperas; en el camino se encuentra con un grupo de americanos, uno de los cuales dibuja con un palo de plátano un diagrama de la región de La Vega y el curso del río Yuna.

records.headline: A correspondent's letter from Santa Barbara, Samana Bay, dated February 13, 1873, describes arriving aboard the…
records.summary_en: A correspondent's letter from Santa Barbara, Samana Bay, dated February 13, 1873, describes arriving aboard the Tybee at sunrise and being welcomed by Colonel Joseph Warren Fabens, presented as governor of the peninsula, and by Mr. Price, the consul. The pioneer emigrants of the Samana Bay Company settlement are aboard inspecting the discharge of the vessel's freight and looking over the village of Santa Barbara, with its eighty-four houses, as the place where their future settlement and homes are to be made.
records.summary_es: La carta de un corresponsal desde Santa Bárbara, bahía de Samaná, fechada el 13 de febrero de 1873, describe la llegada a bordo del Tybee al amanecer y la bienvenida del coronel Joseph Warren Fabens, presentado como gobernador de la península, y del señor Price, el cónsul. Los emigrantes pioneros del asentamiento de la Compañía de la Bahía de Samaná están a bordo inspeccionando la descarga del cargamento del buque y observando el pueblo de Santa Bárbara, con sus ochenta y cuatro casas, como el lugar donde se harán su futuro asentamiento y sus hogares.

records.headline: An editorial presents a first look at the 'dreamland' in St.
records.summary_en: An editorial presents a first look at the 'dreamland' in St. Domingo that speculators of the Samana Bay Company have fenced in with treaties, leases and powers, describing Santa Barbara as a delightful spot, the bay as first-class anchorage, and the soil as fertile. It notes that the $150,000 paid to Baez smoothed away much of the first difficulty and that Baez's ministers reported 22,000 votes cast for the treaty, while questioning what would happen when the people saw how little of the company's money reached beyond Baez's coffers.
records.summary_es: Un editorial presenta una primera mirada al 'país de ensueño' en Santo Domingo que los especuladores de la Samana Bay Company han cercado con tratados, arrendamientos y poderes, describiendo Santa Bárbara como un lugar encantador, la bahía como un fondeadero de primera clase, y el suelo como fértil. Señala que los 150.000 dólares pagados a Báez allanaron gran parte de la primera dificultad y que los ministros de Báez informaron de 22.000 votos a favor del tratado, mientras se pregunta qué pasará cuando la gente vea lo poco del dinero de la compañía que llega más allá de las arcas de Báez.

records.summary_en: A Puerto Plata report prints a letter from the British vice-consul stating that General Juan Nuezl, former governor of the city, and his sons Martin and Claudia had claimed the protection of the British flag at his home. When the authorities ruled that the consul's private house was not his consulate, the mayor surrounded the house, entered it by force after three summonses, and took the three Nuezis prisoner to the fort in irons; one son said his father opposed the Samana lease and had determined to oppose it by physical force.
records.summary_es: Un informe de Puerto Plata publica una carta del vicecónsul británico que declara que el general Juan Nuezl, antiguo gobernador de la ciudad, y sus hijos Martín y Claudia habían reclamado la protección de la bandera británica en su casa. Cuando las autoridades resolvieron que la casa particular del cónsul no era su consulado, el alcalde rodeó la casa, entró en ella por la fuerza tras tres requerimientos, y llevó a los tres Nuezl prisioneros al fuerte con grilletes; un hijo dijo que su padre se oponía al arrendamiento de Samaná y había decidido oponerse a él por la fuerza física.

records.headline: A Herald correspondent interviews an imprisoned former governor who says he took up arms because he wanted liberty…
records.summary_en: A Herald correspondent interviews an imprisoned former governor who says he took up arms because he wanted liberty of expression in the vote concerning the sale of Samana. He insists the people were dragooned into voting for the Baez measure and would have voted against it if the pressure had been taken off, that none of the money paid by the Americans would benefit the country but would go into the pockets of Baez and his associates, and that the government has done nothing for the people toward Monte Cristo who have had no rain in two years.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del Herald entrevista a un exgobernador encarcelado que dice que tomó las armas porque quería libertad de expresión en la votación sobre la venta de Samaná. Insiste en que la gente fue obligada a votar por la medida de Báez y habría votado en contra si se le hubiera quitado la presión, que nada del dinero pagado por los estadounidenses beneficiaría al país sino que iría a los bolsillos de Báez y sus asociados, y que el gobierno no ha hecho nada por la gente de hacia Monte Cristi que lleva dos años sin lluvia.

records.headline: An editorial reports that at Puerto Plata a civil and military force under the Dominican Minister of Finance…
records.summary_en: An editorial reports that at Puerto Plata a civil and military force under the Dominican Minister of Finance forcibly entered the residence of the British Vice Consul, Mr. Hamburger, and seized three citizens, enemies of Baez and opponents of the Samana sale, who were thrown into a dungeon, and that Baez approved the arrests and ordered the prisoners brought to Santo Domingo City. It warns that a British man-of-war is expected to demand satisfaction, and that Baez must not imagine the United States will protect him, since the Americans who paid $150,000 down for a year's rent of Samana Bay represent only themselves and their purchase implies no American protectorate.
records.summary_es: Un editorial informa que en Puerto Plata una fuerza civil y militar bajo el ministro de Finanzas dominicano entró por la fuerza en la residencia del vicecónsul británico, el señor Hamburger, y apresó a tres ciudadanos, enemigos de Baez y opositores a la venta de Samana, que fueron arrojados a un calabozo, y que Baez aprobó los arrestos y ordenó llevar a los prisioneros a la ciudad de Santo Domingo. Advierte que se espera un buque de guerra británico para exigir satisfacción, y que Baez no debe imaginar que los Estados Unidos lo protegerán, pues los americanos que pagaron $150,000 por un año de renta de la bahía de Samana solo se representan a sí mismos y su compra no implica ningún protectorado americano.

records.headline: Writing from Santiago de los Caballeros on March 4, the correspondent describes his eight-day journey across St.
records.summary_en: Writing from Santiago de los Caballeros on March 4, the correspondent describes his eight-day journey across St. Domingo from Samana, three days of it in a canoe slowly ascending the Yuna River from Santa Barbara to Almacen. On the way the party spent a night in hammocks at Bebedero and joined a marriage feast at a house near Santa Capuza, with music, dancing, tiny cups of coffee and revolver shots fired in honour of the event, before entering the small mouth of the Yuna at midday.
records.summary_es: Escribiendo desde Santiago de los Caballeros el 4 de marzo, el corresponsal describe su viaje de ocho días a través de Santo Domingo desde Samaná, tres de ellos en una canoa que remontaba lentamente el río Yuna desde Santa Bárbara hasta Almacén. En el camino el grupo pasó una noche en hamacas en Bebedero y se unió a una fiesta de boda en una casa cerca de Santa Capuza, con música, baile, tacitas de café y disparos de revólver en honor del acontecimiento, antes de entrar al mediodía por la boca pequeña del Yuna.

records.headline: It is a pity both races cannot live on better terms
records.summary_en: According to the *New York Herald* on April 22, 1873, international animosity and border warfare between Hayti and the Dominican Republic had depopulated the border region, reducing towns like Dajabon to near-desolation. While Hayti's President Saget unsuccessfully sought a treaty of amity and commerce through the British consul general, Dominican leader Baez allegedly maintained hostilities to frighten Dominicans into supporting annexation to the United States. Additionally, the article contrasted the two nations' populations, noting that Hayti had a larger population and smaller territory with a seven-eighths black demographic, whereas the Dominican Republic was three-quarters Creole, with Creoles serving as the ruling and aristocratic element in both republics.
records.summary_es: Según *The New York Herald* del 22 de abril de 1873, las querellas internacionales y las guerras de frontera entre Haití y la República Dominicana habían despoblado la comarca limítrofe, sumiendo en la ruina y el abandono a villas como Dajabón. En tanto el presidente haitiano Saget gestionó infructuosamente un convenio de concordia y comercio con la mediación del cónsul general británico, se aseguraba que el gobernante dominicano Báez sostenía los enconos armados para intimidar a sus conciudadanos y forzarlos a cobijarse bajo la anexión a los Estados Unidos. El artículo contrastó asimismo la composición demográfica de ambos estados, refiriendo que Haití contaba con una población más densa en un territorio menor constituida en sus siete octavas partes por negros, en tanto que la República Dominicana era en sus tres cuartas partes criolla, integrando los criollos el estamento dirigente y aristocrático en ambas repúblicas.

records.summary_en: The *New York Herald* reported in April 1873 that annexing Santo Domingo would likely result in disappointment and questioned whether President Grant could guarantee the peaceable behavior of local inhabitants. The article argued that acquiring the island solely for a naval station is an extravagant burden and that annexation would only benefit New England manufactures if foreign commerce from Germany, France, and England were excluded.

records.summary_en: An editorial notes that St. Domingo's difficulties are many and that Cabral, the revolutionary leader interviewed by a Herald correspondent, holds very decided views on them. The epithets he applies to President Baez are strong and numerous, his opinion of the future of the Samana Bay Company is not encouraging to the trusting shareholder, and while he is not himself opposed to the introduction of American hard cash, he is presented as waiting on the mountain ledges to swoop down on Baez.

records.headline: Baez proposes to President Grant to establish a protectorate over Santo
records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported that Mr. Báez proposed that President Grant establish a U.S. protectorate over Santo Domingo to guard against attacks and influences from Hayti, having exhausted other resources after the failure of annexation and the Samana Bay enterprise. Báez also forwarded a disavowed treaty between Hayti and Santo Domingo containing a clause against alienating territory to foreign powers, attempting to provoke national jealousy regarding European machinations. President Grant laid the communication before Congress without making any recommendations, and the scheme was deemed unlikely to receive favor from the National Legislature.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Tribune* informó que el Sr. Báez propuso al presidente Grant erigir un protectorado estadounidense sobre Santo Domingo para repeler las agresiones e influencias procedentes de Haití, habiendo agotado todos sus recursos tras frustrarse la anexión y la empresa de la Samaná Bay Company. Báez remitió asimismo un desautorizado convenio entre Haití y Santo Domingo provisto de una cláusula prohibitiva de toda cesión territorial a potencias foráneas, en una tentativa de azuzar los celos geopolíticos frente a maquinaciones europeas. El presidente Grant dio traslado de dicha comunicación al Congreso sin formular recomendación alguna, juzgándose improbable que el parlamento dispensase una acogida favorable al proyecto.

records.summary_en: The provisional government holds Santo Domingo City with fewer than 200 soldiers and Azua with 300, and would have to concentrate those 500 men in the capital to defend it, leaving Azua exposed. The rest of the island is in revolution, though business remains uninterrupted except where provisional troops move. A letter from the American consul says Puerto Plata decided against Báez and his followers became despondent, while official documents state the government wants to fulfill the Samaná Bay Company treaty and guarantee the rights granted under it.
records.summary_es: El gobierno provisional sostiene la ciudad de Santo Domingo con menos de 200 soldados y Azua con 300, y tendría que concentrar esos 500 hombres en la capital para defenderla, dejando Azua expuesta. El resto de la isla está en revolución, aunque los negocios siguen sin interrupción salvo donde se mueven las tropas provisionales. Una carta del cónsul estadounidense dice que Puerto Plata se pronunció contra Báez y sus seguidores cayeron en el desaliento, mientras documentos oficiales afirman que el gobierno quiere cumplir el tratado con la Compañía de la Bahía de Samaná y garantizar los derechos otorgados en él.

records.summary_en: After the insurgent commander obtained a four-day armistice and President Baez had made his arrangements for leaving the country, Baez sent the Senate a message on January 2, 1874 laying down the presidency, recalling that he had been called in 1868 when paper money had brought bankruptcy and public credit had vanished. That same afternoon Baez left Santo Domingo for St. Thomas on the French war vessel Kersaint, declaring he was in no sense an exile, having left voluntarily, and that he was tired of office and wished to rest and consult physicians about his eyes.
records.summary_es: Después de que el comandante insurgente obtuviera una tregua de cuatro días y el presidente Báez hubiera hecho sus arreglos para salir del país, Báez envió al Senado un mensaje el 2 de enero de 1874 en el que renunciaba a la presidencia, recordando que había sido llamado en 1868 cuando el papel moneda había traído la bancarrota y el crédito público había desaparecido. Esa misma tarde Báez salió de Santo Domingo hacia Saint Thomas en el buque de guerra francés Kersaint, declarando que no era en ningún sentido un exiliado, pues había salido voluntariamente, y que estaba cansado del cargo y deseaba descansar y consultar a médicos sobre sus ojos.

records.summary_en: The *New York Herald* reported on a past scheme led primarily by England and Spain to establish a new power called the Confederation of the Antilles, which would unite St. Domingo, Cuba, Jamaica, and other West India islands to counter rapidly developing American interests. According to the article, General Báez expressed sympathy for the islanders' independence and noted that while St. Domingo harbored sympathies for Spain, Cubans living in St. Domingo opposed his government because he refused to violate neutrality laws by fitting out expeditions against Spain.
records.summary_es: El *New York Herald* informó sobre un proyecto anterior encabezado principalmente por Inglaterra y España para establecer una nueva potencia denominada la Confederación de las Antillas, la cual uniría a Santo Domingo, Cuba, Jamaica y otras islas de las Antillas para contrarrestar el rápido crecimiento de los intereses estadounidenses. Según el artículo, el general Báez expresó simpatía por la independencia de los isleños y señaló que, si bien Santo Domingo albergaba simpatías hacia España, los cubanos residentes en Santo Domingo se oponían a su gobierno porque se negaba a infringir las leyes de neutralidad pertrechando expediciones contra España.

records.headline: The return of ex-Prosident Baez to power, Upon the intercession of
records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported on April 7, 1874, that the return of ex-President Baez to power led to the release of Carlos and Felix Baez upon the intercession of the French Consul, while business remained stagnant and government obligations were offered at an 85 percent discount. Additionally, the announcement that the treaty between the Santo Domingo Government and the Samana Bay Company had been abrogated discouraged promoters and sympathizers, prompting returning Commissioners Capt. Samuels and Gov. Fabens to hold informal consultations with company director Paul N. Spofford and other members in New York.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Tribune* informó el 7 de abril de 1874 que el regreso al poder del expresidente Báez condujo a la liberación de Carlos y Félix Báez tras la intercesión del cónsul francés, mientras que el comercio permanecía paralizado y las obligaciones gubernamentales se ofrecían con un 85 por ciento de descuento. Además, el anuncio de la abrogación del tratado entre el gobierno de Santo Domingo y la Samana Bay Company desalentó a promotores y simpatizantes, lo que motivó a los comisionados retornados, el capitán Samuels y el gobernador Fabens, a sostener consultas informales en Nueva York con el director de la compañía Paul N. Spofford y otros miembros.

records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported on British influence, backed by a promised war vessel and a multi-million-dollar interest-free loan to the Dominican Government, though a director stated that holders of the English Hartmont loan were not responsible for abrogating the treaty. Additionally, a director noted that previous concessions granted to Funkhauser and the Samana Surveying Company were not absorbed by the Samana Bay Company. The article also featured a translated decree from Provisional President Ignacio Maria Gonzales regarding the lease contract for the Peninsula and Bay of Samana.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Tribune* informó sobre la influencia británica, respaldada por la promesa de un buque de guerra y un préstamo multimillonario libre de intereses para el gobierno dominicano, aunque un directivo declaró que los tenedores del préstamo inglés Hartmont no eran responsables de la derogación del tratado. Asimismo, un directivo señaló que las concesiones previas otorgadas a Funkhauser y a la Samana Surveying Company no fueron absorbidas por la Samana Bay Company. records.summary_en: The steamship Tybee, from San Domingo on March 30, brings news that the British Consul-General of Port-au-Prince had toured Samana Bay and visited Santo Domingo with Haitian treaty proposals, said to include cession of the disputed frontier territory and annulment of the Samana Bay Convention in return for a large interest-free loan from Haiti or England. The same advices report that President-elect Gonzalez had not been installed because the constitutional convention could not agree, and that the Provisional Government has declared the Samana Bay Convention null and void, while the company's commissioners protested and demanded arbitration and United States protection.

records.headline: A court report describes an application for a receiver for the Samana Bay Company, which was incorporated in 1873 by…
records.summary_en: A court report describes an application for a receiver for the Samana Bay Company, which was incorporated in 1873 by a special act of the Dominican government, with all its stockholders citizens of the United States and its headquarters in New York, to promote mining, agriculture and railways. Creditor William Rowland argued that General Gonzales's decree had dissolved the company, while director Paul Spofford, himself a creditor for $50,000, argued that Gonzales's act was not the act of the republic; Judge Donohue reserved his decision.
records.summary_es: Un informe judicial describe una solicitud de un síndico para la Samana Bay Company, que fue incorporada en 1873 por un acto especial del gobierno dominicano, con todos sus accionistas ciudadanos de los Estados Unidos y su sede en Nueva York, para promover la minería, la agricultura y los ferrocarriles. El acreedor William Rowland argumentó que el decreto del general Gonzáles había disuelto la compañía, mientras que el director Paul Spofford, él mismo acreedor por 50.000 dólares, argumentó que el acto de Gonzáles no era un acto de la república; el juez Donohue reservó su decisión.

records.summary_en: Santo Domingo City advices of the 12th, received at St. Thomas, reported that President Gonzalez had just returned from his voyage to the Northern provinces and that the whole country was perfectly quiet. A Haitian steamer had arrived at Santo Domingo City, and by her the Dominican Commissioners would leave for Port-au-Prince to conclude the treaty of amity and commerce between the two republics. General Caceres had arrived and met ex-President Baez of Santo Domingo.
records.summary_es: Noticias de la ciudad de Santo Domingo del día 12, recibidas en Saint Thomas, informaban que el presidente González acababa de regresar de su viaje a las provincias del norte y que todo el país estaba en perfecta calma. Un vapor haitiano había llegado a la ciudad de Santo Domingo, y en él partirían los comisionados dominicanos hacia Puerto Príncipe para concluir el tratado de amistad y comercio entre ambas repúblicas. El general Cáceres había llegado y se había reunido con el expresidente Báez, de Santo Domingo.

records.summary_en: The *National Republican* reported on September 29, 1874, that President Gonzales returned from a voyage to the northern provinces and that the country remained completely quiet. Dominican commissioners were set to leave for Port-au-Prince aboard a Haytien steamer to conclude a treaty of amity and commerce, while the Haytien Government had imposed heavy taxation on resident foreigners and foreign clerks. Additionally, General Caeeres arrived and met with ex-President Baez of San Domingo.
records.summary_es: El *National Republican* informó el 29 de septiembre de 1874 que el presidente González regresó de un viaje a las provincias del norte y que el país se mantenía en total tranquilidad. Comisionados dominicanos estaban listos para partir hacia Puerto Príncipe a bordo de un vapor haitiano con el fin de concluir un tratado de amistad y comercio, en momentos en que el Gobierno haitiano había fijado fuertes tributos a los extranjeros residentes y a los dependientes comerciales extranjeros. Asimismo, el general Cáceres llegó y se reunió con el expresidente Báez de Santo Domingo.

records.headline: AFFAIRS IN SANTO DOMINGO.
records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported on April 5, 1875, that a treaty of peace, amity, extradition, and reciprocity between the two republics on the island had been ratified and exchanged, demonstrating an *entente cordiale*. Additionally, the newspaper stated that the Dominican Government was being pressed by about 2,000 citizens—victims of Báez's actions while under the protection of U.S. warships—to present a claim against the United States Government for £3,000,000 in losses and injuries. This prospective claim, drawing its foundation from Senator Sumner's March 27, 1871 speech, argues that Báez was maintained in power by U.S. troops and attempted to dispose of the country and the lease of Samaná.

records.full_text:
AFFAIRS IN SANTO DOMINGO.
THE PRESIDENT IN FAVOR OF FREE SPEECH—
AMICAL RELATIONS WITH HAYTI—CLAIMS FOR
INDEMNITY AGAINST THE UNITED STATES.

SANTO DOMINGO, March 22.—The yacht Tarolinta of the New-York Yacht Club arrived here on the 19th inst. from Porto Rico, having on board Mr. Kent, her owner, and a party of friends who have been making a tour of the islands. Yesterday they called on President Gonzales, who returned the visit in the afternoon, accompanied by two of the ministers and other dignitaries. The President in a speech on the yacht said he was determined to try the experiment of free speech, a free press, and as much liberty as existed in the United States, even though he should perish in the attempt. No one had been exiled but Baez and a few of his family, and they were at liberty to return here now if they wished. The Tarolinta left here this morning for Kingston, Jamaica, from which place she will proceed to Havana, and thence home.

President Gonzales, accompanied by three of his ministers, his staff and some friends, returned a few days since from the province of Azua, where he had a conference with President Domingue of Hayti. The meeting was near the boundary line, and, by preconcert, took place on February 27, the anniversary of the separation of the two Republics in 1844, which is another proof of the entente cordiale now existing between the two Governments and people of the island. The treaty of peace, amity, extradition, reciprocity of trade guarantees to each other that neither any part nor the whole of the territory of either shall be alienated, has been ratified and exchanged.

It is stated that this Government is now being hard pressed by about 2,000 of its citizens, victims of Baez’s action, while under the immediate protection of the United States ships of war, to prepare and present a claim on the United States Government for losses and injuries to the Government and people arising therefrom. The foundation of this claim has been taken from the speech of Senator Sumner, of March 27, 1871, on violations of international law and usurpations of war powers. The Government intends, it is said, to present a claim for $5,000,000, but has not yet decided how or by whom they will present it, having no diplomatic representative in Washington. The argument which it is said the Dominican Government will submit in support of this claim recites the facts in connection with Baez’s accession to power, his attempt to dispose of the country, and the lease of Samana; declares that he was maintained in power by the United States troops, and was compelled to fly when they ceased to support him, and that, while occupying the Presidency, protected by United States ships, he plundered the Treasury of a large portion of its revenue, and ill-treated the citizens; alludes to many other facts in regard to the relations between the United States and Santo Domingo which have occupied attention during several years, and asserts that the acts of the United States Government were in violation of international law, and that it is responsible for the losses and injuries occasioned by the protection of Baez.

records.summary_en: The Dominican Government submitted a claim arguing that the United States Government is responsible for losses and injuries caused by its protection of Baez during his presidency. According to the claim, Baez forced a loan from citizens, plundered the treasury, and ill-treated people while maintained in power by U.S. troops and ships, making the U.S. actions a violation of international law.

Según la reclamación, Báez impuso un préstamo forzoso a los ciudadanos, saqueó el erario público y maltrató al pueblo mientras se mantenía en el poder respaldado por tropas y barcos estadounidenses, lo que convertía las actuaciones de los Estados Unidos en una violación del derecho internacional.

records.summary_en: A Washington dispatch reports fresh disclosures from a British parliamentary inquiry into foreign loans placed in London, centered on the Dominican loan floated by Hartmont and Company in the fall of 1869. It says Hartmont was connected with Fabens and Cazneau and their concessions from the Baez government, including railroad rights, large estates near Samana Bay and commercial privileges there, and that annexation of San Domingo to the United States was necessary to make those concessions immensely valuable, with money spent in New York and Washington to promote President Grant's scheme.

Dice que Hartmont estaba vinculado con Fabens y Cazneau y con sus concesiones del gobierno de Báez, incluidos derechos de ferrocarril, grandes propiedades cerca de la bahía de Samaná y privilegios comerciales en ese lugar, y que la anexión de Santo Domingo a los Estados Unidos era necesaria para que esas concesiones adquirieran un valor inmenso, con dinero gastado en Nueva York y Washington para promover el plan del presidente Grant.

records.summary_en: According to the *Clarksville Weekly Chronicle*, a British House of Commons committee investigated the negotiation of foreign loans in England, hearing testimony from Mr. Edward Hertzberg Hartmont regarding a Dominican loan nominally valued at $3,788,500. Hartmont testified that he received only $1,800,415 in cash—of which the San Domingo government received merely $230,000—with the remainder spent on arms in Berlin and disbursed in Washington, where Hartmont was sent to work for annexation. The newspaper questions whether the unaccounted-for funds were paid to General Grant's military favorites, such as Babcock, who became suddenly prosperous and invested in real estate, and suggests that the next Congress should investigate the matter.
records.summary_es: Según el *Clarksville Weekly Chronicle*, un comité de la Cámara de los Comunes británica investigó la negociación de empréstitos extranjeros en Inglaterra y tomó declaración al Sr. Edward Hertzberg Hartmont acerca de un préstamo dominicano con un valor nominal de 3.788.500 dólares. Hartmont declaró haber recibido únicamente 1.800.415 dólares en efectivo —de los cuales el gobierno de Santo Domingo recibió tan solo 230.000 dólares—, destinándose el resto a la compra de armas en Berlín y a desembolsos en Washington, a donde Hartmont fue enviado para gestionar la anexión. El diario cuestiona si los fondos no rendidos fueron pagados a los militares predilectos del general Grant, tales como Babcock, quien se enriqueció repentinamente e invirtió en bienes raíces, y sugiere que el próximo Congreso debería investigar el asunto.

The paper speculated that such a move would prompt aggressive Spanish countermeasures against Santo Domingo, questioning what obligations the United States would have under those circumstances.

records.summary_en: A traveler arriving from Port-au-Platte on August 24 reported that recent telegrams from Havana concerning a revolution in Santo Domingo were entirely false. According to the source, the rumor was fabricated and circulated by a banished individual named Barrera upon his arrival in Porto Rico. Furthermore, the traveler stated that no general disaffection existed and the government was fully capable of handling any conspirators.
records.summary_es: Un viajero arribado desde Puerto Plata el 24 de agosto informó que los recientes telegramas enviados desde La Habana respecto a una revolución en Santo Domingo carecían enteramente de veracidad. Según la fuente, el rumor fue fraguado y puesto a circular por un individuo desterrado de apellido Barrera tras su llegada a Puerto Rico. Asimismo, el testigo manifestó que no existía descontento generalizado y que el gobierno gozaba de plena capacidad para contener a cualquier conspirador.

records.summary_en: Based on the provided excerpt, the *New-York Tribune* reported on August 31, 1875, that prior reports of a successful revolution in favor of Baez were greatly exaggerated, attributing the rumors to treasonable correspondence by a wealthy Spanish resident who was subsequently expelled. According to advices received by the Dominican Consul and statements from Capt. Gardiner of the steamer *Tybee*, unrest was limited to minor lawlessness and murmurings by some ignorant and uneducated portions of the interior population instigated by Spanish emissaries. The newspaper also described President Don Ignacio Gonzales as a cultured and intelligent leader supported by the intelligent and wealthy classes, ruling against tyranny and oppression.

records.summary_en: A professed agent of the Government of Santo Domingo made overtures to the President regarding the annexation of the island to the United States, though the President initially suspected the agents might be adventurers. To ascertain the real feelings of the people, the President dispatched a confidential agent who found an enthusiastic desire for annexation, leading to a treaty that was subsequently submitted to the Senate for ratification.

Con el fin de constatar el auténtico sentir de la población, el presidente despachó a un enviado confidencial, quien constató un ferviente deseo de anexión, lo que dio origen a un tratado sometido posteriormente al Senado para su ratificación.

records.summary_en: A correspondent writing from Puerto Plata on February 23 traces the revolution to President Gonzales's treaty with Spain binding Santo Domingo to return Cuban refugees accused of incendiarism, and to a governor's decree that Cuban exiles embarking more than three on a vessel would be seized and delivered to Spanish war vessels. He describes street fighting on January 23 and 24 around the government house and General Luperon's residence, Governor Ortea's demand to capture Luperon dead or alive, and troops deserting and fraternizing with the Cubans as families fled the city.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal que escribe desde Puerto Plata el 23 de febrero atribuye la revolución al tratado del presidente Gonzales con España, que obligaba a Santo Domingo a devolver a los refugiados cubanos acusados de incendios, y a un decreto del gobernador según el cual los exiliados cubanos que embarcaran más de tres en un buque serían apresados y entregados a buques de guerra españoles. Describe los tiroteos callejeros del 23 y 24 de enero alrededor de la casa de gobierno y la residencia del general Luperon, la exigencia del gobernador Ortea de capturar a Luperon vivo o muerto, y cómo las tropas desertaban y fraternizaban con los cubanos mientras las familias huían de la ciudad.

records.summary_en: According to the newspaper report, the Dominican government ordered the arrest of a general aboard the steamship *Tyhee* on the grounds of attempting to foment a revolution from the Haytian frontier, but American Consul Paul Jones decided the general was entitled to remain on board under the protection of the American flag. Despite the Consul's protests and Captain Kuhl's preparations to defend the vessel—which included displaying American flags—Dominican authorities brought a field piece to the wharf and sent fifty armed soldiers who tore away the flags and boarded the ship.

records.summary_en: On June 28, a ship arrived at Cap Haitien and took on board Pablo Villanueva, the former Minister of War and Marine under Dominican President Rousales, who carried a Dominican passport bound for St. Domingo City. Upon arriving at the capital, officials recognized Villanueva, but he was subsequently warned that he would be arrested if he came ashore, prompting him to seek the assistance of American Consul Mr. Paul Jones to explain his non-political intentions of visiting his family and collecting money. The following day, the first notification of hostilities by the Dominicans occurred when a cannon was brought down to the wharf.

records.summary_en: According to the *Morning Herald* of July 10, 1876, crew members of the steamship *Tybee* reported that Pablo Villanueva, ex-Minister of War and Marine under Dominican President Gonzales, boarded the vessel at Cape Haytien with a valid Dominican passport and arrived at St. Domingo City. Upon arrival, Villanueva was warned that the newly elected President would order his arrest if he came ashore, prompting Villanueva to summon American Consul Mr. Paul Jones to state that his only intentions were to reunite with his family, collect a debt of $5,000, and depart for New York without causing political strife. Following this conversation, Consul Jones went ashore.
records.summary_es: Según el *Morning Herald* del 10 de julio de 1876, tripulantes del vapor *Tybee* informaron que Pablo Villanueva, exministro de Guerra y Marina del presidente dominicano González, embarcó en Cap-Haïtien con pasaporte dominicano en regla y llegó a la ciudad de Santo Domingo. A su arribo, se advirtió a Villanueva que el recién electo presidente ordenaría su detención si bajaba a tierra, lo que indujo a Villanueva a llamar al cónsul estadounidense, Sr. Paul Jones, para manifestarle que su único propósito era reunirse con su familia, cobrar una acreencia de 5.000 dólares y viajar a Nueva York sin provocar disturbios políticos. Concluida la conversación, el cónsul Jones marchó a tierra.

records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that local hostility toward Cuban emigrants in Puerto Plata—intensified by the murder of a native—alongside revolutionary factions seeking the restoration of either Baez or Gonzales, led to an insurrection. In response, President Espaillat declared the entire republic in a state of siege and sent troops to the area, where insurgents surrounded Puerto Plata and prevented the steamer *Tobcc* from landing its cargo.

En respuesta, el presidente Espaillat declaró a toda la república en estado de sitio y despachó tropas a la comarca, donde los insurgentes cercaron Puerto Plata e impidieron que el vapor *Tybee* desembarcara su carga.

records.summary_en: The *New Orleans Republican* reported in September 1876 that France, Brazil, Costa Rica, Bolivia, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Guatemala, Hayti, Honduras, New Granada, Nicaragua, Paraguay, Peru, San Salvador, Venezuela, and Italy held treaties entitling them to the same commercial and navigation privileges as Hawaii under mutual favored-nation clauses. A congressional memorial presented in May by the Louisiana, South Carolina, and Georgia delegations noted that these countries produce sugar and, in eight cases, rice, which they could demand to enter duty-free. Additionally, the committee warned that the treaty would unfairly favor San Francisco over Atlantic ports due to significantly lower freight rates.

Un memorial elevado al Congreso en mayo por las delegaciones de Luisiana, Carolina del Sur y Georgia advertía de que estos países producían azúcar y, en ocho de ellos, arroz, cuya entrada libre de derechos podían exigir. Asimismo, la comisión alertó de que el tratado beneficiaría injustamente a San Francisco respecto a los puertos del Atlántico debido a fletes ostensiblemente más reducidos.

The newspaper notes that the population of 250,000 welcomes foreign immigration regardless of race or color, drawing individuals with capital from Cuba, the Bahamas, and France. Additionally, Major Stuart expresses the opinion that Samana could become a major commercial emporium if its advantages are fully utilized.

records.headline: Dwelt especially upon the expenditure, by General Babcock, on San Domingo
records.summary_en: According to the newspaper, General Babcock expended a large sum from the Secret Service Fund regarding San Domingo, leading to a misunderstanding between President Grant and Senator Sumner, where the President intended to discuss the treaty for the acquisition of the Dominican Republic while Sumner believed they were discussing the expenditure. Sumner assured the President he was a Republican supporter and intended to examine the papers to sustain the expenditure, while Major Poore's statement purportedly resolves historical doubts regarding the cause of the difficulty between Grant and Sumner.

Sumner aseguró al presidente su lealtad republicana y su disposición a revisar los documentos para respaldar el desembolso, mientras que las declaraciones del mayor Poore esclarecen supuestamente las dudas históricas sobre el origen de las desavenencias entre Grant y Sumner.

records.summary_en: *The Cheyenne Daily Leader* published an account by Major Poore explaining the origin of the feud between President Grant and Senator Charles Sumner over Santo Domingo. records.headline: CAUSE OF THE TROUBLE BETWEEN GRANT AND SUMNER.
records.summary_en: The newspaper reported on a historical misunderstanding between President Grant and Senator Sumner regarding General Babcock's expenditures from the secret service fund for San Domingo versus the treaty for the acquisition of the Dominican Republic. According to Major Poore's statement, Sumner believed the President wanted him to defend the expenditure, while the President actually meant the acquisition treaty.
records.summary_es: El periódico reseñó el histórico malentendido surgido entre el presidente Grant y el senador Sumner con motivo de las erogaciones del fondo de servicios secretos realizadas por el general Babcock en Santo Domingo frente al tratado para la anexión de la República Dominicana. Conforme a las declaraciones del mayor Poore, Sumner creyó que el gobernante deseaba que defendiera el desembolso pecuniario, cuando el mandatario aludía en realidad al tratado de anexión.

records.full_text:
CAUSE OF THE TROUBLE BETWEEN GRANT AND SUMNER.

CHICAGO, October 26.—A Tribune Washington special says: Major Ben. Perley Poore, who was Senator Sumner’s guest at the time of his estrangement from President Grant, has explained the cause of the trouble. He says the removal of James M. Ashley, ex-congressman from Ohio, from the governorship of Montana, and the appointment of Colonel Potts, which had just happened, was the subject of table conversation, and a letter from Ashley, protesting against the change, had been read when the President was announced. He was received, shown Ashley’s letter and became immediately excited, denouncing Ashley as a mischief-maker. The next topic discussed was the San Domingo treaty. Sumner dwelt especially upon the expenditure by General Babcock on San Domingo, of the large sum taken from the secret service fund for promoting intercourse with the West India islands, which Seward had prevailed on Thad. Stevens to have inserted in the appropriation bill during the war, and the President impressed Sumner with the idea that he feared an attack in congress for that expenditure. Poore adds: “My opinion is that Sumner thought that the President had come to enlist his services in defending this expenditure by General Babcock, but the President meant the treaty for the acquisition of the Dominican republic. The President and the senator misunderstood each other. After a while the President promised to send General Babcock to call on the senator next day with copies of the paper and left. As Sumner escorted him to the door he told him that he was a Republican, a supporter of the Republican administration, and that he should sustain the administration in this case, if he possibly could, after he had examined the papers. He meant to sustain the expenditure of $100,000 in cash ($50,000 in a light battery and muskets purchased at New York), but the President meant the treaty.” Major Poore’s statement thus removes a grave historical doubt, and seems to set at rest the stories recently published of the cause of the difficulty between Grant and Sumner.

records.summary_en: Following remarks by Wendell Phillips regarding General Grant's statements on the St. Domingo treaty, a *New York Herald* representative interviewed ex-Secretary of State Fish in Boston. Fish stated that Senate records show multiple drafts of treaties remained in the hands of the Foreign Affairs Committee under Senator Sumner for months—and in some cases over two years—whereas the entire batch was disposed of within four months after Sumner's retirement.
records.summary_es: A raíz de las manifestaciones de Wendell Phillips sobre las declaraciones del general Grant acerca del tratado de Santo Domingo, un reportero de *The New York Herald* entrevistó en Boston al exsecretario de Estado Fish. Este afirmó que las actas del Senado prueban que numerosos proyectos de tratados permanecieron estancados en manos del Comité de Relaciones Exteriores bajo la presidencia del senador Sumner durante meses —y en ciertos casos más de dos años—, en tanto que la totalidad de ellos se despachó a los cuatro meses de su salida.

records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that in late December 1869 or early January 1870, President Grant discussed the features of a treaty orally with Mr. Sumner, who initially expressed warm approval of the measure. According to Mr. Fish, Sumner supported the treaty until J. M. Ashley of Ohio was not nominated as a commissioner to St. Domingo, after which Sumner opposed it. Furthermore, Mr. Fish stated that Senators Carl Schurz and Mr. Stewart determined in February that the Senate would not pass the treaty, and Sumner was not reappointed to the Foreign Affairs Committee upon the meeting of the new Congress in 1871.
records.summary_es: El rotativo dio cuenta de que a finales de diciembre de 1869 o principios de enero de 1870, el presidente Grant expuso verbalmente a Sumner las cláusulas del tratado, ante lo cual este último manifestó inicialmente un cálido beneplácito. Según Fish, Sumner mantuvo su adhesión a la iniciativa hasta que J. M. Ashley, de Ohio, quedó excluido de la designación como comisionado en Santo Domingo, momento a partir del cual combatió el proyecto. Añadió además Fish que los senadores Carl Schurz y Stewart comprobaron en febrero que la cámara alta desestimaría el tratado, no siendo reincorporado Sumner a la Comisión de Relaciones Exteriores al instalarse el nuevo Congreso en 1871.

Babcock's expenditure of a secret service fund. The report states that the President and the Senator misunderstood each other, as Sumner believed the President sought defense for the expenditure of funds, whereas the President intended to discuss the treaty for acquiring the Dominican Republic. Poore's statement regarding the meeting reportedly clarifies a historical doubt and resolves published stories concerning the cause of the difficulty between Grant and Sumner.

La relación del mayor Poore sobre dicha entrevista disipa al parecer una incógnita histórica y desvirtúa versiones divulgadas respecto al origen del distanciamiento entre Grant y Sumner.

records.summary_en: Based on the provided excerpt, Major Poore's statement clarifies a historical misunderstanding between President Grant and Senator Sumner regarding a past expenditure by General Babcock involving secret-service funds and the proposed treaty for the acquisition of the Dominican Republic. While Sumner believed the President sought his defense of a cash and weaponry expenditure, the President was referring to the annexation treaty itself. Additionally, the newspaper briefly reported that General Pope, the Post Commander at Fort Leavenworth, was assaulted at the Leavenworth races.

Mientras Sumner creía que se requería su concurso para legitimar una entrega de fondos y pertrechos, el dignatario se refería al tratado anexionista en sí. Por añadidura, el diario mencionó someramente que el general Pope, jefe de plaza en Fort Leavenworth, sufrió una agresión durante las carreras de dicha localidad.

The revolt is attributed to Báez declaring Romana a port of entry to export cattle under a private contract with a Cuban firm, a scheme the people of Seibo considered a ring speculation damaging to their interests; in the other provinces, victory was favoring the government troops and the revolutionists alternately.

records.headline: An editorial on Puerto Plata says the American consul there has found the country too unsettled to remain and has…
records.summary_en: An editorial on Puerto Plata says the American consul there has found the country too unsettled to remain and has left, leaving as vice consul a native of San Domingo who is a relative of the Minister of War under President Baez. It expresses fear that, after months of revolutionary fighting, this vice consul would try to convince the commander of any American man-of-war coming into the harbor that the warship was not needed.
records.summary_es: Un editorial sobre Puerto Plata dice que el cónsul americano allí ha encontrado el país demasiado revuelto para quedarse y se ha marchado, dejando como vicecónsul a un nativo de Santo Domingo pariente del Ministro de Guerra del presidente Báez. Expresa el temor de que, tras meses de lucha revolucionaria, este vicecónsul intentara convencer al comandante de cualquier buque de guerra americano que entrara en el puerto de que el barco no era necesario.

records.headline: For sixty days preceding the date of our latest dispatches the
records.summary_en: According to the *Daily press and Dakotaian* on January 12, 1878, an incessant revolutionary conflict had prevailed in San Domingo for months, putting foreign merchants and their families in danger while no American naval vessel had appeared at Puerto Plata since the outbreak began over three months prior. Consequently, U.S. Consul Douglass departed, leaving a native Dominican and relative of President Baez's minister of war as vice consul—a succession that alarmed American residents who feared partisan bias and opposition to potential U.S. naval assistance.
records.summary_es: Según el *Daily press and Dakotaian* del 12 de enero de 1878, una incesante contienda armada convulsionaba a Santo Domingo desde hacía meses, arriesgando las vidas y haciendas de los comerciantes extranjeros sin que asomara buque militar estadounidense alguno por Puerto Plata desde el inicio de los disturbios tres meses atrás. Ante ello, el cónsul estadounidense Douglass se ausentó de la plaza, delegando la vicecancillería en un nativo dominicano emparentado con el ministro de Guerra del presidente Báez, relevo que sobresaltó a los residentes norteamericanos ante el temor a sesgos partidistas y trabas a un eventual auxilio naval de los EE. UU.

The paper noted Báez's past attempt to lease Dominican territory to the Samaná Bay Company and predicted he would inevitably return to challenge rivals such as Luperón and González.

La publicación evocó las pretéritas tentativas de Báez para arrendar suelo patrio a la Samana Bay Company y auguró que retornaría indefectiblemente a medir fuerzas con rivales de la talla de Luperón y González.

records.summary_en: Based on the provided excerpt, *The New York Herald* reported that about six months prior, the Spanish mail steamer arriving at Puerto Plata carried two Dominican generals belonging to the Hay party who intended to start a revolution against the Dominican government. Although the steamer's captain initially omitted the generals from his custom-house entries, passenger list, and bill of health, the captain ultimately surrendered them following instructions from the Spanish Consul, and the generals were subsequently court-martialed and shot. The article also asserted that the Dominican Republic, led by President Guilerino and his Cabinet, had acted with moderation and dignity and done nothing against Spain.

records.headline: THE SCANDALS OF GRANTISM.
records.summary_en: According to the newspaper, deposed Dominican President Buenaventura Báez partnered with promoters of the Great San Domingo Copper Company to raise money from investors by falsely claiming General Grant was involved. After distributing stock to Washington officials and raising $200,000—part of which funded camels for the mines—the adventurers fled to San Domingo, where Báez regained the presidency and resumed swindling operations, including granting a coal mine concession to Edward H. Routmont in exchange for a loan from a London firm.

records.full_text:
THE SCANDALS OF GRANTISM.

The San Domingo Job—Its Inception, Prosecution, and Final Failure.
I.

“If Gen. Grant, Gen. Babcock, and others high in office in Washington are so well satisfied with the real value of our prospects, and feel safe in lending their names and influence to carry them out, I cannot for the life of me see why you should hesitate. It was our intention to have sent 1,200 shares of the stock of the San Domingo Copper Company to you, as soon as Knapp shall have signed the certificates, to be distributed among officials of influence in Washington. But from the tone of your letters I suppose we shall have to do our business through some other party.”

These words, which seem like the idle boast of a confidence operator, are in reality the statement of a scandalous fact. They were written on the 21st of December, 1866, by Joseph W. Currier, then of New York, to a friend in Washington, who hesitated to embark in a scheme which looked to the raising of a million of dollars for the avowed purpose of mining copper in the island of San Domingo. Currier had been a quartermaster in the Union Army. He was speculative by nature, and circumstances made him impecunious. He was enthusiastic and credulous, but perhaps not deliberately dishonest. At this time, however, he was in the clutches of two unscrupulous knaves, who, years before, had gone from Massachusetts to the West Indies to teach the Dominicans tricks of which they never dreamt before. These were Joseph W. Fabens and William L. Cazneau. They were both natives of the Bay State. In 1863, Fabens, Cazneau, and Currier established the Great American West India Company, with an office at 5 Pine street, New York. Their rooms were fitted up in sumptuous style, and by the free use of printers’ ink they succeeded in disposing of their worthless stock to the amount of $160,000. Then they closed their doors and disappeared. But they came again in 1866, scattering far and wide their prospectus of the Great San Domingo Copper Company. They were accompanied this time by Buenaventura Baez, the deposed President of the Dominican Republic, who had been driven from the island and was ready for any sort of a job which promised him a good living without work. These conspirators explained that Cabral’s revolution had destroyed the Great American West India Company, but that the present corporation rested on a secure basis. To all doubting inquirers they whispered, “Gen. Grant is in it!” On the strength of his name they raised money from investors. Fabens took $30,000 and started for Africa to buy camels for the copper mines. He was accompanied by Baez. The 1,200 shares of stock were duly distributed among “officials of influence in Washington,” and $200,000 was raised by the sale of shares. Then the doors of the the office were closed again, and the adventurers sought safety in flight. They returned to San Domingo, where Baez reëstablished himself in the Presidency. There they remained till President Grant was inaugurated, and then they began once more their swindling operations in good earnest.

records.summary_en: The newspaper reported on a protocol involving U.S. President Ulysses S. Grant and Dominican Republic Secretary of State Manuel Maria Gautier, wherein President Grant would use his influence to secure the annexation of the Dominican Republic by the United States once assured of a majority in Congress. In exchange for the United States paying $1,500,000 in coin to settle the Dominican Republic's debt, the Dominican Republic agreed to reform its constitution to resemble those of other states in the Union. Additionally, the excerpt notes Senate comments by Charles Sumner questioning the authority of an officer acting as an aide-de-camp to President Grant in relation to the Dominican Republic.
records.summary_es: El rotativo dio cuenta de un protocolo concertado entre el mandatario estadounidense Ulysses S. Grant y el secretario de Estado dominicano Manuel María Gautier, mediante el cual Grant empeñaba su influjo para consumar la anexión de la República Dominicana por los Estados Unidos en cuanto contase con mayoría legislativa en el Capitolio. A cambio del desembolso de 1.500.000 pesos en moneda contante por parte de los Estados Unidos para redimir la deuda dominicana, la República Dominicana se comprometía a reformar su carta magna adaptándola a la de los estados de la Unión. Asimismo, el texto recoge las censuras del senador Charles Sumner impugnando las facultades de un militar que actuaba como edecán de Grant ante el gobierno dominicano.

records.summary_en: The article prints the protocol agreed on September 4, 1869, between General Orville E. Babcock, President Grant's special agent, and Manuel Maria Gautier, the Dominican Secretary of State, as the basis of an annexation treaty. Under it Grant was to use his influence for annexation, the United States was to pay money to clear the republic's debt, estimated at $1,500,000, and other articles fixed the price of Samana, a down payment, American protection for Baez during the negotiations, and absolute secrecy; Senator Charles Sumner is quoted ridiculing Babcock's assumed title of aide-de-camp to the President.
records.summary_es: El artículo reproduce el protocolo acordado el 4 de septiembre de 1869 entre el general Orville E. Babcock, agente especial del presidente Grant, y Manuel María Gautier, secretario de Estado dominicano, como base de un tratado de anexión. Según el protocolo, Grant usaría su influencia a favor de la anexión, los Estados Unidos pagarían dinero para saldar la deuda de la república, estimada en $1,500,000, y otros artículos fijaban el precio de Samaná, un pago inicial, la protección estadounidense para Báez durante las negociaciones y el secreto absoluto; se cita al senador Charles Sumner ridiculizando el título de edecán del Presidente que Babcock se había arrogado.

records.summary_en: According to the New-York Tribune of July 7, 1880, order prevailed during the San Domingo presidential elections, with the Rev. Ferrando Arturo Merino receiving a majority of the votes. Meanwhile, Haitian Commissioner General Caman was in Puerto Plata to arrange for the expulsion of Dominican political refugees from the Haytian frontiers, and plans were underway to begin building a railroad from Santiago to Samana while the Republic was prospering. Additionally, the newspaper reported on General Sherman's arrival at Winnipeg, Manitoba, where he was met by local officials and greeted with a procession, a nineteen-gun salute, and an infantry reception at the Government House.
records.summary_es: Según el *New-York Tribune* del 7 de julio de 1880, reinó absoluto orden durante los comicios presidenciales de Santo Domingo, alcanzando la mayoría del sufragio el presbítero Fernando Arturo de Meriño. Entretanto, el comisionado haitiano general Caman se hallaba en Puerto Plata para convenir la expulsión de asilados políticos dominicanos asentados en la raya fronteriza, prosiguiendo al propio tiempo los proyectos para tender una vía férrea de Santiago a Samaná en momentos de prosperidad para la República. Por añadidura, el diario refirió la llegada del general Sherman a Winnipeg, Manitoba, donde fue agasajado con un desfile, diecinueve salvas de cañón y una guardia de honores en la Casa de Gobierno.

records.summary_en: According to a dispatch from Havana dated July 7, the recent presidential election in San Domingo was conducted peacefully and resulted in a majority of votes for the Rev. Fernando Arturo Merino, whose nomination was expected by the "Blues." General Caman, the Haytian Commissioner, was present in Puerto Plata to arrange for the expulsion of Dominican refugees from the Haytian frontiers. Additionally, the report noted that a railroad from Santiago to Samana was scheduled to begin construction soon and that the republic was prospering.
records.summary_es: A tenor de un despacho de La Habana del 7 de julio, las recientes elecciones presidenciales en Santo Domingo transcurrieron pacíficamente, consagrando el triunfo del presbítero Fernando Arturo de Meriño, cuya postulación auspiciaba el partido de los «azules». El general Caman, delegado haitiano, asistió a Puerto Plata para concertar la expulsión de asilados dominicanos de la línea divisoria. Informóse asimismo del próximo inicio de las obras del ferrocarril entre Santiago y Samaná en medio del florecimiento que experimenta el país.

records.summary_en: *The Indianapolis Leader* described the historical impact of educated, affluent refugees of color from Saint-Domingue who settled in Louisiana, particularly New Orleans, after fleeing the island. Their arrival stimulated the local free colored Creole population to establish new schools and send their children to France for higher education. This educational movement significantly elevated the social and intellectual status of Louisiana's free Black community by the late eighteenth century.

Su radicación espoleó a la población criolla de color libre a erigir escuelas y franquear a sus hijos estudios superiores en Francia. Esta corriente formativa encumbró de manera decisiva la jerarquía social e intelectual de la comunidad negra libre de Luisiana hacia las postrimerías del siglo XVIII.

records.summary_en: The *Omaha daily bee* reported on July 11, 1881, that Father Merino, a regularly ordained priest and the executive of the Dominican Republic, had assumed dictatorial powers by issuing a decree that abolished the right of asylum for political offenders, mandated court-martial trials for political conspirators, and declared that citizens taken with arms would be sentenced to death. Threatened Invasion of San Domingo.

ST. THOMAS, Feb. 4.—Gen. Guillermo, ex-President of San Domingo, with eleven other exiles from that republic, left here on the 29th ult. on board the British steamer Yucatan with the avowed purpose of organizing in Jamaica a formidable party to invade San Domingo and Hayti. It is reported that he has purchased the Victoria, a small steamer, which will form part of a fleet of four vessels. He is said to have in his possession letters of credit to the amount of $80,000. The Dominican Consul here has chartered the British schooner Lillie to convey to the Government of San Domingo intelligence of Gen. Guillermo’s designs.

THE HAYTIAN REBELS.
E. Nadale, an emissary of the Haytian Gov-
ernment, arrived in this city on Monday on a secret
mission. He said that the rebels under Dazelais and La
Forestre numbered nearly 1,000 and were composed
mostly of exiled Haytiaus, Cubans and Dominicans.
Bazelals 1s a very brave man and would fight to the last
before giving up the port of Miragoane. La Forestre,
who was Inspector of Prisons under the late Emperor
Soulougne, was also not wanting in courage. Oa one
occasion he caused all the State prisoners to be shot,
saying that it was cheaper to kill than to feed them. A
stubborn and prolong rage may be expected, but
M. Nadale seemed confident that the insurgents would
finally be overthrown by the Government troops.

records.summary_en: According to dispatches from Santo Domingo brought by a steamer from St. Thomas, the Dominican Congress passed a bill establishing free trade with the United States, and Senor Galvan was appointed Commissioner to finalize arrangements in Washington. Negotiations were also reported to be proceeding with Washington regarding the lease of Samaná Bay, with bondholders of the Samana Bay Company slated to receive the first claim on the lease money. Additionally, the newspaper reported on a dynamite scare affecting English Island and St. Vincent, yellow fever deaths on a vessel at Barbados, and the withdrawal of insurance agencies in Trinidad.
records.summary_es: Según despachos de Santo Domingo traídos por un vapor de Saint Thomas, el Congreso dominicano sancionó un proyecto que consagraba el libre comercio con los Estados Unidos, nombrándose al señor Galván comisionado para ultimar los convenios en Washington. Se refirió igualmente la marcha de negociaciones con Washington en torno al arrendamiento de la bahía de Samaná, reservándose a los obligacionistas de la Samana Bay Company el derecho preferente sobre el canon respectivo. Además, se dio cuenta de una alarma por dinamita en posesiones inglesas y San Vicente, muertes por fiebre amarilla a bordo de un barco en Barbados y el retiro de agencias de seguros en Trinidad.

records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that the President announced the conclusion of a commercial treaty with the Dominican Republic providing for reciprocal trade, similar to one negotiated with Spain for Cuba and Porto Rico. Additionally, the President recommended amending neutrality laws, encouraging the American steamship marine through government subsidies, and restoring the navy's efficiency. The excerpt also detailed federal financial figures, including decreases in expenditures, aggregate receipts, and customs revenue compared to the previous fiscal year.

records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported on a convention detailing various Dominican products, including animal remains, cocoa, coffee, and sugar, to be admitted into the United States. It noted that specific Dominican goods, such as cordials and manufactured tobacco, would receive a twenty-five percent reduction in U.S. customs duties. Additionally, the convention provided that certain United States productions, including ale, beer, and live animals, would be admitted into the Dominican Republic free of duty.

Consignó que determinados efectos dominicanos, tales como licores y tabaco manufacturado, gozarían de una rebaja del veinticinco por ciento en los aranceles estadounidenses. Preveía asimismo el instrumento que ciertos artículos de producción estadounidense, incluyendo cerveza de malta, cerveza común y ganado en pie, entrarían libres de derechos a la República Dominicana.

records.summary_en: Ben Perley Poore recounts how the ill feeling between President Grant and Senator Sumner grew out of a misunderstanding on the evening the San Domingo treaty was sent to the Senate: Sumner thought Grant wanted his help defending General Babcock's expenditures in Santo Domingo, while Grant meant the treaty for acquiring the Dominican Republic. When Babcock read the treaty to Sumner the next day, Sumner objected to the stipulation that Grant would use his influence to make annexation popular in Congress, and became the enemy of the whole scheme.

Cuando Babcock le leyó el tratado a Sumner al día siguiente, Sumner objetó la estipulación de que Grant usaría su influencia para hacer popular la anexión en el Congreso, y se convirtió en enemigo de todo el proyecto.

Furthermore, Senate sycophants and troublemakers worsened relations between Sumner and General Grant by exploiting their differing views on the president acting as a lobbyist and the acceptance of gifts by public men.

Por añadidura, intrigantes y aduladores senatoriales profundizaron el distanciamiento entre Sumner y el general Grant explotando sus divergentes criterios sobre las gestiones oficiosas de un mandatario y la aceptación de dádivas por servidores públicos.

records.headline: Lucas Gibbs, Minister of Finance and Commerce of the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: *The New York Freeman* reported on a meeting in the Dominican Republic presided over by Hon. Lucas Gibbs, Minister of Finance and Commerce, with Hon. Richard Alexander Gross serving as secretary, alongside several appointed vice-presidents and officials. Following his opening remarks, Mr. Gibbs introduced the evening's speaker, Hon. John Mercer Langston, an American citizen who expressed surprise before briefly addressing commercial relations and a reciprocal treaty.
records.summary_es: *The New York Freeman* reseñó una asamblea celebrada en la República Dominicana presidida por el honorable Lucas Gibbs, ministro de Hacienda y Comercio, actuando como secretario el honorable Richard Alexander Gross, junto a varios vicepresidentes y dignatarios designados. Tras sus palabras inaugurales, el Sr. Gibbs presentó al orador de la velada, el honorable John Mercer Langston, ciudadano estadounidense que manifestó su sorpresa antes de disertar brevemente sobre los nexos mercantiles y un convenio recíproco.

records.summary_en: According to the *St. Paul daily globe* of December 9, 1885, a commercial treaty signed with the Dominican Republic was subsequently withdrawn from the Senate for re-examination. The official concluded that entering into such engagements was inexpedient because the treaties required the United States to surrender large revenues on sugar for inadequate advantages, provided only illusory relief to consumers, risked raising embarrassing questions under favored-nation clauses, and diminished independent control over national revenues.
records.summary_es: Según el *St. Paul daily globe* del 9 de diciembre de 1885, un tratado comercial suscrito con la República Dominicana fue formalmente retirado del Senado para un nuevo examen. El mandatario concluyó que concertar tales estipulaciones resultaba improcedente, habida cuenta de que exigían a los Estados Unidos resignar cuantiosas rentas arancelarias sobre el azúcar a cambio de ventajas exiguas, brindaban un alivio ilusorio a los consumidores, arriesgaban suscitar enojosas querellas bajo las cláusulas de nación más favorecida y menoscababan el manejo soberano de los ingresos públicos.

records.summary_en: According to the December 10, 1885 *Austin Weekly Statesman*, commercial treaties signed with Spain and the Dominican Republic, along with unsuccessful overtures from Great Britain, were withdrawn for re-examination upon taking office. The official concluded that endorsing such engagements was inexpedient because they did not cover the entire traffic, required the surrender of large revenues for inadequate considerations—particularly concerning sugar duties—and would create embarrassing questions under favored-nation clauses. Furthermore, the report noted that regulating tariffs by treaty diminishes a government's independent control over its own revenues, which is essential for its safety and welfare.
records.summary_es: A tenor del *Austin Weekly Statesman* del 10 de diciembre de 1885, los convenios mercantiles concluidos con España y la República Dominicana, junto con propuestas infructuosas formuladas por Gran Bretaña, fueron retirados del Senado al asumir el nuevo gobierno. La presidencia consideró improcedente respaldar tales instrumentos por no comprender la totalidad de los intercambios, requerir la renuncia a cuantiosos gravámenes sobre el azúcar a cambio de ventajas mezquinas y amenazar con promover embarazosos litigios bajo las estipulaciones de nación más favorecida. Advirtióse además que supeditar las leyes arancelarias a convenios internacionales erosiona la potestad soberana del Estado sobre sus recursos tributarios, salvaguarda de su prosperidad y decoro.

records.headline: Recognizing the need of less obstructed traffic with Cuba and Porto
records.summary_en: The *Gloucester County Democrat* reported on December 10, 1885, that a commercial treaty had been signed by the Dominican republic following steps taken to establish less obstructed traffic with Cuba and Porto Rico. The newspaper also noted that subsequent overtures for a similar mutual extension of commercial intercourse were made by Her Britannic Majesty's government regarding British West Indian and South American dependencies, but these efforts yielded no result. Additionally, the excerpt urged Congress to recast appropriations for the diplomatic and consular service to ensure adequate salaries while returning notarial and official fees to the treasury.
records.summary_es: El *Gloucester County Democrat* dio cuenta el 10 de diciembre de 1885 de la firma de un tratado de comercio por la República Dominicana tras los pasos encaminados a franquear el tráfico con Cuba y Puerto Rico. Consignó asimismo la publicación que gestiones posteriores formuladas por el gobierno de Su Majestad Británica para ensanchar recíprocamente el comercio con las dependencias británicas antillanas y sudamericanas resultaron infructuosas. Por último, instó al Congreso a reformular el presupuesto del servicio diplomático y consular para dotarlo de haberes decorosos, restituyendo los derechos notariales y de cancillería al tesoro público.

It says the country's only hopes of relief are a commercial treaty with the United States or American capital at a reasonable rate, and praises United States Consul H. C. C. Astwood for settling American claims, including a $63,000 indemnity for the widow of Piatt, an American carpenter shot by government troops.

records.headline: Name to go before the President for consid eration at the
records.summary_en: *The New York Freeman* reported on February 20, 1886, that Mr. Astwood's name was submitted for Presidential consideration for reappointment as United States Consul to San Domingo, whose affairs were described as unsettled with an anticipated upheaval due to the presidential succession. The newspaper also stated that recent reports of the assassination of President Salomon of Hayti were unfounded, praising him as a wise and discreet leader. Additionally, the excerpt criticized a note from the *Norfolk Virginian* regarding a statement made by a colored brother, Rev. Hooper Jolly, at a Methodist conference in Philadelphia.
records.summary_es: *The New York Freeman* informó el 20 de febrero de 1886 de que el pliego con la postulación del Sr. Astwood fue elevado a la consideración del presidente para su confirmación como cónsul de los Estados Unidos en Santo Domingo, demarcación cuyos asuntos se hallaban inestables y con presagios de conmociones por el relevo presidencial. Declaró asimismo el rotativo que las noticias sobre el asesinato del presidente Salomon de Haití carecían de fundamento, ponderándole como un gobernante previsor y juicioso. Fustigó asimismo una nota del *Norfolk Virginian* sobre una alocución pronunciada por un correligionario de color, el reverendo Hooper Jolly, en un congreso metodista en Filadelfia.
